paragraphs.text: PROLOGUE

After my expositions of the Twelve Prophets, of Isaiah, Daniel and Ezekiel, I now at last turn my hand to Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, and dedicate these brief commentaries on him to you, so that you may join this evangelical man to Matthew the evangelist, whom I discussed many years ago, at your urging, in a concise treatment. Because the book is very long and for the most part is woven of plain history, I advise your prudence not to look for a broad exposition in it, especially on matters already dealt with in the other prophets and on things that are clear to the understanding of themselves. So I shall try to write by the hand of secretaries in such a way that nothing is lacking in the sense, even though much is lacking in the words.

I will prepare for you the warp and the woof and the threads; you yourself must make the beautiful garment, so that you may not only listen to me but also teach others. As for the little book of Baruch, which is commonly attached to the Septuagint edition but is not found among the Hebrews, and the pseudepigraphal Letter of Jeremiah, I decided not to comment on them at all. Rather, I thought it better to set in order the sequence of Jeremiah, which the errors of copyists have thrown into confusion, and to fill in from the Hebrew sources the many things that are missing, so that you may have a new prophet in place of the old, a true one in place of one corrupted and falsified. Pay no heed to the rage of the detractors, who carp not only at my words but even at the syllables of my words, thinking they know something if they disparage the works of others.

So recently an ignorant slanderer has burst out who thinks my commentaries on Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians deserve censure. Snoring in his excessive folly, he does not understand the rules of commentaries, in which many opinions of different writers are set out, with the authors' names either withheld or stated, so that it is left to the reader's judgment to decide which he ought most to choose. And yet in the first book of that very work I said in my preface that I would be stating either my own views or those of others, and that the commentaries themselves belonged as much to the ancient writers as to me.

His forerunner Grunnius failed to see this and once tried to pick it to pieces; I answered him in two books. What this man puts forward as if it were his own has already been cleared up when another slanderer raised it. I pass over the volumes against Jovinian, in which he is aggrieved that virginity is preferred to marriage, marriage to a second marriage, and a second marriage to many marriages. That utter blockhead, weighed down with Irish porridge, does not remember that in that very work I said: "I do not condemn the twice-married, nor even the thrice-married, nor, if it can happen, those married eight times. I will go further: I even receive a fornicator who repents. Whatever is equally permitted must be weighed in an equal balance."

Let him read the defence of that same work, which Rome gladly received many years ago, against his master, and then he will see that he blasphemes with other men's voices and is so unskilled that he does not even have abuse of his own, but uses against me the rage of enemies long since dead and buried. But now I must take up the work I have set before me.
BOOK ONE

The words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, of the priests who were in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The word of the Lord came to him in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Josiah [?] son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the deportation of Jerusalem in the fifth month.

The other prophets, such as Isaiah, Hosea and Joel, lived before the captivity of the ten tribes of Israel or of the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin; others came after the captivity, such as Daniel, Haggai and Zechariah. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, however, composed their prophecy when the captivity was imminent, the one in the land of Judah, the other in Babylon.

Jeremiah began to prophesy while still a boy, in the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah. He prophesied for nineteen years during his reign, and afterwards for eleven years under his son Jehoiakim, and under Zedekiah, the last of the kings of Judah, for eleven years, up to the fifth month, when Jerusalem was taken by the Babylonians. The three months each of Jehoahaz and Jeconiah—one of whom was taken to Egypt, the other with his mother to Babylon—are counted within the years mentioned above.

Thus from the beginning of his prophecy to the captivity of Jerusalem, in which he too was taken captive, he prophesied for forty-one years, apart from the time when he was taken to Egypt; and there he prophesied in Tahpanhes, as this very book relates. In place of "the words of Jeremiah" the Septuagint has: "The word of God that came to Jeremiah," meaning, of course, that the words of Jeremiah are the word of the Lord. He was of the priestly line who lived in the little village of Anathoth, three miles north of Jerusalem. Notice at the same time the wonderful mercy of the Lord: even when captivity was near and the Babylonian army was besieging Jerusalem, he still calls the people to repentance, preferring to save them if they turn rather than destroy them as offenders. In place of "deportation," which all the others have translated with one voice, the Seventy put "captivity." Ezekiel began to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been taken captive with him in the thirty-fifth year after the beginning of Jeremiah's prophesying.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you; I gave you as a prophet to the nations. This does not mean that Jeremiah existed before his conception, as heresy supposes, but that the Lord foreknew that he would exist, for to him things not yet done are already done, according to what the apostle says: who calls the things that are not as though they were.

That he is sanctified in the womb we should understand in the light of the apostle's words: But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles. John the Baptist too is sanctified in the womb; he receives the Holy Spirit, stirs in the womb, and speaks through his mother's mouth. And as for his saying:

I gave you as a prophet to the nations, he means what we shall read later in this same prophet: that he prophesied not only to Jerusalem but also to many nations round about. Some understand this passage of the Savior, who was in the proper sense the prophet of the nations and through the apostles called all peoples. For he truly, before he was formed in the virgin's womb and before he came out of his mother's womb, was sanctified in the womb and known to the Father, since he is always in the Father and the Father is always in him.

And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy. The Seventy: And I said, O Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am young. He declines an office which on account of his age he cannot bear, with the same modesty with which Moses too says that his voice is thin and weak. But Moses is rebuked as a man of mature and vigorous age, while to this man pardon is granted for his boyhood, which is adorned with modesty and bashfulness.

And the Lord said to me: Do not say, "I am a boy," for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their faces, for I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord. "Do not consider your age," he says, "for you have learned from another prophet: a man's gray hair is his wisdom. Only let it be your will to go; you will have me as your companion, and with my help you will accomplish everything: open your mouth, and I will fill it.

And do not consider the multitude of those to whom and against whom you are going to speak, but me, who am with you to rescue you, says the Lord." The Lord rescues him, not in the sense that the prophet is free from persecutions and hardships—we read that he suffered much—but so that by enduring he may overcome all things and not give way under distress.

And the Lord put out his hand and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Note that here the hand of God is put out to touch the prophet's mouth, and it is said to him: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; whereas in Isaiah it is written: And one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he held a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins.

There, because Isaiah was of full and mature age and himself frankly confesses that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a people of unclean lips, one of the seraphim is sent to touch his mouth, not with a hand but with tongs and a coal, to take away his iniquities and cleanse his sins. Here, however, the very hand of God is put out, through which he made all things, and which elsewhere is called his arm—not to take away sins, which being a boy he had not committed in great number, but to grant him the gift of speech.

Ezekiel, again, devours a book written within and without, containing both divine mysteries and plain history. Jeremiah's mouth is touched and the words of the Lord are given him, so that he may gain confidence to preach. And it is fitting, according to the letter, that a hand is put out, so that, seeing the likeness of human limbs, he may not dread the touch of the hand.

Behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to root up and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant. The word "overthrow" or "bring down," which I have added from the Hebrew, is not found in the Seventy. And notice that two joyful things follow upon four grim ones. For good things could not be built unless evil things had been pulled down, nor could the best be planted unless the worst had been rooted out.

For every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up, and every building which has no foundation on the rock but is built on sand is undermined and pulled down by the word of God. And that which Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the appearing of his presence—namely, every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine—he will destroy for ever.

Further, the things that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which with God is foolishness, he will overthrow and bring down, so that lowly things may be built in their place, and in place of the lofty things that have been pulled down and rooted up, there may be built and planted what accords with the truth of the Church, and the apostle's words may be fulfilled: you are God's building, God's field.

Many understand this passage of the person of Christ. For "Jeremiah" means "the exalted one of the Lord," who destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him on the height of a mountain, and who destroyed the hostile powers, blotting out on the cross the bond of errors. Of these the psalm too speaks figuratively, after the truth of the history: Why have the nations raged and the peoples plotted vain things? The kings of the earth stood up and the rulers gathered together.

In place of these, rooted up, pulled down, destroyed and cast down to the depths, the Church of God is built and planted. Concerning the person of Jeremiah, however, there is no doubt; for we read later on that he takes in his hand a cup full of wine and is commanded to make all the surrounding nations drink.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see a watchful rod. And the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word to perform it. In place of "a watchful rod" the Seventy translated "a staff of nut-wood." We must therefore take some trouble so that the Latin reader may briefly understand the Hebrew etymology.

"Saced" means "nut," while "watch" or "watchful" or "to watch" is called "soced." Hence later on the watchful leopard is designated by this word. So from the word meaning "nut," because of the similarity of the words, the name plays on the sense of "watchful." The same thing is written in Daniel according to Theodotion, where from the trees schinos and prinos, that is, the mastic and the holm oak, the sentence of being cut in two and sawn asunder is pronounced on the adulterous elders. Likewise at the beginning of Genesis, woman is called "issa" from "man," which is "is," as if to say "she-man," because she was taken from man.

In place of "staff of nut-wood" Aquila and Symmachus translated "watchful rod," but Theodotion "of almond." The rod watches, observing all the sins of the people, in order to strike and correct offenders. Hence the apostle too writes to sinners: What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? This is the rod or staff of which David also speaks: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me. And he rightly says "they have comforted," for the Lord rebukes in order to amend. And just as the nut or almond

has a very bitter rind and is enclosed in a very hard shell, so that when the harsh and hard parts are removed the sweetest fruit is found, so all correction and the toil of self-restraint seem bitter for the present but yield the sweetest fruits. Hence the old saying: the roots of learning are bitter, the fruits sweet. Some understand the watchful rod of nut-wood to be the Lord, of whom Isaiah says: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse. Hence also the rod of Aaron, which was thought to be dead, is said to have blossomed, prefiguring the resurrection of the Lord.

And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see? And I said: I see a boiling pot, and its face is toward the face of the north. And the Lord said to me: Out of the north evils will be opened—or, will blaze forth—upon all the inhabitants of the land.

Punishments are assigned to sinners by certain stages, so that little by little they may come to salvation. Those who refuse to be amended by the striking rod are put into the bronze pot set on fire, of which Ezekiel writes more fully. It is kindled from the face of the north, signifying the king of Babylon and the city of Jerusalem. And it is aptly added: out of the north evils will blaze forth upon all the inhabitants of the land—either the land of Judea or indeed the whole earth—of whom it is also written in the Apocalypse: woe to all the inhabitants of the earth.

For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and sojourners, one of whom says: I am a stranger on the earth and a sojourner, like all my fathers; and another: few and evil have been my days, in which I sojourn on the earth. Hence Peter too writes his catholic epistle to the strangers and sojourners of Pontus, Galatia and Cappadocia. And in a mystical sense Solomon says: The north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called "right"—that is, by those who have grown stiff with its cold and have lost the warmth of faith.

For behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord, and they shall come, and each shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all its walls round about, and against all the cities of Judah. And I will pronounce my judgments upon them for all their wickedness, for they have forsaken me, and poured libations to strange gods, and worshipped the work of their own hands.

No one doubts that many nations, and the kings of the individual nations, were subject to the king of Babylon. When Jerusalem was besieged, they set their thrones and tents all around it, especially at the exits of the gates, so that none of those shut in could break out; and not only Jerusalem but all the cities of Judea were encircled by a similar siege. "And when the city has been taken," he says, "then I will tell them that my judgments were just and that each received what he deserved—not for the other vices to which the human condition is subject, but above all for idolatry, through which they forsook me and worshipped the works of their own hands."

Some take this passage in a good sense: namely, that those who have been boiled in the bronze pot, through torments, and purified, will afterwards be the rulers of Jerusalem, and that after the Lord has had mercy on them, he will then reproach them for having forsaken him and worshipped idols. But this is a forced and perverse interpretation—let no ignorant commentator raise a false charge.

You, therefore, gird up your loins, and arise, and speak to them all that I command you. Job too is commanded to gird up his loins, and the apostles, with loins girded—which Elijah and John the Baptist mortified with leather belts—are told to hold lamps in their hands, the lamps, that is, of gospel preaching.

Whoever, then, is going to speak the words of God must gird up his loins, knowing that all the devil's strength is in the loins, and that the righteous man says in the psalms: My loins are filled with mockeries. And when he has girded his loins, let him hear what is written: Arise, you who sleep, and rise up, and Christ will give you light, so that, ever watchful and rising from sleep, he may speak what God has commanded him.

Do not be afraid of their faces, for I will not make you fear their countenance—or, as the Seventy and the other translators have it: lest I make you afraid. According to our translation the sense is: "Do not be afraid of their faces, for with me as your helper you will be unable to fear them"; according to the Seventy: "Do not be afraid of their faces; have confidence in my command. For if you do not offer what you have so as to stop fearing, I will abandon you and hand you over to fear, and in a sense I shall seem to make you afraid, since I leave you to terror."

This signifies that truth is always bitter, and that the multitude of men is not to be feared, who when rebuked do not bear correction but lay snares for the one who corrects them. And what follows in the Seventy, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord, is not found in the Hebrew. The sense is: "I will rescue you, not in the sense that no one will lay snares for you, but in the sense that, in enduring snares, you will not sin."

For I have made you this day—or, behold, I have set you on this day—a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall against the whole land: against the kings of Judah, its princes and priests, and the people of the land. And they will fight against you, but they will not prevail, for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you. The divine word describes why the prophet ought not to be afraid.

"I have set," he says, or "made you this day"—that is, in the present life, as long as it is called today—"as a most strongly fortified city," not a single house, nor a tower or some walls, but a whole city, which, set on a hill, cannot be hidden, of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God; and: I am a strong city, a city under siege.

"And an iron pillar," he says, of which the apostle writes: the pillar and bulwark of the truth. Hence Peter and John, who were reputed to be pillars of the Church, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship. Nor is this enough, but "a bronze wall," he says, which is not damaged by any rust nor perishes when beaten by rain, but grows stronger with age.

"And you will be such against the kings and princes and people"—not of just any place, but "of the land," people who mind earthly things and do not know heavenly ones, who bear the image of the man of dust and not of the heavenly man. "These," he says, "will fight against you, but they will not prevail." Why, I ask? What is the reason for such great strength that neither kings nor princes nor priests nor peoples prevail against one man? There follows: for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you.

If ever the kings of Judah—which means "confession"—and its princes and priests and peoples, that is, bishops, presbyters and deacons, and the base and ignoble crowd, should choose to rise up against a holy man, let him hold firm in faith and cease to fear, for with the Lord's help he will overcome.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying. This is not found in the Seventy, but has been added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion, who translated the Hebrew word "carath," for which I have said "cry" or "proclaim," as "read." For because of its ambiguity it signifies reading, crying out and proclaiming. The ears of Jerusalem we should take to mean the ears of its inhabitants.

Thus says the Lord: I remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown. The Seventy: Thus says the Lord: I remembered the mercy of your youth and the love of your perfecting. This is said more fully in Ezekiel, where the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and takes her into his embrace in the character of a wife; or, to show a more ardent affection, he calls her a girl, a young maiden and betrothed. For what we have not yet obtained we desire all the more to obtain.

"When," he says, "you followed me in the wilderness, and, as betrothal gifts and dowry, I bestowed on you the ornaments of the law and the necklaces of words." And he attributes all this not to her merit but to his own mercy, through which love also followed. This too, which I have set down, in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown, is not found in the Seventy.

Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest; all who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord. When he calls Israel the firstfruits of the Lord's harvest, he shows that the people gathered from the Gentiles came after the firstfruits, as is written elsewhere: Remember your congregation, which you have possessed from the beginning. Firstfruits, however, belong to the priests, not to enemies. What follows, all who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord, has this sense: just as those who devour the firstfruits, though they are in no way of priestly stock, are guilty of a crime, so those who defile Israel will be made subject to evils. This agrees with what the holy man says in the twenty-sixth psalm: While the wicked draw near against me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me, my enemies themselves have grown weak and have fallen. For they will not be exempt from punishment just because they carry out God's sentence, and evils will come upon them; for offenses must come, but woe to him through whom the offenses come!

Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What wrong did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me and walked after vanity and became vain? Another prophet also bears witness to this sense: My people, what have I done to you, and how have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slaves.

Both names, [Jacob?] and Israel, are used here. They do not mark off the two tribes from the ten but refer to the whole people, since Jacob himself was afterwards called Israel. He traces the offense back to the fathers. This is not because the sins of the fathers are charged to the children. It is because the children too, bearing the likeness of their fathers, are punished both for their own crime and for their parents'. We often read that God shows mercy to the children for the sake of holy fathers.

The fathers of the sinful people forsook God, and not briefly but for a long time. Instead of God they followed vanity, that is, idols, which do their worshipers no good, and they became like them, as it is written: Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.

And they did not say: Where is the Lord, who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the desert, through a land uninhabitable and pathless, through a land of thirst and the image of death, through a land in which no man walked and no human being dwelt? For "human being" the Septuagint translated "son of man", and for "image of death" the words "shadow of death" were added from Theodotion.

This is plain according to the history. But according to the anagogical sense we should consider that, as long as we are in this world and are being led out of Egypt, we ascend little by little. First we cross deserts and an uninhabitable land, which the saint ought not to inhabit, and a pathless one, a word that shows how hard the journey is. We pass through a land of thirst, where we always crave greater things and are never content with what we have; and through the image or shadow of death, for we always stand in danger and the devil sets his snares everywhere. We pass through a land in which no man walked who is of full age in Christ, for we shall all rise to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. Nor does anyone who is a man of God, or a son of man, ever dwell in it; he always hastens on to greater things.

From this it is clear that perfection is not found on the way but at the end of the way, in the dwelling prepared in heaven for the saints, to whom it is said: You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In vain, then, does the new heresy sprung from the old suppose that perfect victory is found here, where there is battle and struggle and the outcome of things to come is uncertain.

And I brought you into the land of Carmel, to eat its fruit and its good things. And you entered and defiled my land and made my inheritance an abomination. That is: "In return for the toil of a very hard journey I gave you an abundance of all things." For this is what "Carmel" signifies; in Hebrew it is called "Chermel", and in our language it means "knowledge of [circumcision?]".

That people polluted and violated with idolatry the holy land, which was fertile in every good thing. In the same way we, having received the knowledge of true circumcision, eat its fruit, but if negligence creeps in, we defile God's land and make his inheritance abominable.

The priests did not say, Where is the Lord? Those who handled the law did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me. The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed idols. After such great benefits they turned the privileges of their rank into contempt. The priests did not seek the Lord, and the teachers of the law, who ought to have taught others, did not know him. The shepherds became transgressors through negligence, and the prophets, who discourse among the peoples, speak not for God but for an idol and venerate their own inventions. These words should be turned against the teachers of our own order, who devour God's people as they would eat bread and, by their evil works, do not call upon the Lord.

Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and I will dispute with your sons. So as not to seem to strike by sheer power, he contends by reason, as though with equals. David sings of this, and the apostle takes it up: That you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged. By putting "still", he testifies that he has often done this. By adding "with your sons", he shows that the same obstinacy is found in the sons of the wicked too. He hints covertly that their sons also, at the coming of the Lord, followed the ancient denial of God.

Cross over to the islands of Kittim and see, and send to Kedar and consider carefully, and see whether such a thing has happened: whether a nation has changed its gods (or: its own gods), even though they are not gods. But my people have changed their glory for an idol (or: [?]), which will do them no good. He makes a comparison of something that admits no comparison, and sets the true God beside false ones.

"Go," he says, "to the islands of Kittim." We should take these as the islands of Italy or of the western regions. The name comes from the island of Cyprus, which lies near the land of Judea and has a city called by this name; Zeno, the founder of the Stoics, also came from there. Kedar is a desert region of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens. A prophecy of this same prophet against it is set out in the final part of his book, and David mentions it, saying: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner.

The sense is: "Go west, or send into the desert, and see whether any nation has done what you have done. None of them has spurned its gods or exchanged its wooden and stone gods for golden ones. Each has followed its ancient error and held fast to what it received from its ancestors, and this even though none of these is a god, but only likenesses of men made by hand. But my people have exchanged the truth for a lie and preferred to me an idol, which will not be able to help them in their time of need."

We can also say this against those who pursue vices with greater zeal than virtues. The apostle admonishes them, saying: I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification.

Be astonished at this, O heavens; its gates, be utterly desolate, says the Lord. For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water. The Septuagint has: The heaven was astonished at this and shuddered exceedingly and greatly; the rest is the same. The heaven was once told: Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak, and: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth. Now, seeing God's commandments trampled underfoot, it shudders and cannot hide its astonishment. For the whole creation groans and grieves over the sins of men.

The people of God did two perverse things. First, they forsook God, who is the fountain of life and who gave the commandment: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Second, they acted against what is written in the same place: You shall have no gods before me. Instead of him they followed demons, whom he calls broken cisterns because they cannot keep God's commandments.

Note also that a fountain is perpetual and has living waters, while cisterns and pits are filled from torrents, from the muddy waters of the earth, or from rain. By the gates of the heavens he means those of which it is written in the twenty-third psalm: Lift up your heads, O gates, and the King of glory shall come in. For this the Septuagint translated: Lift up your gates, O princes. These will be discussed more fully in their proper place.

Let no one be troubled that Aquila and Symmachus translated "heavens" while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated "heaven". The Hebrew "samaim" is of common number, and both "heavens" and "heaven" are called by the same name, like Thebes, Athens and Salonae.

Is Israel a slave, or a servant born in the house? I think it was from this passage that the Jews, puffed up with pride, said to the Savior: We are the seed of Abraham and have never been slaves to anyone; how can you say, You will be free? They did not know that everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, and that each person serves whatever has overcome him. So, though born of Abraham, the friend of God, by their own fault they became like sons of Ham, to whom it was said: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.

Why then has he become a prey? Lions have roared over him and raised their voice; they have made his land a wilderness, and his cities are burned, and there is no one to dwell in them. The divine word asks the question so that it may answer it itself.

By lions he means the princes of Babylon, who made his land a wilderness and destroyed his cities by fire. Or in the anagogical sense we may understand the lions as the hostile powers, or the leaders of the heretics. They lay waste the land of the church and ravage all its cities with heretical fire, the fire of which it is written: All are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven.

For they truly raise their voice. In this same prophet, in the guise of the partridge, they cry out and gather what they did not hatch, and they gain riches unjustly. Its cities are laid waste and destroyed because they do not have God dwelling in them, as Scripture says: and there is no one to dwell in them.

The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have also defiled you to the crown of your head. Has this not happened to you because you forsook the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you on the way? The words we rendered "at the time when he was leading you on the way" are not found in the Septuagint. He names two very great cities of Egypt, Memphis and Tahpanhes, and says that their sons defiled Israel to the crown of the head. He means this in the sense in which Isaiah said: From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him. So great was the lust of the Egyptians, who are "great of flesh", that they spared no member but defiled them all. In the literal sense, refer this to the idols of the Egyptians. In the spiritual sense, refer it to teachers of perverse doctrine, who pollute the purity of the church with their own foulness. These things will happen to her because she forsook the Lord her God, and above all at the very time when she ought to have followed him as her guide.

And now what do you want on the way to Egypt, to drink the water of Shihor? And what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river? For "Shihor" we have put "muddy", which is what the Hebrew word means. For it the common edition has "Gihon".

Above he had mentioned the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who defiled Israel to the crown of the head; now he names Egypt itself more plainly. No one doubts that the Nile has muddy waters. By the river of the Assyrians he means the Euphrates, for Scripture says that the land of promise stretches from the torrent of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.

Some forsake Christ, the fountain of life, and dig for themselves the pits of the heretics, which cannot hold the waters of doctrine. They must inevitably fall prey to lions, who turn their land into a wilderness and destroy all their churches. They must be defiled to the crown of the head and drink muddy waters, the streams of the Assyrian river and of the north, from which evils blaze out over the earth.

Your wickedness will rebuke you (or: your transgression will instruct you), and your turning away will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to have forsaken the Lord your God and to have no fear of me, says the Lord God of hosts. Note that wickedness or transgression first glutted the transgressor and, like the quails, filled him until he was sick of it, and only then instructs him to repent. He is commanded to see what he has left and what he has followed, and how he spurned good and sweet things and chose evil and bitter ones.

All this has happened because he forsook the Lord his God and the fear of him is not in him. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Because he did not have it, he is handed over to evil and bitterness.

Long ago you broke my yoke (or: your yoke), you burst my bonds (or: your bonds), and you said: I will not serve [?]. For on every high hill and under every leafy tree you lay down as a harlot (or: there you poured yourself out in fornication). He speaks to Israel as to a harlot, because she broke the marriage covenant and said, I will not serve (understand: "the Lord" or "my husband"). Instead, on every high hill and under every leafy tree she lay prostrate in idolatry, for pleasant and lofty places are always dedicated to idols.

This can also be said of someone who was a Christian from the start and was partly educated in the sacred writings, but who later, out of desire for secular literature (signified by the hills) and for the charms of eloquence (shown by the leafy trees), prostrates himself before demons. Under the pretext of learning and lofty knowledge, the demons pollute the souls of believers and make them spread their legs for every passer-by.

Yet I planted you as a choice vine, wholly of true seed. How then have you turned against me into a degenerate, foreign vine? The Septuagint has: Yet I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you turned into bitterness, a foreign vine? For "choice" or "fruitful" vine the Hebrew has "sorec", the word used in Isaiah's song. It is a kind of excellent vine, and the Lord says that he planted Israel from its shoot. He marvels that the true seed and choice vine has turned to bitterness and so become a foreign vine.

Let no one feel secure, then, if even the Lord's planting, the true seed, the sorec vine, can be so changed by its own fault that it departs from the Lord through bitterness and becomes a foreign vine. Here we should also consider the Creator's clemency. He who said in the Gospel, I am the true vine, granted his disciples too, and the people who believe in him, to be a choice or true vine, if it does not refuse to remain what it was planted as.

Though you wash yourself with lye and use much of the herb borith, you are stained by your iniquity before me, says the Lord God. For "herb borith", which we have kept as it stands in the Hebrew, the Septuagint put poa ("grass"), meaning the fullers' herb. In the province of Palestine this grows in green and moist places, and for washing away dirt it has the same power as lye. Our "lye" and "fullers' herb" is repentance. The word of the church, which reproves, rebukes and corrects the sinner, is also like a sharper lye.

Someone stained only with the light dirt of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions. But grave sins, which drag a person to death, cannot be washed out with lye or with the herb borith; they need harsher torments. For the fire will test what sort of work each one's is, and it will be revealed in fire. He aptly added: you are stained by your iniquity in my sight, meaning: "Even if you seem clean to men, you are not clean to me, for I know the conscience of each one." Hence it is also said elsewhere: No one living will be justified in your sight.

How can you say, I am not defiled, I have not gone after the Baals? Look at your ways in the valley (or: [?]). In Hebrew the valley is called "ge", and the Septuagint translates it polyandrion, which in our language can be called "the tomb of the multitude". "In vain," he says, "you refuse to confess your crimes and boast of your cleanness, when you are polluted with the filth of idolatry, and shamelessly deny that you worshiped the idol of the Baals. Look at the valley of the sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Siloam, and there you will see the shrine of Baal, whom you worshiped after forsaking God."

The words that follow, Know what you have done, open the closed eyes of the one who denies, so that she may see what she blushes to look at. In the tropological sense, let us use their own works to refute the brazenness of those who will not confess their vices. People like this do not walk on the strait and narrow way that leads to life. They walk on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, by which very many enter. That is why it is meaningfully named polyandrion. Or, according to the history, it was so named because a multitude of the people was slain and perished there through the evil of idolatry.

A swift runner tracing out her ways, a wild ass used to the wilderness, in the desire of her heart she sniffed the wind of her love; no one will turn her back. None who seek her will weary themselves; in her months they will find her. The Septuagint has: Toward evening her night howled; she widened her ways over the waters of the desert; in the desire of her soul she was borne along by the spirit; she was handed over; who will turn her back? None who seek her will toil; in her humiliation they will find her. In this passage the Septuagint edition differs greatly from the Hebrew truth, yet each has its own sense.

Above she had said, I am not defiled, and he was speaking as to a woman who had behaved shamefully; now he describes her fornication. "As a nimble doe" (which we have called by the common-gender word "runner", and which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion rendered more expressively as dromas kouphē, "a light runner") "traces out her ways and is carried swiftly to pasture, and as a wild ass used to the wilderness draws in, in the desire of her heart, the wind or spirit of her love" (for among the Hebrews both "wind" and "spirit" are called by the one name "ruha"), "so Israel, or Jerusalem, was carried headlong toward the desire of lust and burned with every love of idols. No one can turn her from this headlong rush by his warnings. This is not because the prophets were unable to do it but because of the perverse wickedness of her desire." "Whoever,"

he says, "seeks her will not have to toil much; in her menstruation and uncleanness they will find her." For this Aquila translated neomenia, that is, "the new moon", Symmachus "month", and the Septuagint and Theodotion "humiliation". According to the Septuagint the sense is this. The harlot Jerusalem, like the woman described in Proverbs, howled toward evening and enticed lovers to lust. She opened the ways of her shame and spread her legs for every passer-by. And there was a place made pleasant by flowing waters, which becomes more delightful when there is solitude all around, so that no one sees the one committing fornication.

"In the desire of her soul," he says, "she was pneumatophoreito": either she was led by a perverse spirit, or she drew in the cool breath of love, or else she sang the songs of her shame. "She was handed over," he says, to her vices and lust; no one will be able to turn her back. All who wish to find her will find her in the abasement of her shame, so that she can never be satisfied in her love of pleasure.

Keep your foot from going bare and your throat from thirst. But you said: I have lost hope; I will by no means do it, for I have loved strangers, and I will go after them. The Septuagint has: Turn your foot from the rough way and your throat from thirst. But she said: I will act manfully, because she loved strangers and walked after them. Those who are about to keep the Passover are commanded to have sandals on their feet.

The apostle, too, speaks of the shod feet of those who are made ready for the gospel. While they walk through the wilderness of this world they must not be exposed to venomous creatures, which ought to be trampled and crushed by the foot of the gospel. We keep our throat from thirst when we accept the commands of the Savior, who says: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. But she, despairing of better things, refused to do what the Lord commanded. She gave her reason, saying, I have loved strangers and will follow them, and she thought that by this shameless confession she could escape her crimes.

According to the Septuagint, the way of sinners is rough, and the Lord turns it into a smooth way. Whoever follows heretics should be branded with the verdict of these verses, for having said: I have lost hope (or: I will act manfully in my evil purpose), and I will be strong in my error. Whoever follows a doctrine foreign to the church's must inevitably love strangers and follow in their footsteps. These are either demons or the leaders of the heretics, who are strangers to God.

As a thief is put to shame when he is caught, so the house of Israel is put to shame, they and their kings, their princes and their priests and their prophets. However shameless and brazen the faces of thieves may be, they still blush when they are caught in the act of theft. So Israel too, saying to a piece of wood, "You are my father," and to a stone, "You gave birth to me," calling those things parents which he himself had made, is put to shame when he is caught in his idolatry.

And so that we should not think he says this of the common people, he names their kings and princes and priests and prophets. Let us use this testimony whenever our own leaders, and those who are regarded as leaders in the Church, are caught in shameful sins.

They have turned their back to me and not their face. Those who cast the words of God behind them turn their back against him and not their face. For when a teacher gives instruction, it is a sign of obedience if the hearer listens facing him with head bowed; but if he turns his back, it is a sign of contempt, as is written in another place: "And they turned to me a shoulder that drew away." "So greatly," says God, "have they despised my commands that they would not even listen to them, but showed the swelling of their mind by the bearing of their body."
And in the time of their affliction they will say: Arise and save us. Let those who did not perceive God through his benefits perceive him through torments.

Where are your gods, whom you made for yourself? Let them arise and save you in the time of your affliction. It is a shameless request, in a time of need and distress, to seek help from the one whom they despised in time of peace. And it should be read with the tone of one rebuking: "Let your gods save you, whom you made for yourself," so that, since God is the creator of human beings while a human being has made a god, necessity may prove what those gods can do whom you worshipped before, when you felt secure.

According to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah. The individual cities worshipped either the same gods or separate and different ones, so that they did not seem to share agreement even in their impiety; rather, a superstition at war with itself followed diverse errors. And what follows, "and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal," was added by the Septuagint.

Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord. Human perversity is quick to excuse itself, so that whatever people deservedly suffer they make out to be suffered unjustly, and they lay their own fault at the door of God's judgment. "In vain, then," he says, "do you put forward complaints and accuse the judge of injustice, when what you suffer comes from your own impiety." And what follows, "and you have all acted wickedly against me," was likewise added by the Septuagint.

In vain have I struck your sons; they did not accept discipline — for which the Septuagint put: "you did not accept." The sense in the Hebrew is: "Those very ones who were struck refused to accept discipline." But in the Septuagint it is: "I struck your sons for this reason, that you might be instructed by their death. And lest perhaps you should say, 'You would not correct us when we sinned,' learn from the blows dealt to your sons that I wished to cure you with a harsher medicine."

Your sword has devoured your prophets. "Not my prophets but yours; and not my sword at all, but your own sword devoured them, the sword you brought upon yourselves by your sins." The Septuagint, however, does not have "your," but translated simply: "The sword has devoured your prophets," "so that it may be shown to be either the enemy's sword or my sword, by which your sins were pierced through."

Like a ravaging lion is your generation. Septuagint: "like a ravaging lion, and you did not fear." "The sword," he says, "which devoured your prophets" — there is no doubt that he means the soothsayers of Baal and of the idols — "laid everything waste like a lion; and yet your generation, which ought to have been corrected by the slaughter of a few, persisted wholly in its wickedness."

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is this: "Thus the sword of the Lord, which displayed the sword of the enemies, devoured and tore your false prophets like a lion that most greedily tears the prey it has found; and yet not even by the punishment of your prophets could you be turned to better things."

See the word of the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a late-yielding land? Why then has my people said: We have withdrawn, we will come to you no more? Septuagint: "Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a land full of thorns? For my people said: We will not be ruled, and we will not come to you." Moses too saw the voice of God, and the apostle John says that he saw and handled the Word of God.

He marvels that the people of Israel should have regarded God as a wilderness, while they followed idols as though they were the bustle of cities. A late-yielding land is one that does not receive the rains of teaching or the discipline of the gospel, and it is full of thorns because it had not been cultivated. So the people who were once God's are the more wicked in this, that they withdrew from the Lord and are unwilling ever again to return to their God. It is a grave offense to refuse to appease the one you have offended.

Will a virgin forget her ornament, or a bride the sash on her breast? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number. From this we learn that Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin Church, which has no spot or wrinkle. And if he is the bridegroom, these are his words — the one of whom John the Baptist also speaks: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom."

So whoever withdraws from the Lord loses his ornament and loses the understanding of doctrine, which is signified by the breast. That is why John the Evangelist reclines on the Lord's breast, and why, among other portions, the breast of the victims is set apart for the priests. And the greater the length of time during which we forget God, the greater the punishment of the sin, since not even the passing of ages could subdue it.

Why do you strive to show your way to be good, in order to seek love? You who have even taught your ways to your wickedness, and on your skirts — or, in your hands — has been found the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent. I did not find them in pits, but in all these things — or, under every oak.

"In vain," he says, "do you wish to defend yourself by skill with words and to show your works as good, so as to earn love — you who have even taught others your ways and have been an example of evil works to all. For on your skirts — or, in your hands — has been found the blood of the innocent, whom you sacrificed to idols, or whose souls you destroyed by the likeness of sacrifices."

We have put "the poor" from the Hebrew; it is not found in the Septuagint. "These poor and innocent people," he says, "I did not find slain in pits" — as usually happens through the ambushes of robbers — "but in all the things I mentioned above, or under the oak" — which in Hebrew is called ella, a word that also means "these," so that the sense is "in all these things, or under the oak and terebinth" — "under whose shade and foliage, as in pleasant places, you took your enjoyment in the crimes of idolatry."

And you said: I am without sin and innocent, and therefore let your anger be turned away from me. Behold, I will contend with you in judgment because you said: I have not sinned. How utterly vile you have become — or, since you have been exceedingly contemptuous — repeating your ways! These words are to be used against those who refuse to acknowledge their sins, but who in a time of affliction and distress say that they suffer unjustly what they suffer, and so provoke God's anger all the more, since it is a second and greater sin not to mourn what they have done but to put forward empty excuses for their sins.

"I will contend with you in judgment," he says, "because you said: I have not sinned," as though anything were greater than this sin: to have one thing in one's conscience and to utter another with one's tongue. Let the new heresy sprung from the old hear that God's anger is greatest of all against those who refuse humbly to confess their sin and instead shamelessly boast of their righteousness.

And you will be put to shame by Egypt, as you were put to shame by Assyria. For you will go out from her too, with your hands upon your head, because the Lord has crushed your confidence — or, your hope — and you will have no success in it. To avoid an attack by the Egyptians they used to flee to the Assyrians, whose protection proved useless, for we read that they were defeated by the Egyptians. Again, to escape the wrath of the Assyrians they relied on the help of the Egyptians, who, as history relates, were overcome by the Assyrians.

So they are rebuked because, abandoning their hope in God, they rely on human help, which has all been crushed and so overthrown that they can find nothing useful in it. Hence he says: "And you will go out from her too," that is, from Egypt, just as you went out from the Assyrians, "and your hands will be upon your head," and you will mourn that you looked for protection from the Egyptians in vain. Let us recall the story of how Tamar, after she had been defiled and violated by her most wicked brother Amnon, put her hands on her head, which was strewn with ashes, and so returned to her house.

It is commonly said — for which the Septuagint rendered only "It is said" — if a man sends away his wife, and she leaves him and takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will not that woman — or, that land — be polluted and defiled? But you have played the harlot with many lovers — or, shepherds. For the word [?], which is written with the four letters resh, ayin, yod, mem, means both "lovers" and "shepherds": if we read rehim, it means "lovers"; if rohim, "shepherds."

Yet return to me, says the Lord — or, and you were returning to me, says the Lord. In the Hebrew he receives her as a penitent even after her harlotry and urges her to return to him; but in the Septuagint he does not call her to repentance but rebukes the shamelessness of the harlot for daring to return to her husband after adultery.

And where he says "and that woman will be defiled," for which we read "land" in the Hebrew, he leaves the comparison and speaks more plainly of the land of Israel, which is likened to an adulterous woman. Let us use this testimony against those who abandon faith in the Lord and, entangled in the errors of heretics, after many acts of harlotry and the deceiving of souls, pretend to return to the original truth — not to rid their hearts of poison, but to instill it into others.

Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not been prostituted. You sat by the roads waiting for them like a robber in the wilderness — or, like a deserted crow. For "robber" and "crow" the Hebrew has arabe, which can also mean "Arab" — a people given to brigandage who to this day raid the borders of Palestine and beset the roads of those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, something the Lord also recalls in the Gospel.

"Lift up your eyes, then, O Jerusalem, look around this way and that, and see where you have not been prostituted in harlotry. For just as robbers are accustomed to lay ambushes for travelers toward evening and in deserted places, so you, like the harlot in Proverbs, sat by the roads toward evening, so that by lying with them you might kill the souls of those who committed harlotry with you. Because of this the whole

land has been polluted by your harlotries." And it is significant that, in the anagogical sense, those who promise to abandon heretical errors are commanded to lift their eyes straight ahead. For unless they begin to see what is straight, they cannot condemn their former crookedness.

You have polluted — or, killed — the land with your harlotries and your wickedness. Therefore the drops of rain were withheld and there was no late rain — or, and you had many shepherds to your own stumbling. The land was killed, or polluted, through the killing of those who perished in the harlotry of idolatry; for this reason the blessing of all things was taken away, so that they suffered a drought of the word of God. Or else: it had shepherds through whom it offended God, so that those who ought to have been teachers, to keep others from error, became the authors of impiety.

You had the brow of a harlot; you refused to blush. Septuagint: "You had the face of a harlot; you became shameless toward all." Because he had said above, "I have not sinned," and had sinned the more by denying her crimes, he now rebukes her as a brazen woman of excessive shamelessness, who does not go to just one or two men with a brazen face but blushes before no one. Let us use this saying against the conventicle of heretics who glory in their errors.

Then at least from now on call to me: My father, you are the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry forever, or will you keep it up to the end? Let the heretics blush, who refuse to turn to better things or to go back to their Father and Creator, and let them hear: "At least from now on call to me: My father, you are the guide of my virginity."

He betrothed your soul in his embrace, and he teaches how it ought to pray and do penance. And the more merciful he is, who shows the way of salvation even after harlotry, the more wretched is the harlot who will not receive healing after her wounds.

Behold, you have spoken and done evil, and you have been able. "Instead of words of repentance you have blasphemed with words of pride, and you have carried out your evil design and displayed your strength against your husband, so that you are able to do what you have talked of."

And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what faithless Israel has done? She went up onto every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there she played the harlot. And I said, after she had done all these things: Return to me; and she did not return.

And her treacherous sister Judah saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I had sent her away and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the harlot, and by the ease of her harlotry she defiled the land and committed adultery with stone and wood. And in all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood, says the Lord.

The punishments of some are the remedies of others: when a murderer is punished, he himself receives what he did, but others are deterred from crime. So when the ten tribes, which were called Israel, had been taken captive by the Assyrians and carried off to Media, the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, which ought to have feared a similar fate and turned to God with their whole mind, outdid the crimes of the ten tribes and followed idols to such a degree that they set up a statue of Baal in the temple of God, which in Ezekiel is called the idol set up to provoke the Lord's jealousy and rivalry.

He speaks under the figure of two sisters, because they were born of one stock — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — and he calls the first "faithless" and the second "treacherous." For the first turned away from God entirely, at once worshipping the golden calves in Dan and Bethel; but the second, with whom were the temple and the religion of the true God, withdrew from the Lord gradually in imitation of her sister, and is therefore called "treacherous." In the anagogical sense, however, the prophecy concerns heretics, who, while they think they are pursuing knowledge falsely so called with heretical subtlety, climb the mountain of pride and, beguiled by the pleasures of this flesh, display their harlotry under every leafy and pleasant tree. And when they are handed over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh, it often happens that the house of Judah — that is, of confession and true faith — is not at all frightened by the example, but commits far greater sins, and by the ease of its harlotry defiles the land of the Church and commits adultery with stone and wood, following doctrines that are hostile to God.

But if a churchman wishes to correct the one who errs, to cut away the rotting flesh and to draw back to repentance those who had followed falsehood, and they nonetheless follow their old error under the guise of the Church's truth, it can be said of them: "In all this treacherous Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood." This prophecy was given in the time of Josiah, a righteous king, under whom Jeremiah also began to prophesy.

And the Lord said to me: Faithless Israel has justified herself in comparison with treacherous Judah. "Israel," he says, "is more righteous in comparison with Judah, because she perished right at the beginning, while Judah could have been corrected by her torments." Let the new heresy sprung from the old note that Israel is said to be justified in comparison with one who is worse. Nor is this surprising in the case of sisters of one nation, since even Sodom receives the name of righteousness in comparison with Jerusalem, as the Lord says through Ezekiel, "Sodom was justified by you," and the tax collector becomes righteous in comparison with the Pharisee.

Go and proclaim — or, read — these words toward the north, and say: Return, faithless Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn away — or, I will set — my face from you — or, against you — for I am holy — or, merciful — says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your iniquity, that you have transgressed against the Lord your God — or, acted impiously — and have scattered — or, poured out — your ways to strangers under every leafy tree, and you have not listened to my voice, says the Lord.

The Hebrew word carath is understood both as "call" or "proclaim" and as "read"; hence Aquila and Symmachus translated "cry out," while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated "read." The message is directed toward the north and against Babylon and the Assyrians, to the ten tribes and to the two, and their return is foretold. "And I will not turn away," he says, "my face from you — or, I will not set my face against you — so that I will receive you not with the severity of a judge but with a face of mercy.

For I am holy and merciful, so that I will no longer remember your iniquity, nor recall that you withdrew from the Lord, that in his place idols delighted you, and that you played the harlot under every shady and leafy tree." This can fittingly be said also to heretics, or to those who are negligent within the Church, who are daily called to repentance by churchmen, and to whom these words can properly be applied: "And you have not listened to my voice."

Every heretic dwells in the north and has lost the warmth of faith, and cannot heed the Apostle's words, "fervent in spirit"; and because he has given himself over to pleasures, he has withdrawn from the Lord, scattered his ways to alien doctrines, and followed pleasure. For no heresy is built up except for the sake of the gullet and the belly, so as to lead astray silly women burdened with sins, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth. Of such men it is truly said, "who devour my people as they eat bread," and they are the ones whom Christ censures as devouring widows' houses.

"And when I have had mercy on you," he says, "do not think yourself righteous, but always remember your iniquity and know that you have committed harlotry against the Lord, and bow your proud neck, so that you who offended through arrogance may appease God through humility." And to what we cited above, "and I will not set my face against you," the prophet's words are fitting: "Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities."

Return, O returning children — or, wandering and departing ones — says the Lord, for I am your husband — or, I will rule over you — and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you into Zion. And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and understanding. And when you have multiplied and increased in the land in those days, says the Lord, they will no longer say, "The ark of the covenant — or, of the testament — of the Lord"; it will not come to mind, nor will they remember it, nor will it be visited, nor will it be made any more.

The Jews think this was fulfilled after the return from Babylon under Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, since not all returned; and that this is what is meant by "I will take one from a city and two from a family." But it is better taken of the coming of Christ, when a remnant was saved, as the Apostle says in his exposition: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Then they were brought into Zion, of which it is written, "Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God." And shepherds after his own heart were given — the apostles and apostolic men — and they fed the multitude of believers not in Jewish ceremonies but in the knowledge and teaching of Christ, once the preaching of the gospel had been sown throughout the whole world.

They will by no means place their confidence in the ark of the Lord, which was the guardian of the law of Moses, but they themselves will be the temple of God; nor, like the erring Nazarenes, will they serve sacrifices that have been abolished, but they will pursue spiritual worship. Others, however, understand this of the end of time, when, once the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel will be saved.

At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all nations will gather to it in the name of the Lord in Jerusalem, and they will no longer walk after the perversity of their most wicked heart. The Lord will by no means sit upon the ark of the covenant and the cherubim — to whom that people formerly used to say, "You who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself" — but all who believe with a perfect mind will be the throne of God.

Or surely it is better to understand the whole of this of the Church, when all nations are gathered in the name of the Lord into Jerusalem, in which is the vision of peace; and they by no means walk after the perversity of their most wicked heart, to do what they desire, nor do they follow their own errors, but they say with the prophet: "My soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me."

"In those days the house of Judah will go to [?] the house of Israel, and together they will come from the land of the north to the land that I gave to your fathers." This is properly fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when people of the twelve tribes together believed the gospel. Leaving the land of the north, with its bitter cold, and turning away from the devil's rule, they then received the land of promise that he had promised to their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. I recently published a small book on the land of promise.

"But I said: How shall I set you among the sons and give you a desirable land, the glorious inheritance of the hosts of the nations! I said: You will call me Father, and you will not cease [?] to walk after me." For "the glorious inheritance of the hosts of the nations," which the Septuagint translated "the renowned inheritance of the almighty God of the nations," Theodotion translated more expressively: "the famous inheritance of the mightiest strength of the nations." This signifies Christ, who is the leader and Lord of all the nations that believe in his name and his passion.

It is he who said to Israel, "You will call me Father," and, "Whoever believes in me believes in the Father." It is he who promised, "I will set you among the sons," that is, "in the number of my sons who have believed in me from among the people of the Gentiles, and to whom I have given the desirable land." For "to all who received him he gave power to become children of God."

"But as a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me, says the Lord." This is the voice of Christ concerning the Jewish people, to whom he had said, "I will set you among the sons and give you a desirable land, and you will call me Father and will not cease to walk after me."

"Just as," he says, "a woman despises not her husband but her lover, once she has slept with him and sees him serving her lust, and sees the law of nature reversed in her own case—the law by which she was once made subject to her husband, when the Lord said, 'and your turning shall be toward him'—so the house of Israel, that is, the Jewish people, has despised the Lord and Savior, to its own ruin."

"A voice was heard on the roads"—or "on the lips"—"the weeping and wailing of the sons of Israel, because they have made their way wicked; they have forgotten the Lord their God. Turn, returning sons, and I will heal your turnings away"—or "your bruises"—for which Symmachus translated "your conversions." God gladly receives the penitent. He runs to meet the son worn out by want and filth, at once clothes him in his former garments, and restores glory to the one who returns—provided only that he returns with weeping and wailing.

For it was by his own fault that he made his way wicked and forgot the Lord his God and Father. To such the prophetic word now speaks: "Turn, returning sons. I call you sons for this reason: that, having recognized your sins, you return to your Father with weeping and wailing. And when," he says, "you have returned to the Lord, he will heal all your bruises"—or "turnings away," by which you had departed from the Lord—"or, indeed, your conversions."

For although we return to the Lord by our own will, yet unless he draws us and strengthens our desire with his protection, we cannot be saved. Let us understand this both of the Jewish people returning to the Lord and of heretics who have abandoned the Lord.

"Behold, we come to you, for you are the Lord our God. Truly the hills were liars, and the multitude"—or "the strength"—"of the mountains; truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel." Let the penitent say this, abandoning all pride and the multitude, or height, of the mountains and hills through which he was proud against God; and, laid low in humility, let him say: "Truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel."

"Shame has devoured the labor of our fathers from our youth: their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters." All the labors of the heretics—of whom it is written, "They have failed, searching out searches"—from the youth of those whom they had deceived, their sons and daughters who had advanced in heresy or were simply held fast by self-indulgence: all this our shame has overwhelmed. Hence they go on:

"We shall lie down in our shame, and our disgrace shall cover us, for we have sinned against our God, we and our fathers, from our youth to this day, and we have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God." Let Israel, which did not listen to its Lord, say this; let every heretic who does penance say this. And yet it is a part of salvation to confess and acknowledge one's sins. "Tell first your iniquities," he says, "that you may be justified."

For truly Israel abandoned Christ, the Lord its God, and sinned against him, not only at the time when he was seen in the flesh but also before his coming. Hence they say: "We and our fathers, from our youth to this day, have not listened to the voice of our God," who spoke to our fathers: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote of me."

"If you return, Israel, says the Lord, turn to me." For this the Septuagint translated: "If Israel [?] turns, says the Lord, to me he shall return." And the sense is: "If he has returned to me, he will return from captivity," or otherwise: "when he has offered what he has." For "to him who has, it will be given; but from him who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken away."

But according to the Hebrew the sense is this: "If you return to me, Israel, and once and for all desire salvation, and say that you have sinned and have not listened to the voice of your Lord, then turn fully: believe in him whom you denied, and then your conversion will be complete."

"If you take away your [?] stumbling blocks from before my face, you will not be shaken." So when we are shaken and say, "But my feet were almost moved," we suffer this not from the weakness of our nature but because we set up our stumbling blocks and our idols against the Lord.

"And you will swear, 'As the Lord lives,' in truth and in judgment and in righteousness; and the nations will bless him and praise him." How, then, does the gospel forbid us to swear? But here "you will swear" is said in the sense of confession, and as a condemnation of the idols by which Israel used to swear. Finally the stumbling blocks are taken away and he swears by the Lord.

And the phrase "As the Lord lives" is, in the Old Testament, an oath that condemns the dead gods by whom all idolatry swears. At the same time we should note that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment and righteousness. If these are lacking, it will be no oath at all, but perjury. "And when," he says, "Israel has done this too, and through the apostles has become the teacher of the nations, then all nations will bless him—or be blessed in him—and will praise him, because salvation has come forth from Israel."

"For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns. Be circumcised to the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest my wrath go forth like fire and burn, with no one to quench it, because of the wickedness of your thoughts"—or "of your devices."

Where we have said, "Be circumcised to the Lord, and remove the foreskin of your hearts," Symmachus put, "Be purified to the Lord, and remove the wickedness of your hearts," understanding circumcision as cleansing and foreskins as vices. This is commanded to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, who follow the true faith and dwell in the Church: that they should not sow among thorns—which the word of the gospel signifies, thorns that choke the seed of God—but should first break up the fallow ground, dig out all the brambles and pull up the briars, so that clean fields may receive clean seed.

This is what is said in another place: "Do not cast your pearls before swine, and do not give what is holy to dogs." For how can someone whose mind is full of the troubles of the world hear the word of God, receive the seed and bear fruit? And what follows—"Be circumcised to the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts"—is commanded to no one but the man of Judah and the inhabitant of Jerusalem, so that they may abandon the letter that kills and follow the Spirit that gives life.

"For if you do not do this," he says, "my wrath will go forth like fire and burn, with no one to quench it." He warns and foretells it for this reason: so that he may not be compelled to do it. We see this proved in the Ninevites, to whom the sentence was announced in advance so that by repentance they might turn aside the impending fury. All these evils will come because of the wickedness of our thoughts or devices. Where now are those who say there is no sin in thoughts, when according to the truth of the gospel all vices proceed from the heart?

"Declare in Judah, and make it heard in Jerusalem; speak, blow the trumpet in the land, cry aloud, say: Gather together, and let us go into the fortified cities." Let Judah hear this; let Jerusalem hear it, in which is the confession of faith, in which the peace of Christ dwells, and to which it was said through Isaiah: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice, you who bring good news to Jerusalem." Let him cry aloud and command thus:

"Let us go into the fortified cities—the wars of the heretics are rising; let the defenses of Christ hold us. Raise the sign of the cross on the watchtower and on the height of the Church. Take courage, you who are afraid; do not stand still, but run to Christ for help. For I," he says, "am bringing evil from the north, and great destruction: the true Nebuchadnezzar, whom I permit to exist in this world for this reason, that your strength and victory may be proved."

"The lion has come up from his lair, and the plunderer of nations has roused himself; he has gone out from his place to make your land a desolation; your cities will be laid waste, left without inhabitant." This, as we have said, is the true Nebuchadnezzar, of whom Peter also speaks: "Our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion."

And he comes up from the abyss, to which he is to be banished, and he begs not to be sent there. And the plunderer, or destroyer, of nations has roused himself—he of whom it was said, "He will rule over all his enemies," and who boasts in the sight of the Lord, "I have gone around the whole earth and trampled it." For who is there whom the devil's poisons do not touch, except him alone who can say, "Behold, the prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me"?

He often makes the whole land of the Church a desolation, so that those who have gone out from the Church fight against the Church. Of these the evangelist John also speaks: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us." The cities of the land of Judea are laid waste, and the conventicles of the heretics flourish. So if anyone is a supporter of the authors of perverse doctrines, of him it can be said: "The lion has come up from his lair, and the plunderer of nations has roused himself," and the rest.

"For this gird yourselves with sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned away from us"—or, as the Septuagint translated, "from us." There is no other way for us to escape the lion and that most savage beast, unless we do penance and turn to the Lord not only in mind but also in deed. For as long as he lays waste the Church and the land of Judah, and ravages Jerusalem too, God's anger is plain to see.

"And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that the heart of the king will perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests will be astounded and the prophets dismayed." When the plunderer lays waste the Church of the Lord and the Lord's anger against us remains, every help will be useless. "The heart of the king will perish"—the king whose heart ought to be in the hand of God—"and the heart of the princes," who were thought to be wise; for God has made foolish the wisdom of the world, because through it they did not know God.

The priests themselves too, who ought to teach the law of the Lord and defend the peoples under them from the lion's fury, will be dazed by a kind of stupor and turned to madness—for so the Septuagint translated it, rendering "stupor" as "ecstasy of mind"—and the prophets will be dismayed, or, as Aquila translated the Hebrew word "iethmau," they will be out of their minds.
