For who would not go mad, who would not lose heart, on seeing princes and kings and priests and prophets, once his own, beneath the lion?

"And I said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God"—for which the Septuagint translated, "O Lord God"—"have you then deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'You shall have peace'? And behold, the sword has reached even to the soul."

Because he had said above, "At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of God, and all nations shall be gathered to it in the name of the Lord in Jerusalem," and now he says, "The heart of the king will perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests will be astounded and the prophets dismayed," the prophet is troubled and thinks that God has lied to him. He does not understand that the former was promised for a time long afterward, while the latter would happen in the near future—just as the apostle also says: "Has God rejected his people?

By no means!" And the sword reaches even to the soul when nothing living is left in the soul. At the same time this also shows that unless the sword goes first, to cut away and purge the vices of the soul, peace and the promise do not follow.

"At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem: A burning wind"—or "a wind of error"—"on the roads that are in the desert, the way of the daughter of my people, not for winnowing and cleansing; a full wind will come to me from these." When the sword has reached even to the soul and the threshing floor is finished, then a burning wind will come from the desert. It will not cleanse and winnow the floor, so that the chaff is scattered here and there and the grain stored in the barns; rather, a full wind will come, not to the people but to me, so that my wheat is scattered.

Among the Hebrews "wind" and "spirit" are called by the same name, "ruha," and depending on the nature of the passage we should take it as either "wind" or "spirit." Others explain this passage as meaning that after the threshing floor has been cleansed, a remnant will be saved, which is why it is written, "A spirit of fullness will come to me," as the evangelist says, "We have all received from his fullness, and we shall obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit." According to the historical sense, take the burning wind as Nebuchadnezzar, who consumes everything; according to the tropological sense, as the hostile power which, coming from the desert and the wilderness, where there is no dwelling place of God, tries to overthrow his Church.

"And now I—but I will speak my judgments with them." This is aposiopesis, like that line of Virgil: "Whom I—but better first to calm the troubled waves." So, being about to speak of prosperity, he checks himself and joins sorrows to sorrows. For these are the judgments that God speaks with the people that was once his, so that they may know they justly suffer what they suffer.

"Behold, he will come up like clouds, and his chariots like a whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, for we are laid waste!" He sees future things as present and describes the Babylonian army: the din of its chariots and wheels is compared to a most violent storm, and the speed of its horses is likened to eagles.

When the prophet had said this and, as it were, pointed with his finger at the approaching enemy, the people groan and feel these things not as future but as already done, saying, "Woe to us, for we are laid waste!" Apply this same passage to the Church: every day the army of the true Nebuchadnezzar attacks us, and the chariots of Pharaoh and all his cavalry outdo the onslaught of eagles. If a churchman understands this, believing the saying, "When you turn and groan, then you will be saved," he will say, "Woe to us, for we are laid waste!"

"Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved; how long will harmful thoughts linger in you?" To the people who say, "Woe to us, we are laid waste," the prophet replies—or rather God through the prophet: "Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem," with that water of which Isaiah also speaks: "Wash yourselves, be clean"—the water of saving baptism,

the water of penance. He is speaking to the capital of the Jews, so that by the city its people may be understood: "How long will you be subject to the wicked thoughts that proceed from your heart?" In the holy Scriptures we should take "heart" to mean the soul and the mind.

"For a voice is declaring from Dan, and announcing an idol"—or "pain"—"from Mount Ephraim." The divine word now speaks according to the layout of the land of Judea. For the tribe of Dan, near Mount Lebanon and the city now called Paneas, faces the north, from which Nebuchadnezzar was to come.

He describes an idol—whether Bel, or pain, or iniquity—as coming from Mount Ephraim. For after the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one reaches Jerusalem. "Dan" means "judgment," "Ephraim" means "abundance." So the judgment of the Lord will come upon a land that sins against the Lord, with all abundance of punishment.

"Tell the nations: Behold, it has been heard in Jerusalem that watchmen are coming from a distant land; and they have raised their voice against the cities of Judah. Like keepers of fields they have surrounded her on every side, because she has provoked me to anger, says the Lord." He wants all the surrounding nations to know God's sentence, and all to learn discipline from the scourging of Jerusalem.

"It is widely reported in Jerusalem," he says, "that enemies are coming from a distant land, and that the roar of a howling army is rising against her. They will besiege the city so closely and shut it in with siegeworks that you would think them not so much enemies as keepers of fields and vineyards. But all this has happened not through the strength of the enemy but through the fault of Jerusalem, because she provoked God to anger." For if the hostile powers have no power over swine, how much less over human beings—and human beings who were once of the city of God!

"Your ways and your thoughts have done these things to you; this is your wickedness, because it is bitter, it has touched your heart." He turns to address the city of Jerusalem: her ways and thoughts, by which she sinned in deed and word, have brought upon her everything that has come; and her wickedness, bitter in itself, has touched her heart and pierced the inner depths of her soul. So whatever happens to us happens through our own fault, for we turn the sweet God to bitterness and force him to rage against his will.

"My belly, my belly, I am in pain; the senses of my heart are troubled. I will not keep silent, for my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the clamor of battle. Destruction upon destruction is proclaimed, and the whole land is laid waste; suddenly my tents are laid waste, in a moment my curtains." Where, following Symmachus, we have put "are troubled," and the Hebrew has "homae," the Septuagint and Theodotion put μαιμάσσει, a word whose meaning I do not know to this day. Aquila put ὀχλάζει, which itself also means "tumult."

Let this suffice about the word, over which I know there is great dispute among many. The voice of the prophet—and through the prophet, of God speaking—is introduced as grieving over the destruction of his people, his inner organs torn as a man's would be, just as the Savior grieved over the death of Lazarus and wept over Jerusalem, so as not to hide his grief in silence. Every blast of the trumpet and the roar of her battles disturbs his feelings, as evils are heaped upon evils and the whole land of the two tribes is laid waste. "When I did not expect it," he says, "my tents, once [?]

and my curtains were plundered by the raging Babylonian, and what were once my dwellings have passed into the hands of the enemy as spoil." God says this same thing when he sees the turmoil of sedition and discord in the Church, the partridge calling out in its conventicles, and the rest of God turned into wars. Hence there follows:
"How long shall I see people fleeing, and hear the sound of the trumpet?" Either people fleeing the king of Babylon, or people fleeing me and withdrawing from my service.

"For my people are foolish; they have not known me. They are senseless and witless children; they are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good." This is the cause of the destruction, the devastation, the flight and the trumpet: the people have become foolish, not by nature but by the bent of their will. And their very foolishness is proved by this, that they did not know God; instead of wise children they have become foolish and witless children.

For what greater foolishness can there be than that, while the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's crib, Israel should not know its Lord, and should despise him when he was present—him whom it had always longed to see? As for what follows—"They are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good"—here wisdom is to be taken as malice, in the sense in which "the children of this age are wiser than the children of light," and the steward of iniquity is said to have acted wisely in certain things, and the serpent in paradise is said to have been more prudent than all the beasts.

True wisdom, then, is the wisdom joined to the fear of God; otherwise, where there are plots and evasion, it should be called not wisdom but cunning and craftiness. Where we have said, "For my people are foolish; they have not known me," the Septuagint translated, "For the princes of my people have not known me," so that the fault lies more with the teachers than with the people who lacked the knowledge of God.

I looked at the earth, and behold, it was empty and nothing; and at the heavens, and there was no light in them. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were moving, and all the hills were thrown into confusion. I looked, and there was no human being, and the birds of the sky had gone away. I looked, and behold, Carmel was a desert, and all its cities were destroyed before the face of the Lord and before the face of the wrath of his fury. The prophet sees in the Spirit what is to come, so that the people, hearing it, may be terrified, and, having done penance, may in no way suffer what they dread.

The earth is empty because its inhabitants have been wiped out; the heavens have no light because the people, in the greatness of their terror, cannot see. The mountains and hills themselves have no safe hiding places, and by hyperbole they are said to move and be thrown into confusion. He looked and gazed around this way and that, and not even a bird could be found; for even the mute elements feel the wrath of God, and creatures without reason are filled with dread.

That this is true the whole world now shows: when a multitude of people has been slaughtered, even the birds that usually follow human habitation have gone away and perished. Carmel itself, too, which overlooks the Great Sea, planted with olives and thick with orchards and vineyards, will come to such desolation that it will have the waste of a wilderness; and all its cities will also become deserted.

And the cause of all these evils is that the wrath of the Lord has been roused by the vice of a sinning people. Whatever we have said about Jerusalem and Judea according to the historical sense, let us apply to the church of God when she has offended God and been laid waste either by vices or by persecution, so that where once there was a chorus of virtues and joy, there a multitude of sins and sorrows now dwells.

For thus says the Lord: The whole land will be a desert, but yet I will not make a full end. The earth will mourn, and the heavens above will grieve, because I have spoken; I have purposed, and I have not repented, nor have I turned back from it. With God's mercy mingled with his wrath, the whole land is made desert, but there is no full end, so that there may be some who understand his clemency.

The sky above, too, will look sorrowful, and the earth itself will mourn, because the Lord's sentence has been carried through to the end and he has not repented of what he purposed and spoke. God is said to repent, however, when a sentence he has pronounced is withdrawn and his raging wrath does not go through to the end. He threatened through Jonah, and a multitude of tears and groans overcame the impending sword.

At the sound of the horseman and of the one who shoots arrows — or, who bends the bow — the whole city — or, region — has fled; they have gone into the heights and climbed up the rocks — and what follows, "and they went into the thickets" or "caves," was added by the Seventy — all the cities have been abandoned, and no one lives in them.

The divine word here describes the army of the raging Babylonian: in terror of it the whole people abandoned the city and climbed every high place, and yet could not escape the wrath of the Lord. But whatever, as we said above, is understood in the historical sense against Jerusalem, apply to the church when she has offended God and been handed over to her adversaries, either in a time of persecution or certainly through vices and sins.

But you, laid waste, what will you do? For "laid waste" — which in Hebrew is "sadud," and which Aquila alone translated this way — the others rendered "wretched" and "pitiable": wretched by her own fault, since she offended a merciful God. Then follows:

Though you clothe yourself in scarlet and adorn yourself with a golden necklace and paint your eyes with kohl, in vain will you make yourself beautiful: your lovers have despised you; they will seek your life. He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman: "Once you have offended God and, as it were, left your husband, your Creator, it is in vain that you go looking for ornaments; the demons, your lovers, have despised you, and they will seek not the filth of debauchery but the destruction of your soul."

This same thing is to be understood spiritually against those who have lost their marital affection and the chastity of the true faith. "If," he says, "you clothe yourself in scarlet — take up faith in the blood of Christ — if you adorn yourself with a golden necklace — practice meditation on spiritual sense and understanding — and paint your eyes with kohl — have zeal for the mysteries and for knowing the secrets of God — in vain will you make yourself beautiful. For you had prepared these things for your lovers too, and therefore the narrow bed cannot hold both, nor does God accept the ornaments with which you previously pleased your lovers."

For I have heard a voice as of a woman in labor, anguish — or, groans — as of one bearing her first child; the voice of the daughter of Zion fainting away and spreading out her hands: Woe is me, for my soul has failed because of the slain! In the likeness of a woman in childbirth, that is, one giving birth to her first offspring, he describes the city of Jerusalem wailing and crying out.

For just as a woman giving birth, who has not yet experienced the pains of labor, faints away — she suffers anguish, can scarcely breathe, and with hands flung out collapses — so too the daughter of Zion, when she sees her children slain, bursts out into these words and says: Woe is me, for my soul has failed because of the slain! Two images have been brought together in one passage, that of a woman bearing children and that of a woman mourning them, so that whatever a woman suffers in childbirth or in the deaths of her children, Jerusalem suffers in her peoples.

Go around the streets of Jerusalem, and look and consider, and search in her squares, whether you can find a man who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to her. And even if they say, "As the Lord lives," they will swear this falsely. Great is his love of justice: not, as in Abraham's question and God's answer, will God deliver the city for the sake of ten just men; rather, if he finds just one in Jerusalem, now on the very point of perishing, who does justice and seeks faithfulness — or, as Symmachus translated, truth — God will still have mercy on Jerusalem.

And because it could happen that some might be found among the people who feigned the worship of God and swore by the Lord, he forestalls this, saying that God takes no delight in empty words but in the truth of faith, and he says: "I do not love them because they swear by me, for they swear falsely, but those whose hearts and lips agree."

Lord, your eyes look upon faithfulness. You struck them, and they felt no pain; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction; they have made their faces harder than rock and refused to return. After the words of the Lord, in which he had given the command, "Go around the streets of Jerusalem," and so on, the prophet speaks to the Lord: Lord, your eyes look upon faithfulness — which in Hebrew is "emunah" — not upon the works of the Jews, in which they exulted according to the ceremonies of the law, but upon the faith of Christians, through which we have been saved by grace.

From this passage we learn that punishments are inflicted so that vices may be corrected. Thus he says: You struck them, and they felt no pain; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction. For Jerusalem is being corrected through every torment and scourge; and on top of all this they did not even feel shame for their vices, but, hardening the shamelessness of their brow like rock, they refused to turn to better things.

But I said: Perhaps these are the poor and foolish — or, they were not able — ignorant of the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. I will go, then, to the great men and speak to them, for they have known the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. By "poor" and "great men" here he does not mean poverty and wealth; rather, he contrasts the people with their leaders. The sense is: "Seeing the obstinacy of the unbelieving people, and that with hardened face they refused to accept correction, I reasoned this out with myself: perhaps the common crowd cannot know God's teaching and is therefore excusable, because through ignorance it is unable to know God's commandments.

I will go, then, to the priests and to those who are over the people, and speak to them; for they have known the will of the Lord and know the judgment of their God." He says this in the language of one in doubt, as in that saying of the Gospel: "I will send my son; perhaps they will respect him" — so that by the uncertainty of the statement and the suspense of the words the free will of man may be shown.

And behold, these all the more have together broken the yoke and burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest has struck them, a wolf at evening has laid them waste, a leopard keeps watch over their cities; everyone who goes out of them will be captured, because their transgressions are multiplied, their turnings away have grown strong. "Those I took for teachers have been found to be worse than their disciples, and the greater the authority of the rich, the greater the insolence of their sins."

For they broke the yoke of the law, as the apostle says: "Now then, why do you put God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are." And they burst the bonds of God's precepts — not those of the Pharisees, of which it is said in the second Psalm: "Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us."

Since, then, they have done these things, a lion from the forest has struck them — that is, the kingdom of Babylon; a wolf at evening has laid them waste — signifying the Medes and Persians, in whose place in Daniel's vision a "bear" is set, in whose mouth were three rows; a leopard keeps watch over their cities — prefiguring the onslaught of Alexander and his swift sweep from the west all the way to India. He calls him a leopard because of his variegation, since he fought against the Medes and Persians with a great many nations subject to him. "And the beast," it says, "had four heads, and dominion was given to it."

And since he is not prophesying about the distant future, but weaving a history of what is past or of what is about to come at any moment, he therefore says nothing of the Roman Empire, of which perhaps it is said: everyone who goes out of them will be captured. And he gives the reasons why they suffered these things: because their transgressions were multiplied and they persisted in their transgressions. Hence it is said: and their turnings away have grown strong.

What we set down at the beginning — that the Hebrew word "shaqad" means "watching" — is shown in the present passage; for where we have said "a leopard keeping watch," in the Hebrew it is written "namer shoqed." According to the tropological sense: those who are thought great in the church, because they break the yoke and burst the bonds, are therefore handed over to shameful passions, so that they do what is unfitting.

On what grounds can I be merciful to you? Your children have forsaken me and swear by those who are not gods. I fed them to the full, and they committed adultery and reveled in the house of the harlot. They have become to me like horses in love with mares, like stallions; each one neighed after his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; and on such a nation shall my soul not take vengeance? A catalogue of Jerusalem's sins, while God says he does not know on what ground he could have mercy on her.

"Your children," he says, "have forsaken me — not mine, but yours — because they swear by those who are not gods. I fed them to the full, and they committed adultery." Let those hear this who, having received riches from the Lord, brood over them and serve luxury. They have become like horses in love with mares. For "stallions" the Hebrew has "moshekhim," which all with one voice have translated ἕλκοντες, that is, "drawing," to show the size of their genitals, as in that passage of Ezekiel: "their flesh is like the flesh of asses."

This is what is written elsewhere: "They have been compared to senseless beasts and have become like them." At the same time he shows so great a madness of lust that he calls it not a desire for pleasure but χρεμετισμός, that is, "neighing," keeping the metaphor of horses raging with lust. "Since you have done these things," he says, "do you not deserve a fitting visitation?" And note that here "visitation" is used for penalty and punishment, as in what is written: "I will visit their iniquities with the rod."

And on such a nation shall my soul not take vengeance? Once she has been bound by sins, she is no longer called the people of God, but a nation, from which the soul of God has departed, as it is written: "Your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates." What in the Old Testament is said with reference to feeling is written in the New with reference to truth, as the Savior says: "I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again."

Go up onto her walls — or, ramparts — and tear them down, but do not make a full end! Take away her branches — or, supports — for they are not the Lord's! For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord.

He commands the nations of which he had spoken above — "a lion from the forest has struck them, a wolf has laid them waste, and a leopard in their cities" — to go up onto the walls or ramparts of Jerusalem and tear her down, but not to make a full end, so that a remnant may be saved and there may be someone to proclaim the glory of God among the nations; and he mingles clemency with severity.

And in adding, Take away her branches — or, supports — he orders the removal of every help that she lost by her own vice, because the house of Israel and the house of Judah have transgressed against God, meaning the ten tribes and the two. Let the church hear this: the walls and ramparts of those who have no hope in the Lord and transgress against him are quickly torn down; yet a full end is not made, because of the clemency of the judge, not because of the merits of the offenders.

They have denied the Lord and said: It is not he — or, these things are not so — and no evil will come upon us; we shall not see sword or famine. The prophets have become wind, and there is no answer — or, word — in them. These things, therefore, will happen to them.

Because they have denied the Lord — or, lied to the Lord — and said: "It is not he by whose judgment all things come about; rather, all these things have happened by chance, and what the voices of the prophets threaten us with will not happen; we shall not see the sword or endure the famine of a siege; whatever the prophets have said, they have said to the wind, and it has all passed away without effect, and they have had no answer, that is, no oracle, or, the word of God was not in them" — therefore they will suffer what the following passage describes. Let the careless church that rejects the providence of God hear this: it will suffer both sword and famine unless it believes that what is foretold will come.

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it will devour them. "You have said: 'The prophets have become wind, and what they threaten will not come.' Therefore, O prophet, I put my words in your mouth, to have the power of fire and to turn this people into wood, so that the unbelieving may be burned up by your word and prophecy." So God is called a consuming fire, that he may consume in us whatever hay, wood or stubble we have built upon the foundation of Christ.

Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, says the Lord, a mighty nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, nor will you understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open grave; they are all mighty men. It will eat up your harvest and your bread; it will devour your sons and your daughters; it will eat up your flocks and your herds; it will eat up your vine and your fig tree; and it will shatter with the sword your fortified cities in which you trust. Yet even in those days, he says, I will not make a full end of you.

"Not long from now, and not as you falsely believe that the prophets speak to you to the wind, but even now I will bring upon you the nation of the Babylonians, which will come from afar, a mighty nation" — for which the Hebrew has "ethan" — "an ancient nation" — over which the giant Nimrod once ruled — "whose language you will not know, or" — as it is written in the Hebrew — "nor will you understand what it says; for it is some consolation in misfortune to have enemies whom you can entreat and who understand your prayers."

What follows, Its quiver is like an open grave, which is not found in the Septuagint edition, signifies the Babylonian weaponry. Nor is there any doubt that the kingdom of the Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians is highly skilled in archery. At the same time he describes the devastation of the land of Judea, the slaughter of many, the driving off of livestock, the overthrow of cities and walls, since everything is taken by the enemy's sword; and yet amid such great evils he does not destroy them to the point of annihilation, but saves a remnant — either of those who were led into Babylon and of those who were left to cultivate the fields of the land of Judea, or of those who, after the heat of persecution, kept faith with the Lord either by flight or by confession.

And if you say, "Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us?" you shall say to them: "As you have forsaken me and served a foreign god — or, foreign gods — in your own land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours." It is great folly not to know why they have suffered when they have sinned so greatly, and to those in doubt the answer is brief: just as you served a foreign god — that is, Baal — or the foreign gods of all the nations in the land of Judea, so you shall serve foreign gods in a land not yours, no doubt among the Babylonians and Chaldeans.

"For if a foreign religion delights you, why need you take up an error from far away? Go and live with such people." [?] This may also be understood of the heretics, of whom it is written: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us" — namely, that the Lord casts out of the church the heretics who for a long time, under his name, have worshiped the idols of their own lies, so that they may worship outside what they previously venerated within, and the chaff may be separated from the wheat.
BOOK TWO

Brother Eusebius, I am dictating this second book on Jeremiah with rapid speech, turning my ears away for a little while so as not to hear the judgment of blood and weep for the souls of the slain — those who, on the strength of a reputation for virtue, daily fall headlong into pride and think themselves like God, so that the equality which the impious heresy of the Arians denies to the Son they ascribe to all human beings, setting their mouth against heaven and leaving nothing more for the future blessedness of the saints.

I have answered their madness as best I could, and, if the Lord grants me life, I intend to answer more fully. Now I must take up the road I began and dictate these little commentaries, neither stretching the work to excessive length nor stripping away its sense by immoderate brevity: the former burdens the minds of readers, the latter cuts short the desire of the studious.

Proclaim this to the house of Jacob and make it heard in Judah, saying: Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart, who have eyes and do not see, and ears and do not hear! In many ways he draws sinners back to salvation; he calls the people foolish for having forsaken the author of wisdom, and he compares them to idols, of which it is written: "They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear. May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them."

He speaks specifically to Judah and to the house of Jacob — for Israel had long since been in exile among the Assyrians — and at the same time he gives us to understand that even without a commandment we ought to grasp by natural sense what is right.

Will you not fear me, then, says the Lord, and will you not grieve — or, tremble — before my face? I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting decree that it will not pass. Its waves will be stirred up and will not prevail — or, it will be troubled and will not prevail — and they will swell — or, roar — and they will not pass over it.

But this people has acquired an unbelieving and provoking heart; they have turned aside and gone away, and they did not say in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives us the early and the late rain in its season, who keeps for us the fullness of the yearly harvest! He recounts his benefits in order to convict the ungrateful.

"Will you not fear me," he says, "who have bestowed so much on you? I do not ask for the love of the perfect, but for the fear of beginners — I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, who by my command have reined in with shores so mighty an element and the immense masses of the deep, as it is written: 'He set a decree, and it will not pass away.' Things that have no sense of hearing hear me and perceive me; and the people that was once mine, made foolish by its own vice, not only despises but even provokes its gentle God.

They have turned aside," he says, "from me and turned their backs on me, and gone away at a rapid pace; nor did a silent conscience draw them back, so that they would say in their hearts: Let us fear him who gives us the early and the late rain!" Through all these things he showed his good gifts: "the fullness of the yearly harvest" — for which the first edition of Aquila and Symmachus translated "weeks"; for in the Hebrew it is written "sabaoth," which, because of the ambiguity of the word, means both "weeks" and "fullness."

Our iniquities have turned these things aside, and our sins have kept good from us. So if at any time the sea overflows its bounds and the rain is withheld, it is by no means that the hand of the Lord has been shortened so that he does not do these things; rather, our sins have turned them aside as they were coming to us, so that they might go on to others who have not sinned.

"And they have kept back," he says, "the good that was already coming to us," in accordance with what is written in the literal sense: "I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it." But we can also take the early and the late rain as the law and the gospel, and as the various callings from the first hour to the eleventh, in which one reward of eternal life is promised to the laborers in the vineyard.

For wicked men have been found among my people, lying in wait like fowlers, setting snares and traps to catch men! Like a trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. Why the early and the late rain turned away from them and no good things came: the causes are set out — because wicked men were found among his people.

He did not say "unjust" and "sinners," as the new heresy would have it, but "wicked." Wickedness openly denies God; injustice and sin, if one confesses the error, easily bend God to mercy. As for what we have rendered "lying in wait like fowlers," it is not found in the Septuagint; Aquila and Symmachus translated the word "iasir" as "like a fowler's net." The meaning is that even the one among them who seems good and upright lays snares like a fowler, while they hunt one another to death and fill their own houses with the losses and costs of others. So that saying of the philosophers is fulfilled: every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.

And would that these things were done only by those who are plainly outside, whom the Lord judges, and were not carried out in our own little gatherings, which are possessed by greed, the root of all evils, so that we look not at the faces of those who come to us but at their hands!

Therefore they have become great and rich. They have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed over my words most wickedly. They did not judge the cause; the cause — or: the judgment — of the orphan they did not set right, and the right of the poor — or: the judgment — they did not judge. Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; or shall my soul not take vengeance on a nation such as this?

If I wished to note one by one the things omitted in the Septuagint edition, it would take a long time. "Those who lay snares," he says, "and rejoice at the stripping of others have therefore become great and rich." Because they did these things, they grew fat and sleek, as it is written: The beloved grew fat and sleek, and kicked. And they passed over my words. For, conscious of their wealth, they said what we find in the Gospel: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; take your rest, eat, drink, be merry!

They passed over my words to their own harm, and, despising all men, they did not set God's judgment before their eyes. They despised the orphan and the poor. Here the Septuagint said "widows," which is not in the Hebrew; for "hebionim" properly means "poor," not "widows." As for what follows — Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; or shall my soul not take vengeance on a nation such as this? — it has already been discussed above.

Astonishing and marvellous things have come to pass in the land: the prophets prophesied a lie — or: unjust things — and the priests clapped their hands, and my people loved such things! What then will you do at the end — or: after these things? Earlier he had said: I will go to the great men and speak to them; perhaps they have known the way of the Lord. And behold, these men above all had together broken the yoke and burst the bonds. Now he describes who the great men are: namely, the prophets and the priests, of whom the former foretell what is to come, the latter decide from the law what is to be done.

"And behold," he says, "while they prophesied a lie, the priests clapped their hands." And to show that the people, who are led astray by such men, are not without fault either, it is written: and my people loved such things. Once they were mine; but after they loved such things, they ceased to be mine. What then will they do when the last time of judgment comes, or the hard necessity of captivity? Hence the astonishing and marvellous things: that neither among the leaders nor among the people was anyone found who thought rightly.

Be strong, sons of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem, and in Tekoa sound the trumpet, and over Beth-haccherem raise a signal — or: a standard — for evil has been seen — or: has appeared — from the north, and great destruction! No one is unaware that Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin. Tekoa, too, a small village set on a hill twelve miles from Jerusalem, we see with our own eyes every day. Between these lies another village, which in the Syriac and Hebrew language is called Bethacharma, and it too is set on a hill. What he says, then, is this:

"Since Nebuchadnezzar is about to come from the north at any moment and captivity is close at hand, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, take up arms, sound the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise the standard in Beth-haccherem," he says, "so that you may be able to resist the enemy!" Benjamin means "son of the right hand," Tekoa "trumpet," Beth-haccherem "vineyard estate." Let us apply all this to the church, so that if she has sinned and an onslaught of persecution comes, she may prepare herself to resist.

I have likened the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman. Shepherds will come to her with their flocks; they have pitched — or: will pitch — their tents around her; each will feed those who are under his hand. Sanctify — or: prepare — war against her; rise up and let us go up at noon!

The beauty of Jerusalem, which is the same as Zion, is described here, though the one name denotes the whole city and the other the city's citadel. For Zion means "citadel," that is, watchtower, and it is compared to a beautiful woman; and as lovers gather to such a woman, so shepherds are said to gather to this city. And quite elegantly, in Hebrew the word written with the four letters resh, ayin, yod, mem means "lovers" if it is read "reim," and "shepherds" if it is read "roim." So we may understand either lovers, following the metaphor of the beautiful woman, or shepherds, following the overthrow of the city: some of them hasten to defile the harlot,

others to besiege and overthrow the city. In the shepherds and their flocks let us understand the princes and the army of the Chaldeans. They will pitch their tents all around during the siege of the city, and each will feed those who are under his hand, namely his own squadrons and companies. These princes, or shepherds, will say to their flocks: "Sanctify war against Jerusalem, for it is the Lord's command. Rise up and let us go up at noon — not by night and by ambush, but let us fight in full daylight; for no one can resist us."

Woe to us, for the day has declined, for the evening shadows have grown longer — or: have faded! Rise up and let us go up by night and destroy her houses — or: foundations! The one side says: "Rise up and let us go up at noon and fight in broad daylight"; the other answers: "Woe to us, for the evening shadows have grown longer," as in that line of Virgil: "And now far off the rooftops of the farmhouses smoke, and longer shadows fall from the high mountains." And the sense is:

"If we suffer these things by day, what shall we suffer by night?" And again, those who had said above, "Sanctify war against her and rise up," now urge themselves on to fight, saying: "Rise up and let us go up by night, so that our adversaries may know that victory depends not on the time of day but on strength; and let us destroy the houses that are fortified in vain by the strength of their walls."

For thus says the Lord of hosts: Cut down her tree — or: her trees — pour out — or: heap up — a siege mound around Jerusalem! "For this reason," they say, "we are sure of victory: because it is the command of the Lord, who orders the Chaldeans: Cut down the trees and heap up a mound for the siege works to come!" This shows that, before [?] it came to pass, the city was not to be taken at once by an encircling assault, but by a long siege, as we read later.

This is the city of visitation — or: lying city — all slander — or: oppression — is in her midst. As a cistern — or: pit — keeps its water cold, so she has kept her wickedness cold. The Lord commands that trees be cut down and mounds be heaped up all around, because the time of her visitation has come, so that she may receive the due of her sins. The greatest of these is sycophancy (συκοφαντία): oppressing the innocent by false accusation.

So, just as a cistern or pit keeps its water cold, so in the midst of Jerusalem the wickedness within her has lost all the warmth of life. And it should be noted that the saints are called fervent in spirit, while evil things are cold. Hence it is also written that in the last days, when iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. I think this is also what is meant by: I am counted among those who go down into the pit.

Let the Latin reader understand this — and let it suffice to have said it once — that among the Greeks "lacus" means not "pond" but "cistern," which in Syriac and Hebrew is called "gubba." In the present passage, however, where all the translators alike have "lacus," the Hebrew has "bor."

Iniquity and devastation will be heard in her; sickness and wounds are always before me. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you, lest I make you a desolate, uninhabitable land! The Septuagint has: Impiety and misery will be heard in her, before her face. Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you, lest I make you a trackless land that is not inhabited. From this we learn that the Lord scourges every son whom he receives. And so Jerusalem is instructed by blows and torments, so that she may be corrected, and God's soul may not depart from her, and she may not be reduced to a wilderness. If ever, then, we are subjected to frequent distresses, let us remember this little verse for our consolation: Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem.

Thus says the Lord of hosts: They will glean the remnant of Israel down to the last cluster, as in a vineyard; turn back your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket! The Septuagint has: For thus says the Lord of powers: Glean, glean the remnant of Israel as in a vineyard; return like a grape-gatherer to his basket!

Some take these words in a good sense, others in a bad one. In the good sense: "When Jerusalem has been laid waste, let a remnant be saved." In the bad sense, thus: "Let not even one cluster or small bunch remain in the vineyard; let everything be gathered; and whatever you find, throw it into the basket like a grape-gatherer, so that, as he hauls the clusters to the winepress, so you may haul the captives to Babylon."

To whom shall I speak, and whom shall I warn, that he may hear? Behold, their — or: your — ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear! Behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach to them, and they will not receive it! They cannot hear because they refused to circumcise their ears; yet an inability that springs from contempt and unbelief is not exempt from punishment.

If anyone, then, does not receive God's words and has no understanding of his commandments, he has uncircumcised ears. At the same time it should be noted that Scripture speaks of three kinds of circumcision: of the foreskin, of the heart, and of the ears. Hence the Lord too says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. It is by our own will, then, that we do not receive the word of God; and so it becomes a reproach to us, so that what was given for salvation is turned by our own fault into punishment.

Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I have toiled to hold it in. The Septuagint has: And I have filled up my fury, and I held it in, and I did not use it all up. According to the Hebrew this is spoken in the person of the prophet: he foresees the coming wrath of God and is full of the Lord's fury and anger; he can hold it in no longer, nor does he dare to entreat the Lord for sinners.

According to the Septuagint, however, a different sense is given: that the Lord himself speaks and says, "I have fulfilled my fury by striking the sinful people," and yet held it back and did not pour it all out, so that a remnant might be saved. This seems to me self-contradictory; for if he fulfilled his fury, how did he hold it back so as not to fulfil it?

Pour it out — or: he poured it out — on the little child outside and on the gathering of young men alike; for husband with wife will be taken, the old man with him who is full of days, and their houses will pass to others, their fields and wives together. Either the prophet, in the spirit, commands the Chaldean who is coming to pour out the Lord's fury on the little ones and to spare not even that innocent age; or else he relates what was done to the gathering of young men alike, who had taken up arms to resist.

For husband with wife will be taken: those who bear the names dearest to each other will experience captivity together. The old man with him who is full of days: so old age is not the last stage of life; the last stage belongs to those who are "full of days," whom in our language we call "at death's door" or "decrepit." There follows: and their houses will pass to others through the evil of captivity, their fields and wives together, so that both wife and property pass to the enemy. Whatever we understand literally of Jerusalem, let us apply according to the spiritual sense to the church, should she offend God.

For I will stretch out my hand over the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. For from the least to the greatest, all are given over to greed, and from prophet to priest, all practise deceit. And they treated the wound of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: Peace, peace! And there was no peace.

Where the Hebrew says, I will stretch out my hand over the sinners — or: the inhabitants — of the land, the Septuagint always writes "I will lift up"; both are the posture of one about to strike, as it is written: And still the hand of the Lord is stretched out — or: lifted high. Now the inhabitants of the earth are always at fault; hence in the Apocalypse too it is often said: Woe to the inhabitants of the earth! From the least to the greatest, all are given over to greed, according to the apostle's saying:

The root of all evils is greed. And from prophet to priest, all practise deceit: the prophets by prophesying a lie, the priests by perversely interpreting the law of God; for in another place the prophet says: Seek the law from the priests. "And although they did such things," he says, "they announced every kind of prosperity

to my people and, as it were, sought to heal the wound and the disgrace of my daughter, saying: Peace, peace, when there was no peace at all." This is properly to be understood of priests and teachers who promise prosperity to the rich and to those they see set in the highest honour, and preach a merciful God, when in fact they are preparing them for punishment and wrath.

Were they ashamed because they had committed abomination? No; rather they were not confounded with confusion, and they did not know how to blush. This should be read more precisely according to the Hebrew: "And when they had done such things," he says, "were they ashamed? Did they blush at their crimes? No; rather they grew in contempt and did not know how to blush" — here he put "did not know" for "would not" — "or else, through excessive contempt and the vice of ingrained evil, they could not even understand."

Therefore they will fall among those who fall; in the time of their visitation they will collapse, says the Lord. "Since," he says, "they did not know how to blush, and had not only no deed of repentance but not even the knowledge and sense of it, therefore those who once stood will fall among those who will collapse through their own vices; and when the time of their visitation and punishment comes, they will join all who are falling." It is great impiety not only not to guard against sins but not even to want to understand them, and to see no difference between good and evil works.

Thus says the Lord: Stand by the roads and look, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it! And you will find refreshment — or: purification — for your souls. And they said: We will not walk in it — or: we will not go. And I set watchmen over you: Hear the sound of the trumpet! And they said: We will not hear.

Therefore hear — or: they heard — O nations, and know, O assembly — or: you who pasture flocks, or, according to Symmachus: and know the testimony that is in them — what great things I will do to them! Hear, O earth! The Gospel parable, if it is understood, will give the understanding of this passage. In it the good merchant is said to sell all his pearls in order to buy with their price one most precious pearl: that is, through the patriarchs and prophets we come to him who says, I am the way.

We must therefore stand in the prophets, and most diligently consider and ask about the ancient — or: everlasting — paths, worn by the footsteps of many saints, which are more expressively called in Greek τρίβοι, which is the good way in the Gospel; and we must walk in it. When this way has been found, it gives refreshment, or purification, to the souls of believers. But they, on the contrary, answered: We will not walk in the way of the Gospel. Here the prophet is speaking specifically of the faithlessness of the Jews.

And at once he adds: "And I set watchmen over you" — without doubt the band of the apostles is meant, as in Ezekiel: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel — "and I commanded you to hear the sound of the trumpet," that is, either the commands of the Gospel or the teaching of the apostles, according to that saying of Isaiah: Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who bring tidings to Jerusalem.

They said, We will not hear, and when invited to the supper they refused to come; therefore it is said: Hear, O nations! The apostles also followed this when they speak in Lycaonia: It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.

And know, O assembly — by no means the Jewish assembly, but that of all nations. Or: you who pasture flocks — bishops and presbyters and the whole order of the church. Or: know the testimony that is in them; for the testimony of God is sure, giving wisdom to little ones. To them the Lord also says: Do not be afraid, little flock; and: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me. "Know, then, what great things I will do to the people that does not believe." And what is added:
Hear, O earth — the whole world is called to hear, as we also read at the beginning of Isaiah: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth — namely, what the Lord is going to do to the people of the Jews.

Behold, I will bring evils upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts — or: of their turning away — because they did not hear my words and they cast away my law. By "evils" he means the punishments and penalties of those who suffer them: not upon the nations, who are called to the truth of the Gospel, but upon the people who answered, We will not hear. And it will receive the fruit of its thoughts, or of its turning away, as David says: You shall eat the labours of your hands. And the reason is plain: because they did not hear the words of the Lord and cast away his law.

Why do you bring me incense from Sheba and sweet-smelling cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me. That incense comes from Sheba no one doubts; hence that line of Virgil: "and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense." As for the "cane," which in Hebrew is called "qaneh,"

and which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as "cinnamon," the prophetic word shows that it comes from a distant land, so that we are to understand India, from which many spices come by way of the Red Sea. Physicians call this kind of spice "pipe cassia" (κασσία σύριγγος). And the sense is: "In vain do you bring me spices of the sweetest scent for making the ointments prescribed in the law, and kindle burnt offerings, you who do not do my will in the law" — as was said above: they did not hear my words and they cast away my law.

This properly applies to those who offer sacrifices from what they have plundered and stripped from the wretched, and who think they can redeem their sins with alms gained by iniquity. For Scripture says: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches — riches gathered not by iniquity but by labour and justice.

Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will set ruin before this people, and they will fall in it — or: weakness, and they will be weakened by it — fathers and sons together, neighbour and friend, and they will perish. We see fulfilled everything that the Lord threatened against that people: for every day they fall in their blasphemies, and there is nothing strong in them, but all among them is weakness.

The sons follow the blasphemies of the fathers and every day take upon themselves that imprecation: His blood be on us and on our children. And not only they themselves but also their neighbours and friends — all who follow the Law and the Prophets according to the letter that kills and not according to the spirit that gives life — will all perish alike, because they sinned alike.

Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people comes from the land of the north, and a great nation will rise from the ends of the earth. It will seize arrow and shield — or: hunting spear —; it is cruel — or: shameless — and will show no mercy; its voice will roar like the sea, and they will mount horses, arrayed like a man for battle against you, O daughter of Zion. This is properly a prophecy about the Babylonians, who were to come against the people of Jerusalem. The whole array of their armour and the onslaught of the fighters is described so that, shaken by the terror of these words, the people might repent and appease the most merciful God.

In the end he gives them occasion to entreat him when he says: against you, O daughter of Zion. We may also apply this testimony to a time of persecution, when the whole fury of the devil is roused against us, and there is no mercy, and it overwhelms those who resist like the waves of a most violent sea.

We have heard the report of it; our hands have grown weak; anguish has seized us, pains like a woman in labour. The people answers — the people whom the prophet, or rather the Lord through the prophet, had threatened with the Babylonians: that even before the enemy comes they are overcome by fear and cannot lift their hands, and anguish has seized them like the pain of a woman in labour. Women who have felt that pain affirm that nothing is more grievous.

“Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror on every side!” The Gospel teaches that we must not go out into the field, nor come down from the housetop, but must listen to the words, “Save yourself on the mountain,” the mountain to which Isaiah and Micah command us to run and climb. According to the letter, however, they are ordered not to go outside and not to abandon the walls, but to protect themselves behind strong fortifications.

“Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes; make mourning for yourself as for an only son — or a beloved one —, a bitter lament — or a pitiful one —, for suddenly the destroyer — or misery — will come upon us — or upon you —!” He had said above, “Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror on every side,” and so had forbidden flight as well. Now he teaches what they ought to do: that they should turn to repentance and hold it as their strongest and safest armour.

Where we have translated “make mourning for yourself as for an only son,” the Hebrew for “only son” is “iaid,” which means “solitary” rather than “only-begotten.” For if it meant “beloved” or “lovable,” as the Septuagint translated, the word would be “ididia,” the name God gave to Solomon. Nothing is more grievous than to lose one son, an only son.

And where we have translated “for suddenly the destroyer, or misery, will come upon us,” the Septuagint put “upon you,” although God spoke far more mercifully, testifying that whatever was to come upon his people would come upon himself as well. “The destroyer” properly signifies either Nebuchadnezzar or the devil.

“I have made you a strong tester among my people, and you will know and test their way. All these princes are turning aside — or disobedient —, walking deceitfully — or perversely —; they are bronze and iron; all of them are corrupt. The bellows have failed in the fire — the Greeks call it more expressively a physētēr —, the lead is consumed, in vain has the smelter smelted — or the silversmith —, for their wickedness has not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, for the Lord has cast them away!”

The prophet is given to an unbelieving people as a “strong tester,” which in Hebrew is “mabsar.” According to Aquila this means “fortified,” and according to Symmachus and the Septuagint “shut in” and “surrounded,” like a very strong city, so that he need fear no plots from the people. “So that when you have tested,” he says, “and known the way of the sinning people, you may then understand that silver mixed with bronze can by no means be purified.” For lead is mixed with metals that are adulterated and debased in order to separate the foreign matter; and if they are not purified, all the lead is consumed and reduced to nothing. In the same way all the eloquence of teaching and all prophetic speech is wasted on those who refuse to listen.

We may say this also of those who, like deaf adders, stop their ears so as not to hear the voices of the charmers. For in vain has the silversmith, or smelter, smelted; their wickedness has not been consumed. That is why they are not called “silver” at all, but “rejected silver,” because the Lord has cast them off. The princes are those who depart from the Lord, or are disobedient, and walk perversely and deceitfully.

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord, and proclaim — or read — this word there, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all you of Judah who enter through these gates to worship the Lord!” This is not found in the Septuagint edition, but was added from Theodotion on the basis of the Hebrew.

The prophet is commanded to stand in the gate of the Lord, through which the multitude of the people enters to pray to the Lord, so that on this occasion they may hear what the Lord commands. From this we understand the hardness of the Jewish people: they regarded the prophets as liars and madmen, since it was only the occasion and the crowds of the place that compelled them to hear the words of the Lord, and not the fact that these were the words of the Lord.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Make good — or direct — your ways and your pursuits — or your devices —, and I will dwell with you in this place — or I will make you dwell in this place.” The most merciful physician wishes to heal the wounded with every remedy. When he says, “Make good, or correct, your ways,” he shows that they are crooked and have nothing good in them.

And since it is natural for everyone to love the soil of his birth and to hold nothing sweeter than his homeland, he promises rewards to the obedient. “I will dwell with you,” he says, “so as to make you secure in your dwelling”; or, according to Symmachus, “I will establish you yourselves in a firm dwelling,” for Symmachus says, “and I will establish you in this place.”

“Do not trust in lying words, saying: This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord! For if you rightly direct — or direct — your ways and your pursuits, if you do justice between a man and his neighbour, if you do not wrong the stranger and the orphan and the widow — or do not oppress them —, nor shed innocent blood in this place, nor walk after foreign gods to your own harm, then I will dwell with you — or make you dwell — in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers from age to age.” What the Septuagint added at the beginning of this passage,

“in lying words, which will not profit you at all,” is not found in the Hebrew. He commands both the Jewish people of that time and us today, who appear to be established in the church, not to put our trust in the splendour of buildings, in gilded coffered ceilings and walls clad in marble veneer, and say, “This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.” For the temple of the Lord is that in which true faith dwells, holy conduct, and the whole choir of the virtues.

Then he adds: “If you make your ways straight, and your thoughts do not go off after error, and you follow justice and do no evil, and do not shed innocent blood by causing the simple to stumble, and do not walk after foreign gods by worshipping perverse doctrines that you have invented in your own hearts to your own harm, then I will dwell with you in this place, which you call the temple of God, and in the land that I gave to your fathers — that is, the apostles and apostolic men —, or at least I will make you dwell in a firm station from the beginning to the end.”

This can also apply to those virgins who boast of their purity and display their chastity with a shameless face, while their conscience holds something else. They do not know the apostle's definition of a virgin, that she should be holy in body and in spirit. For what use is purity of body when the mind has been defiled, if she lacks the other virtues that the prophetic word has described?

“Behold, you trust in lying words — or lies — which will not profit you: you steal, kill, commit adultery, swear falsely, pour libations to the Baals and go after foreign gods whom you do not know. And you have come and stood before me in this house, on which my name is called, and said: We are delivered — or we have ceased — because we have done all these abominations.”

The sins that follow show that they trust in the temple in vain. For what use is it to cross the threshold of God's house boldly and stand there with neck held high, while not only your heart but your hands are polluted with theft, murder, adultery, perjury, sacrilege and the worship of gods you do not know? No one doubts that these things happen in a spiritual sense in the church, when people look at their present prosperity, take no account of their sins, and suppose that God does not notice because punishment does not follow at once. Indeed, they break out into such madness that they think themselves delivered, because after their evil works they have even abandoned the worship of the Lord.

“Has this house — or my house —, on which my name is called, become a den of robbers in your eyes? I, I am; I have seen, says the Lord.” I think the Gospel took from this passage the words: “It is written: My Father's house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers,” or, as another Gospel has it, “a house of trade.” The church of God is turned into a den of robbers when thefts,

murders, adulteries, perjuries, sacrilege, the invention of heresy and every crime are practised in it; when its leaders burn with the torches of greed, and a cheap little cloak — or rather one not so cheap — possesses what was once the wealth of kings. Hence he adds: “I, I am,

I have seen, says the Lord; my eyes have beheld what you think is hidden. The darkness of your treasuries does not escape my knowledge.” He who was rich and became poor for our sake now blushes at our riches and says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation!”

“Go to my place in Shiloh, where my name dwelt at the beginning, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of my people Israel!” He teaches the present from the past. To those who say, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord,” and who delight in the splendour of a costly house, he recalls the history of Shiloh, where the tabernacle of God first stood, of which the psalm says, “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh.” Just as that place collapsed into ruins and ashes, so too the temple will fall, since it has become the dwelling of the same sins. As Shiloh is an example for the temple, then, so the temple is an example for us, when the time of that testimony comes: “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith on the earth?”

“And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord, and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, and you did not listen, and I called you and you did not answer, I will do to this house, on which my name is called and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you out from my sight, as I cast out all your brothers, the whole seed of Ephraim.”

The words we have set down, “rising early and speaking,” are not in the Septuagint. God rises early not because there is any time for him without daylight, but because after the night's rest, when the body's strength has been restored, the human soul is livelier and, not yet taken up with pleasures or the desire for food, is able to hear and do what is said.

So we also read in the psalm: “In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and will see”; and in Isaiah: “In the night — or at dawn — my spirit will rise to you, O God, for your precepts are a light upon the earth.” That is why the apostle Paul calls us children of light, not of night or darkness, and not sleepers, as the others sleep, who do not perceive the commandments of God. Since God, then, called them, rising in the night in order to set them free from darkness too, he threatens to do to the temple in Jerusalem what he did to Shiloh, where the tabernacle first stood, so that like sins may be struck with a like sentence.

And just as the Lord cast out the seed of Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes, which were called Israel and had their own rulers, on account of Jeroboam son of Nebat of the tribe of Ephraim, also called the tribe of Joseph, so too he declares that he will cast off Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah together with Benjamin. He cast off Shiloh, and he will cast off the temple too; he cast off the ten tribes, and he will cast off the two as well. Whatever is said to that people, let us understand it as said to us also, if we do the same things.

“As for you, do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer for them — or do not ask that they may obtain mercy —, and do not stand against me, for I will not hear you.” So that the prophet should not seem to ask and not obtain what he asks, God commands him not to intercede for a sinful people that does no penance. When he says, “and do not resist me,” he shows that the prayers of the saints can resist the wrath of God.

So too the Lord says to Moses: “Let me alone, that I may strike this people, and I will make you a great nation”; and in the Psalms it is written: “And Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Aaron also took up a censer and stood between the fire and the people who were about to burn, and the wrath of God ceased. And so that we should not think God cruel for not even allowing himself to be asked, he gives the reasons why he will not listen, saying:

“Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The sons gather wood and the fathers kindle the fire and the women knead fat to make cakes — or chavonas — for the queen — or the host — of heaven, and they pour libations to foreign gods to provoke me to anger. Is it I whom they provoke to anger? says the Lord. Is it not themselves, to the shame of their own faces?”

“Prophet,” he says, “do you wish to hear why I told you, Do not pray for this people? This is what they do: inside and outside, in the streets and at the gates of Jerusalem, the sons carry wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead fat with flour to make chavonim” — which we have translated as “cakes,” or “preparations” — so as to indicate every kind of sacrifice offered to the queen of heaven, whom we should take to be the moon, or else to the host of heaven, by which we should understand all the stars — “and after this they pour libations to foreign gods” — not that these gods exist, but under their names they burn incense to demons — “and they provoke me to anger by doing these things.

Nor do the wretches understand that this quarrel of theirs does not harm me, whom anger never changes, but themselves, to the shame of their faces and to everlasting disgrace.” So whatever we do, we do not harm God, who can never be harmed, but prepare destruction for ourselves, storing up wrath for the day of wrath. He set out the different tasks of sons, fathers, and mothers or wives, to show that there was no age that held back from impiety.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my fury and my indignation is kindled — or has dripped — upon this place, upon men and upon beasts and upon the trees of the field and upon the fruits of the ground, and it will burn and will not be quenched.” He had said above, “Is it I whom they provoke to anger?” How then does he now say, “Behold, my fury and my indignation has dripped upon this place”?

The sense is this: “I by nature do not grow angry, but they act in such a way as to provoke me to anger, so that I seem to change my nature. Let them feel, then, the anger that, as far as it lies in them, they are trying to produce.” And he finely does not say, “my fury has been poured out upon this place,” but “has dripped,” to signify a moderate punishment. But if a single drop of his fury is so harsh, what will happen when the whole downpour is poured out?

“Kindling” can also be understood to mean that he is compelled by the multitude of sins to do what he long refused to do. And when God is angry, both men and what belongs to men will suffer a like destruction. “And it will burn,” he says — no doubt the fury of the Lord — “and will not be quenched, because the people do nothing by which it could be quenched.”

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the meat. For on the day I brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt I did not speak to them or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but this is the command I gave them: Hear my voice, and I will be your God and you will be my people; and walk in every way that I have commanded you, that it may be well with you.” Having rejected their temple, he goes on to reject their sacrifices too, and obliquely accuses them of offering victims not out of reverence for him but from a craving for feasts.

When he says, “I did not speak to your fathers or command them on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices,” it is clearly understood that he first gave the Ten Commandments, written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, and that only later, after the offence of idolatry and the calf's head, did he order sacrifices to be made to himself rather than to demons, taking from them the pure religion of God's commandments and conceding to them the blood of victims and their craving for meat.

“But they did not listen or incline their ear, but walked in their own wills — or desires — and in the perversity of their evil heart, and went backward and not forward, from the day their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day.”

“When I said, Hear my voice and I will be your God, and the rest, they did not listen or incline their ear, but did what their own hearts desired. Contrary to the teaching of the apostle, who forgot what lay behind and strained forward to what lay ahead, they did the opposite: they longed for the past and despised the future!” And when he says,

“from the day their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day,” he means that they spent the whole intervening time offending the Lord. That is why the grace of the gospel was necessary, which preserved them not by their own merit but by the mercy of the Lord.

“And I sent to you my servants the prophets, day after day, rising at dawn and sending them; and they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but hardened their neck and did worse than their fathers.” Just, then, is the wrath of the Lord, which was kindled and dripped upon a people that was contemptuous, stiff-necked and unwilling to hear the words of God. How God sends prophets in the night, or at dawn and by day, we explained above.

“And you will speak all these words to them, and they will not listen to you; and you will call them, and they will not answer you. And you will say to them: This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God, nor accept discipline; faith has perished and has been taken from their mouth.” “Do not doubt,” he says, “that they have hardened their neck and done worse than their fathers. See, I give room for repentance; I do not speak so that these things may happen, but I foretell them because they are going to happen.

At least now speak to them with my words; and yet they will not listen to you, and you will call them and they will not answer you. For they will be so proud that when you call them to listen, no one will deign to answer. And you will say to them: This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God, nor accept discipline.” He finely calls them, as I have already said, not his people but a nation.

Although this was partly fulfilled in the time of the prophets, and went before in shadow and image, it was more fully fulfilled in Christ, when they refused to accept discipline and scorned the voice of their Lord. Hence it is fittingly added: “faith has perished” — faith which properly belongs to Christians — “and has been taken from their mouth,” that is, every confession of the Son of God and of the faith.

“Cut off your hair and throw it away, and raise a lament on the heights — or upon your lips —, for the Lord has rejected and forsaken the generation of his fury.” We read that Job too cut off his hair when he heard of the death of his sons and daughters, and among the ancients it was the custom of all mourners to cut their hair; but now, on the contrary, letting the hair grow long is the sign of grief.

The whole lament and prophetic lamentation is taken up because the Lord has rejected and forsaken the generation of his fury; there is no doubt that he means the Jewish people. And this is properly to be referred to the times of Christ, when faith perished and was taken from the mouth of the people who blasphemed the Lord.

“For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, says the Lord; they have set up their stumbling blocks in the house on which my name is called, to defile it, and they have built the high places — or the altar — of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it enter my heart.”

That the sons of Judah set up a statue of Baal in the temple of God we learn at the beginning of Ezekiel. The “high places,” called “bamath” in Hebrew, or the “altar” of Topheth, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, refers to the place watered by the springs of Siloam, which is pleasant and wooded and even today provides the delights of gardens. This error of paganism took hold of every province, so that people sacrificed victims at the sources of springs and in the loveliest groves, and the rites of every depraved superstition were kept there.

“Topheth” in the Hebrew language means “breadth.” It is said to be mentioned in the book of Joshua son of Nun, in connection with this place, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom and in Hebrew is called “Gehennom”: “ge” means pharanx, that is, “valley,” and “hennom” is either a man's name or means “grace.” The Hebrews have a tradition that “Gehenna” is named after this place, because the whole Jewish people perished there by offending God; for in this place they consecrated their sons to idols in the fire, or offered them as burnt offerings, which God had not commanded them nor ordered by any ordinance of the law.

And if Jephthah offered his virgin daughter to God, it is not the sacrifice that pleases God but the intention of the one offering it. For if a dog or an ass or any unclean animal had been the first to meet the father as he returned from slaughtering the enemy, he ought not to have offered that to God.

Therefore behold, the days will come, says the Lord, when it will no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter; and they will bury in Topheth, because there will be no other room. And the corpses of this people will be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and there will be no one to drive them away. He means the time of the siege, which they endured from the ninth year of King Zedekiah to the eleventh. The valley itself will no longer be called "gehennom", that is, "the valley of Hinnom" or "of the sons of Hinnom", but, because of the slaughter of so many, "the valley of killing".

So great will the slaughter be that in the place once given to worship there will be countless tombs. Those whom they cannot bury will be torn by birds and devoured by beasts, and there will be no one to drive them away, since everyone fears the same fate and is overwhelmed by the task of burial. We pass quickly over what is plain, so that wherever there is room we may linger over what is obscure. The sheer size of the book can weary its readers; how much more if we discuss it at greater length!

And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride; for the land will become a desolation. When the place of idolatry has been turned into a burial ground, so that their unburied corpses lie in the very place where they had offended God, then all joy will be taken away from what was once the city of Jerusalem and from the other cities under its rule, and everything will be filled with grief, groaning and desolation.
