At that time, says the Lord, they will cast out of their tombs the bones of the king of Judah, the bones of his princes, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of those who lived in Jerusalem. And they will spread them out before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they loved and served, which they followed, sought and worshipped. They will not be gathered up or buried; they will be like dung on the face of the earth. And all who remain of this most wicked family will choose death rather than life, in all the places that are left, to which I have driven them, says the Lord of hosts.

Everything the prophetic word describes we have seen happen in our own time, not to Jerusalem alone, which suffered these things at the hands of the Chaldeans and the Romans, but to the whole world, so that tears have run dry and everything is filled with the bones of the dead. And because by ancient custom people used to place gold and various ornaments of women or men in tombs, greed broke these open too and dug them up, exposing them to the sky and the light.

And so, first of all, the bones of the kings of Judah and of its princes, of the priests and prophets too, and of the whole people who had been in Jerusalem, were brought out of their graves and left lying open to the sun and the moon and the full sight of the stars. Thus they lay exposed to the gaze of the very things they had served after forsaking God, and were consumed and dissolved into dung and ashes. And if anyone in the multitude managed to escape, wherever he came he preferred death to life and thought destruction the cure for his unhappy soul.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Shall one who falls not rise again? And shall one who has turned away not return (or: not turn away)? After such great evils he calls to repentance those who were able to survive; or else, before the things he has threatened come to pass, he urges them to conversion and gives them room for repentance.

As for the Hebrew reading, "and shall one who has turned away not turn away?", it means that one who has turned away from God, if he is willing to be converted to better things, can also turn God's fury in a better direction, withstand what is coming, and escape the blows by his prayers.

Why then has this people in Jerusalem turned away in contentious rebellion? They have laid hold of falsehood and refused to return. "The more I called them to repentance," he says, "the further they withdrew from me, not so much from eagerness to sin as from a wish to get the better of me. For they have laid firm hold of falsehood, whether idols or any perverse things contrary to truth and justice, and they refused to return" (he did not say "they could not"), "but pursued wickedness with all their zeal."

I paid attention and listened; no one speaks what is good. There is no one who repents of his sin, saying: What have I done? All have turned to their own course, like a horse charging headlong into battle. Called back to repentance, they scorn to listen. It is not enough for them to have offended against the Lord and spoken blasphemy; like horses rushing into battle at a furious gallop, none of them reflects on his sin or says: What have I done?

From this we understand that these things are said either of the whole human race, because it is prone to vice, or of the time of the Savior, when all turned aside and together became worthless; there was no one who did good, not even one. Hence he himself also cries out in a mystical sense: Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed! But if this is so, where are those who say that it lies within our own will to be wholly without sin? No one, he says, speaks what is good, since we shall have to give an account even for an idle word on the day of judgment.

The kite in the sky has known its season; the turtledove, the swallow and the stork have kept the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. For "kite", which is how Symmachus translated it, the Septuagint and Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, "asida", and Aquila "herodios" [heron]. Again, for "swallow" Symmachus rendered "cicada", which in Hebrew is called "sis". And for what we have rendered "stork", both Aquila and Symmachus put "agur", as it is written in the Hebrew, where the Septuagint translated "sparrows of the field".

The sense, however, is one and the same as at the beginning of Isaiah: The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood. Even little birds know their seasons: they know when to hasten to warm places and escape the harshness of winter, and when to come back to their usual haunts at the start of spring. Here we should take "sky" to mean the air above us.

How can you say: We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us? Truly the lying pen of the scribes has worked falsehood. He is speaking to the scribes and Pharisees, who boast of their knowledge of the law and, when they write, write iniquity. And as for what he says:

The wise have been put to shame, terrified and captured: it is not that those who do these things are wise, but he calls them wise so that they may be condemned by their own judgment, and so that, on the contrary, their wisdom may be convicted as foolishness, as Paul says: You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? And because they have cast away the word of the Lord, there is no wisdom in them. In vain, then, do they boast of knowing the law, who destroy its teaching by their works.

Therefore I will give their women (or: their wives) to strangers and their fields to heirs, because from the least to the greatest all are bent on greed; from prophet to priest, all practice falsehood (or: iniquity). And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people to her disgrace, saying: Peace, peace, when there was no peace.

They have received the reward of their deeds: those who cast away the word of the Lord have themselves been cast away by him. "Their wives," he says, "and their possessions I will hand over to their enemies. And so that my sentence may not be thought cruel, let the hearer learn the reasons. From the least to the greatest all are bent on greed (for greed is the root of all evils), from prophet to priest. Those who ought to restrain others from sinning are the first to fall into crime, and all of them either practice iniquity, plundering what belongs to others, or at any rate practice falsehood, so that there is no truth in their mouths." And after all this, like good physicians, they wanted to heal the wounds of others with words, though they themselves were pierced through with the wounds of every outrage.

We see this daily among our own people too, as the apostle says: You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? and the rest. When such men see sinners who are rich, they are eager to heal the brokenness of the daughter of God's people, that is, the church, to the disgrace either of those who are deceived or of those who deceive others, saying to people covered in every kind of crime: Peace, peace, when there is no peace and the war of their sins hangs over them.

They were put to shame because they committed abomination; nay rather, they were not put to shame by their shame, and they did not know how to blush. This should be read as a question, so that the sense is: "Did they blush at their crimes? Did they understand the abominations they had committed?" "Not at all; they broke out into such madness that neither did shame make them want to amend their vices, nor did the hope of pardon make them confess their crimes."

Therefore they will fall among those who fall; in the time of their visitation they will fall, says the Lord. This is the reward of those who did not know how to blush: those whose rank was higher than the people's are caught up in the people's ruin. For from the least to the greatest all are bent on greed, and from prophet to priest all practice falsehood. The time of visitation is the approaching captivity.

Gathering, I will gather them, says the Lord; there are no grapes on the vines and no figs on the fig tree; the leaf has fallen, and I have given them things that have passed away. He shows more clearly what the time of visitation is, in which the wrongdoers will fall, when he says, "Gathering, I will gather them" (no doubt into Jerusalem), so that they may be besieged by the Chaldeans for a long time and endure the evils of famine. "While the seasons pass," he says, "and autumn follows summer and the leaves fall from the trees in winter, you will see it all from far off and take no food from any of it. For there are no grapes on the vines for you,

since you do not gather the fruit of the vines." And there are no figs on the fig tree for a besieged people, who watch the fruit of their own trees being plundered by the enemy. "The leaves," he says, "will fall when summer and autumn are over. For I gave them things that they would see pass away, so that they would lose, with all the greater grief, an abundance of everything that they were not permitted to touch."

Why do we sit still? Gather together, and let us enter the fortified city (or: the fortified cities) and be silent there (or: be cast away there), for the Lord our God has cast us away (or: has silenced us) and given us water of gall to drink; for we have sinned against the Lord. We waited for peace, and no good came; for a time of healing, and behold, terror.

The people are brought in speaking, answering and confessing their vices and urging one another to enter the walled cities, or the one city of Jerusalem, for the rest had already been captured. "And let us be silent there," he says, "because our Lord has silenced us (for we have no confidence to plead with him); or, let us be cast away there, or thrown out like dung. He himself has made us drink waters of gall, because we turned the sweet God into bitterness.

And the reason we drank such waters is plain: we sinned against the Lord, and we waited for peace though we had done no good work, and we thought the time of healing had come for us, when everything was filled with fear and terror." Changes of speaker, especially in the prophets, make understanding difficult; but if they are assigned to their proper places, reasons and times, what seemed obscure will become plain.

From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard; at the sound of the neighing of his warriors (or: his cavalry) the whole land shook; and they came and devoured (or: and they will come and devour) the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it.

So the people did not say, as the Septuagint translated above, "let us enter the fortified cities", but "the fortified city", meaning Jerusalem. Accordingly he now adds: the city and those who dwell in it. Nebuchadnezzar is described as coming with his army from Dan by way of Phoenicia, the place where the river Jordan rises. And what the Septuagint presents as future, the Hebrew records as already done, true to what actually happened.

For behold, I will send among you serpents, basilisks (or: most evil ones, or, as the Septuagint translated, deadly ones), against which there is no charm; and they will bite you, says the Lord, incurably, with the pain of your failing heart.

Who they are that come from Dan, whose snorting was heard and who reduced the whole land to a wilderness, the same prophetic word shows under another figure, calling them "serpents", "most evil" or "deadly", and, as Aquila translated, "basilisks", which in Hebrew are called "sapphonim". Why his second edition put "watchmen" here I do not understand, unless perhaps because of the similarity of the word. Against which, he says, there is no charm.

For those who have despised God's commandments pour out their prayers to God in vain against the ancient serpent, the twisting snake. Let us apply this passage against those who despise the words of the Savior and are handed over to the hostile powers.

My sorrow is beyond sorrow; my heart within me grieves. Here, as we said above, the Septuagint joined these words to the preceding sentence, so as to read: and they will bite you, says the Lord, incurably, with the pain of your failing heart. But in the Hebrew the word is not so much "pain", which in Greek is called odynē, as meidiama, which we can render as the "grimace" of a mouth twisted by pain so that it looks like a smile. These words should be read with emphasis, as spoken in the person of God, who laments the overthrow of Jerusalem and cannot bear its miseries.
Listen! The sound of the cry of the daughter of my people from a distant land! He describes the weeping and wailing of the city of Jerusalem once the enemy has entered it.

Is the Lord not in Zion? Is her king not in her? Either the Lord himself is the king, or else "Lord" refers to the Father and "king" to the Son, as in what is written under the name of Solomon: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king's son. The reason why there is the sound of crying in Jerusalem, and why the cry itself comes from a distant land, is plain: the Lord is not in her, and her king has withdrawn from her.

Why then have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with foreign vanities? "The Lord has withdrawn from them," he says, "because by worshipping idols they provoked me, their Lord and King, to anger."

The harvest is past, the summer is over, and we are not saved. Again it is the people speaking, shut up in Jerusalem by a long siege: the seasons have changed, the year has come full circle, and all their hope has come to nothing and passed away.

Over the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am broken and saddened; astonishment has seized me. God answers that in Jerusalem's affliction he himself appears afflicted and, in the manner of a human being, is crushed with astonishment.

Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the wound of the daughter of my people not healed over? Not only in this passage but in many other testimonies of Scripture we find the balm of Gilead standing for repentance and for healing. Here God wonders why the wounds of Jerusalem have not been cured at all and why scars have not yet formed over the skin: it is because there are no prophets or priests whose remedies might cure them.

Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes? And I will weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people. "Even if I were turned wholly into weeping," he says, "and there were no longer drops of tears but a river in flood, I still could not weep worthily for the slain of the daughter of my people. For the evils are so great that their magnitude surpasses all grief." This can be understood as spoken in the person of the prophet as well as of the Lord.

Who will give me a travelers' lodging in the wilderness? Then I would leave my people and go away from them. The Septuagint has: Who would give me in the wilderness a last lodging, so that I might leave my people and go away from them? "It is better," he says, "to live in the farthest wilderness than to remain among such great crimes of men." Hence the Savior also said in the Gospel: How long shall I bear with you? And in another place it is written: At that time he who understands will sit and keep silent, for it is an evil time.

For they are all adulterers, a band of transgressors; they have bent their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth; they have grown strong in the land, for they have gone from evil to evil, and they have not known me, says the Lord. Sinners go from evil to evil when they exchange one idol for another and pass from sins to further sins, or else when they pass from the evil of the siege to captivity.

Of the saints it is said: They will go from strength to strength; but of sinners: They have gone from evil to evil. The cause of all their miseries is that they have not known the Lord, and that they are a band of transgressors who arm their tongue for blasphemy like a drawn bow. And they have grown strong in the land, so that they deserve to hear: You are earth, and to earth you shall go.

Let each of you guard himself against his neighbor and put no trust in any brother, for every brother supplants by trickery and every friend goes about deceitfully. A man will mock his brother, and they will not speak the truth; for their tongue has learned to speak falsehood (or: for they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood). They have labored to do wrong (or: they have done wrong and have not paused so as to turn back). Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit; in deceit (or: usury upon usury and deceit upon deceit) they have refused (or: they have not wished) to know me, says the Lord.

This passage is to be applied in a time of persecution and distress, when faith is rare or altogether absent, when neither brother nor neighbor can be trusted and a man's enemies are those of his own household, when, as the Gospel says, father will betray son and son father, and two are divided against three and three against two. As for what he adds, "they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood" or "their tongue has learned to speak falsehood", it shows that the habit of lying has in a sense become second nature, and that they work zealously at doing wrong. And as for what follows: "your dwelling is in the midst of deceit;

in deceit", these words are directed specifically to the prophet, because he lives among a lying people (or, as the Septuagint translated: usury upon usury and deceit upon deceit), and because they daily increase their crimes and never repent of what they did before, but heap new sins on the old; and in doing these things they strive with all their zeal not to know the Lord, who commanded that such things must not be done.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will smelt them (or: test them with fire) and try them; for what else shall I do in the face of the daughter of my people? (or: for I will act in the face of the wickedness of the daughter of my people). Whenever we are subjected to distress, we receive evils from God and are tested by persecutions, so that whatever base alloy is in us may be smelted out by the heat of tribulations and miseries; for the silver of the Lord is tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified seven times.

Their tongue is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit. With his mouth he speaks peace to his friend, and secretly he lays an ambush for him. Shall I not punish them for these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation as this?

Every heretic who wounds the hearts of his hearers, people who do not know the scripture "Guard your heart with all vigilance", holds a wounding arrow and speaks deceitfully; and while with his mouth he promises peace to his neighbor, he secretly lays snares. As for the verses that follow, in which he says, "Shall I not punish them for these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation as this?", this prophet uses them frequently: when he has listed their evil deeds one by one, he adds that he is acting justly in what he does.

On the mountains I will take up (or: take up) weeping and lament, and over the beautiful places (or: the paths) of the wilderness a dirge, for they have been burned (or: have failed), so that no man (or: no human being) passes through; and they have not heard the voice of the owner (or: of substance). From the birds of the sky to the cattle, they have fled and gone away.

The desolation of the province is prophesied, when the Babylonian comes upon it and lays everything waste: there is mourning on the mountains and weeping in the wilderness, or on the paths of the wasteland; everything has failed and been burned; there is no one to walk through the land, since all have been slain; and nothing is left that can breathe and live. For "owner" the Septuagint translated "of substance"; in Hebrew the word is "macne". Here "substance" is taken not in the sense of ousia, that is, "essence", but in the sense of "wealth" and "riches".

And what he adds, "from the birds of the sky to the cattle they have gone away and departed", shows what we have often said: that the whole creation feels God's anger, and that not only the birds of the air but even the fish of the sea fail. In the figurative sense, weeping is taken up on the mountains and lamentation over the beautiful places of the wilderness when the leaders of the church sin and nothing of God's substance is found in it, and the voice of the Lord who owns the church is not heard through holy and apostolic men, and when, from the birds of the sky to the cattle (that is, from those who can rise to the heights down to all the irrational and simpler folk), people have departed from the assembly of God.

"And I will make Jerusalem heaps of sand (or: a deportation) and lairs of dragons, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without an inhabitant." When the men of the Church and all its teachers have failed, then Jerusalem is given over to deportation, or to heaps of sand. Heretical teaching then prevails in her, she becomes a lair of dragons, and her cities are reduced to a wilderness. The divine word no longer dwells in her, nor does he who says, "I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God."

"Who is the wise man who may understand this, to whom the word of the Lord's mouth may come, so that he may declare it: why has the land perished and been burned up like a desert, so that no one passes through it? And the Lord said: Because they have forsaken my law, which I gave them, and have not listened to my voice nor walked in it, but have gone after the perversity of their own heart and after the Baals, which they learned from their fathers."

The prophet asks whether he can find anyone among the wise in Jerusalem, anyone to whom the word of God comes, who could declare the Lord's will and give the reasons why Judaea has been reduced to a wilderness, with everyone slain and no one left to pass through it. And he brings in the Lord answering and giving the reasons: because they forsook his law, which he had given them, did not listen to his voice, and did not do what was commanded, but went after the perversity of their own heart.

We must therefore trust not in our own will but in the Lord, for the heart of human beings is perverse, and out of our heart come the worst thoughts. "And they went after the Baals," he says, "which they learned from their fathers." Baal was the idol of the Sidonians, and the word is singular, while Baalim is plural. So we must follow neither the error of our parents nor that of our ancestors, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches us.

"Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed them, this people, with wormwood (or: with distress), and give them water of gall to drink, and I will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed." This can be taken as a prophecy about the near future, when they were taken captive by the Chaldeans, and more properly about the present time, when they have been scattered among nations that neither they nor their fathers had known, and, divided throughout the whole world, have been fed with wormwood, that is, with hardship and distress.

And they have received water of gall to drink. This signifies either the greatness of their misfortunes and the everlasting yoke of captivity, or else that, through ignorance of God's law, they are going to receive the Antichrist in place of Christ. The sword is sent after them so that they are consumed to the point of destruction; or else it is a sword that divides them and does not allow them to be of one mind in evil, so that they may perish in respect of what makes them evil.

"Thus says the Lord of hosts: Consider (or: understand), and call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for those who are skilled, that they may hasten (or: speak). Let them make haste and raise a lament over us (or: over you), that our eyes (or: your eyes) may shed tears and our eyelids (or: your eyelids) flow with water, for a voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion (or: in Zion)."

Because of the coming captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem he orders the mourning women to be called, who in times of grief are accustomed to move the people to tears with tearful voices, beating their arms with their hands. This custom survives in Judaea to this day: women with their hair loosed and their breasts bared stir everyone to weeping with a chanting voice. God, or the prophet, joins himself to them with fellow-suffering affection, so as to say that whatever the people endure, he himself endures and feels. And as for what he adds, "for a voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion," he immediately goes on to say what that voice is.

"How we are laid waste and utterly confounded! For we have forsaken the land, because our tents have been thrown down (or: we have cast away our tents)." This is the voice of those lamenting in Zion: "How we are laid waste and utterly confounded!"

And immediately they answer themselves and set out the reasons for the devastation, saying: "Because we have forsaken the land through our own fault and sin, and our tents have been thrown down," the tents they once held as if passing through. The crowds of believers in a time of persecution might also say this: that they have been laid waste and confounded because they forsook the land of the Lord and deserted their own tents.

"Hear, then, O women, the word of the Lord, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach your daughters a lament, and each woman her neighbor a dirge. For death has come up through our windows, it has entered our houses, to cut off the little children from the streets and the young men from the squares!" In the preceding section he had said, "Call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for those who are skilled, that they may hasten." Now he speaks to them as if they were present, to the condemnation of the priests and teachers and all the men: since these have ceased to teach, the women are to hear the word of the Lord, receive the words of his mouth, and teach their daughters and neighbors a dirge and the reasons for their tears, "for death," he says, "has come up through our windows, it has entered our houses."

Although this can also be understood spiritually, in that the death of sins enters through all the senses to the destruction of the soul, it can also be understood of the onslaught of the Babylonians: their strength and speed in battle will be so great that they will not wait to unbar the doors but will climb in through the windows and roofs to lay waste the houses of Jerusalem. Those who perish are the little children who are outside and go out of Jerusalem, and the young men, to whom John also writes, who do not enter by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, but walk through the squares, of which it is written: "How wide and spacious is the way that leads to death!"

"Speak: Thus says the Lord: And the dead body of man (or: the corpses of men) shall fall like dung upon the face of the countryside (or: of the field), and like hay behind the reaper, and there is no one to gather it." The Hebrew word, which is written with three letters, daleth, beth, resh (for it has no vowels in the middle), means "word" if, according to the context and the reader's judgment, it is read dabar; "death" if deber; and "speak" if dabber. That is why the Septuagint and Theodotion attached it to the preceding section, so as to say: "to cut off the little children from the streets and the young men from the squares by death."

Aquila and Symmachus, however, translated it λάλησον, "speak," so that God commands the prophet to speak what follows: "Thus says the Lord," and so on. The sense is this: when death has come up through our windows and entered the houses of Jerusalem, and the little children and young men have perished in the streets and squares, then their dead bodies, the corpses of the slain, will lie upon the face of the earth as on a dunghill, and like stubble left behind the reapers and not gathered because it is useless. By this he means to show that there will be such slaughter in and around Jerusalem that there will be no one to bury the fallen.

"Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the strong man glory in his strength, let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he knows (or: understands) and recognizes me, that I am the Lord who show mercy and judgment and righteousness on the earth! For these things please me (or: for in these is my will), says the Lord."

All human pride is taken away when people's wisdom, strength and wealth are counted as nothing. This is the only true glorying: to know and understand that he himself is the Lord who shows mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth; that all things are governed by God's providence and justice; and that the things that seem to us to lack reason are full of justice and reason.

For these things alone please God, and in these is his will. Where, then, are those who say that man is ruled by his own choice, and that the power of free will has been given in such a way that God's mercy and justice are done away with? Hence the apostle, too, takes up this testimony and sets it as an example: "Let him who glories glory in the Lord."

"Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will punish all who are circumcised in the foreskin: Egypt and Judah and Edom and the sons of Ammon and Moab, and all who are shorn at the hair, who dwell in the desert. For all the nations have the foreskin, but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart."

Among a number of nations, at least in part, and especially those bordering on Judaea and Palestine, the peoples are circumcised to this day: above all the Egyptians and Idumaeans, the Ammonites and Moabites, and the whole region of the Saracens, who live in the wilderness, of whom it is said, "upon all who are shorn at the hair, who dwell in the desert."

Judah, then, who is mixed with the nations named above, ought not to glory in not having a foreskin but in being circumcised according to the law of God, since others also do this who do not keep the commandments of the law and do not know the God of Israel. Nor does circumcision, which was given as a sign, profit anything unless the Lord's precepts are fulfilled, just as the hair marks out a people and does not signify bodily strength or the valor of warriors.

What follows, "For all the nations have the foreskin, but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart," has this sense: whereas, apart from the Egyptians, Idumaeans, Ammonites and Moabites, and the Ishmaelites who live in the wilderness, a large part of whom are circumcised, all the other nations throughout the world are uncircumcised in the flesh, the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart, not in the flesh; and it is this uncircumcision that leads to death. For the one belongs to the flesh, the other to the spirit.

"Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, O house of Israel! Thus says the Lord: Do not learn the ways of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of heaven, which the nations fear, for the laws of the peoples are vain!"

He speaks specifically against those who revere the heavenly bodies and suppose that the human race is ruled by the things that have been set as signs of years, seasons, months and days, and that earthly affairs are directed by heavenly causes. And when he says, "the laws (or: statutes) of the peoples are vain," he shows that all human wisdom is futile and has no usefulness in it.

"For one cuts a tree from the forest, the work of the craftsman's hands with the axe; he adorns it with silver and gold, he fastens it with nails and hammers so that it will not come apart (or: will not move). They are fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree, and they will not speak; they must be carried, because they cannot walk. So do not fear them, for they can do neither harm nor good."

This is a description of the idols that the nations worship. "One cuts a tree from the forest," he says: so the material of idols is cheap and perishable. "The work of the craftsman's hands": since the craftsman is mortal, what he fashions is mortal too. "He adorns it with silver and gold," so that it may deceive the simple with the gleam of both metals. This error has indeed come down even to us, so that we think religion consists in riches.

"He fastens it with nails and hammers so that it will not come apart, or will not move." How great is the power of idols that cannot stand by themselves unless they are fastened with nails and hammers! "Fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree," they have the beauty of metals and are adorned with the art of painting, but they have no usefulness to yield any fruit to their maker.

"And they will not speak," for they have nothing living in them; of them it is written, "They have mouths but will not speak; they have ears but will not hear." "They must be carried": the one who carries is stronger than the things carried; indeed, in him there is feeling, in this a shape without feeling.

"So do not fear them, for they can do neither good nor harm." For many of the pagans are accustomed to worship some demons so that they will do no harm, and to entreat others so that they will bestow benefits; hence that line of Virgil: "a black sheep to the Storm, a white to the favoring Zephyrs." Whatever we have said about idols can be applied to all doctrines that are contrary to the truth.

For their authors, too, promise great things and fashion from their own heart the image of a vain worship. They make grand boasts, and to deceive all the simple they dazzle the eyes of the unlearned with golden notions, as it were, and with words gleaming with the splendor of silver. They are exalted by those who invented them, yet there is no usefulness in them, and their worship properly belongs to the nations and to those who do not know God.

"There is none like you, O Lord; you are great, and great is your name in might. Who will not fear you, O King of the nations? For yours is the glory; among all the wise of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you. The wise and the foolish alike will be proved;

the teaching of their vanity is wood. Rolled-out (or: drawn-out) silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the craftsman and of the smith's hands; blue and purple are their clothing; all these are the work of craftsmen (or: of the wise). But the Lord is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth will quake, and the nations will not endure his threatening."

These verses are not found in the Seventy, but in most copies they have been added from the edition of Theodotion. And though they seem plain according to the letter, according to the anagogical sense they present great difficulty. For none of those gods fashioned by heretical art is like the true God. All will fear him who is King of the nations, for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and from it we advance to love. "Yours is,"

he says, "the glory": in truth there is beauty, in falsehood ugliness. Although the heretics seem to themselves to be wise according to the wisdom of the world, which is being destroyed, yet in all the kingdoms with which they tear the Church apart there is none like you, as the divine word says: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject."

They are at once wise and foolish. Their teaching, according to the quality of their talent, is either cheap and compared to wood, or like silver because of the charm of its eloquence. It is brought from Tarshish, which is either a region of India, as Josephus holds, or else the whole sea is called Tarshish, and it resembles the sky. And yet it is wrapped up in verbal artifice, for if it were laid open, it could not deceive. "And gold from Uphaz."

Among the Hebrews gold is called by seven names, one of which is ophaz, which we can call "refined gold" (obryzum), so that what is inwardly wood and cheap material may gleam on the surface of the idols. They are covered with blue and purple so as to deceive the eyes with their outward show, while they promise themselves the color of the heavens and the heavenly kingdom. And yet all these are the works of the wise, who are thought wise in this world but are foolish before God.

"But the Lord our God is the true God": so all those things are lies. "And he is the living God": so those things that are fashioned are dead. "And the everlasting King": the shadows of the heretics prevail for a time, but over a long time they decay. "At his wrath the earth will quake": that is, those who have earthly works and fashion earthly images. "And the nations will not endure": by no means the people of the Lord, but the multitude of the nations, who cannot bear God's threatening.

"Thus you shall say to them: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth and from among the things under heaven!" These words are to be spoken to the false gods and to those that have been put together by craft, for they made neither the heavens nor the earth; whereas Christ's fellow workers, who are called gods and lords, are for the most part fashioned through the Church's teaching [?].

"The Lord, who makes (or: made) the earth by his might, establishes the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretches out the heavens. At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heavens, and raises (or: brings up) the mists from the ends of the earth; he made lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind (or: the winds) from his storehouses.

Every man has become foolish in his knowledge; every craftsman is put to shame by his carved image, for what he has cast is a falsehood, and there is no breath in them. They are vain and works worthy of ridicule; in the time of their visitation they will perish. The portion of Jacob is not like these, for he who formed all things is himself his portion, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name."

He who makes the earth by his might is God the Father. He makes it by his might, that is, by the Lord and Savior, for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He is also the understanding by which he stretches out the heavens. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created, saying to the Son: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." "At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heavens."

For all the Lord's teaching flows from heavenly sources, as David says: "You set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened, but you perfected it." "And he raises (or: brings up) the mists from the ends of the earth." The mists, or clouds, which the Lord commanded not to rain upon Israel, are brought up from the ends of the earth. One of these clouds said: "For I think that God has displayed us apostles as last of all, like men condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels and to men."

"He made lightnings for the rain." For when the shower of teaching has come from heaven and soaked the parched hearts of men, then you will find the flashes and bright lightnings of wisdom. "And he brings forth the winds from his storehouses," in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. "Every man has become foolish in his knowledge." Though it be Paul, though it be Peter, though it be Moses or Abraham, in comparison with God all their wisdom will be counted as nothing; hence also "the foolishness of God is wiser than men."

"Every craftsman is put to shame by his carved image": he who has fashioned images from his own heart; and what he has cast is false. But if every man has become foolish in his knowledge, then everything he has made is foolish and false. "And there is no breath in them." Note that in this passage too "wind" and "spirit" are called by a single name among the Hebrews, ruah. He means the spirit of sanctification, which cannot be found in the minds of heretics.

"They are vain and a work worthy of ridicule." For who would not laugh on seeing the images of the heretics? Either what they say is boorish, and it is wood; or it is composed in fine language, and is found to be silver; or else it is feigned out of their own minds, and they vainly promise the likeness of gold. "In the time of their visitation they will perish." Heresy has strength for a time, so that all the elect may be made manifest and proved; but when God's visitation comes and his eye looks upon their follies, all things fall silent. "The portion of Jacob is not like these," the portion of those

who supplanted the Jews and daily overthrow the heretics. The portion of the saints is God, of whom the prophet says, "The Lord is my portion." "For he who formed all things is himself" the one who made and fashioned all things, in soul as well as in body, "and Israel is the rod of his inheritance." Everyone who is upright with God, or who perceives God with his mind, is the scepter of his inheritance, whose name is "Lord Almighty" or "of powers"; for that is the meaning of "Lord of hosts," which in the Hebrew is written "Lord Sabaoth."

"Gather up from the land your shame, you who dwell under siege, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will hurl the inhabitants of the land far away at this time, and I will distress them, so that they may be found." The Seventy: "She has gathered her substance from outside, she who dwells in the fortress, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will trip up the inhabitants of this land and distress them, so that they may be found."

Jerusalem is commanded to gather into the strongly fortified city whatever substance she has outside, and to prepare provisions for a long siege. For he says that he is no longer threatening, as before, about a future and distant time, but about an imminent captivity that is about to come at any moment. "Gather," he says, both from outside and from the land, that is, from the fields, "your substance into shame."

"For whatever you have deserves shame. Though you lay these things up, learn what the Lord says about them: Behold, at this time, in this very season, I will hurl, or fling as from a sling, the inhabitants of this land far away." For this the Seventy translated "I will trip up and make to fall"; for this Hebrew word, that is, cole, Aquila and Symmachus translated σφενδονίσω, "I will sling." The sense is: "I will cast them away with all force, as from a sling, and so I will have them besieged, and so I will distress and hem them in, that they will all be found within the city and unable to escape the evil."

"Woe is me for my breaking, my wound is grievous!" The Seventy: "Woe for your breaking, your wound is grievous!" According to the Hebrew, Jerusalem herself speaks, because she is grievously afflicted and suffers an incurable wound; according to the Seventy, the prophet speaks to Jerusalem and laments over her breaking and her wound.

"But I said: Surely this is my sickness (or: my wound), and I will bear it (or: it has seized me)." Jerusalem herself speaks: "Whatever I suffer, I suffer through my own fault. I recognize my wound, which has seized me; or, I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him."

My tent has been laid waste [?]; all my cords are broken — or, all my skins are torn —; my sons have gone out from me — or, my sheep — and they are no more; there is no one to stretch out my tent any longer — or, there is no place any longer for my tent — and to set up my skins.

Jerusalem laments the overthrow of her city as something so easy that you would think it was not the walls and all the fortifications razed to the ground, but the taking down of a tent and pavilion. "My tent," she says (that is, my dwelling), "has suddenly been taken away. All my cords are broken" — she keeps the metaphor of the tent — "or, all my skins are torn."

"My sons have gone out from me, or, my flocks": what the Septuagint added does not fit the history, for in a long siege how could sheep and flocks be carried off from Jerusalem, when, even if there had been any, famine would have consumed them? "And they do not survive," she says, "or, they are not"; for they were not transported to Chaldea, but a great part of them was killed and utterly destroyed. "There is no one to stretch out my tent any longer. There is no one to restore me and lay the foundations of my walls, which have been leveled to the ground."

Because the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord, therefore they have not understood, and all their flock has been scattered. By the metaphor of shepherds and sheep the guilt of the leaders and the scattering of the people are described. For because the leaders acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, whom they ought to have sought with their whole heart, therefore they did not see the evils that were coming — or, did not understand the Lord — and the whole multitude of Jerusalem has been scattered this way and that.

Behold, the sound of a report comes, and a great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling of dragons — or, a lair of ostriches, and, as Symmachus translated, of sirens — for which the Hebrew has "thannim."

Near [?]: "Behold," he says, "the sound and roar of the Babylonian approaching is heard, and a great commotion, or earthquake, from the land of the north, to kill the inhabitants of all the cities of Judea and reduce them to desolation, and to make dragons and every venomous creature dwell there in place of men, or ostriches" — for this animal too is at home in the wilderness and is born and reared in deserts; or at any rate we can understand sirens, certain monsters and phantoms of demons.

Let us apply all these things, which both the previous passage and the present one have described, to the times of persecution of the church, when the tents of the Lord are overturned and every dwelling of the church is reduced to desolation. And that all this happens is the fault of the shepherds, who acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord nor understand him; and therefore the whole flock has been scattered.

I know, O Lord, that a man's way is not his own, nor is it in a man to walk and direct his steps. Let the new preachers blush, who say that each person is governed by his own free will, when this prophet too says, "A man's way is not his own," and David sings in a lyric song: "The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will greatly desire his way." Or else the sense is this: "What we suffer at the hands of the Babylonians is not due to how fearsome they are, but to our deserts and to your indignation."

Correct me, O Lord, but in judgment and not in your fury, lest you reduce me to nothing! Pour out your indignation on the nations that have not known you, and on the provinces — or, generations — that have not called on your name, for they have devoured Jacob and consumed his place and have scattered his glory — or, pastures — or, reduced it to desolation.

We read this passage in the Psalm: "O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath!" And the sense is: "We do indeed deserve all that we suffer, and we deserve far greater things than we endure; yet this I beg, that you correct me as a father, not as an adversary, that you amend me as a son and not punish me as an enemy. For you chastise every son whom you receive, and through every pain and scourge you amend Jerusalem.

But the enemies who have not known you, and the provinces or regions that have not called on your name, ought to feel not your judgment but your indignation. For you handed us over to be corrected, but they made their yoke heavy; they did not spare the old and they afflicted the little ones; they ate us up and devoured us completely, and reduced Jerusalem to such desolation that they demolished every building, public and private, and killed your people."

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this covenant — or, testament — and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel. The title does not state at what time, or under which king and in what year of his reign, this prophecy was given; but we understand either that it is to be joined to the previous prophecy and its time, or at any rate that this word of the Lord came to the prophet some interval of time after the previous prophecy.

It should be noted, moreover, that Aquila and Symmachus always translated the word "berith" as "pact," while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as "testament." Here the speech is directed specifically to Jerusalem and to the men of the tribe of Judah.

Cursed is the man who does not hear the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, saying: Hear my voice and do all that I command you, and you shall be my people and I will be your Lord.

It is not because of the privileges of their race, nor because of the injury of circumcision and the idleness of the sabbath, but because of obedience that God becomes the God of the people of Israel and Israel becomes his people. And here indeed he speaks as to servants, that they may please God; but in the Gospel the Lord says to his disciples: "You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants, for a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you."

And once they have become friends, they pass from friends to sons; for as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God. Hence he commands his friends and sons: "Be perfect, as your Father is perfect," enjoining likeness, not equality. There it is obedience to the commandments; here it is likeness to God. And when he says, "on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace," he gives us to understand that the kiln and the iron, blazing furnace signify the magnitude of tribulation and punishment, not some place of punishment constructed out of iron.

That I may confirm the oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. The fathers are considered to receive when their sons receive, and the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in his descendants.

The land flowing with milk and honey we should take hyperbolically as an abundance of all things, as in the lines: "Let honey flow for them, and let the rough bramble bear amomum," and again: "and he stopped the wine that ran everywhere in streams"; or at any rate let us understand the land flowing with milk and honey tropologically as the church of Christ, in which we are brought up through faith as little ones and sucklings, so that we may be able to take solid food.

And I answered and said: Amen, O Lord — for which the Septuagint translated, "So be it, O Lord," since that is what "amen" means. The Lord had said: "I swore to your fathers to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as is proved today by the facts themselves." The prophet, loving his people, catches up the Lord's word and longs for what has been given to be true and to remain forever. Hence he says: "Truly, O Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised"; or, "So be it, O Lord," that is: "May what you have given remain always!"

And the Lord said to me: Cry out — or, read — all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this covenant and do them! The most merciful God often foretells what is to come, so that a mind slow to believe may at last be softened. And he foretells it both in the city of Jerusalem and outside in the countryside, so that those who share a common danger may share the same repentance.

For I solemnly warned your fathers from the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt until this day; rising early I warned them and said: Hear my voice! And they did not hear nor incline their ear, but each of them walked in the perversity of his evil heart; and I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do.

Up to this point the passage is not found in the Septuagint; and what follows, "and they did not do them," was placed by them and joined to the end of the previous section, in which it is written: "Hear the words of this covenant and do them!" — and they did not do them. As for what it means for God to rise early and press his words on them frequently through the prophets, to bring them out of Egypt, to admonish them repeatedly and say, "Hear my voice," and for them to go off after the perversity of their heart, and for him afterward to render to them what they deserve to receive — we have already discussed this earlier.

And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the former iniquities of their fathers, who refused to hear my words; and so these too have gone after foreign gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant, which I made with their fathers.
For "conspiracy," which we have translated following Symmachus, Aquila, the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered σύνδεσμον, which we could call a "binding together." Hence Athaliah too,

when she discovered that a plot was being laid against her in the temple, used the same word: "Conspiracy, conspiracy!" Scripture applies this word specifically when people strive toward wrongdoing not through a sudden and chance sin, but through premeditated plots and conspiracy, and with one mind and one purpose set themselves to despise the commandments of God. And he says that both fathers and sons, with one mind and a common resolve, neglected God and worshipped idols — namely both Israel and the house of Judah, that is, both the ten tribes and the two whose government was in Jerusalem — so that those who were of one zeal in contempt of God might suffer an equal punishment in enduring captivity.

Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring upon them evils from which they will not be able to escape; and they will cry to me, and I will not hear them. And the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they pour libations, and they will not save them in the time of their affliction.

God does not hear in the time of need and distress, because they too were unwilling to hear the voice of the Lord. Saul also experienced this: when, dreading the Philistine armies, he had not been found worthy to receive a word from the Lord, he turned to the woman with a spirit of divination, to learn from idols what he ought to have wrested from the Lord by persistent prayer and weeping.

From this we learn that even if the Lord does not hear, we must by no means give up or take refuge with demons, who cannot help their worshippers, but must flee to the help of the Lord, who, though angered, is quickly moved and changes his sentence if those with whom he was angry also change. But all that is said here pertains to the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, on whom captivity is pressing.

For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah, and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem you have set up altars of shame to pour libations to the Baals. Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we will find that Judah and Jerusalem did far worse than Israel, so that as many cities as they had, so many kinds of idols they had too, and as many streets and crossroads as there were in the city of Jerusalem, so many altars they had, to their own shame, on which they sacrificed victims to the idols of the Baals.

You, therefore, do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer on their behalf, for I will not hear in the time of their crying to me, in the time of their affliction! Jeremiah is commanded not to entreat the Lord for those against whom the sentence has already been finally passed, lest his prayer appear weak and go unheard because of their own crimes.

"Do not pray for them," he says, "nor take up praise, trying to change my sentence by recounting the mercy of ancient history with which I have always pitied this people, and by praising me! For even if you do this, I will not hear those who are forced to ask me only in a time of necessity." From this we learn that it is in vain for anyone to ask on behalf of another when the one for whom God is being asked does not deserve to receive.

Why is it that my beloved has committed many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh take away from you your wickednesses, in which you have gloried? A rich olive tree, beautiful, fruitful, fair — so the Lord called your name; at the sound of a mighty speech a fire blazed up in it, and its thickets were burned.

He calls the people of Judah beloved and most dear — a people who set up and worshipped idols in his temple, who think they appease God's wrath by sacrificing many victims, and who glory in the multitude of sacrifices that cannot take away the wickedness of sins.

And he compares Jerusalem, or the whole Jewish people, to a beautiful and fruitful olive tree which, exalted by pride, by no means behaved humbly nor understood its creator and ruler, but, puffed up with pride and speaking grandly, was set ablaze by the fire of the Lord, so that its branches or thickets were burned and reduced to nothing — that is, the whole people was destroyed by the sword of its adversaries.

This is the sense also in another place, where it is said to Jerusalem: "I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly genuine; how have you turned into bitterness, a foreign vine?" — when its walls are torn down, and the boar from the forest lays it waste, and all the beasts devour its fruit. Let us address this passage to the leaders of the churches: "Why is it that my beloved has committed many crimes in my house?" Or else to the rich, who plunder what belongs to others and do not take away the wickedness of their hearts, yet think they merit God's mercy: "Will holy flesh take away from you your wickednesses, in which you have gloried?" But now the names of those who make offerings are read out in public, and the redemption of sins is turned into a matter of praise, and they do not remember that widow in the Gospel who, by putting two coins into the treasury, surpassed the gifts of all the rich.

And the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you because of the evils of the house of Israel and the house of Judah, which they did to themselves to provoke me, pouring libations to the Baals. "A rich olive tree," he says,

"beautiful, fruitful — so the Lord your God called you and planted you; but because at the sound of God's mighty speech a flame came down upon you and consumed all your branches, therefore he who had planted you has now pronounced evil against you — not from injustice in his sentence nor from some sudden perversity of speech, but because of the evils which the house of Israel and the house of Judah did to themselves, and zealously practiced, pouring libations to the Baals in order to provoke me to anger." And though God can do whatever he wills, he gives his reasons, lest he seem to act unjustly, according to what is written: "that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged."

But you, O Lord, showed me and I knew; then you showed me their designs. And I was like a gentle lamb that is carried to the slaughter, and I did not know that they had devised plans against me: "Let us put wood into his bread, and crush him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more!" But you, O Lord of Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the reins and the heart, let me see your vengeance on them! For to you I have revealed my cause.

It is the consensus of all the churches that these words are to be understood as spoken by Christ in the person of Jeremiah: that the Father showed him how he ought to speak, and showed him the designs of the Jews; and that he himself, like a lamb led to the slaughter, did not open his mouth and did not know — "sin" is to be understood, according to what the apostle says: "who, though he knew no sin, was made sin for us" —; and that they said: "Let us put wood into his bread" — namely the cross onto the body of the Savior, for he is the one who says, "I am the bread that came down from heaven" — "and let us uproot" — or, "crush" — "him from the land of the living!"

For this crime they plotted in their minds: to blot out his name forever. But on the contrary, in keeping with the mystery of the body he had assumed, the Son speaks to the Father and calls down his judgment, praising his justice and invoking God as the examiner of the reins and the heart, so that he himself may render to the people what it deserves; and he says: "Let me see your vengeance on them" — that is, on those who persist in their crime, not on those who turn to repentance; of these he says on the cross: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" —; and he reveals and lays open his cause to the Father: that he was crucified through no fault of his own, but through the crime of the people, saying: "Behold, the ruler of this world is coming and finds nothing in me."

The Jews, and our own Judaizers, understand these words as spoken in the person of Jeremiah, and maintain that he suffered these evils at the hands of the people because of his prophecy of the future and of the calamities of the impending captivity. But I do not know how they can prove that Jeremiah was crucified, since Scripture does not record this — unless perhaps they plotted it but did not carry it out.

Therefore thus says the Lord to the men of Anathoth, who seek your life and say: "You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and you will not die at our hands." Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will visit upon them; the young men will die by the sword, their sons and their daughters will die by famine, and no remnant of them will be left; for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation.

This seems to contradict the earlier view, by which we wish to show that what was said was spoken in the person of Christ and not of Jeremiah, who actually lived in the village of Anathoth, three miles from Jerusalem. But if we grasp the etymology of the town of Anathoth, which is interpreted "obedience," it will be clearly shown that the men of Anathoth, who once obeyed the commandments of the Lord, stand for all the Jews, and especially for the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, upon whom the final sentence came, that they should perish through the evils of siege — by sword, famine and pestilence.

But to free ourselves from all difficulty of interpretation, let us follow this rule: that all the prophets did most things as a type of the Lord and Savior, and that whatever was fulfilled in Jeremiah in his own time is prophesied of the Lord for the future.
BOOK THREE.

The fables tell that the Lernaean serpent sprouted many snakes from its central head, and that Scylla, the monster of the Sicilian strait, with the face of a maiden but girt about with dogs, tore apart the shipwrecked wretches, while the deadly song of the Sirens sounded on the same shore; and to escape them, Homer's Ulysses is said to have stopped his ears and avoided an insuperable evil by prudent counsel.

I wanted to do just that and to avoid the rage of the heretics, singing, like the Ismenian poet, for myself and my own, and I was turning over in my mind that prophetic word: "When the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and kept silent even from good things." But the devil did not allow me, content with the quiet I longed for, to devote myself to explaining the holy Scriptures and to passing on to the people of my own tongue the learning of the Hebrews and Greeks. Instead he works at this day and night, openly and by ambush, mixing falsehood with truth — or rather smearing all his lies with treacherous honey, so that whoever hears the sweetness of his words may not fear the poison in his heart. He promises peace in order to wage worse wars; he smiles in order to bite; he holds out his hand in order to kill the guileless Abner unawares.

No doubt this is what the apostle meant when he said: "For we are not ignorant of his schemes." Here he keeps silent, there he accuses; he sends papyrus letters throughout the whole world, once bearing gold, now bearing slander, and he interprets our patience, which comes from the humility of Christ, as the sign of a bad conscience. And though mute himself, he barks through an Alpine dog, huge and corpulent, who can do more damage with his heels than with his teeth.

For he comes of the race of the Scots, from the neighborhood of the Britons, and, as in the fables of the poets, like Cerberus he must be struck with a spiritual club, so that he may fall silent in eternal silence along with his master Pluto. But more of this elsewhere. Now I shall begin the third book on Jeremiah, in which I shall try, brother Eusebius, to compress the broad fields of explanation into the narrow path of a commentary.

You are indeed righteous, O Lord, if I dispute with you — or: so that I may give you satisfaction —; yet I will speak of judgments to you: why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why is it well with all who transgress and act unjustly? You planted them and they took root; they thrive — or: they have begotten sons — and bear fruit; you are near to their mouth and far from their kidneys. This dispute is directed against all who act unjustly, and it briefly sums up the meaning of the seventy-second psalm, in which the prophet says: How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! But my feet had almost slipped, my steps had nearly given way, for I was envious of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners, and so on. But it is said properly against the heretics. Though they are wicked, their way prospers, and they beget sons, namely those whom they have deceived into heresy; and they transgress and act unjustly, so that they despoil the Church, and while they persist in the perversity of their opinions, they boast that they have been planted by God, have taken root, have begotten sons and have borne fruit. Though they repeat the name of Christ again and again, they do not have God dwelling in them, according to that saying of Isaiah: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

And you, O Lord, know me; you have seen me and tested my heart toward you. Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them for the day of slaughter! "It is no stumbling block," he says, "that the wicked, or all the heretics, flourish for a time; for you, O Lord, know me, and have seen me, and have tested my heart toward you."

Whom does God the Father know in this way, as he knows his own Son? For no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. "Although," he says, "the heretics thrive, although they beget sons and bear fruit, and you are near to their mouth and far from their kidneys, that is, from their conscience, it is still no small consolation that they are being fattened like cattle for sacrifice.

You gather them into the city of Jerusalem, or into their own conventicles, so that they may be slaughtered like victims unto death, and they will be sanctified only when they have been slain by the Church's sword; for the slaying of the heretics is the salvation of those who had been deceived."

How long will the land mourn, and the grass of every region wither, because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it? Beast and bird are consumed, because they said: He will not see our end — or: God will not see our ways. Whatever happens in the world, whether good or evil, happens not apart from providence or by blind chance, but by the judgment of God. The land is now barren and the grass withers: do you want to know the reason? The wickedness of its inhabitants causes this, so that both the animals on the earth and the birds of the sky are consumed, since all these things were created for human use. And these people rose to such blasphemy as to say that God does not know their ways and does not know what each one is going to suffer. And when he says "how long," he means that the wrath of God remains, because the mind of the sinners does not change.

If you have run with men on foot and grown weary, how will you be able to compete with horses? If you felt secure in a land of peace, what will you do in the pride — or: the roaring — of the Jordan? "If," he says, "frequent captivity at the hands of the neighboring nations has worn you out — the Moabites and Ammonites, the Philistines and Edomites — what will you do in the long captivity that is going to carry you all the way to Chaldea?" And he compares foot soldiers with horsemen because, in fact and according to history, the whole of Persia and all

Chaldea, and the armies of those regions, delight in cavalry. But the nations I mentioned above, because of the difficulty of their terrain, are suited less to pitched battle than to raiding. He keeps the metaphor and says: "If you have collapsed from exhaustion running with men on foot, what will you do if you try to match your pace with horses? And if you had some confidence in your own land, what will you do when you have crossed the Jordan and must endure its whirlpools?"

For even your brothers and your father's house, they too have fought against you and have cried out after you at the top of their voices; do not trust them when they speak fair words to you! "You will be so overwhelmed," he says, "by the most violent waves of the Jordan, and the host of horsemen coming from afar will so lay you waste, that even your brothers the Edomites, and your father's house, Moab and Ammon, who were born of the stock of Lot, will themselves fight against you and mock you in your time of need and distress.

So beware of trusting them and placing your hope in kinship; because of it they will rage against you with greater hatred than your enemies." This can also be taken of the Savior: his brothers and his father's house fought against him and cried out at the top of their voices, saying: Crucify him, crucify him; we have no king but Caesar.

I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hand of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me, therefore I have hated her. He who said in the Gospel, Rise, let us go from here, and again, Your house will be left to you desolate, here too in the prophet threatens the same thing, and he says that he has done what he is going to do. For Israel is the Lord's inheritance and the measuring cord of his inheritance.

And when he says, I have given my beloved soul into the hand of her enemies, this is the same as: I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. And the Jewish people, once the Lord's inheritance, became like a lion in the forest against him when, at his Passion, it cried out against him with one voice. And because it raised its voice against him, he therefore hated and rejected it, and she who was once beloved and most dear is now called hateful.

Is my inheritance to me a speckled bird? Is it a bird dyed all over? Come, gather together, all you beasts of the earth, hurry to devour! The Septuagint: Is my inheritance to me a hyena's cave? Or a cave all around it, over it? Go, gather all the beasts of the field, and

let them come to devour her. By the speckled bird, dyed all over, he means, according to the letter, the peacock. "Israel had such beauty," he says, "and Jerusalem was adorned with such virtues, that there was no good thing that could not be seen in her. Since, then, my former inheritance, that is, the people of Israel, has become to me like a lion in the forest and has raised its voice against me, and I have come to loathe it with all hatred, therefore come and gather together against her, all you beasts of the earth, the multitude of various nations, and devour her who did not know her Lord!" But if,

as the Septuagint and other translators rendered it, we read: Is my inheritance to me a hyena's cave?, we should refer this to the uncleanness of that nocturnal beast, which lives on the carcasses of the dead, is accustomed to digging bodies out of tombs, and will feed on any uncleanness whatever. Such is Israel, which offended its Lord and was handed over to be torn by the teeth of every beast.

Many shepherds have destroyed — or: corrupted — my vineyard, they have trampled — or: defiled — my portion, they have turned my desirable portion into a desolate wilderness — or: a trackless place —. They have made it — or: it has been made — a ruin, and it mourned over me — or: it perished.

Let those hear this who long to be leaders of the peoples, and who will have to render account on the day of judgment not only for themselves but also for the flocks entrusted to them; for because of them the Lord's portion is trampled and defiled, so that where once God had his lodging, there is now a lair of beasts. Others, however, understand this not of the overseers of the people and the priests, but of the commanders of the enemy, who laid waste Jerusalem, that is, the Lord's vineyard.

And it mourned over me; the whole land has been made utterly desolate, because there is no one who reflects in his heart. Over all the ways of the desert the destroyers have come, for the sword of the Lord has devoured from one end of the land to the other; there is no peace for any flesh. The Septuagint: Because of me the land has been utterly ravaged, and the rest.

The words we have set down, and it mourned over me, are joined in the Hebrew to the preceding verse, so that it reads: They have made it, that is, my inheritance, a ruin, and it mourned over me, bereft of my help. According to the Septuagint, however, God says that because of him the land has been ravaged and reduced to a wilderness, since there is no one who reflects in his heart, and there is no peace for any flesh. For flesh cannot receive the peace of God: for the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

But according to the Hebrew, all Judea is desolate because there is no one who reflects on God in his heart, nor anyone left who can escape. For over all the ways of the wilderness the destroyers have come, that is, the enemy army, and the sword of the Lord has devoured from border to border, and there was no rest for those fleeing the city. Hence it is said: There is no peace for any flesh.

They sowed wheat and reaped thorns; they received an inheritance, and it will not profit them. The Septuagint: You sowed wheat and reaped thorns; their clergy will not profit them. "They expected better things," he says, "and the worst came; they hoped for prosperity and suffered adversity; they received from the Lord an abundance of all things, and it will not profit them."

According to the Septuagint, however, all heretics sow as if it were wheat and reap thorns, while the Lord waited for them to bear fruit; and they did not do justice, but brought forth an outcry. This is also said to churchmen who ruin the words of the Lord and his teaching by their bad way of life, and of whom it is added: their clergy will not profit them. For what help can the title of bishop or presbyter or any other ecclesiastical rank be to them, when they are rather weighed down by their dignities, and the mighty will be mightily tormented, and the more has been entrusted to them, the more will be required of them?

Be ashamed of your fruits — or: of your boasting — because of the fierce anger of the Lord — or: because of reproach in the sight of the Lord —. Thus says the Lord against all my most wicked neighbors who touch the inheritance I apportioned to my people Israel: Behold, I will uproot them from their land, and I will uproot — or: cast out — the house of Judah from among them. And when I have uprooted them, I will turn — or: return — and have mercy on them, and I will bring them back — or: make them dwell —, each man to his inheritance and each man to his land. This is said to those

whom their clergy and the ecclesiastical order will not profit, that they may be ashamed of their boasting and of their reproach before the Lord. And as for what he adds, against all my most wicked neighbors: according to the letter, the neighbors of the holy land are the Edomites, the Philistines, Moab and Ammon. According to the tropological sense, however, they are all the heretics, who are counted under the name of Christ and are neighbors of the holy land rather than its inhabitants, who touch God's inheritance and lay it waste. And it is said of them that they will be removed from the midst of the land, and that the house of Judah will be taken out from among them. When these have been uprooted and freed from the jaws of the heretics, they will obtain God's mercy and be brought back to their inheritance and their land.

And it shall be that, if, once instructed, they learn the ways of my people, so as to swear by my name, As the Lord lives, just as they taught my people to swear by Baal, they will be built up in the midst of my people; but if they will not listen, I will uproot that nation with uprooting and destruction, says the Lord. If those who have passed over from heresy into the Church learn the ways of God's people and swear by the name of the Lord and not by the names of the idols they have fashioned out of their own hearts, they will be built up by the Lord and will be part of his people.

But if, having passed over into the Church, they cling to remnants of their perverse doctrines and do not listen to the words of the Lord, that nation will be uprooted from the midst of God's people with uprooting and everlasting destruction, so that no place of repentance whatever is left to them. We see this every day and prove it by experience: heretics feign the truth of the faith precisely in order to deceive the simple, not so that they themselves may be converted to the faith, but so that they may drag the faithful into unbelief.

Thus says the Lord to me: Go and get yourself a linen loincloth — or: girdle — and put it on your loins, and do not put it in water — or: it shall not pass through water —! So I got a loincloth according to the word of the Lord and put it around my loins. And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: Take the loincloth — or: girdle — that you got, which is around your loins, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock!

So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the Lord had commanded me.
