And after many days the Lord said to me: Arise, go to the Euphrates and take from there the loincloth — or: girdle — which I commanded you to hide there! So I went to the Euphrates and dug, and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, the loincloth — or: girdle — had rotted, so that it was fit for no use.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord: So will I make the pride — or: the injustice — of Judah rot, and the great pride of Jerusalem, and this most wicked people, who refuse to hear my words and walk in the perversity — or: the direction — of their most wicked heart, and have gone after foreign gods to serve them and worship them; and they shall be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use. For as

the loincloth clings to a man's loins, so I bound to myself the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, says the Lord, that they might be my people, and a name, and a praise, and a glory; but they did not listen.

The girdle or loincloth that is bound to God's loins is the people of Israel. Taken from the earth like flax, and unwashed, it had neither softness nor whiteness, and yet through his mercy it clung to God. And when it had sinned — for linen and a loincloth of this kind are endowed with reason — it was carried across the Euphrates, that is, to the Assyrians, and there it is hidden; that is, it is in a sense swallowed up by the multitude of great and countless nations and counted as nothing.

After a long time, however, the prophet himself, as a type of God, frees the people from captivity. Yet even after its return it did not keep God's commandments, but followed foreign gods, and at the last even laid hands on the Son of God and wasted away in everlasting perdition. Every holy man, too, is a loincloth of God: taken from the earth and from the clay of the earth, he is joined in fellowship with God, and in a sense he covers and surrounds with greater care the parts of his Church that seem unseemly, so that they may not be exposed to the bites of pagans and heretics.

If this loincloth touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, so as to be soaked in the moisture of the Assyrian region, it loses its former strength and rots and falls apart; and even if it returns to God's use, it still cannot have its former beauty. This happens not through God's harshness, but through its own fault, because they refuse to hear his words and walk in the perversity of their heart, or rather do whatever seems right to themselves.

And the divine word itself explains why it set forth this comparison, saying: "For as the loincloth clings to a man's loins, so I bound to myself and made to cling to me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah" — that is, the ten tribes and the two — "that they might be my people, called by my name, and a praise, and a glory; and in return for all this they did not listen to me, but followed their own vices."

Let anyone who can say, But for me it is good to cling to God, take care, then, that he is not through negligence separated from God's loins, and does not cross the Euphrates and get handed over into the power of the king of Assyria, and lodged not on the most solid rock but in a cleft of a rock that is corrupt and decayed, that is, in the filth and vices of the heretics, and does not come to such rottenness that he can never again return to the Lord's use and be his girdle.

You shall therefore say to them — or: to the people — this word: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Every flask — or: wineskin — will be filled with wine. And they will say to you: Do we not know that every flask — or: wineskin — will be filled with wine? And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings of the stock — or: the sons — of David who sit upon his throne, and the priests and the prophets and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness, and I will scatter them, a man from his brother, and fathers and sons together, says the Lord; I will not spare — or: I will not long for them — nor relent nor have mercy, but will destroy them. The Hebrew word nebel was rendered by Aquila's first edition as "flask," by his second as nebel itself, by Symmachus as "bowl," by the Septuagint as "wineskin," and by Theodotion as "vessel." All of it is filled not with oil, not with water, not with honey, not with milk, nor with any other liquid substance, but with wine and drunkenness. This shows that we are a fragile vessel, according to the Apostle, who says: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels; and that it cannot be that what is written should not be fulfilled in us: For nothing good dwells in my flesh; and again: For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do; and then: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? With this drunkenness, by which we forget the commandments of God, and with vices and sins, the whole human condition is filled, as the prophet says: No one living will be justified in your sight — not in comparison with God, as heretics old and new and the patrons of heretics would have it, but with respect to his knowledge; for man sees the face, but God the heart — and what sometimes seems clean to us is found to be filthy in his eyes. Not only the base mob and the worthless rabble are filled, but the kings of the churches, of the stock or sons of David, who sit lolling back with necks held high and bellies thrust out upon his throne; the priests too, the second rank in ecclesiastical honor; and the prophets, who seem to have knowledge of the Scriptures; and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem — or Judah, as the Septuagint added — are filled according to the variety of their sins. And when they are drunk, they are scattered from fellowship with one another, and fathers are separated from sons and sons from fathers, so that they are defiled by various heresies, and under the name of Christ they fight with swords among themselves and wage war against their mother, the Church, who bore them. Hence he says: "I will not long for them, but will hold them in everlasting hatred; I will not spare nor relent nor have mercy" — not from cruelty of sentence, but from the truth of judgment. "For those who slaughtered my peoples will themselves perish forever." This can also be taken simply according to history: that the kings and the priests and the prophets and all the people of Jerusalem were to be made drunk with the cup of Babylon and overwhelmed by the evils of captivity.

Hear and give ear, do not be exalted, for the Lord has spoken! Since he had said above, Every wineskin will be filled with wine, so that the kings too and the priests and the prophets and every inhabitant of Jerusalem would be filled with drunkenness, he therefore adds and says: Hear and give ear, outwardly as well as inwardly, with the mind as well as with the body, and do not be exalted through pride, but consider your frailty and that there is no one who, according to the nature of sin, is free from this drunkenness. Hence the one who exalts himself against him through pride is ruined and corrupted and is unworthy of God's mercy.

Give glory to the Lord your God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble on the gloomy — or dark — mountains! You will look for light, and there will be the shadow of death, and they will be set in darkness — or, according to the Hebrew: and he will turn it into the shadow of death and into gloom. But if you will not listen, (my — or) your soul will weep in secret before the face of pride — or of injury [?]. Those to whom the divine word had said:

"Hear and give ear, and do not be lifted up," he now calls to repentance, so that they may give glory to God before they are led off to Babylon and their feet stumble on the dark or gloomy mountains. This is why sinners are often told: "Give glory to God!"

That Babylon and the whole region of the Chaldeans are called gloomy or dark mountains we read at the beginning of Isaiah's prophecy against Babylon, where it is written: "Lift up a signal on the gloomy mountain," which in Hebrew is called 'neseptha'. So he commands this: that before they are led into captivity and feel the evils of slavery, they should repent, since while they look for light they are going to sit in darkness.

"But if," he says, "you will not listen to me, my soul" — or, according to the Septuagint, "your soul" — "will weep in secret" — according to Aquila, "in darkness" — "before the face of pride, so that not even groaning and weeping will be free, lest the eyes of the victors be offended." We can also interpret this passage in this way. The Savior says: "Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work any longer."

Isaiah's prophecy also concerns this time: "For the stars of heaven and Orion and all the array of heaven will not give their light, and the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light." Zephaniah too agrees in the same words, saying: "A day of trouble and distress, a day of misery and ruin, a day of darkness and whirlwind, a day of cloud and gloom."

Therefore, before the time of judgment comes and our feet stumble on the dark mountains — that is, the hostile powers set over torments and tortures — let us repent, so that we are not wrapped in the darkness of night while we look for light. And let us know that, unless we do this, the soul either of God or of the prophet will weep before the face of our pride, since we refuse to hear the words of God. This is why the prophet himself says:

Weeping, Jerusalem will weep — or, weeping, it will weep — and my eye will shed tears, and I cannot hide my grief with silent groans. But the whole cause of the torments is that the Lord's flock has been taken captive.

Let us say to the Jews, and to the judaizers among us who follow only the plain history that kills: unless you listen in secret — that is, in a mystery, or in the darkness which God made his hiding place, and, as Solomon says, so as to understand a parable and an obscure saying — the soul of the prophet, or their own soul, will weep before the face of pride, while they resist God in their stubbornness. Hence there will be unceasing weeping and perpetual tears, because the Lord's flock has been captured and corrupted by the true Nebuchadnezzar.

Say to the king and to the lady ruler — or, say to the king and to the mighty —: Humble yourselves, sit down, for the crown of your glory has come down — or has been taken away — from your head! The cities of the south are shut up, and there is no one to open them; all Judea has been carried away — or all Judah has been carried away — in a complete deportation — or captivity.

The prophet is commanded to speak to King Jeconiah and to his mother, whom he calls lady and ruler, or queen, telling them to humble themselves and sit in the dust; for they have lost their royal dignity and are to be handed over to the king of Babylon. "The cities of the south are shut up": that is, the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem, which faces south toward the desert; "and there is no one to open them" once they are surrounded by siege.

"All Judea — or all Judah — has been carried away in a complete deportation," or "it has received what it deserved, and it has been fulfilled in it"; for that is how the Septuagint translated it. In this passage the one who takes the king to be Christ, and the mighty to be the angels or the apostles, is raving: they are supposed to take on the body of humiliation and sit in the dust, and lose — whether the king or the mighty — the crown from their head and the glory of their strength.

He also interprets the cities of the south that are shut up as the underworld, which is opened to no one, and says that all the glory of Judah was carried away when, at the Passion, this was fulfilled: "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one." The Hebrew word 'gebira' Aquila and Symmachus translated as 'lady ruler' and 'lady', whereas the Septuagint thought it was 'geburoth' and rendered it 'the mighty'.

Lift up your eyes and see those who come — or you who come — from the north! Where is the flock that was given to you, your splendid sheep? What will you say when he visits you? For you teach them against yourself and train them against your own head.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem are commanded to lift up their eyes and see the Chaldeans coming from the north, and the city itself is questioned and told: "Where is the flock that was given to you, your splendid sheep? Where is your people, whom you had received from God? Where is that great and splendid multitude, so large that you would have thought the crowd of an entire province had been gathered into one place?

What will you say when the Lord visits you with his rod and hands you over to your Babylonian enemies, whom you yourself taught against you, or against your head, or from the beginning, when you fled to them for help and followed their idols — they who, on the pretext of your friendship, learned by what road they should come against you?" Let the negligent church hear this: that it is itself teaching its enemies how they may seize it in spiritual captivity and tear its flock to pieces with the cruelty of wild beasts.

Will not pains seize you like a woman in labor? And if you say in your heart: "Why have these things come upon me?" — because of the multitude of your iniquity your more shameful parts have been uncovered, the soles of your feet have been defiled — or disgraced.

"While you are unaware, captivity will seize you suddenly, as sudden childbirth seizes a woman. And if you will not make excuses but ask why you have been handed over to your enemies, hear plainly that it is the multitude of your iniquity that has done this to you, so that, like a harlot whose clothes are stripped off, your disgrace has been uncovered and your fornications publicly exposed." From this we learn that as long as sins are lesser, God acts patiently and waits for our repentance; but if we choose [?] to join sins to sins and pile up a heap of transgressions, our shameful parts will be uncovered and the soles of our feet shown to all, either in the present age or in the age to come. For nothing is hidden that will not be made known, when that word of Daniel is fulfilled: "These shall rise to everlasting life, and those to reproach and everlasting shame."

If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard its spots, then you too will be able to do good, though you have learned evil. This text is used against the church by those who wish to assert different natures; they say that the blackness or the spottedness of sins is so great that they cannot pass over into whiteness and the beauty of a single color. They do not attend to what follows: "you too will be able to do good, though you have learned evil."

For whatever is learned belongs not to nature but to effort and one's own will, which through long habit and the love of sinning is in a certain way turned into nature. But what is impossible for men is possible for God: so that it is not the Ethiopian and the leopard who are seen to change their nature, but he who works in the Ethiopian and the leopard, as the apostle says: "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me."

Hence he says in another place: "I labored more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that is in me," and: "I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me." And again we read it written: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" For these reasons let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, nor the chaste man in his chastity, knowing that in all these things the power is Christ's, not that of those who boast in their own virtues.

And I will scatter them like stubble swept away by the wind in the desert. This is your lot and the portion of your measure from me, says the Lord — or, and the portion of your disobedience against me. "Because through long habit in evil they could not change their nature — not through any fault of the Creator, but through their zeal for ingrained wickedness — therefore I will scatter them into the wilderness like stubble swept away by the wind, as is written elsewhere: like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth." And he turns to address Jerusalem herself: this is her lot and this her portion, which she has chosen for herself — a measure heaped up, full and running over — or the portion of her disobedience, by which she refused to submit to the Lord. For with the measure she has measured, it will be measured back to her.

Because you have forgotten me and trusted — or hoped — in a lie, therefore I too have stripped bare — or will strip bare and uncover — your thighs — and your hindparts — before your face, and your disgrace will appear: your adulteries and your neighing, the wickedness — or the estrangement — of your fornication.

The cause of Jerusalem's scattering is that she forgot God and trusted or hoped in lies. Whoever trusts in the things of this world rather than in God forgets God. So his thighs or hindparts are uncovered, so that he may see his disgrace, and what ought to be behind may be in front, and he may see for himself what he has done, and his disgrace may appear not only to himself but to everyone.

"Your adulteries," he says, "and your neighing": this shows not lust alone but the madness of lust, like that of mares eager for mating, as in that line of Virgil: "Then the slow poison drips from the groin, which the shepherds call by its true name, hippomanes." Let us ask Jesus not to uncover our thighs and hindparts, either in the present age or in the age to come, but to blot out our iniquities and not let any of our crimes be seen.

On the hills in the field I have seen your abominations. Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be made clean — or, because you have not been made clean — after me; how much longer? "Not only in the middle of the city of Jerusalem, but on every hill and in every region I have seen your idols." Hence it is said to her: "Woe to you, Jerusalem, because you have not been made clean after me; for although you boasted that you were following in my footsteps and paraded the confession of my name, you were never purified, because you forgot me and hoped in lies."

So he rebukes her and says: "How much longer?" The sense is: "How long shall I wait for you? How long shall I bear with you? How long will you go on forgetting me to the end and despising my commandments?" Whoever does not humble himself under the mighty hand of God, but holds his neck stiff in pride and trusts in his own crimes and vices, commits fornication on the hills and in the fields and is never made clean.

The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought. All things are in agreement with the wrath of God: hence the sun sets at noon over sinners, and the moon and the other stars do not give their light. And we should suppose that during the time of the siege there were no rains, so that the besieged suffered a lack of water. For the city uses only one spring, Siloam, and even that does not flow continually, and to this present day the failure of rain causes a scarcity not only of crops but also of drinking water.

Judea — or Judah — has mourned, and her gates have fallen — or have become empty — and have been darkened — or made dark — upon the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem has gone up. Her nobles sent their lesser ones — or their young men — for water; they came to draw — or to the wells — and found no water; they brought back their vessels empty. They were confounded and afflicted — or they blushed — and covered their heads. Because of the desolation of the land — or, and because the works of the land failed — since no rain came — or there was no rain — upon the land, the farmers were confounded; they covered their heads.

In a time of drought, when the multitude suffers a famine of hearing and learning the word of God, Judea mourns — she who boasts that she holds first place in the worship of God and in the confession of the true faith — and her gates are either emptied or fall down; these gates we should refer to the senses, through which the soul takes in instruction. Then everything is darkened and wrapped in shadows, and in Jerusalem it is not reason and the word of teaching that reign, but clamor and confusion. The elders too, who ought to go themselves to draw water, send the young, in whom there is no gray hair of wisdom; and so they come to the wells and do not find the water which, as the history tells, the patriarchs found. They bring back their vessels empty — the young men, that is — not because there was no water, but because they could not find it. "They were confounded and afflicted — or they blushed — and covered their heads" — because they could not say with the apostle: "But we all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord" — "because of the desolation of the land," or "and the works of the land failed," the works by which we advance to the knowledge of God. And the cause is plain: "because no rain came upon the land." For the clouds were commanded not to rain upon it. The farmers too — one of whom says: "You are God's field, God's building," and [in another place]: "We are God's fellow workers" — cover their heads and are confounded, understanding that without the grace and help of God they strive in vain.

For even the hind — or the hinds — gave birth in the field and abandoned her young — or they gave birth and abandoned them — because there was no grass. And the wild asses stood on the crags; they panted for air like dragons; their eyes failed, because there was no grass — or hay.

Great is the barrenness when even the hinds give birth in the field and abandon their young because there is no grass or hay, so that they — who by the breath of their nostrils draw serpents out of their holes and kill venomous creatures — have no food of grace to eat. The wild asses too, of whom it is written: "Who has set the wild ass free in the wilderness?", leave the plains and open country and stand on the crags; they cannot run, and they gasp for air like dragons, and their eyes fail and cannot see the clear light, because the food of reason has been withdrawn from them.

This drought often happens in the churches, when there are both harts and wild asses among the people, and they waste away for lack of teachers. There are those who could learn, and there are none who can teach.

Though our iniquities have answered — or have stood up — against us, O Lord, act for your name's sake, for our turnings away — or our sins — are many. We have sinned against you, O hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble. If we wonder why the rains do not come down upon the earth, why everything withers in drought, let us hear: "Our iniquities have stood up against us. Therefore, O Lord, not according to our works but according to your holy name, overcome our many turnings away.

For we have sinned against you, from whom the secrets of the heart are not hidden, and we wait for you, who are the true hope and expectation of Israel and save him in time of trouble," as it is written: "In my trouble I cried to the Lord, and he heard me." Let us too say, in a time of drought and lack of water: "We have sinned against you and done evil in your sight; we wait for your coming, you who save Israel not for its own merit but by your mercy."

Why will you be like a sojourner in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay the night? Why will you be like a wandering man, or a mighty man who cannot save? The Septuagint: Why have you become like a stranger in the land, and like a native turning aside to lodge? Will you be like a man asleep, and like a man who cannot save?

The Jews understand this passage as follows: "Why do you separate yourself from your people and, like a traveler seeking an hour's rest, not care what lodging you use, but, intending to move on elsewhere, fail to save your people and abandon the once-splendid temple?" Our interpreters, however, think it is said of the future dispensation of Christ: that he would be a stranger on earth and would make use of earth's hospitality for a short time, and, like a man passing through and strong, would leave Israel behind and make for the multitude of the nations, so as to pass from place to place, from people to people, from temple to church.

As for what is said according to the Septuagint — "Will you be like a man asleep, and like a man who cannot save?" — he is offering a likeness, not the reality of the matter, as in the text: "Rise up, why do you sleep, O Lord?" It is not that the Lord sleeps — of whom it is said: "He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" — but that he seems to be asleep to those whom he abandons. Indeed, in what follows it is not written: "a man" asleep who cannot save, but: "like a man"; in both cases it is said anthropopathically.

But you are among us, O Lord, and your name has been called upon us; do not forsake us — or do not forget us! "You who among the Jews will be like a stranger and a traveler and a wandering man abandoning his old dwelling, you dwell in us, and your name has been called upon us, so that we are called Christians. Therefore do not forsake us or forget us, for whom the mouths of all the prophets have sung of your coming."

Thus says the Lord to this people: Because it loved — or they loved — to move their feet, and did not rest — or did not refrain — and it did not please the Lord — or, and God took no pleasure in them — now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins.

When the people say: "Why have you become like a stranger, a traveler and a wanderer, abandoning your dwelling?", the Lord answers his former people: "Do you want to know the reason? Listen to what is said: because the people loved to move their feet and did not take them out of the fetters of sin — or did not rest and could not stand still — therefore I too have abandoned them, and I take no pleasure in them."

So he who long delayed and in his patience refused to punish sinners will, because they persisted in wickedness, remember their iniquities and visit their sins, as one visits the sick and those who have no sense of God, so that they may cease to sin any longer. Note, moreover, that in the holy Scriptures it is always the feet of sinners that move, while to the saints it is said, as to Moses: "But you, stand here with me," and elsewhere it is written: "Praise the Lord, you servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God!"

And the Lord said to me: Do not pray for the good of this people! When they fast, I will not hear their prayers, and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, for I will consume them by the sword, by famine and by pestilence. It is foolish to pray for one who has sinned unto death, as John says: "There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All iniquity is sin, and there is sin that is not unto death."

Fasts and prayers and sacrifices and burnt offerings are of benefit when we turn away from vices and weep over our former sins. But if we persist in our crimes and imagine we can buy the ears of God with vows and sacrifices, we are badly mistaken, for we take God to be unjust. Whoever has once been destined for sword, famine and pestilence cannot be rescued by any prayers. That is why the prophet is told not to ask in vain for what he cannot obtain.

And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God — or, you who are, Lord God — the prophets are telling them: You will not see the sword, and there will be no famine among you, but he will give you true peace in this place. And the Lord said to me: The prophets are prophesying falsely in my name. I did not send them, I did not command them, nor did I speak to them; they are prophesying to you a lying vision, a deceitful divination and the delusion of their own heart.

Let the teachers hear this who promise prosperity to those who sin and persist in their vices, who say to the rich: "You will not see the sword of God's torments, and there will be no famine among you, for you will be filled with the words of God, and the Lord will give you the truest peace in the place of the church" — or of Jerusalem. As for his saying "ah, ah, ah" three times, according to the Hebrew, he was responding to the earlier words, where the Lord had threatened, saying: "By the sword, by famine and by pestilence I will consume them."

Since, then, the prophets — or rather the false prophets — had made false promises, the Lord spoke through Jeremiah: "Do not listen to the words of the false prophets, who were not sent by me but came of their own will! So those who speak delusion to the people should be called not prophets at all but diviners." For it is far better to amend our sins through fear of punishment than to fall under the divine sentence through hope of prosperity.

Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, whom I did not send, and who say, “Sword and famine shall not come upon this land”: by sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed. And the peoples to whom they prophesied shall be cast out into the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there shall be no one to bury them, them and their wives, their sons and their daughters; and I will pour out upon them their evil — or, their evils.

Let the false prophets beware, who trip up the people of God by promising them prosperity. Otherwise they too will perish, and the people they have deceived will be destroyed by a like death and lie in the streets of Jerusalem. Having trampled on the Lord's commandments, they will perish by famine and sword, and there will be no one to bury them or to cover their disgrace with the dust of repentance.

For the prophets themselves and the people, their wives, their sons and daughters and their whole generation, will lie on the dunghill with no one to prepare them for burial. How many lie in the streets of Jerusalem! How many do we see unburied, receiving their own evils, which they suffer as the Lord pours them out!

And you shall say this word to them: Let my eyes shed tears — or, let your eyes shed tears — night and day, and let them not be silent — or, not cease — for the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a most grievous wound. This passage is understood in two ways. Either God himself laments his people and his eyes do not cease to weep, or else he commands that the eyes of the peoples should flow with tears. And what must be lamented is no light thing, since the virgin daughter of his people has been struck with the greatest crushing and an unbearable wound. Others think these words are spoken in the person of the prophet.

If I go out into the fields, behold, those slain by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, those wasted by famine — or, the pain of famine! Prophet and priest alike have gone into a land they did not know. There is just cause for lament: the virgin has been crushed, the daughter struck, the people destroyed. “For if,” he says, “I choose to go outside, I will see the slain; if I enter the city, I will behold people wasted away and barely clinging to their bones through the pressure of hunger.”

And what wonder is it to say this of the common people and the lowly crowd, when even the prophets and priests, who prophesied prosperity to others and whose duty was to open up the commandments of the law, themselves went into a land they did not know and endured the evil of captivity? Let our own prophets and priests hear this: that through their negligence there is no security either within or without, since they both scandalize those who are outside and let those within perish of hunger, and those who were the authors of sin become partners in the torments.

Have you utterly rejected Judah, or does your soul loathe Zion? Why then have you struck us, so that there is no healing? We waited for peace, and there is no good, and for a time of healing, and behold, turmoil! The prophet marvels that the Lord has so suddenly cast off Judah and Jerusalem, that is, the kingdom of the two tribes, where the religion of God and the ceremonies of the temple were found, and has struck them with so great a blow that no medicine can be applied.

“We waited,” he says, “for peace and a time of healing, and there is no good, but on the contrary turmoil, so that where once there had been the worship of God and tranquillity, everything is now filled with sedition and the roar of the enemy.” If ever, then, our own Zion and our own Judah is cast off and the soul of God loathes it, let us by no means be surprised, but rather say what follows:

We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness, the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you. “Both we,” he says, “and our fathers, with the same madness, neglected the commands of God, and the measure of our forebears has been filled up in us, so that whatever they lacked has been made up by our own heap of sins.” Hence it is also said of Judas: Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered in the sight of the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out! Let them be before the Lord always, and let their memory perish from the earth!

Do not give us up to reproach for your name's sake, and do not bring dishonor upon the throne of your glory! Remember: do not make void your covenant with us! Let us not suppose that the throne of God's glory is only the temple of Judea, which was often destroyed. It is every saint. As it is written, You have dashed his throne to the ground, and such a throne is dashed down and destroyed when the saint has offended God by a multitude of sins. Yet one who has perished by his own fault is upheld by the Lord's mercy. That mercy would be changed into a severe sentence only if the Lord were to make void his covenant, in which he promised that we would be saved.

Are there any among the carved idols of the nations who can bring rain, or can the heavens give showers? Are you not the one, O Lord God, whom we have waited for? For you have made all these things. After many and varied discourses he returns to the title of the prophecy, where it is written: The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought.

What he says, then, is this: “Because the images of demons cannot give rain, nor can the heavens give their showers by themselves, therefore you, O Lord our God, for whom we have always waited and toward whom we turn our hopes and prayers, give your rain! For all things are yours, and whatever is good cannot be given without you, to whom it belongs.” Let us say this also against the heretics,

who cannot bestow the rain of teaching. Though they claim to be heavens and boast that of them it is written, The heavens declare the glory of God, they still cannot give the showers of doctrine. For God alone instructs his people and bestows varieties of grace on those who wait for him.

And the Lord said to me: Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before me — or, against me — my soul is not toward this people. For we read that these men withstood the Lord's wrath on behalf of the people and turned aside a sentence that was already impending. “Even if,” he says, “they should stand either in my sight or against me” — to one of them God said, Let me alone, and I will strike this people — “yet I will not hear, because the crimes of the sinning people have reached their full measure.”

Cast them out — or, send them away — from my presence, and let them go forth! Sinners depart from God not in place but in will, although we do read that both Adam and Cain were cast out from the face of God.

And if they say to you, “Where shall we go?”, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Those for death, to death; and those for the sword, to the sword; and those for famine, to famine; and those for captivity, to captivity! And I will visit upon them four kinds, says the Lord: the sword to slay, and dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.

The prophecy of Ezekiel also shows the four plagues to which the people of the Jews were handed over: sword, pestilence from famine, wild beasts, captivity. Among the beasts, understand the dogs and birds as well, to which their bodies were handed over to be torn, devoured and scattered. For once the Creator had been neglected, the whole creation could not fail to rise up against the sinners.

And I will make them an object of agitation — or, of commotion and distress — to all the kingdoms of the earth because of Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for all that he did in Jerusalem. We read in the book of Chronicles that Manasseh, after his captivity and repentance, returned to Jerusalem and reigned. But just as the merits of the saints, such as David and others, pass down to their descendants, so the crimes of sinners reach their descendants if their children and grandchildren act in the same way. As for the words, “I will make them an object of agitation, or of commotion and distress, to the whole earth,” this was fulfilled in part under the Babylonians and is now being fulfilled completely, since an impious people has imitated that most wicked king who filled Jerusalem from gate to gate with the blood of the righteous. From this we learn that peoples are very often destroyed through the wickedness of kings, princes and rulers.

For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve for you? Or who will go to ask for your peace? When God has been offended, no one can intercede for the crimes of sinners. No creature can be as merciful as the Creator, nor can anyone spare those who are not his own as readily as the Lord spares his own.

You have forsaken me, says the Lord; you have gone backward. The reason is given why no one has pity on Jerusalem, grieves for her, or pleads for her peace. According to the apostle, she ought to have forgotten what lies behind and stretched forward to what lies ahead. Instead she turned back and longed for the flesh of Egypt.

And I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you; I am weary of being entreated — or, of entreating. For this the Seventy translated: I will no longer let them go. An outstretched hand is the sign of one who strikes, and the slaying of sinners signifies wrath brought to completion. What he added, “I am weary of being entreated,” or “of entreating,” has a double sense: that God has grown faint from pardoning them so often, and that he is tired of always calling them to salvation.

And I will scatter them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land — or, of my people; I have slain and destroyed my people, and yet they have not turned back from their ways. “What use is it to be entreated again and again, when they do not turn back from their wicked ways or repent? For I scattered them as with a winnowing fork in order to cleanse my threshing floor. I scattered them in the gates of the land, so that in a sense they might tread the threshold of the underworld. And I slew and destroyed my people, so that, driven by the pressure of their evils, they might avoid the evils that were impending.”

Their widows have been multiplied before me beyond the sand of the sea; I have brought upon them, upon the mother of the young man, a destroyer at noonday; I have sent terror suddenly upon the cities. God wishes to save sinners by various remedies, so that those who despised him when he coaxed them may fear him when he threatens.

Widows have been multiplied beyond the sand of the sea because their husbands were slain. Mothers who lost their children felt the destroyer not at night or by ambush but in broad daylight, which shows the open force of a stronger adversary. “I have sent,” he says, “upon the cities” — undoubtedly those of Judah and of the sinning people — “sudden terror, so that the more sudden the evil, the harder it would be to escape.”

She who bore seven — or, very many — has languished — or, has cast off, or, has been made empty; her soul has fainted; her sun has gone down while it was still day — or, at midday; she has been confounded and put to shame. And the remnant of them I will give to the sword in the sight of their enemies, says the Lord. We have often said that the Hebrew word saba means “seven,” or “oath,” or “very many.” Hence the translations also differ: Aquila, the Seventy and Theodotion render it “seven,” Symmachus “very many.”

She who was rich in children, then, was suddenly made childless, perished in broad daylight, and was put to shame in her desolation. “And the rest of the people,” he says, “I will hand over to the sword, so that no one may escape death and the wrath of God.” Others refer this to the synagogue, which was weakened so that the multitude of the church might grow, according to what is written: The barren woman has borne seven — or, many — and she who had many children has languished. Hence the sun of righteousness, in whose wings is healing, has set for her, and she is therefore covered with everlasting shame, losing her people by the spiritual sword.

Woe is me, my mother! Why did you bear me a man of strife — or, of judgment — a man of discord — or, one to be judged — in all the earth? This can be understood of Jeremiah by synecdoche, since he was judged not in the whole world but in the land of Judea. But it truly fits the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind; and of whom it is written: Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against.

For which of the philosophers, which of the Gentiles, which of the heretics does not judge Christ, laying down laws for him about his birth, his passion, his resurrection and his substance? Nor is it surprising that Christ, according to the reality of the body he assumed, should say, Woe is me, my mother, since in another place too these words plainly fit his person: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest, and like a cluster at the vintage, with no ear of grain to eat the firstfruits!

And lest we should think that the lowliness of these groans refers to the Word of God, the passage at once shows who it is that laments: Woe is me, my soul, for the godly man has perished from the earth! We do not mean that we divide the persons, as the impious do. We mean that one and the same Son of God speaks now according to the flesh, now as the Word of God.

I have not lent at interest, nor has anyone lent to me; all curse me. For this the Seventy have: I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me; Theodotion: I have not owed, nor has anyone owed me. In the person of Christ, all these have this sense: “No one has offered himself to receive my money worthily, nor has anyone lent to me by cherishing the saints and the poor and so making me his debtor.” Or: “I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me; for no one was willing to receive as much as I desired to give.

Nor has anyone profited me, for the salvation of the creature is the Creator's gain.” Or else: “I have not owed, nor has anyone owed me; no one has given me as much as I longed to receive, nor has anyone made me his debtor in anything.” And what he adds, “nor has anyone owed me,” has this sense: “For how could anyone owe me interest who did not deign to accept a loan?” All, he says, curse me. For which of the heretics and those in error does not curse Christ by believing perversely and blaspheming more perversely still?

The Lord says: Surely your remnant shall be for good; surely I came to meet you in the time of affliction and in the time of tribulation — and distress — against the enemy. These words can also be taken as spoken in the person of Jeremiah, who was compelled to prophesy in the worst of times, when captivity was already imminent, and to suffer harsh treatment from an unbelieving people.

To what he had said above, Woe is me, mother, why did you bear me a man to be judged and set apart by all the earth? and the rest, the Lord replies: “Do not consider the present but the future, for your remnant and your latter end will be for good. Indeed, even now, when your enemies longed to crush you, I stood by you, and you were protected by my help.” This can be referred both to Jeremiah and, by the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, to the Savior.

In place of what we have translated from the Hebrew, from all curse me down to the place where it is written in the time of tribulation against the enemy, I found the following in the common edition: My strength has failed among those who curse me. So be it, Lord, as they prosper, if I did not stand before you in the time of their affliction and in the time of their tribulation, for good, against the enemy! The sense is: “My strength has failed among those who curse me. For they do not understand my power, which is made perfect in weakness, and the more they curse me, the more my strength fails in them.”

And either the prophet or the Lord adds: So be it, Lord, as they prosper! That is: “Let the curses that my enemies speak come upon me, and let them be guided toward good, if I did not stand in your sight in the time of their tribulation and distress, when the enemy was laying them waste and hastening to capture them, and pray to you for them and say: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” But we also often find Jeremiah praying for the people in this book.

Shall iron be allied with iron from the north, and bronze? Symmachus: Shall iron harm iron from the north, and bronze? The Seventy and Theodotion: Will iron know, and a covering of bronze? The reason for the variation is clear. The word iare, which is written in this place, means both “friendship” and “malice” because of the ambiguity of its pronunciation; and if the letter daleth is read in place of the letter resh, which looks like daleth, it means “knowledge” and “recognition.” What is said should be understood as follows:

“Do not grieve that the people is your enemy; for when you announce harsh things, one who is hard cannot love you.” Or: the Babylonians, who come from the north and are the hardest iron, will not be able to join in friendship with this people, which is harder still and untamed like bronze. Or: the hardest iron, that is, the people of Israel, is unworthy of the knowledge of God, for it has come to such malice that it is encased in a harder metal, bronze.

Your wealth and your treasures I will give up to plunder for nothing — or, without price — for all your sins, throughout all your borders. And I will bring your enemies — or, I will make you serve your enemies — from a land you do not know; for a fire has been kindled in my fury; it will burn upon you. “All your substance,” he says, “I will hand over to your enemies without any price because of the sins you have committed throughout all your borders. Therefore I will bring your enemies, or make you serve them in the land of the Chaldeans, because my fire, once kindled in my fury, will burn in you and cannot be quenched. For you have supplied the fuel for your own burning, so that my fire consumes the wood, hay and stubble that are in you.” Thus the cause of the burning lies not in the Lord but in those who supplied fuel for the fire.

You know, O Lord; remember me and visit me, and rescue me from those who persecute me! Do not, in your patience, take me away; know that for your sake I have borne reproach! Your words were found, and I ate them — or, from those who reject your words; consume them — and your word became — or, will be — to me the joy and gladness of my heart, for your name is called upon me, O Lord God of hosts!

The words we have given, “You know,” are not found in the Seventy. Happy is the conscience that bears reproach for God's sake. Therefore he says: “Your words were found, which you spoke through my mouth, and I ate them; that is, they became food for me.” Or, according to Symmachus: “I received them, so that words which had formerly brought me reproach might be turned into gladness for me.”

Hence even the Babylonians acknowledge that what Jeremiah had foretold was fulfilled. Or the sense is this: “I felt distress, I bore the miseries inflicted by a persecuting people, yet I rejoiced that I had obeyed your commands, and for your name's sake I endured hardships.”

I did not sit in the council of revelers, and I gloried — or, I was afraid; because of your hand I sat alone, for you filled me with bitterness. Why has my pain become perpetual — or, why are those who grieve me made strong — and my wound past hope, refusing to be healed — or, my wound is severe; how shall I be healed? It has become to me like the deceit of faithless waters — or, like deceptive water that cannot be trusted.

The Hebrews think these words are spoken in the person of Jerusalem: that she sat alone, was filled with bitterness, and her pain became perpetual, and that the words of the prophets, by which the people promised themselves prosperity, passed away falsely as waters pass by. But it is better for us to take these words as spoken in the person of the prophet, as the words of a holy man who did not sit in the council, or secret gathering, of revelers, either because he feared the hand of God hanging over him, or rather because he gloried in having no fellowship with the wicked.

“I sat alone,” he says, in keeping with what is written: I have not sat with the council of vanity, nor will I go in with those who do wicked things. I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly; and in another place: I am solitary until I pass on. “Because of your hand,” he says, “I sat alone, fearing you and always expecting your hand to fall upon me. I refused to sit in the council of revelers; instead I swallowed

my bitterness, so that I might prepare joy for myself in the future. Nor did I have any respite from my pain; I was weighed down by unceasing misery, so that I looked for no remedy. For those who grieved me prevailed, and my wound became severe. But I had this consolation, that it was like deceptive and passing water. For just as passing waters are seen while they flow and then glide away, so every assault of the enemies has passed away with your help.”

May the Lord grant us too not to sit in the council of revelers and of those who give no thought to the future, nor to yield to adversity, but always to dread the sentence of God and to say with the prophet: I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness! “Let the hidden and secret gathering of revelers, then, rejoice in the present time, and by no means the council of the wise. For me, let it be good to cleave to God, to place my hope in the Lord, to be filled with reproaches, and to await the sentence of my judge. When the end comes, that sentence will show in deed that all sorrow and bitterness have flowed away like waters.”

Therefore thus says the Lord: If you turn back, I will turn you back, and you shall stand before my face; and if you separate the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you to this people a wall of bronze, strong; and they will fight against you and will not prevail, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, says the Lord. And I will free you from the hand of the most wicked, and redeem you from the hand of the strong, or of the pestilent.

It is clear that the preceding words were spoken not by Jerusalem at all but by the prophet. The Lord answers him: 'If you turn the people back from their sins, I too will turn you from tribulation to gladness, and you shall stand before my face, just as the angels stand in God's presence, daily beholding his face; and if you separate the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth. Do not think,' he says, 'that a good work has no reward. If by your words you set apart all my holy ones from the number of sinners, you shall be as my mouth and shall be joined to my commandments. For they ought to imitate you, not you them.'

'Do not be afraid and say, "Why has my pain become perpetual, and my wound severe" (or "desperate"), "so that I despair of being able to be healed?" For I will make you like a wall of bronze, very strong, so that you may resist the adversary with all your strength and have me as your helper; and I will free you from the hand of the most wicked (or "the pestilent"), and redeem you, either with my own blood or, for the present, with my help.' Let us consider how great a reward the teacher's word has if it is able to free someone from error and lead him out of the number of sinners!

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons and daughters in this place. For thus says the Lord concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them, and concerning their fathers from whose stock they were born in this land: They shall die deaths of sickness; they shall not be lamented and they shall not be buried; they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth, and they shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, and their corpses shall be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth.

If, at a time when captivity was imminent, the prophet is forbidden to marry a wife, so that he may not have tribulation of the flesh and, on top of his own grief, be tormented by the miseries of a wife and children as well, how much more does the apostle command, since the time has been shortened and the end is at hand, that even those who have wives should be as though they had none!

Hence the new heretic's censure is superfluous, by which he attacks our teaching that second and third marriages do not come from the law but from indulgence. For it is one thing to do what is good in itself, another for something to be permitted so that you may not do worse. Indeed, the apostle himself gives the reasons why he wants young widows to marry, adding: For some of them have already turned aside after Satan. And yet this man, at once a teacher of continence and perpetual chastity and blasphemously making himself equal to God, praises third and fourth marriages, which I would call not so much marriages as consolations for misery and the last plank for the shipwrecked—unless perhaps he grants this indulgence to his Amazons so that they may go on waging the wars of lust right up to decrepit old age.

Why the prophet is barred from marrying a wife has an obvious reason: because, with the siege close at hand, all would perish by pestilence, sword and famine, and the number of the dying would be so great that the duty of burial would be overwhelmed, and the corpses would lie like dung, to be torn apart by birds and beasts.

And this should be noted: that to waste away through sickness and long infirmity is the wrath of God. Thus Joram, the son of Jehoshaphat, is consumed by disease, and the apostle teaches that those who have profaned holy things fall sick, waste away and die.

For thus says the Lord: Do not enter the house of feasting, nor go to lament, nor console them, for I have taken away my peace from this people, says the Lord, my mercy and compassion. Both great and small shall die in this land; they shall not be buried nor lamented, and no one shall cut himself or make himself bald for them. And they shall not break bread among them for the mourner, to console him over the dead, nor give them the cup to drink to console them for their father and mother. And you shall not enter the house of feasting, to sit with them and eat and drink.

The apostle commands that we should not even take food with those who turn away from God; and further: Do not even say "Greetings" to such people! The Savior also forbids the apostles to greet anyone on the road; and so Elisha too forbids Gehazi, as he goes to heal the boy, to exchange greetings. Now it is customary to bring food to mourners and to prepare a feast, which the Greeks call perideipna, and which among our people are commonly called parentalia, because the due rites are celebrated for parents. And elsewhere divine Scripture says: Give wine to those who are in mourning—that is, so that they may forget their grief.

The prophet is therefore commanded not to console anyone of the people, not to mingle in the feasts of God's enemies, and not to perform the due rites over the funerals of the dead. For it is one thing to die by the common law of nature, another to have been slain by the sentence of God. 'I have taken away,' he says, 'my peace from this people, and they are unworthy of mercy; I will spare no age, but great and small alike will perish, so that they will even lack burial.' Nor will they cut themselves, he says, nor will anyone make himself bald for them.

This was a custom among the ancients, and it persists to this day among some of the Jews: in mourning they cut their arms and shave themselves bald, which we read Job also did. Hence the prophet too is told not to break bread among them, nor go in to console anyone for the dead, not to offer drink, not to enter the house of feasting, and not to mingle with those who have been made ready for God's sentence. And if this is said about mourners, what will become of heretics, whose word spreads like a cancer, and who daily lay low in the church the corpses of those they have deceived?

For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will take away from this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.

And when you have announced all these words to this people, and they say to you, "Why has the Lord pronounced all this great evil against us? What is our iniquity, and what is our sin that we have sinned against the Lord our God?" you shall say to them: Because your fathers forsook me, says the Lord, and went after foreign gods, and served them and worshipped them, and forsook me and did not keep my law. And you too have done worse than your fathers.

When the church has sinned, all joy and all gladness are taken from it—that gladness of which the apostle says: Rejoice; again I say, rejoice; and the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, of whom it is written: He who has the bride is the bridegroom. 'But if,' he says, 'the people ask you why they suffer these things, and seek the causes of their miseries, you shall answer them: Because your fathers forsook me, says the Lord—those who preside over you in the churches—and went after foreign gods—whose god is their belly, and avarice and luxury, and whose glory is in their shame—and served them—for by whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also a slave—and worshipped them—for each one worships what he loves—and forsook me and did not keep my law.'

It belongs properly to priests not only to teach the law but also to do it, so that they teach the peoples subject to them and the flock entrusted to them not by words alone but by example. And lest perhaps they should say, 'It is an unjust sentence that the fathers eat sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge,' he adds: And you too have done worse than your fathers, so that just punishments may fall upon those who have sinned worse than their fathers.

For behold, each of you walks after the perversity of his evil heart, so as not to listen to me. And I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve foreign gods day and night, who will give you no rest.

Once forsaken by the Lord, they do what is not fitting, going after the desires of their evil heart, from which come forth the worst thoughts; and therefore they are separated from the church, so as to go into a far country which neither they nor their fathers had known before they sinned, there to serve foreign gods, which are not gods but are thought to be so through the error of those who worship them.

As for his adding [?] 'day and night,' this shows the perpetual persistence of sinners in wickedness, since they serve shameful deeds by day and lust by night. Who will give you no rest, he says—there is no doubt that he means the false gods, of whom he said: and there you shall serve foreign gods.

So whatever we sin, whatever we do day and night and whatever evil works we commit, is the command of the demons, who never give us rest but always drive us to add offenses to offenses and to pile up a heap of sins.

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when it shall no longer be said, "As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt," but, "As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north and out of all the lands to which I had driven them"; and I will bring them back to their own land, which I gave to their fathers.

Here the future restoration of the people of Israel is plainly foretold, and mercy after the captivity. In the literal sense this was partly fulfilled under Zerubbabel, Jeshua the high priest and Ezra; according to the spiritual understanding it is described as something to be fulfilled more truly and more perfectly in Christ. 'The time will come,' he says, 'when it will no longer be said that the people was brought back from Egypt by Moses and Aaron, but that it was brought back from the land of the north when Cyrus, king of the Persians, released the captives.'

And from all the lands, he says—which will be fulfilled not in the time of Cyrus but at the very end, as the apostle says: 'After the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.' We can also apply this to the persecutions that befell our people from the days of Nero—of whom the apostle writes, And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion—up to the time of Maximinus: how the Lord had mercy on his people and brought them back to their own land, that is, without doubt, into the church, which he gave to their fathers, the apostles and apostolic men.

Behold, I will send many fishers, says the Lord, and they shall fish for them; and after this I will send them many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and from every hill and from the caves of the rocks. For my eyes are upon all their ways; they are not hidden from my face, nor has their iniquity been concealed from my eyes. And first I will repay double their iniquities and their sins, by which they defiled my land with the carcasses of their idols and filled my inheritance with their abominations.

There are different interpretations of this passage. The Jews hold that it signifies the Chaldeans, who are described under the name of fishers, and afterwards the Romans, who are compared to hunters and who hunted down the unhappy people from the mountains and hills and the caves of the rocks. The Lord says that he himself did this because he had looked upon their ways and repaid their iniquities, by which they had defiled the land in venerating images, and polluted his inheritance with the abominations of idols.

Our writers, however, more rightly and better think that the prophet prophesied this of the future. For since he had said above, I will bring them back to their own land, which I gave to their fathers, he now shows how they are to be brought back: that he first sends the apostles, to whom the Savior said, Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men, and afterwards hunters—whom we may take to be either churchmen or angels—who, when the time of the consummation has come, will hunt all the saints from the mountains of lofty doctrines, from the hills of good works, and from the caves of the rocks, that is, the apostles and apostolic men.

For not only is Christ the rock, but he also granted to the apostle Peter to be called a rock, and those who rest in his understanding are rightly said to have been brought out of the rock. And he shows that either the apostles or those who are to be hunted afterwards had sins and received double for their iniquities. For the servant who knows his master's will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows. It should also be known that 'first' is found in the Hebrew but omitted in the Septuagint edition.

When he says, First I will repay double their iniquities and their sins, he implies that after they have received evils they will also receive good things. Those who are to be brought over afterwards defiled the Lord's land with the carcasses of their idols and filled his inheritance with their abominations, so that the whole world may become subject to God and be preserved not by its own merit but by his mercy. What we have given here from the Hebrew, they are not hidden from my face, is not found in the Septuagint.

O Lord, my strength and my might, and my refuge in the day of tribulation (or "of evils")! All human strength without the power of God, which is Christ, is reckoned weak and worthless. Hence we must flee to God and say: Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation; and in another place: He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.
The day of tribulation or of evils is to be understood as that of which the apostle also speaks: to rescue us from the present evil age, and: redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

To you the nations will come from the ends of the earth and will say: Truly our fathers possessed a lie, a vanity that did not profit them. The Septuagint: To you the nations will come from the ends of the earth and will say: How false were the idols our fathers possessed, and there is no profit in them!

After Israel has been cast out and carried off by the fishers and hunters, the multitude of the Gentiles is then called to faith and confesses that it, or its fathers, had lived in former error. And those who say, 'How false were the idols our fathers possessed, in which there is no profit!' confess that the things to which they are passing over are true and supported by every safeguard.

Shall a man make gods for himself, and they are not gods? This too is spoken by the Gentiles who have come to the Savior from the ends of the earth, reproaching the ignorance both of themselves and of their ancestors, by which they thought gods could be made by man, when it belongs to God to make men.

Therefore, behold, I will show them this time, I will show them my hand and my power, and they shall know that my name is the Lord. The hand of God, through which he made all things, and the power of which the apostle said, 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God,' is shown to the Gentiles once the Son's passion has been accomplished.

And he put it beautifully: 'I will show them this time; I will show them openly, and not as before in shadow and image and the prophecy of things to come, so that, once they have come to know, they may know my name and hear from the Son: Father, I have made your name known to men.'

The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with a point of diamond, engraved upon the breadth of their heart (or "on the breast of their heart") and on the horns of their altars. Concerning the nations that had turned to the Lord it was said above: Behold, I will show them this time, I will show them my hand and my power; now he speaks of Israel, which has been cast off: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with a point of diamond, and so on.

Why this was omitted by the Septuagint I do not know, unless perhaps they were sparing their own people, as it is clear they did in Isaiah too: Cease then from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself has been reckoned exalted; and many things of this kind, which, if I wished to set them all out, would require not a book but books. The sins of the Gentiles have been blotted out, because, having turned to the Lord from the ends of the earth, they heard this: Praise the Lord, all you nations; praise him, all you peoples, for his mercy has been confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord endures for ever; and of them he had said to Moses: Let me alone, that I may destroy this people, and I will make of you a great nation.

But the sin of Judah, indelible and, so to speak, impossible to abolish by any means, is written with a pen of iron, with a point of diamond, which in Hebrew is called samir—not that there is any point called samir, but that the diamond stone, which received this name because it is untameable and unbreakable, has such brilliance and smoothness that one can write on it with an iron pen without any hindrance, so that the hard substance of iron writes on the harder tablet of diamond, and what is written lasts for ever. For they themselves said: His blood be upon us and upon our children.

Hence it is also engraved, or carved, on the horns of their altars, so that the works of their sacrilege may endure in everlasting memory. And if this is so, where is that notion, invented by a doting old woman, that a man can be without sin if he wishes, and that God's commandments are easy?

When their children remember their altars and their groves and the leafy trees on the high mountains, sacrificing in the field, I will give your strength and all your treasures as plunder, and your high places, because of your sins in all your borders. And you shall be left alone, cut off from your inheritance which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land you do not know, because you have kindled a fire in my fury; it shall burn for ever.

These words too are not found in the Septuagint, for the same reason, I think, that we gave above: namely, so that an eternal sentence should not remain upon them. You shall be left alone, he says, cut off from your inheritance which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land you do not know—either under the Babylonians or, as is truer, under the Romans. For they themselves kindled the fire and provoked the most merciful Lord to fury, and the fire of his fury will burn for ever.

I am ashamed of the contentiousness of our own people, who find fault with the Hebrew truth. The Jews read what tells against themselves, and the church does not know what tells in its favor. Therefore let us, who are sons of the apostles, remember the iniquities of the former people and bear witness that they suffered justly.

The 'high places,' which in Hebrew are called bamoth, can also be taken as directed against heretics, who have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has gone over the earth; who have broken out into such madness that they alone have remained without the grace of the Holy Spirit and have lost the Lord's inheritance, namely the original truth of the faith. Hence an eternal burning is prepared for them, and slavery to the demons, who are their enemies and avengers.

Thus says the Lord: Cursed is the man who trusts (or "has hope") in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. For he shall be like a tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see when good comes, but shall dwell in dry places in the desert, in a salt land and uninhabitable.

If every man who trusts in man is cursed, and Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior holy and exalted above all in virtues, nevertheless confess him to be a mere man, then they will be cursed, having their hope in man. But if it is objected to us that we too believe in him who says, But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God; this Abraham did not do. You do the works of your father, we will answer with the apostle's words: Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.

Indeed, the same apostle writes to the Galatians at the beginning of his letter: Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me. For if death has been swallowed up in victory, why should not the lowliness of the flesh, which was assumed for the salvation of mankind, have passed into the majesty of the Godhead, so that he made both one, and we worship not the creature but the Creator, who is blessed for ever?

Cursed, then, is not only he who has hope in man, but he who makes flesh his arm—that is, his strength—and who thinks that whatever he has done is due not to the Lord's mercy but to his own power. For whoever does this, his heart departs from the Lord, claiming that he can do what he cannot. And he will be like a tamarisk—which in Hebrew is called aroher, or, as Symmachus translated, an unfruitful tree in the wilderness—and he will not see when the good things come which the multitude of the Gentiles is to see, but will dwell in dry places in the desert.

This is said of the Jewish people, who dwell in the desert and bear no fruit, and are in a salt land, which produces no fruit, and an uninhabitable one, which has neither God as its guest, nor the protection of angels, nor the grace of the Holy Spirit, nor the knowledge of teachers.

Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence (or: his hope). He will be like a tree that has been transplanted (or: a fruitful tree) by the waters, that sends out its roots toward the moisture. It will not fear when the heat comes, and its leaf will be green (or: its little branches will be in leaf), and in the time (or: year) of drought it will not be anxious (or: it will not fear), nor will it ever cease to bear fruit.

That earlier saying may be taken as spoken of the Jews and of the heretics, who place their hope in a man, namely in their own Christ, whom they suppose will come not as the Son of God but as a mere man. By contrast, the man of the Church, who trusts in the Lord, hears this: "Know that the Lord himself is God." He trusts in the Lord, and he will be compared to that tree of which the first psalm also sings: "He will be like a tree planted beside the streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall."

"By the waters" means the grace of the Holy Spirit, his various gifts. "That sends out its roots toward the moisture" means that it receives its fruitfulness from the Lord. But we can also put it another way: we have been transplanted out of the drought of the Jews into the everlasting grace of baptism.

"And it will not fear," he says, "when the heat comes" — whether the time of persecution or the day of judgment — "and its leaf will be green" (or: "it will have little branches in leaf"), so that it never fears drought but blossoms with the grace of every virtue. And when the time or year of drought comes, it will not be afraid, when the Lord in his anger commands the clouds not to pour rain on Israel.

What follows, "nor will it cease to bear fruit," can explain the passage written in Mark, that the Lord came to the fig tree and found no fruit on it, because it was not yet the season, and cursed it, so that it should never bear fruit again. For whoever trusts in the Lord, and whose confidence is the Lord, will not be afraid even in the time of the Jews' drought, but will always bear fruit, believing in him who died once for us and dies no more, and who says: "I am the life."

The heart of all is perverse and unsearchable; who can know it? I the Lord search the heart and test the inner parts, who give to each according to his way and according to the fruit of his devices. The Septuagint has: "The heart is deep above all things, and it is man; who can know him?" and the rest likewise. The Hebrew word enos is written with four letters, aleph, nun, waw and shin. If it is read enos, it means "man"; but if anus, it means "unsearchable" or "desperate," because no one is able to discover the hearts of men.

Symmachus, however, translated this passage as follows: "The heart of all is unsearchable; and who is the man who can find it out?" Our people are accustomed, with good intentions indeed but not according to knowledge, to use this passage against the Jews: that the Lord and Savior is a man according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, and that no one can know the mystery of his birth — in line with what is written, "Who will declare his generation?" — except God alone, who searches out hidden things and renders to each according to his works.

It is better, however, to take it simply: no one knows the secrets of men's thoughts except God alone. For he had said above, "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man," and by contrast, "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord."

So, lest we should think human judgment reliable, he added that the hearts of nearly everyone are perverse, as the psalmist says: "Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others" — undoubtedly meaning thoughts. And in Genesis: "But God saw that the wickedness of men on the earth was great, and that every thought of their heart was bent on evil at all times"; and again: "For the mind and thought of the human heart are inclined to evil from youth." Through these we learn that God alone knows their thoughts. But if it is said of the Savior, "But Jesus, seeing their thoughts," and no one can see thoughts except God alone, then Christ is God, who searches hearts and tests the inner parts and will render to each according to his works.

The partridge has hatched (or: gathered) what it did not lay — and as the Septuagint translated: "The partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not lay" — it makes its riches without justice; in the middle of its days it will leave them (or: in the middle of his days they will leave him), and at its end it will be a fool.

The writers of natural history — of beasts and birds as well as of trees and plants — chief among whom are Aristotle and Theophrastus among the Greeks and Pliny the Elder among us, say that it is the nature of the partridge to steal the eggs of another partridge, that is, eggs not its own, and to sit on them and keep them warm; and when the young have grown, they fly away from it and abandon their foster parent.

Of this kind are the rich who plunder what belongs to others and, with no thought for God's judgment, make riches without justice, which they leave behind halfway through their lives when they are carried off by sudden death, when it is said to them: "Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" And nothing is more foolish than not to look ahead to the last things and to think brief things everlasting.

Others, however, because of the account above, and because of another one in which they say the partridge is most quarrelsome and unclean, to the point of defiling the one it has defeated, interpret the devil under its name, since he gathered to himself riches not his own, saying to the Lord: "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." His riches, wickedly gathered by him, will leave him and through the apostles will return to the Lord; and he who thought himself most prudent will be judged a fool by all.
