As for the Septuagint's "The partridge cried out," it should be referred to the heretics: this partridge, the devil, cried out through the leaders of the heretics and gathered what he did not lay, gathering to himself a multitude of the deceived, who will afterward abandon him, and he will be proved by the judgment of all to be the greatest fool.

A throne of glory on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctification, O Lord, the hope of Israel. All who forsake you will be put to shame! Those who turn away will be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the spring (or: fountain) of living waters, the Lord.

The partridge having been abandoned for its folly, the hope of Israel — that is, of the people of God who believe in the Lord — is he who made all things, whose throne is glorious and exalted from the beginning, and who is the place of sanctification for all believers; for the Lord is not in a place, but wherever he is, that place is sanctified. By contrast, those who forsake the Lord will be put to everlasting shame, and those who turn away or depart from him will be written in the earth, blotted out of the book of the living.

For just as one who can say with the apostle, "But our citizenship is in heaven," is written in heaven, so one who forsakes the Lord or turns away from him will be written in the earth with those who set their minds on earthly things. And the reason why they are written in the earth is plain: because they have forsaken the fountain of life, the Lord, or the fountain of living waters, the Lord, who says in the Gospel: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink! Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive.

Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise! In the Gospel many physicians had treated the woman with the flow of blood, who had spent all her property on them, and yet she could be cured by none of them except by him who is the true physician and in whose wings is healing. So now too the prophet, having suffered reproaches from the people and having often been beset by plots, longs to be healed and saved by him who is his true praise and true medicine.

See, they say to me: "Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!" But I have not been troubled in following you as shepherd (or: I have not grown weary following you), and I have not desired the day of man; you know. What came out of my lips was right in your sight (or: is before your face). Do not be a terror to me, you who are my hope in the day of affliction (or: do not become a stranger to me, sparing me in the evil day)!

Those who do not believe that what has been spoken will come to pass say to the prophet, "Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!" — taking the postponement of the sentence for its abandonment. But while they are saying this, he says: "I have not been troubled or grown weary following you as shepherd, or walking in your footsteps; nor was I content with this alone, but I have not desired the day of man" — whether a longer life or any of the prosperous things of this world. And he calls as witness the one who is also judge: "You know." There follows: "What came out of my lips

was right in your sight" — so that he never lied and never said anything contrary to the will of the Lord. "Do not be a terror to me," he says, "you who are my hope in the day of affliction!" This is clear according to the Hebrew.

But according to what the Septuagint translated, saying, "Do not become a stranger to me, sparing me in the evil day," the sense is: "Do not spare me in the present age, which is evil, but repay me according to my sins, so that I may have everlasting rest. For I know it is written: Whom the Lord loves he reproves, and he scourges every son whom he receives." The evil day is either the whole present age, or the day of judgment for those who are tormented for their sins.

Let those who persecute me be put to shame, and let me not be put to shame! Let them be dismayed, and let me not be dismayed! Bring upon them the day of affliction and crush them with a double crushing! The prophet calls down curses on those who taunt him about the word of the Lord and say, "Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!" — that those who persecute him may be put to shame and blush and return to salvation; that they who lie may be dismayed, and not he who foretells the truth; and that when the day of vengeance comes, God may crush them with a double crushing, by famine and by sword.

Thus says the Lord to me: Go and stand in the gate (or: the gates) of the children of the people, through which the kings of Judah come in and go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say to them: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah and all Judah (or: Judea) and all inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates! "Since,"

he says, "they scorn to listen to your words and do not come to you to ask what God's sentence is, go yourself to the busiest place, whether the gates of the temple or of the city, through which the kings and all the common people go in and out, so that they are forced to hear, and so that you may preach the word of God in season and out of season, and no excuse may be left to them that they failed to act because they had not heard."

Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the sabbath day or bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem! Do not carry loads out of your houses on the sabbath day, and do no work at all, but keep the sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers! Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but hardened their neck — and, which is not in the Hebrew, "more than their fathers" — so as not to hear me and not to receive instruction.

"And it shall be," he says, "if you listen to me, says the Lord, and do not bring burdens through the gates of this city on the sabbath day, and if you keep the sabbath day holy and do no work on it, then there will enter through the gates of this city kings and princes sitting on the throne of David and riding in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and this city will be inhabited forever.

And they will come from the cities of Judah and from the area around Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin, and from the lowlands and from the hill country and from the south, bringing whole burnt offerings and victims (or: incense) and sacrifice (or: manna) and frankincense, and they will bring an offering (or: praise) into the house of the Lord.

But if you do not listen to me, to keep the sabbath day holy and not to carry a burden or bring it in through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day, I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem and will not be quenched."

So as not to tear into pieces the commandment of the sabbath renewed through Jeremiah, I decided to set down the whole of it, so that we might understand everything together. He guards his soul who does not carry the burdens of sins on the day of rest, the sabbath, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem, by which we ought to understand the virtues. "And do not," he says, "carry loads out of your houses" — for they are not to be carried but cast away entirely — "and do no work at all," whether servile work or that of which it is written, "Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both the one and the other"; rather, that work is to be done of which the Savior speaks: "Work for the food that does not perish."

"Keep the sabbath day holy," he says, so that we may spend the whole time of our life in holiness, as our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did. And though God commanded these things, they did not incline their ear — the ear of the mind, of course, not of the flesh — but hardened their neck, throwing off the yoke of the law and, by a metaphor, taking on the likeness of untamed animals.

Let us see what the reward is of those who do not carry burdens on the sabbath day and keep it holy. "There will enter," he says, "through the gates of this city kings" — those whose heart is in the hand of God and who rule their own bodies — "and princes sitting on the throne of David," so as to imitate the example of Christ, "and riding in chariots and on horses," of which it is written: "The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the holy place," and elsewhere: "Your riding is salvation"; every man who confesses God and who dwells in Jerusalem, of which it was said, "His place was made in Salem" — that is, in peace — "and his dwelling in Zion"; and the Church of God will be inhabited forever.

And they will come from the cities of Judah and from the area around Jerusalem, of which we have already spoken; and from the land of Benjamin, who is the son of power and of the right hand; and from the lowlands, which in Hebrew is called sephela and signifies the plain, historical understanding; and from the hill country, that is, from lofty doctrines; and from the south, of which it is written, "God will come from the south," the source of warmth and full light, where all cold is driven out.

"Bringing," he says, "whole burnt offerings" — consecrating themselves to God — "and a victim" or "incense," so that they may say: "A sacrifice to the Lord is a troubled spirit," and "We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place," and elsewhere, "Let my prayer rise like incense in your sight"; "and sacrifice," for which the Septuagint put the Hebrew word itself, manaa, which through a very bad habit, or rather through the carelessness of copyists, is read as "manna" in our books; "and frankincense," of which it was said, "Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba?"; "and they will bring an offering," which in Hebrew is called thoda and can be translated "thanksgiving," and which the Septuagint rendered "praise," "into the house of David" — undoubtedly meaning into the Church.

These are the rewards of those who keep the sabbath holy and are weighed down by no burden. "But if," he says, "you do not listen to my commandments, and do what I commanded should not be done, I will kindle a fire in its gates" — that is, in Jerusalem's — the fire of which it is said, "They are all adulterers; their hearts are like an oven" — "which will devour the houses," or streets, "of Jerusalem" — which the Septuagint rendered ἄμφοδα, and Aquila and Symmachus βάρεις, that is, "towered houses," and which in Hebrew are called armanoth — "and this fire will never be quenched," as the apostle says: "The fire will test what sort of work each one's is," and again: "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire."

But if our Judaizers reject the figurative interpretation, they will be forced either to be Jews and, along with keeping the sabbath, to be circumcised, or else to find fault with the Savior, who on the sabbath ordered the paralytic to carry his bed, as the evangelist says: "For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he was not only breaking the sabbath but also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God."
BOOK FOUR

The devil always lies in wait for a good work and sets snares everywhere for those who walk, as the prophet tells of the plots of his henchmen: "Beside the path they have set a stumbling block for me"; and the Gospel teaches this same thing more fully, saying that the birds of the air snatch away and destroy the seeds scattered along the road.

Why I have used this opening, brother Eusebius, what follows will show. Busy with the many crowds streaming here from all over the world, and with the care of the holy brothers and of the monastery, I was dictating commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what was lacking in leisure might be made up by diligence, when suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno — their apatheia and anamartesia, that is, "impassibility" and "sinlessness" — which was long ago slain in Origen, and more recently in his disciples Grunnius, Evagrius of Pontus and Jovinian, began to come back to life, and to hiss not only in the West but also in parts of the East, and in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, to stain a great many and to grow day by day, while they teach it in secret and deny it in public.

After keeping silent a long time and swallowing my pain in silence, I was compelled by the repeated demands of the brothers to answer it; yet even so I have not gone so far as to name its authors, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced; for I am an enemy not of men but of error. They, to pay me back in kind and sink the tooth of their resentment into me, have patched together the old slanders of their masters, and have been shown to be so tongue-tied and wretched that they could not even speak ill of me in words of their own.

Their dirges were refuted at that time by the books published against them; whoever cares to read these will see clearly that they are, as Isaiah says, dumb dogs that cannot bark — having indeed the will and the frenzy to lie, but lacking the skill to invent and to bark.

To them I will speak briefly: what you teach is either good or bad. If good, defend it openly; if bad, why do you secretly slaughter wretched people by your error, and parade an exposition of the right faith in order to deceive the simple? If it is true, why is it hidden? If it is false, why is it written? What madness is this, I ask? The apostle instructs us to be ready to give satisfaction to everyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us, and the prophet cries out, "I spoke of your testimonies before kings and was not put to shame"; yet these people shun the public eye and whisper in the corners of the lost, and they grieve as if on their own behalf over things they fear to own as theirs [?].

And when we have spoken in general terms against [?] and heretics, they complain that they are the target, and, their indignation long concealed, they reveal the bad state of their conscience. But if we must take care not to seem to wound an old friendship by cutting off this most arrogant heresy with the spiritual sword, then we shall have to endure the torments of a betrayed faith and say with the prophet: "I was turned about in misery while the thorn was fixed in me."

Let them rather hear that apostolic saying: "We must obey God rather than men," and again: "If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ." But I will pursue these matters more fully in a work of their own, unless they fall silent. Now let us take up again the journey we began through Jeremiah, and running briefly through the fourth book on him, let us linger only on what is obscure.

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down to the potter's house, and there you will hear my words! And I went down to the potter's house, and behold, he was doing his work at the wheel — or: on the stones. And the vessel that he was making from clay with his hands was spoiled; and turning — or: and again — he made it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his eyes to make it.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not do with you as this potter has done, O house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, like clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel! Suddenly — or: in the end — I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root it out — or: to take it away — and to pull it down and destroy it.

If that nation repents of its evil, for which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil that I planned to do to it. And suddenly — or: in the end — I shall speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so as not to listen to my voice, I will repent of the good that I said I would do to it.

Through all the senses, it is true, things reach the mind's judgment and understanding: through hearing, smell, taste and touch. But what is seen with the eyes is held more firmly in the mind. That is why the prophet is told to go to the potter's house and hear the Lord's commands there. 'And when,' he says, 'I had gone and gone down to the potter's house, he was doing his work at the wheel.' The Septuagint, misled by an ambiguous word, translated this as 'stones'; for 'abanim', depending on the context and on differences of pronunciation, means both an 'instrument', that is, the potter's 'wheel', and 'stones'.

'And when,' he says, 'I saw a vessel being made from clay, suddenly it was spoiled.' This happened through the working of God's providence, so that the craftsman's hand, without knowing it, shaped a parable through its own mistake. And that potter, who had lost the clay vessel on the turning wheel, made himself another one, as seemed good to him. And at once the Lord said to the prophet: 'If a potter has this power, to make again from the same clay what had been spoiled, shall I not be able to do this with you, who, as far as it depends on you, seem to have perished?'

And to indicate free will, he says that he announces evils to this or that nation and kingdom, and again good things; and yet what he has foretold does not come to pass, but the opposite happens. Good things come to the wicked if they repent, and evils to the good if, after receiving promises, they have turned to sin. We say this not because God does not know that this or that nation or kingdom is going to do this or that, but because he leaves man to his own will, so that he may receive rewards or punishments according to his own deserts.

Yet what happens will not, on that account, belong wholly to man, but to the grace of him who has bestowed all things. For freedom of choice must be preserved in such a way that the grace of the Giver surpasses it in everything, according to the prophetic saying: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman has kept watch in vain. For it depends not on him who wills, nor on him who runs, but on God who shows mercy.

Now therefore speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying: These things — or: thus — says the Lord: Behold, I am fashioning evil against you and devising a plan against you. Let each of you turn back from his evil way, and set right your ways and your pursuits! But they said: We have lost hope — or: we shall be strong —; for we will follow our own plans, and each of us will do the wickedness — or: what has pleased — of his evil heart. Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask among the nations: who has heard such horrible things as the virgin Israel has done to excess?

The Lord completes the parable that he had taught both by sight and by words, and says: 'Behold, I am fashioning evil against you, as a potter fashions clay.' Here 'evil' is meant in the sense of Isaiah, who says: making peace and creating evil, not that it is evil in itself, but that it seems evil to those who suffer it. 'And I am devising a plan against you,' that is, to pass sentence according to what you deserve. 'Change your works and set right your ways, so that the punishment too may be changed into prosperity!'

'But they,' he says, 'answered on the contrary: We shall be strong' — that is, in evil works. Or, according to Aquila, 'we have lost hope', and according to Symmachus, 'we have given up'. Both offend God: either one thinks he can by no means be saved, or he has lost heart in seeking to appease God. 'And we will follow,' he says, 'our own plans.' Where then, apart from the grace [?]

of God, is the power of free choice and the judgment of one's own will, when it is a grave offense against God to follow one's own plans and do the will of a depraved heart? That is why he adds: 'Ask among the nations and all the peoples round about who, in serving idols, has done or has heard of the things that the virgin Israel has done to excess.' He calls her a virgin because she had served the one God, as the prophet says: God is known in Judah, his name is great in Israel.

Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Or can the cold waters that burst forth and flow down be plucked up? The Septuagint: Will breasts fail from the rock, or snow from Lebanon? Or will water turn aside when it is driven violently by the wind?

Something similar is expressed in that line of Virgil: 'Sooner, then, will nimble stags graze in the sky, and the seas leave their fish stranded bare upon the shore, than his face will slip from my heart.' And in another place: 'While rivers run into the seas, while shadows pass over the slopes of the mountains, while the heavens feed the stars, your honor, your name and your praises will always remain.'

'Just as,' he says, 'the snow cannot fail from the summits of Lebanon, nor is it ever so overcome by the heat of the sun that it melts away entirely, and the streams flowing down from the mountains never dry up at their springs, so my name, which is in itself steadfast and everlasting, cannot be changed. And yet, while everything else keeps the order of nature, my people have forgotten me.' For there follows:

Because my people have forgotten me, pouring out libations in vain and stumbling in their ways, in the paths of the age — or: the everlasting paths —, so as to walk in them on an untrodden road. Whoever forgets God and abandons him who says, I am the way, and pours libations to foreign gods, stumbles in his own ways, which are not God's at all but his own. He abandons the ancient and everlasting paths, worn smooth by the footsteps of all the saints who worship God. These people, however, walked on an untrodden road, and abandoning the worship of God they venerated idols. For this, punishment is brought upon them. It follows:

So that their land should become a desolation and an everlasting hissing; everyone who passes through it will be astonished and shake his head. 'And because they have abandoned the worship of God,' he says, 'and followed the crooked paths of idolatry, their land has been reduced to a wilderness, and has become a wonder and a thing to hiss at for everyone. Those who see a land and a city that once flourished greatly, now collapsed into desert and ashes, will marvel and be astounded and show the confusion of their souls by the gestures of their bodies.' For this is what it means to shake the head and to express the mind's astonishment by hissing.

We understand that this was fulfilled more fully and more properly after the coming of the Lord, when no Jew is permitted by law to enter the land and the city that was once holy. When they come to mourn, they marvel and weep at the oracles of the prophets fulfilled in fact.

Like a scorching wind I will scatter them before the enemy — or: the enemies —; I will show them my back and not my face in the day of their ruin. To this day God's sentence remains upon the Jews. They are scattered throughout the whole world before the enemy, the devil, or before the hostile demons. And while day and night they call on the name of God in the synagogues of Satan, God shows them his back and not his face, so that they may understand that he is always moving away and never coming to them.
The day of the ruin of the Jews is the whole time from the Savior's passion until the end of the age, so that, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel may be saved.

And they said: Come, let us devise plans against Jeremiah! For the law will not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue and pay no attention to any of his words!

This was the plan of the Jews then against Jeremiah, or against the Lord and Savior, and it is the plan of the heretics today against his servants: to fabricate slanders and to strike first at holy men with accusations. They do not consider what truth those men speak, only what lies they themselves can fabricate. For they boast that the law of God, and counsel, and the word remain with their priests, their wise men and their false prophets, although Scripture says: Wisdom will not enter a perverse soul.

Give heed to me, O Lord, and hear the voice of my adversaries! Is evil repaid for good, that they have dug a pit for my life? Remember that I stood before you to speak good on their behalf and to turn your wrath away from them. Therefore give their children over to famine and deliver them into the power of the sword; let their wives become childless and widows, let their husbands be put to death, and their young men be pierced by the sword in battle; let a cry be heard from their houses!

As a figure of the Savior, Jeremiah suffers all these things at the hands of the Jewish people, who were afterwards laid waste when the Babylonian came. But they are fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ. When the city was overthrown, they were slaughtered by the Roman sword, not for idolatry, which did not exist at that time, but for killing the Son of God, when the whole people cried out together: Away, away with such a man; we have no king but Caesar!

And their curse upon themselves has been fulfilled in everlasting condemnation: His blood be on us and on our children! For they had dug a pit for Christ and had said: Let us cut him off from the land of the living! Yet he had such great mercy toward them, and stood before the Father to speak good on their behalf and to turn his wrath away from them, that on the cross too he said: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.

We pass quickly over what is plain, so as to dwell on what is more obscure. We will by no means interpret the ravings of certain people about the captivity of the heavenly Jerusalem, but will follow the clear history and the most evident prophecy with full confidence in both words and meaning.

For you will bring a robber upon them suddenly, because they have dug a pit to catch me and hidden snares for my feet. But you, O Lord, know all their plotting against me to put me to death. Do not forgive their iniquity, and do not let their sin be blotted out from your sight; let them be falling — or: stumbling — before you; in the time of your fury deal with them — or: act against them!

If we understand this of Jeremiah, we should take the sudden robber to be Nebuchadnezzar; if of the Savior, which is truer and better, the Roman army. And lest God's sentence seem unjust, he sets out what they did against Christ, the Son of God, and what they suffered.

What he adds, Do not forgive their iniquity, and do not let their sin be blotted out from your sight, is in no way contrary to the earlier statement in which he intercedes with the Father for the people. Rather, once the time granted for repentance has passed and they persist in their crime, they are punished not so much for their own sake as for the sake of others, lest sin left unpunished harm the rest by its example.

And what he adds, Let them be stumbling — or: falling — before you, is like the saying of Isaiah and of the apostle Peter: and you will not stumble as on a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling. The prophet also mentions this stone in the Psalms: The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this is the Lord's doing.

Thus says the Lord: Go and take a potter's earthenware flask, and some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests, and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is by the entrance of the Earthenware Gate — or: Charsith —, and there you shall proclaim — or: cry out, or: read — the words that I will speak to you, and you shall say: Hear the word of the Lord, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem!

For 'potter's flask', which in Hebrew is called 'bocboc', the Septuagint translated 'little jar'. For 'Earthenware Gate', Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, 'Harsith'. In its place the Septuagint, following its custom, added a Greek 'chi' for the aspiration of the letter 'heth', so as to say 'Charsith' for 'Harsith', just as it says 'Chebron' for 'Hebron' and 'Hiericho' for 'Hieriho'.

Divine Scripture wants the people to be taught not only through their ears but also through their eyes. For, as we have already said, what reaches the mind through sight is retained more firmly than what reaches it through hearing. 'Take,' he says, 'a flask' — or: an earthenware jar — 'and some of the elders of the people and of the priests, and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom.' We spoke of this valley above: there stood the shrine of Baal, with a grove and a wood watered by the springs of Siloam. 'This valley,' he says, 'is next to the gate,' which in the Hebrew language is called 'Harsith', that is, 'earthen'.

'And there you shall proclaim — or: read — the words that I will speak with you,' so that what I am about to say may be heard there. As we have already said, 'proclaim', 'cry out' and 'read' are all given because the Hebrew word 'carath' means all three. And he wants both the kings of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that is, both the royal line and the whole people, to hear what he is about to say, so that those who refuse to listen may be without excuse.

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring affliction — or: evils — upon this place, so that the ears of everyone who hears of it — or: of them — will tingle. For they have forsaken me and made this place alien, and in it they have poured out libations to foreign gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah knew. They have filled this place with the blood of the innocent and built the high places of the Baals, to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to the Baals, which I did not command — or: think of — nor speak of, nor did they enter my heart.

Some people foolishly refer this passage too to the heavenly Jerusalem. So that I need not keep warning about it, let it be enough to have said this once: such an interpretation is to be avoided, or rather such a heresy, which overturns what is plain and tries to bring certain illusions into the churches of Christ. No one doubts that they set up the idol of Baal in the temple of God, or else in the shrine in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, where Baal's grove and his altar stood, on which they sacrificed and burned their sons.

The Lord neither thought of these things nor spoke of them, nor did they enter his heart. This is not because God did not know the future, but because he says he does not know things unworthy of his knowledge, as in the Gospel saying: Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I do not know you! For the Lord knows those who are his, and whoever does not know will not be known. Or, at any rate, these words too, like others, are to be understood of God in human terms.

Every heretic forsakes God and makes the place of God's dwelling alien, having polluted it by his deceit. He pours libations to foreign gods whom neither he nor his fathers knew, his fathers being, of course, the apostles and apostolic men. The kings of Judah, that is, the patriarchs of the heretics, fill the place that once belonged to God with the blood of the deceived and the innocent; for unless a man is foolish and simple, he is not quickly led astray. They build the high places of the Baals when they claim to be discussing lofty matters, and they burn to the idol their sons, whom they have begotten in heresy. The Lord says that he does not know any of these things and that they never entered his thought.

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when this place will no longer be called Topheth and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. The Septuagint: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and this place will no longer be called Downfall and Polyandrion of the Son of Ennom, but Polyandrion of Slaughter.

We have said above what the Valley of the Son of Hinnom is: in Hebrew it is called 'gehennom', and people think that 'Gehenna' took its name from it. But I wonder what the Septuagint meant by putting diaptōsis, that is, 'downfall', for 'Topheth', and polyandrion, which means 'a multitude of men', for 'valley'. Perhaps it is because the people fell there and a multitude of men was slaughtered, either spiritually, in the error of idolatry, or literally, by the Babylonian army, as is read more plainly in what follows.

And I will bring to nothing the plans of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword before their enemies and by the hand of those who seek their lives. I will give their corpses as food to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and I will make this city an object of horror and of hissing; everyone who passes through it will be horrified and will hiss at all its wounds.

And I will feed them the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and each will eat the flesh of his friend in the siege and in the distress with which their enemies, and those who seek their lives, will hem them in.

We know that these things also happened to the people in the Babylonian captivity. Yet they apply more fully to the times of the Savior, when they were besieged by Vespasian and Titus, and when, in Hadrian's time, their city collapsed into everlasting ashes. Those who had offered their sons to idols were afterwards themselves driven by the necessity of famine to use them as food, and the flesh of all was given to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth. Thus those who had abused God's gifts for impiety and sacrificed their own offspring to idols made their bellies the tombs of their children.

And you shall break the flask before the eyes of the men who go — or: go out — with you, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as a potter's vessel is broken, which can never be mended again.

This is clearly said not of the Babylonian captivity but of the Roman. After the Babylonians, the city was rebuilt, and the people were brought back into Judea and restored to their former abundance. But after the captivity that came under Vespasian and Titus, and later under Hadrian, the ruins of Jerusalem will remain until the end of the age. The Jews, however, think that a Jerusalem of gold and jewels is to be restored to them, and with it victims and sacrifices, the marriages of the saints, and the reign of the Lord and Savior on earth.
Although we do not follow these views, we still cannot condemn them, because many churchmen and martyrs have held them. So let each be fully convinced in his own mind, and

let all things be left to the Lord's judgment. Just as an earthen clay vessel, once broken, cannot be reshaped to its former appearance, so the Jewish people and overthrown Jerusalem will not regain their former state. Indeed, even the city's own name is lost today. It is called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian, and along with its former inhabitants it also lost its former name, so as to strike down the pride of those who lived there.

The names of the Holy Cross and of the Resurrection denote not a city but a place. They signify not the great wealth of former days, through which the Jewish people perished, but the glory of holiness, which our poor little Bethlehem possesses. She has no gold and jewels, but she has the Bread that was born in her.

And they will be buried — or: they will bury — in Topheth, because there will be no other place to bury. Thus will I do to this place, says the Lord, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth — or: like a ruin. And the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah will be like the place Topheth, or of ruin. But what is added in the Septuagint, all the houses of the kings of Judah like the place Topheth, is not found in the Hebrew. And there follows:

All the houses will be unclean on whose roofs — or: housetops — they sacrificed to all the host of heaven and poured out libations to foreign gods. He had said above, This place will no longer be called Topheth and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. Now he states more plainly that there will be such slaughter in that very place that the people will be buried there in heaps, and the place that was once one of worship will become a tomb of the dead. The city too, which overlooks this place, will become like Topheth, for which the Septuagint translated 'ruin', and the houses of Jerusalem and the palaces of the kings will likewise be turned to ruins.

And the reason is given: they were unclean and polluted by the crime of idolatry, because on their roofs and housetops they offered sacrifices and burned incense to the sun and the moon and the stars of heaven. Nor were they content with this error, but they also sacrificed to demons and poured out libations to foreign gods.

Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the house of the Lord and said to all the people: "Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all its towns all the evils that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their necks so as not to hear my words."

In Topheth, before the elders of the people whom Jeremiah had brought with him, he broke the flask, or jar, and prophesied the words of the Lord about the crushing of the people and of the city of Jerusalem. After this he returns, stands in the court of the house of the Lord and speaks to the whole crowd that had refused to go to Topheth. He tells them that the Lord will bring upon the city of Jerusalem and upon all its towns the evils he has pronounced against it.

So that we do not think the sentence cruel, he gives the reasons why the Lord will bring these evils: "because," he says, "they have stiffened their necks so as not to hear my words, and even after many impieties they refuse to repent."

Now Pashhur son of Immer, the priest, who had been appointed chief officer in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words. And Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate in the house of the Lord.

For "Pashhur" the Septuagint has "Phaschor," which means "blackness of mouth." Where we have "stocks," the Septuagint and Theodotion have "cataract," and Symmachus has basanistērion or streblōtērion, both of which mean "instruments of torture." We, however, have said "stocks" in the ordinary way of speaking. We also read of this kind of torture in the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles Paul and Silas were put in prison under guard.

This man was the high priest of the temple. Having been given the dignity of the priesthood, he perversely abuses it, not to teach and rebuke with words, but to terrify with torture. So also the Saviour and the apostle Paul are beaten at the high priest's command. Nor is it surprising if even today the servants of God are beaten by Phaschor, thrown into prison and kept in dreadful custody. This power is granted by God so that the faith of the prophets may be shown. Yet the one who strikes is not the greater; the one who is struck is the stronger. The prophet patiently accepts God's judgment and does not cry out against the blows, but considers the one who gives the command. "Immer" means "word."

"Blackness" is often born from an egg [?], not by the parent's fault but by the wickedness of a degenerate offspring. The "torture" with which the prophet is tormented is seen "on the right side," which is the meaning of "Benjamin," and in the "high" gate, which points not to truth but to the high priest's unjust power.

When it grew light the next day, Pashhur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him: "The Lord has not called your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side." Here, too, all the translators rendered both the high priest's name and the kind of torture just as above. The high priest's name is changed so that his future punishment may be shown by the name.

"By no means," he says, "will you keep your blackness of mouth and your rule of unjust power. Instead you will be led captive to Babylon." That is what "terror on every side," or "round about," means. "So, trembling and unsure of your own safety, you will look around this way and that, and dread your adversaries coming against you!" For "terror," which is written magur in Hebrew, the Septuagint and Theodotion have metoikon, that is, "one who migrates." Aquila's second edition has "stranger" and his first "one who looks around." Symmachus translated it "taken away" or ("gathered") and "driven."

"For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will make you a terror, you and all your friends, and they will fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes will see it. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will carry them away to Babylon and strike them with the sword.

And I will give all the wealth (or strength) of this city, all its labour and all its precious things (or glory), and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies. They will plunder them, seize them and carry them off to Babylon. And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house shall go into captivity. You shall come to Babylon, and there you shall die and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends to whom you prophesied lies."

In keeping with the earlier rendering, in which Pashhur's name had been changed so that he was called "Magur," all the translators likewise rendered it so as to mean "terror," "sojourning," "removal," "transfer" or "migration."

He threatens that Pashhur and his friends will at any moment be captured and handed over to their enemies. The whole people of the tribe of Judah will fall into the hands of the Babylonian king, some to be killed by the sword and others to be led into captivity. All the riches of the city and of the royal treasuries will be seized by the enemy. Pashhur himself, with all his kin and household, will be led into captivity and will die in Babylon, because he deceived the people with his lie. He did not promise them what was true and grim, but falsely promised prosperity.

At the same time we should note the prophet's patience and prudence. When he is put in prison he keeps silent and overcomes the injury by silence. Yet he does not hide what he knows will come, so that at least in this way the false-prophet high priest may stop sinning and beg for God's mercy.

"You enticed me, Lord, and I was enticed" (or "You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived"). "You were stronger than I, and you prevailed" (or "you overcame me and had your way"). "I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me. For long since I have been speaking, crying out injustice, and I keep shouting 'Devastation!'" Or: "For with my bitter word I will laugh; I will call on transgression and misery."

The prophet says that the Lord deceived him. At the beginning he had heard: "I have appointed you a prophet to the nations," and again: "Behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to scatter, to build and to plant." So he thought he would say nothing against the Jewish people, only against the various nations round about, and for that reason he gladly took up the prophetic office. But the opposite happened: he preached the captivity of Jerusalem and so endured persecution and distress.

He adds: "I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me." This is because they thought he had lied about everything and that all he had foretold was false. The prophet had thought that what the Lord threatened would happen at once, and the people thought that what had not come at once would never come at all. "And I cry out the devastation from Babylon and the injustice of the enemies

by which my people is to be crushed." If, however, we follow the Septuagint, which says, "For with my bitter word I will laugh; I will call on transgression and misery," the sense is this: "I know that present sorrow will be exchanged for future joy, as it is written: 'Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh.' Therefore I gladly endure misery, injustice and affliction. I even long for them and call on them, and I offset the brief injury with eternal happiness."

"For the word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and a derision all day long. And I said, 'I will not remember him' (or 'I will not name the Lord'), 'nor will I speak any more in his name.' But there was in my heart something like a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I grew weary (or I was undone) and could not bear it. For I heard the insults (or the abuse) of many, and terror on every side (or of those gathered from every side): 'Persecute him, and let us persecute him!'"

"As I cried out and said that the Babylonian army was already coming and that the enemy's sword would plunder everything, the word of the Lord turned into reproach and derision for me, since they take the delay of the prophecy for a lie. So I resolved in my mind that I would no longer speak words to the people of God nor name his name.

When, overcome by shame, I had made this resolve, modestly indeed but foolishly," he says, "there was in my heart something like a burning fire shut up in my bones, (and I grew weary)," or "I was undone on every side, so that I could not bear it."

For the divine word, once conceived in the mind, burns in the breast if it is not spoken aloud. So Paul also says: "If I preach the gospel, I have nothing to boast of, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship." And in Athens, when he saw the city given over to idolatry, his spirit was stirred and his whole mind burned. A little later in the same book we read: "When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul was pressing on with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ."
Even today many teachers in the church endure similar things. They hear the abuse of many who gather round against them and say: "Persecute them, and let us persecute them!"

"All the men who were at peace with me and guarded my side say: 'Perhaps he can be deceived, and we will prevail against him and take our revenge on him!' But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior." When adversaries rise up, and those who were once friends and at peace with us turn to war and want to lay traps for us, let us not be greatly troubled. Let us rather choose to say what the prophet also says: "But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior."

"Therefore those who persecute me will fall and be weak" (or "therefore they persecuted and could not understand"); "they will be greatly put to shame, because they did not understand the everlasting reproach" (or "disgrace") "that will never be blotted out." Because they persecuted, they could not understand the prophetic word. Great shame followed their ignorance, and they did not understand the everlasting disgrace that will take hold of them and that no forgetting will blot out.

So let them say what they like, these men who were once at peace with me and guarded my side, and let them long to deceive me, so long as a just man and teacher of the church receives such vindication and such rewards after persecution.

"And you, Lord of hosts, who test the just" (or "who test what is just"), "who see the heart and the mind, let me see, I pray, your vengeance on them! For to you I have laid open my cause." The Lord alone knows how to test justice, just as he alone sees the inner depths of the heart. So Jesus too, who knew people's thoughts, is God not by advancement, as some think, but by nature. The Psalms say something similar: "No one living will be justified in your sight." If even one who lives in virtue is not justified, how much less one who is dead in sins!

The just man knows that he has God as his defender. Yet in the impatience of human frailty he longs to see even now what he knows will come. He has laid open his cause to the one who says elsewhere: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord." Happy is the conscience whose cause is laid open to the Lord, for the apostle says: "Everything that is made manifest is light."

"Sing to the Lord, praise the Lord, for he has rescued the soul of the poor from the hand of the wicked!" The one who is poor in spirit lacks the riches that have received their consolation in this world. Of such poor Paul says: "only that we should remember the poor." When he has obtained vindication from the Lord, he praises the Lord in spirit and glories that he has been rescued from the hand of the wicked. All this comes about not by our merit but by the grace of him who set the poor man free. That man does not have the riches of pride that falls to ruin, but the humility of the poor man set free.

"Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day on which my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man (or the person) who brought the news to my father, saying, 'A son, a male child, is born to you,' and made him glad as if with joy! Let that man be like the cities that the Lord overthrew without relenting. Let him hear a cry in the morning and wailing at noon, who (or because he) did not kill me in the womb, so that my mother would have been my grave and her womb pregnant for ever. Why did I come out of the womb to see toil and sorrow, and for my days to be spent in shame?"

Some think that souls existed in the heavens and were cast down from a better state into a worse one. They use this and similar texts to argue that it would have been better to stay in the heavens than to live on earth and take on the body of humiliation. In this way they look for new, or rather already old, arguments for their heresy.

But we read the words of blessed Job: "Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the night in which they said, 'Behold, a male child,'" and: "Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, saying, 'A boy is born to you.'" We fit this to the present text, taking it to mean that it is better not to exist than to live in torment. As it is written: "Death is rest to a man whose way God has hidden," and again: "Why is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are bitter in soul?"

In the Gospel too we read the plain statement: "It would have been better for him if he had not been born." This does not mean that there exists someone who was never born. It means that it is better not to exist than to exist in misery. For it is one thing not to exist at all, and another to exist and be tormented without any respite, just as we prefer a peaceful death to a wretched life. So Amos calls the day a day of darkness and affliction. Jacob, because he lived in toil and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil. And the apostle Paul says, "to rescue us from the present evil age," and again, "making the most of the time, because the days are evil." The Hebrews reckon that the fifth month,

in which Jerusalem was captured and the temple overthrown, was the month of Jeremiah's birth, using certain tangled and incredible arguments. Even if they could prove this, I do not know how they would be able to interpret Job's testimony, unless perhaps they claim that his day too was a prefiguration and prophecy of the future overthrow of the temple.

When he calls down on that man the fate of the overthrown cities, I think Sodom and Gomorrah are meant, and that the man's whole life is to be spent in mourning, with a cry in the morning and wailing at noon. As for what he adds, "who did not kill me in the womb," they think God is meant.

"So that," he says, "my mother's womb would have been pregnant for ever." All of this is said by way of hyperbole. Finally he sets out the reasons why he prefers death to life, and not existing at all to existing in misery. He adds: "Why did I come out of the womb to see toil and sorrow, and for my days to be spent in shame?"

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, saying: "Inquire of the Lord for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the Lord will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds, and he will withdraw from us."

Above, the high priest Pashhur, or Phaschor, who struck Jeremiah, had Immer as his father. This Pashhur, however, is the son of Malchiah. This is pointed out so that no one thinks they are the same man. King Zedekiah sends to the prophet without wanting either the people or the princes to know. Through envoys, by a secret message, he wants to learn what sentence the Lord has passed on the city of Jerusalem and on the Jewish people. He adds, "for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us." This shows that Zedekiah asked the prophet this when Jerusalem was already under siege.

Note also that in the prophets, especially Ezekiel and Jeremiah, the order of kings and times is not kept at all. It is reversed: what happened later in history is told first, and what was done first is told later. Writing history is one thing, and writing prophecy is another. So in the present passage Zedekiah, who was captured along with the city of Jerusalem, is described as sending to Jeremiah, and that at the time when Jerusalem was under siege. Afterwards comes the story of his brother Jehoiakim, who was king before him, and of Jehoiachin, that is, Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim. We will speak about them in what follows.

And Jeremiah said to them: "This is what you shall say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war (or the arms of war) that are in your hands, with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. I will gather them (or those men) into the middle of this city. I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a strong (or lofty) arm, in fury, in indignation and in great wrath. And I will strike the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast; they shall die of a great pestilence."

"In vain," he says, "do you want to resist the besieging Chaldeans. You prepare weapons of war, but you will use them only in the middle of the city, just to look armed. While they besiege you, I will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm, and I will strike you in my fury and indignation, so that you and every living thing will die of famine and pestilence in the middle of the city." And we read that this is just what happened. Without any ring of attackers or din of battle, the city was taken by siege alone. So the enemy had no one to defeat, only people to capture. "Better off," it says, "were those wounded by the sword than those killed by famine."

"And after this," says the Lord, "I will give Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants and his people, and those in this city who survive the pestilence, the sword and the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their lives. He will strike them with the edge of the sword. He will not relent, he will not spare and he will not have mercy."

The Septuagint does not have what we have translated as "into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies." And where we have "He will not relent, he will not spare and he will not have mercy," the Septuagint has "I will not spare and I will not have mercy."

The Hebrew reading is better, because then the cruel and unbending sentence seems to belong to the Babylonian king rather than to the Lord. The first prophecy concerned the whole city. Now it is foretold specifically to Zedekiah and to those of his people who survive the pestilence, the sword and the famine. Zedekiah will be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, and killed by the sword together with his friends. He must hope for no mercy from the one whose treaty and alliance he abandoned by breaking his oath.

"And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. Whoever stays in this city will die by the sword, by famine and by pestilence. But whoever goes out and deserts to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live; he will have his life as his spoil. For I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good, says the Lord. It will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire."

The king had sent men who came to beg the prophet to inquire of the Lord for them. He gave them the answer above, a message to take back to King Zedekiah. Now he urges them to give an answer to the people, and he advises that the people desert to the Chaldeans against the king's will. Everyone knows how dangerous this was for the prophet. So he also calls down death on himself and says:

"Cursed be the day on which I was born," and "Why did I come out of the womb to see toil and sorrow?" Advising people not yet captured to hand themselves over to captivity of their own accord is no small thing. It is as if people about to be shipwrecked were ordered to seize the oars and planks and throw themselves into the waves before the ship had even been wrecked and broken up. But it is easier to bear living as a captive, however that may be, than being consumed by the sword, famine and pestilence. There are

some who explain this passage tropologically as follows. It is better to give oneself to secular learning, and above all to philosophy, than to remain in a church where there is a famine of the word of God, and where the whole people is dying by the sword of the heretics, by the lack of teaching and by the plague of heresy.

And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, O house of David! Thus says the Lord: Judge justly in the morning, and rescue the one who is violently oppressed from the hand of the slanderer, lest perhaps — or, so that it may not happen that — my indignation go forth like fire and burn, and there be no one to quench it. What follows, "because of the wickedness of your pursuits," is not found in the Septuagint.

Since he had said above, "And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord," he now goes on to add, "and to the house of the king of Judah," so that "you shall say: Thus says the Lord" is to be understood; for the preceding and the following words are joined by a term shared between them. So the sense is: "And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord, and to the house of the king of Judah you shall say: Thus says the Lord." The word is addressed specifically to the royal house, since it is above all through its guilt that the city is under siege, so that it may correct its error by repentance and obtain the Lord's mercy.

"Judge," he says, "justly in the morning" — not in the darkness of iniquity, but in the light of justice — "and rescue the one who is violently oppressed from the hand of the slanderer. Do not show partiality in judgment; rather, when the rich oppress the poor, let God's command carry more weight with you than the power of the persecutor! And if," he says, "you do this, the fire of my fury will by no means be kindled among you, nor will it find

anything to consume." In this passage God's incredible mercy is shown. Of these same people he had said above, "For I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good; it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and fire shall burn it"; yet now, with the Lord's sentence already bearing down on them, he calls them to salvation. This is not because he does not know that the city of Jerusalem is to be captured, but so that human free will may be preserved, and they may be seen to perish not through ignorance of the future but by their own will. In the same way the Savior knew that the people would deny him and that he was to be crucified — indeed he had often foretold this to the apostles — and nevertheless he kept admonishing them, wishing to correct them and bring them to repentance, so that whatever they suffered afterward would befall them through their own fault, not through the harshness of the one who threatened.

Behold, I am against you, inhabitant of the solid and level valley, says the Lord, you who say: Who will strike — or, terrify — us, and who will enter our houses? And I will visit upon you (what follows, "according to the fruit of your pursuits, says the Lord," is not found in the Septuagint), and I will kindle, he says, a fire in her forest, and it shall devour everything around her.

For "inhabitant of the solid and level valley" the Septuagint translated: "Behold, I am against you who dwell in the valley of Sor, the plain." Here Symmachus rendered "rock," Theodotion "besieged"; Aquila's first edition has "solid," his second "Tyre." For "Sor" or "Sur" in Hebrew means "Tyre," and also "flint" and "hemmed in."

He is speaking against Jerusalem, which has been surrounded by siege; or which, like Tyre encircled by the great sea, is encircled by the Babylonian army and cannot escape; or at any rate which thinks itself impregnable and strong like the hardest rock because of the solidity and size of its walls, and says, "Who can terrify us, and who will enter our houses?" God, on the contrary, says: "I will visit you. You will not be able to escape my eye.

I will visit you for destruction and repay you the fruit of your wickedness, and it is I who will kindle the fire in your forest — not the Babylonian, as you think, not the king of the Chaldeans; it is my wrath that will accomplish all these things." He calls Jerusalem and the whole region around it a "forest" because it has no fruit-bearing trees of good works and so is ready for burning. And he fittingly calls it a "level valley" because it lies open to enemies, rather than a "lofty mountain," which can be climbed only with difficulty; as it is also said in Isaiah: "The vision of the valley of Zion."

Whatever is prophesied to the royal house and to the capital city, let us apply to the ecclesiastical order and the leaders of the churches — at least to those who have given themselves over to pride, riches and wantonness. Being a royal house will not immediately free it from destruction, just as very few of David's stock were found to please the Lord as David himself did, and Hezekiah and Josiah; a great part of the princes and of the royal stock provoked the Lord's wrath against the whole people.

Thus says the Lord: Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak this word there, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, who sit upon the throne of David, you and your servants and your people who enter by these gates! Thus says the Lord: Do judgment and justice, and rescue the one who is violently oppressed from the hand of the slanderers; do not grieve the stranger, the orphan and the widow, nor oppress them unjustly — or, impiously — and do not shed innocent blood in this place!

For if you truly carry out this word, then kings of the line of David, sitting upon his throne, shall enter through the gates of this house, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not hear these words, I have sworn by myself, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation. This vision —

or rather this word of the Lord — came to the prophet either before Zedekiah sent messengers to him, or at any rate after he had instructed the messengers what they were to report to the king. Jeremiah is commanded not to speak to the king through messengers at all, but to go to the palace himself and speak to him there.

Let us also note the divine wisdom here. Through the messengers he orders sad news to be announced, mixed with favorable news if the king is willing to repent. Here, however, since Jeremiah himself is commanded to go, he does not announce sad tidings and the captivity now on the point of arriving; instead he advises the king what he must do to escape God's impending sentence. It is the proper task of kings to do judgment and justice, to rescue those violently oppressed from the hand of slanderers, and to give help to the stranger, the orphan and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful.

And to make them take greater care over God's commandments, he added: "Do not grieve them — that is, not only rescue them, but do not even allow them to be grieved by others through your connivance — and do not shed innocent blood in this place!" For to punish murderers, the sacrilegious and poisoners is not the shedding of blood but the ministry of the laws.

"If," he says, "you do these things, O kings of Judah, you will keep your former power and enter the gates of Jerusalem in state; but if you refuse to do them, O royal house, it will be due not so much to the Lord's cruelty as to your own will that the whole city is reduced to desolation."

Whatever was said to the royal house, let bishops and their associates, the presbyters and deacons, and the whole ecclesiastical order understand as said to them. If they do what has been commanded, and among other things do not shed innocent blood by scandalizing even the least and wounding the consciences of individuals, they will retain the dignity entrusted to them by the Lord; but if they refuse to do so and treat it with contempt, it is they themselves who reduce the church to desolation.

Those of the line of David — a name that is interpreted "strong of hand" — enter through the gates of Jerusalem and sit upon his throne, and ride in chariots and on horses, when they rein in both their own disturbances and those of the people, and enter the church with composed step, accompanied by a choir of many virtues singing in harmony with them on every side. And so that we may believe this to be true, he swears by himself, since, as the apostle says, he has no one greater by whom he could swear.

For thus says the Lord concerning — or, to — the house of the king of Judah: You are Gilead to me, the head — or, the beginning — of Lebanon; yet surely I will make you a desolation, cities without inhabitants. And I will sanctify against you a slayer, a man with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choice cedars and hurl — or, throw — them into the fire. And many nations shall pass by this city, and each shall say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord done this to this great city? And they shall answer: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God, and worshiped other gods and served them.

Scripture records that Gilead, which the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed, lies beyond the Jordan. It was on this mountain that Laban overtook the fleeing Jacob, and according to Genesis the mountain received the name [?], that is, "mound of testimony," because Jacob and Laban swore an oath there over a heap of stones gathered together.

It is also the head or beginning of Lebanon, a lofty mountain that is entirely planted with cedars, as David sings: "And the Lord will shake the cedars of Lebanon," and elsewhere: "I saw the wicked exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon"; and in Zechariah we read: "Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars!" Therefore in the present passage,

since he was speaking to the royal house, he speaks metaphorically to the temple, or to the house of the line of Judah, either because it stands on high or because remedies for all sins were sought from the temple and sanctuary. Hence this same prophet also says: "Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why then has the healing of the daughter of my people not come about?"

He therefore threatens the royal house, the city of Jerusalem and the temple, which he calls the head of Lebanon, that it is to be reduced to desolation together with all its cities — not by the power of the Babylonian king, but at the command of the Lord, who says: "I will sanctify against you a slayer." Nebuchadnezzar and his whole army are called "holy" because he is carrying out God's sentence.

"And they shall cut down," he says, "your choice cedars" — all the powerful men and princes of the city — "and throw them into the fire, so that the all-devouring flame may consume them. And when everything has been destroyed, many nations shall pass through the city and the temple, which before they were not permitted to enter. And each shall say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord brought so sudden and so great an overthrow on so famous and great a city? And those who are asked," he says, "shall answer and explain the causes of the ruin, saying: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God and worshiped idols in place of God."

Let the royal house of our own city hear this too, and its princes and cedars, which lift their heads up to the clouds and say in their pride, "Who will not see us?" — let them hear that they will quickly be consumed by the Lord's flame if they refuse to comply with his commandments. But the sanctification of the slayer and his weapons is one thing, and that of the priests and of those who minister to the Lord is another.

Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn over him; weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall not return again nor see the land of his birth! For thus says the Lord concerning Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, and who went out from this place: He shall not return here any more, but he shall die in the place to which I have carried him away, and he shall not see this land again. Josiah, a just king, had three sons:

Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. The first of these Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, took captive to Egypt, and he died there; and in his place Pharaoh made his brother Eliakim king (and changed his name to Jehoiakim). When Jehoiakim died, his son Jeconiah reigned, who was led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, together with his mother and the princes. In his place his uncle Zedekiah reigned, who, when Jerusalem was taken, was led to Babylon.

The question therefore arises who this is who should not be wept for, who is to be led into captivity and never return, since three of them were captured and carried off. The Hebrews think this applies to all of them, that is, to Jehoahaz, Jeconiah and Zedekiah, and that all the sons of Josiah are called "Shallem" or "Shallum," which means "consummation" or "completion," because the kingdom of Judah came to an end in them. To me, however, it seems that this is said specifically of Zedekiah. The prophecy of both the present chapter and the previous one concerns him; in him the kingdom of Judah truly came to an end; under him the city was captured; and he was led to Babylon and is recorded to have died there. He is "Shallum," that is, "consummation" and "completion," the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father.

Jeconiah, on the other hand, was not the son but the grandson of Josiah, being the son of Jehoiakim. So we should understand that everything from the beginning of the vision — when King Zedekiah sent Pashhur son of Malchiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah to Jeremiah — up to this chapter is spoken to King Zedekiah and about him.

Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness and his upper rooms by injustice, who oppresses his friend for nothing and does not pay him his wages; who says: I will build myself a wide house and spacious upper rooms, who cuts out windows for himself, makes ceilings of cedar and paints them with vermilion! Will you reign because you compare yourself to the cedar?

Did not your father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it went well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy to his own good; was it not because he knew me? says the Lord. But your eyes and your heart are set on greed, on shedding innocent blood, on false accusation, and on the pursuit of evil deeds.

The Septuagint: "O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! With him his neighbor works for nothing, and he will not pay him his wages. You have built yourself a little house, airy upper rooms, divided by windows, floored with cedar and painted with vermilion.

Will you reign because you contend against Ahaz your father? They will not eat and will not drink; it was better for you to do judgment and good justice. They did not know, they did not judge judgment for the lowly, nor the judgment of the poor. Is this not your failure to know me? says the Lord. Behold, your eyes are not upright nor your heart good, but they are set on your greed, and on shedding innocent blood, and on iniquity and murder, to commit them."

I have set out both editions in full, so that both the Hebrew truth and the difficulty of the common edition may be more easily recognized. The passage is directed against Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, of whom we spoke above, whom Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, set up in place of his brother Jehoahaz, whom he led in chains to Egypt. We read, moreover, in the history narrated by both Kings and Chronicles, that Jehoiakim son of Josiah reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, that he reigned cruelly and proved impious, and that he afterward died; yet his burial is not recorded, although it is the custom of Holy Scripture to report of all the kings both that they died and that they were buried. This one, however, it specifically records as dead and not buried, a matter we shall discuss later.

He therefore laments over this king, because he trusts in injustice and thinks his royal dignity will last forever; because he builds himself upper rooms, oppresses his friends, does not pay the workers their wages, and imagines that the building of his palace is eternal.

"Will you be able," says the divine word, "to reign forever because you wish to compare yourself to a lofty cedar, namely your father Josiah, a just king? Your father," he says, "both ate and drank and enjoyed the wealth of a king; yet he did not offend God by having riches, but pleased him by doing judgment and justice, and therefore it went well with him in the present age and will go well with him in the age to come.

He judged," he says, "the cause of the poor and needy, both for the relief of those whom he heard and, in a particular sense, for his own good. All this turned out prosperously for him because he knew me, says the Lord. But your eyes, O Jehoiakim, turn aside to greed and to shedding innocent blood,

to false accusation and to the pursuit of evil deeds!" What sense these words have according to the Septuagint I cannot understand. For although the rest agree with one another in some part, the words that are added — "Will you reign because you contend in Ahaz your father?" — where the Hebrew has "araz," a word that means "cedar," plainly make no sense. The same is true of what follows, "they will not eat and will not drink," and the rest, which are so scattered and confused among themselves that without the truth of the Hebrew reading they cannot be understood at all.

We can, however, take this passage anagogically as directed against the heretics. They build for themselves not a great house, made very wide by the abundance of the church, but a little one. And they build it without justice and judgment, eager to plunder what belongs to others. Hence it is said: "You have built yourself a little house, airy upper rooms" — which are carried about by every wind of doctrine — "divided by windows"; for they have no lasting building and no solid firmness.

"And floored," he says, "with cedar": they seem indeed to have a very beautiful floor, but in the rains and the storm of persecutions it quickly rots and collapses. "And painted with vermilion": for they too promise the Lord's passion and blood, but they do not reign forever, because they contend against "araz," that is, "the cedar," their father, and provoke him to anger. For every heretic is born in the church, but is cast out of the church, and contends and fights against his parent.

And in what he adds, "they will not eat and will not drink," the words "the body and blood of the Savior" are to be understood, and the rest in like manner. And he says that all their error comes from this: that they have not known God, nor do they have upright eyes, but their heart is inclined to greed, to plunder what belongs to others and to shed the blood of those they have deceived; for this is to commit murder. Obscure passages call for fuller discussion.

Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: They shall not lament for him: "Alas, my brother!" and "Alas, my sister!" They shall not cry out for him: "Alas, lord!" and "Alas, glorious one!" But he shall be buried with the burial of an ass, rotting and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem. The words we have translated from the Hebrew, "They shall not lament for him: Alas, my brother, and alas, my sister," are not found in the Septuagint.

This is said specifically against Jehoiakim, king of Judah. The riddle that previously seemed hidden is now opened, and the ambiguity among the three brothers is resolved: the passage is not about Jehoahaz or Zedekiah, but specifically about Jehoiakim, who, as Hebrew history relates, was killed by raiding bands of the Chaldeans, of Syria, of the Ammonites and of the Moabites. That is why in Kings he is recorded as having died, while his burial is passed over in silence. In the book of Chronicles we read that he was bound in chains and led to Babylon, and nothing more is reported about him.

And he fittingly says that he will be buried with "the burial of an ass," to indicate in other words that he will remain unburied, that is, torn apart by beasts and birds. For this is the burial of an ass.

Go up to Lebanon and cry out, and in Bashan raise your voice, and cry out to those passing by, for all your lovers have been crushed! I spoke to you; in your abundance you said: I will not listen! This has been your way from your youth, that you have not heard my voice. All [?] your shepherds — or, lovers — the wind shall feed, and your lovers — or, friends — shall go into captivity; and then you will be put to shame and confounded for all your wickedness. You who sit in Lebanon and make your nest in the cedars, how you groaned when pains came upon you like the pains of a woman in labor!

Through the metaphor of Lebanon and Bashan, regions and mountains beyond the Jordan, the word is addressed to Jerusalem, because it trusted in Egypt in vain. Or it is addressed to Jehoiakim himself, who was reigning in Jerusalem at that time and had been made king by the Egyptians, because he hopes in vain for help from the Egyptians, who themselves are to be conquered by the Babylonian king and led into captivity.

When he says, "I spoke to you" — that is, God himself through the prophets — or, "they spoke to you" — so that "my prophets" is understood — "and in your abundance you said: I will not listen," he convicts her of pride, and of having abused her great wealth to show contempt for God.
