And he relates that not only at this time but from the very beginning, when she was brought out of Egypt, she did not listen to God's voice; and for this reason all her shepherds and princes have been scattered here and there and have bowed their necks to Babylonian captivity. And what he adds,

"You who sit in Lebanon and make your nest in the cedars," mocks her arrogance, which had grown out of her abundance of everything, and declares that sudden pain and sudden captivity will come upon her like a woman in childbirth. Where we have translated "cry out to those passing by," and the Hebrew has "meabarim," the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered "beyond the sea," and Symmachus "from the opposite side," meaning that the prophet's voice must carry from Jerusalem all the way to Mount Lebanon and Bashan.

As I live, says the Lord, even if Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him off from there — or "you" — and I will give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whose face you dread, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon — this is not found in the Septuagint — and into the hand of the Chaldeans. And I will send you — or "cast you out" — and your mother who bore you into a foreign land where you were not born, and there you shall die; but to the land to which they lift up their soul to return, there they shall not return.

He had said above, "You shall speak these things to the house of the king of Judah," and then, "Go down to the house of the king of Judah," and again, "Thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah." Then, reversing the order, after speaking of Zedekiah, who was the last of the kings in Jerusalem, he goes back to Jehoiakim, his brother, who reigned before him. With that prophecy completed, he now speaks to the son of Jehoiakim and grandson of Josiah, Jeconiah king of Jerusalem. Jeconiah is also called by another name, Jehoiachin. He was captured by Nebuchadnezzar and led into Chaldea together with his mother, the princes, the craftsmen and many nobles, and he died there.

So this is what is being said: "A ring does not leave the hand of the one who wears it, and it slips off the finger only with difficulty. Yet even if Jeconiah were on my hand like that, I will tear him off and hand him over to the king of Babylon. There he will die with his mother and all his companions, and he will never again see the land of Judea, which he longs for." The wretched Grunnius,

who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue to lie, translated into Latin a book by Sextus the Pythagorean, an utterly pagan man. He divided it into two volumes and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome. These volumes make no mention of Christ, none of the Holy Spirit, none of God the Father, and none of the patriarchs, prophets or apostles. With his usual rashness and madness he named this book "The Ring." It is read in many provinces, especially by those who preach apatheia and sinlessness.

So, just as the Lord threatens to cast Jeconiah from his hand and finger like a ring, I beg the reader to throw away this wicked book. If he does want to read it, let him read it like the other books of the philosophers, and not as a book of the Church.

In commentaries and expositions, where it is customary to set out the differing opinions of interpreters, I usually work in phrases of this kind: "Some say this, others maintain that, some think thus." For this the wretched Grunnius himself, and many years later the disciple of Jovinian and of that man, have slandered me and still slander me, claiming that I put forward my own opinions under other people's names. I do it out of kindness, so as not to seem to tear anyone to pieces by name.

Since my kindness has been turned into slander, I now say plainly, both to the one who is dead and to the one who is alive and trying to revive the other's heresy, that their master Origen refers this passage to Christ. He says that Christ was torn like a ring from the hand of God the Father, sent into the land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and handed over to the cross, and that his mother too — the synagogue, no doubt — was captured and cast out.

Nor, in recounting these things, is he afraid to understand what follows as referring to the Lord of majesty: "Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord! Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as abominable" — or "barren" — and the rest. He writes this in the fifth book of the Stromata, so his disciples should not dare to deny it.

Is this man Coniah a clay vessel, and broken? Is he a vessel without any delight — or "usefulness"? Why have they been cast out, he and his seed, and thrown into a land they did not know? Where we have put "Is he a clay vessel, and broken?", Symmachus translated, "Is he refuse, or worthless and discarded rubbish [?]?" The Septuagint has nothing for this; its translators rendered only, "Jeconiah has been dishonoured like a vessel in which there is no use."

Although this is said of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, does anyone dare to apply it to Christ as a type? Because the Apostle says that the Lord and Saviour is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation — that is, wisdom, the Word, truth, life and righteousness — does anyone dare to call him the ring that is cast off or torn from the Lord's hand and handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar?

"They have been cast out," he says, "he and his seed, and thrown into a land they did not know." No one doubts that this happened to Jeconiah. "Jeconiah" means "preparation of the Lord." In the present passage his first syllable, that is, the name of the Lord, is taken away and he is called "Coniah," so that "prepared for perdition and destruction" is understood.

Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord! Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as barren, a man who will not prosper in his days; for no man of his seed will sit on the throne of David and hold power in Judah any longer.

If I tried to note, passage by passage, how much the Septuagint has left out or changed, it would take a long time, especially since a careful reader can compare the two editions and see what has been changed, what added and what removed. For "barren" the Hebrew has "ariri." Aquila's first edition translated this "barren" and his second anauxētos, that is, "not growing"; Symmachus translated it "empty," and the Septuagint and Theodotion "abominable" and "disowned."

The question then arises how the prophecy can stand that no one born of his stock would sit on David's throne or ever again be a prince in Judah, since our Lord and Saviour was born of his seed. Concerning his birth Gabriel says to Mary: Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

We can say, then, that the problem arose for those unaware of the words missing from the Septuagint, namely "in his days he will not prosper" — or "will not grow." For the Septuagint translated: "Write this man down as a disowned man, for no man of his seed will grow to sit on the throne of David, a prince any longer in Judah." In the Hebrew this word is set down twice, and the earliest copyists, thinking it had been added in the Greek books, removed it.

Our answer, then, is that in Jeconiah's days no man succeeded him and sat on his throne, but a long time afterward one was born of his seed who did take possession of his throne. The problem can also be solved another way: a man, a human being, will indeed not sit on David's throne, but God will. His kingdom will not be earthly and brief, as David's was, but everlasting and heavenly, as Scripture says: He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. So Jeconiah was born of Jehoiakim,

Shealtiel of Jeconiah, and Zerubbabel of Shealtiel, and so the line comes down in order to Christ. But in the days of Jehoiachin no son succeeded him as king, as he himself had succeeded his father. He was in captivity, and so were Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and no one held royal power until Christ. This is why the Hebrew has "in his days": in the very time in which he lived there would be no man to sit on the throne of David. For they were all captives, and from then on no one of David's stock held rule in the land of Judea.

So Josephus too records that the rulers were of priestly lineage and of the tribe of Levi, that Herod, son of the proselyte Antipater, succeeded them, and that afterward, under Vespasian, the kingdom of this nation — or rather the mere semblance of rule — was utterly destroyed.

Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear apart the flock of my pasture — or "O shepherds, who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture" — says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock and driven them away, and you have not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your doings, says the Lord.

And I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the lands to which I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fields — or "restore them to their pastures" — and they will grow and multiply. And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they will feed them. They will no longer fear or be dismayed, and none will be missing from their number, says the Lord.

The prophetic word is addressed to the shepherds, or concerns the shepherds. Of Jeconiah, the second-to-last king of Judea, who was of David's stock, we read: Earth, earth, earth, hear the words of the Lord! Write this man down as disowned — or "barren" — and no man of his seed will sit on the throne of David. All hope of the Judean kingdom had been cut off, so the word passes to the leaders of the Church. The synagogue and its shepherds are abandoned and condemned, and the word is addressed to the apostles, of whom it is said: And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they will feed them; they will no longer fear or be dismayed, and none will be missing from their number,

says the Lord. For the apostles will feed the Church's flock with confidence and without any fear, and the remnant of the people of Israel will be saved out of all lands and brought back to their fields, or pastures, and they will grow and multiply. But the Lord will visit the evil shepherds, the scribes and Pharisees, for the wickedness of their doings.

In the tropological sense we can also understand this of the leaders of the Church who do not rule the Lord's sheep worthily. When they are cast off and condemned, the people may be saved by being entrusted to others who prove worthy, and the remnant may be saved. Shepherds who teach heresy destroy the sheep; those who make schisms tear them apart and scatter them; those who unjustly cut them off from the Church drive them out; those who withhold their hand from penitents do not visit them. The Lord will have mercy on all these sheep, giving them back their former pastures and taking away the evil shepherds.

Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous branch — or "a righteous dawn" — and a king shall reign and be wise — or "understand" — and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land. In those days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell in confidence, and this is the name by which they will call him — or "he will call him": the Lord our righteous one, or "our righteousness," which in Hebrew is "sadecenu." The phrase

"among the prophets," wrongly added in the Septuagint, must be cut out entirely. Another section follows, which they left out, and at its end comes the heading "To the prophets" or "Against the prophets." We will discuss it in its place. So once the shepherds of the synagogue have been cast off,

namely the scribes and Pharisees, and the remnant of Israel has been saved, and the apostles of the gospel have been set in place of the former leaders, the shepherd of shepherds is brought in, the prince of princes, the King of kings and Lord of lords: Christ our Saviour. He is properly the "righteous branch" or "righteous dawn," of whom we read, "In his days righteousness shall arise," and elsewhere, "Behold a man whose name is the Dawn; beneath him it shall spring up, and he shall build a temple to the Lord." Just as in Isaiah he is called "Emmanuel," that is, "God with us," so in Jeremiah he receives the name "our righteousness." So the Apostle also says: who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. Opposed to him is the Antichrist, together with the devil who dwells in him, who in Zechariah is called "the foolish shepherd."

"And he shall execute," it says, "judgment and righteousness in the land"; for the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. In those days both the two tribes and the ten, Judah and Israel, will be saved together, and, as in Ezekiel, the two rods will become one rod. As for his name: if we follow the Septuagint, which says the Lord will call him, he will be named Josedech, that is, "the Lord is righteous." If we follow the Hebrew, which says "they will call his name," he will be called "the Lord our righteousness," since that is what adonai sadecenu means. Symmachus rendered it, "Lord, make us righteous!"

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when they will no longer say, "As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel up out of the land of Egypt," but, "As the Lord lives, who brought out and led back the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands to which I had driven them"; and they shall dwell in their own land. This whole section is not in the Septuagint. Its meaning is this: the people of God are set free not from Egypt through Moses, but through Jesus Christ from the whole world, over which they had been scattered. This is partly being fulfilled in the world even now, and it will be fulfilled completely when they come from east and west, from north and south, and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that once the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel may be saved.

To the prophets, or Among the prophets, or Against the prophets. As we said above, in the Septuagint edition this heading is placed at the end of the preceding section, where we read: "And this is the name by which the Lord will call him: Josedech, among the prophets." Most interpreters, unaware of this, invent all kinds of absurd explanations. It would have been much better simply to admit their ignorance than to make others heirs of their own lack of skill.

This word is aimed at the prophets — or rather the false prophets — of Jerusalem and Samaria, whom he now calls "prophets" by the common, everyday name. Of them it is written in what follows, "And in the prophets of Samaria I saw iniquity," and immediately after, "And in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw horrible things." By putting the conjunction "and," he shows that what came before was said about prophets of the Lord who had themselves become like the false prophets.

My heart is broken within me — or "in me" — all my bones tremble — or "are shaken"; I have become like a drunken man, like a man soaked — or "overcome" — with wine, because of the Lord and because of his holy words — or "and because of the beauty of his glory."

Having contemplated the countenance of almighty God, that is, the Father, and the countenance of the Son, whom the Apostle calls the "radiance of his glory" and the "form of God's substance," the prophet shudders in mind and body and understands that he is nothing. As it says in another place: I became like a beast of burden before you. Or else he offers God the sacrifice of his conscience and humility, as is written in the Psalms: The sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.

As for the bones that trembled, or were shaken, let us understand them as those of which the same David sings: All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you? He became like a drunk man, like a man soaked — or "overcome" — with wine, having no understanding and no wisdom; for the Lord knows the thoughts of men,

that they are vain. If this is so, where are those who preach perfect righteousness in man? If they reply that they say this of the saints and not of themselves, I certainly think no one is holier than Jeremiah. He was a virgin and a prophet, sanctified in the womb, and by his very name he prefigures the Lord and Saviour, for Jeremiah means "the exalted one of the Lord."

For the land is full of adulterers; for because of the curse — or "the oath" — the land mourns; the fields — or "pastures" — of the wilderness have dried up; their course has become evil and their strength is unlike what it should be. The words we have given from the Hebrew, "for the land is full of adulterers," are not in the Septuagint, which has "oath" in place of "curse."

He also gives the reasons: barren crops followed because of adulteries and cursing, or needless swearing — indeed, perjury. Whatever you understand literally of the land of Judea, apply to the congregation of believers: because of adulteries and lies, or perjuries, the churches are barren of God's powers and gifts.

For prophet and priest alike are defiled, and in my house I have found their wickedness, says the Lord. Therefore their way will be like a slippery path in the dark; they will be pushed and fall on it, for I will bring — or "bring down" — evils upon them, the year of their visitation, says the Lord. When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially in its leaders, let us know that this is being fulfilled: Prophet and priest are defiled; in my house I have found their evils, says the Lord.

The house of Christ is the Church, of which Paul also writes to Timothy: so that you may know how one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. By the prophet understand the teacher, and by the priest the dignity of the ministry. If they go along with a perverse mind, their way will be slippery and in darkness, and they will not have the Lord saying to them: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness. So the holy man, fleeing all darkness, says: The light of your countenance has been stamped upon us, O Lord; you have put gladness in my heart.

Once they are in darkness and on a slippery way — that is, in heretical error — they will be pushed at every movement and will fall. And the Lord brings evils upon them. This is not because the things the Lord brings are evil in themselves; they are evils to those who suffer punishment. Otherwise the same things are both evil and good: evil for those whom they torment,

and good for those whom they correct. We should also note that the year of the Lord's visitation means the correction and chastisement of sinners, as it is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with stripes; but my mercy I will not take away from him.

And in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly — or "iniquity"; they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray. In the mystical sense, I think the prophets of Samaria properly stand for heretics and for all who boast of knowledge falsely so called.

The prophets of Samaria, whatever they said, prophesied by Baal, an idol consecrated to demons. In the same way heretics, whatever they say inside or outside the Church to trip up the people of Israel, who once beheld God, speak by demons. That is why he says so pointedly: And in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly. For they do not have him of whom it is said, "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God."

And in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw a likeness — or "horrible things": adultery and the way of falsehood. They strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that no one turned back from his wickedness — or "from his evil way." They have all become to me like Sodom, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah.

"Not only," he says, "have these things been found in the gatherings of heretics. In the prophets of Jerusalem too, that is, the teachers of the Church, I have seen similar — or horrible — things. They adulterate the word of God and walk in the way of falsehood. They give in to the deceits of heretics, strengthen the hands of the wicked, add the wicked's evils to their own crimes, and lead to destruction those whom they ought to have corrected.

Let those who have done this not imagine that they will go unpunished! Both they and those whom they favour will be like Sodom, and all who live with them and do not withdraw from such people will be like Gomorrah." So let this wicked doctrine exult as much as it likes, and let the prophets of Jerusalem boast that they have won through falsehood and strengthened the hands of the wicked: their end will be like Sodom and Gomorrah.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts to the prophets: Behold, I will feed them with wormwood — or "with pains," or, in Symmachus, "with bitterness" — and give them gall to drink — or "bitter water"; for from the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone out into the whole land.

Let us use this testimony against those who send letters full of lies, fraud and perjury around the world to pollute the ears of their hearers and damage the good name of simple people, so that what is written is fulfilled in them: From the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone out into the whole land. It is not enough for them to devour their own iniquity and harm their neighbours. Anyone they have once come to hate they try to defame throughout the whole world, sowing blasphemies everywhere.

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you! They speak a vision from their own heart, not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who blaspheme me — or "reject my word": The Lord has spoken: You shall have peace. And to everyone who walks in the perversity of his own heart they have said: No evils will come upon you.

So that the people would not think themselves free of guilt if they gave in to perverse teachers, he says: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy lies to you and deceive you" — for teacher and disciple will receive the same punishment. "They do not speak from the mouth of the Lord, but what they have made up in their own heart. They say to those who blaspheme me" — that is, to heretics and perverse men — "or who reject my word. What do they say? 'The Lord has spoken: You shall have peace. Do not fear harsh punishments or let empty threats frighten you. You will have peace and calm. Whatever we tell you and proclaim to you, the Lord has spoken. The evil you fear because of a bad conscience will not come upon you, but the good which the Lord has promised you.'"

For who has stood in the counsel of the Lord, and seen and heard his word? Who has considered his word and heard it? Where we have translated "in the counsel of the Lord," and the Hebrew has "bassod," Aquila translated "secret," Symmachus "discourse," and the Septuagint and Theodotion "substance" or "subsistence."

And the sense is: "Do not believe, you untaught crowd, the prophets who announce falsehoods to you, who say: 'The Lord has spoken: you will have peace; no evil will come upon you!' For how can they know the secrets of God, or from what source [?] did they learn the counsel of the Lord? How did the word of the divine plan reach them?" Some of our own writers think they have found in this passage a place where the substance of God is written of.

Behold, the whirlwind (or: the storm and upheaval) of the Lord's indignation goes forth, and a storm breaking out will come upon the head of the wicked; and the fury of the Lord will not turn back until he has carried out and fulfilled the purpose of his heart. In the last days you will understand his counsel.

Above, he had rebuked those who said, "The Lord has spoken to us: you will have peace," because they could not know what was to come or know God's sentence. Now he shows by contraries that they know nothing at all. Instead of peace and security, a Babylonian storm is coming, and it is coming not upon just anyone, but upon the heads of the wicked, whether of the whole people or of those who announced falsehoods to the people. Nor is God's wrath and fury to be appeased as in times past. Rather, what he foretold and very often threatened is to be fulfilled in deed, and his purpose and sentence are to be proven by the punishments of the wicked.

"When," he says, "the final time of captivity has come, and the exulting victor has seized you and bound your hands with clanking chains, then you will understand his counsel, which you now vainly boast that you know."

I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. If they had stood in my counsel and made my words known to my people, I would surely have turned them from their evil way and from their most wicked thoughts.

The Apostle also explains this sense to the Romans: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting, filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, wickedness, greed, and the rest. For once false teachers have given themselves over to lies and perjuries and to the deaths
of those they deceive, they run not step by step or with measured pace, but headlong to destruction, both their own and that of those whom they have deceived.

Nor does the Lord speak to them; they speak as if from the Lord's mouth. Of them it is said: "If they had stood in my counsel (that is, if they had been willing to submit to my will) and made my words known to my people, instead of flattering them and ruining them with adulation by saying, 'You have no sins, you possess perfect righteousness; holiness and chastity and righteousness are found in you alone,' then I would not have handed them over to uncleanness and disgrace, to do what is not fitting and to follow their own most wicked thoughts."

Let us look at the heretics: once they despair of salvation, they give themselves over to gluttony and luxury, eat meat, frequent the baths, smell of musk, and, anointed with various perfumes, seek bodily beauty. For they have given up all hope of what is to come and do not believe in the resurrection. What they do not reveal in speech, they show in deeds: if they believed, they would not do these things. In this passage too, where it is written, If they had stood in my counsel, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and the Septuagint translated in the same way as above.

Am I a God near at hand, says the Lord, and not a God far off? If a man hides in secret places, will I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord. The Septuagint: I am a God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar. If a man is hidden in secret places, will I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.

Aquila and Symmachus translated in the same way: Am I a God from nearby (or: near at hand) and not a God from afar? But the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered it in the opposite sense, saying: I am a God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar. The former, that is, assert that God knows not only what is near but also what is far off, and sees not only the present but the future. The latter hold that God is present everywhere, and that there is no place where God is not present. For God draws near to all, and especially to the saints, as a garment clings to the skin; but sinners, withdrawing far from him, will perish.

We read this sense in the Psalms too: Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me. Amos also agrees with these words, saying:

Though they go down to hell, from there my hand will bring them out; and though they climb up to heaven, from there I will drag them down. Though they hide on the top of Carmel, I will search them out and take them from there; and though they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I will command the serpent and it will bite them. And again, earlier in the same psalm: For darkness, it says, will not be dark to you, and the night will be lit up like the day; as its darkness is, so is its light.

The phrase "Thus says the Lord" is used so often in the prophets, and is always added, so that their words will not be despised as merely the words of prophets, and so that people will be continually reminded that what the prophets speak are the words of God.

I have heard what the prophets said who prophesy lies in my name, saying: I have dreamed, I have dreamed (or: I have seen a dream). How long will this be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies and prophesy the deceptions (or: the desires) of their own heart? They want (or: they plan) to make my people forget my name through their dreams, which each one tells to his neighbor, just as their fathers forgot my name for Baal (or: in Baal).

The preceding heading is against the prophets (or: to the prophets), whom we clearly understand to be false prophets. There are many kinds of prophesying, one of which is through dreams, as in Daniel. Therefore the prophetic word is also directed at those who believe in dreams and think that everything they see is divine revelation, which is properly disclosed to the saints and servants of God. And if we read that Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar, wicked kings, saw dreams that were true, this was not due to the merit of those who saw them. It happened so that through them the holy men Joseph and Daniel might become renowned, and the hard and untamable hearts of tyrants might perceive the majesty of the Lord in their own conscience.

Even today there are dreamers in the church, especially in our own flock, who boast of their errors as the Lord's prophecy and keep pressing on us: "I have dreamed, I have dreamed." The Lord rebukes them, saying: "How long will this be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies and prophesy the deceptions of their own heart?

They do this so that, just as the ancient people who came out of Egypt forgot the name of God, their descendants too may forget me." Prophecy of this kind is not in the name of the Lord but in the name of Baal, which is properly the idol of the Sidonians, or else the Babylonian one, and is called Bel by a similar name.

Let the prophet who has a dream tell his dream, and let him who has my word speak my word truly! What has chaff to do with wheat? says the Lord. Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer (or: an axe) that shatters the rock? It belongs to those who deserve to have God's word to expound a dream and to say "Thus says the Lord": to those to whom the Lord has spoken, in whom there is truth and not deceitful lies.

What has the chaff of the heretics to do with the wheat of the church? John the Baptist speaks of this more fully: Christ will clear his threshing floor and with his winnowing fan leave the chaff to be scattered by the blasts of the winds and burned with fire, but he will store the wheat in barns, so that heavenly bread may be made of it, and each believer may say: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet! And perverse doctrine is fittingly compared to chaff, which has no kernel and cannot nourish the believing peoples, but is threshed from empty stalks.

The heretics always promise prosperity and open the kingdom of heaven to sinners, saying: "The kingdom of heaven is prepared for you; you can imitate the majesty of God so as to be without sin. For you have received the power of free will and the knowledge of the law, through which you may attain whatever you wish." They deceive the wretched with flattery, especially silly women laden with sins, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth, and they deceive all their hearers with adulation. For this reason the Lord, comparing his words with the chaff of the heretics, says: "Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer that shatters the rock?

For my word," he says, "announces punishments to come, to deter people from sinning." And he threatens the chaff of sinners with burning, so that the hearts of the heretics, hard and untamable like flint, may be shattered by the hammer of his word. Then he may take away the heart of stone and put in its place a heart of flesh: one that is soft and able to receive and perceive the commands of God.

The Lord says something similar through Ezekiel: the false prophets with their flatteries daub a wall without proper mortar, and it is afterward overthrown by violent rain and by the truth of judgment; and the false prophetesses sew pillows under every elbow, to let sinners rest easy and never soften God's wrath with tears.

For "hammer" the Septuagint translated "axe," namely the one John the Baptist speaks of: Already the axe is laid to the root of the trees. This axe cuts down unfruitful trees, and this hammer shatters the hardest stones. Hence the prophet Nahum also says: His fury (God's, no doubt) will consume principalities, and the rocks will be shattered by him. This is against the heretics. But of churchmen it is written that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of God.

Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who steal my words, each from his neighbor. Behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who take up their tongues and say: He says (or: they slumber a slumber). Behold, I am against the prophets who dream lies, says the Lord, who tell them and lead my people astray with their lies and their marvels (or: their astonishments and terrors), though I did not send them or command them; they have not profited this people at all, says the Lord.

Falsehood always imitates truth, and unless it has some likeness to what is right, it cannot deceive the innocent. Among the former people, the prophets lied and said "Thus says the Lord," and "I saw the Lord," and "The word of the Lord that came to him" or "[?]". In the same way the heretics take up testimonies of Scripture from the Old and New Testaments, and steal the words of the Savior, each from his neighbor: from the prophets, apostles and evangelists. They take up their tongues to utter with their mouths the poisons of their hearts, and they slumber a slumber. Of them it is truly said: They have slept their sleep and found nothing. Or, according to the Hebrew: and they say: He says, with "the Lord" or else "the divine word" understood.

So the Lord threatens that he himself will come against teachers of this kind, who lead his people astray with their lies and with astonishments and marvels. For they promise great, incredible and enormous things to seduce the wretched. They have not profited the people of God at all, and they fulfill the apostle's saying, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain. They are accustomed to announce prosperity to the wicked, and adversity [?].

If, then, this people or a prophet or a priest asks you, saying, What is the burden of the Lord? (or: What is the taking up of the Lord?), you shall say to them: You are the burden (or: the taking up); for I will cast you off (or: dash you down), says the Lord. And as for the prophet and the priest and the people who say, The burden (or: taking up) of the Lord, I will visit (or: take vengeance) upon that man and upon his house.

This is what each of you shall say to his friend and to his brother: What did the Lord answer, and what did the Lord say? And the burden (or: taking up) of the Lord shall be mentioned no more, for each man's own word will be his burden (or: taking up).

Aquila translates the Hebrew word "massa" as ἆρμα, that is, "burden" and "weight"; Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion translate it "taking up." So wherever what the Lord threatens is grievous, full of weight and toil and unbearable, the heading also says ἆρμα, that is, "weight." But wherever the Lord promises prosperity, or promises better things after a threat, there it says "vision" or else "word of the Lord." So from the very heading of the prophecy, "weight" or else "vision" and "word of God," it was clear what kind of prophecy would follow.

The prophets used to announce sad things to the sinning people and threaten punishments, to draw them back to repentance. But the Lord, merciful and compassionate, long delayed his sentence, and so the people, deceived and led astray by the fraud of the false prophets, thought that what the Lord threatened would not come. They had turned a serious matter into sport and jest, and when the prophets prophesied they would say mockingly: "Here he is again, seeing a weight and burden of the Lord!" And so it came about that it was no longer called a "vision," but in jest and derision a "burden" and a "weight."

So the Lord commands that, whether the people or a prophet or a priest asks Jeremiah what the weight or the taking up of the Lord is, he should answer them and say: "You are the burden, and you are the taking up; for I will take you up and cast you off and dash you down and make you perish. And if anyone hereafter, whether of the prophets or the priests or the people, dares to speak of the burden and weight of the Lord, I will visit," he says, "upon that man and upon his house, and I will destroy him forever."

So let each one say to his neighbor and friend, not "What is the burden of the Lord?" but: "What did the Lord answer, and what did the Lord say? Forget the old ways; let 'burden' and 'weight' or 'taking up' no longer sound in your mouth. For each person's own word and own work will be reckoned to him as a burden and a weight, according to what is written: By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned."
And you pervert the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God. Thus you shall say (or: you all shall say) to the prophet: What did the Lord answer you, and what did the Lord say?

But if you say "the burden of the Lord" (up to this point the text is not found in the Septuagint), it continues: therefore thus says the Lord [?]: Because you have spoken this word, "the burden (or: taking up) of the Lord," and I sent to you saying, Do not say "the burden (or: taking up) of the Lord," therefore, behold, I will lift you up (or: take you up) and carry you, and I will abandon you, and the city which I gave to you and your fathers, away from my presence. And I will make you an everlasting reproach and an eternal disgrace that will never be blotted out by forgetfulness.

The Lord commanded that the words "burden," "weight" and "taking up" should no longer be spoken among the people, but rather "answer" and "word of God." Because the people scorned to obey, he turns that very word against them and says: "Since you have said what I did not want, and this when I often sent prophets and commanded you not to say it, I will therefore fulfill in deed upon you your own word of taking up, burden and weight. I will take you up and lift you and carry you, and dash you down and make you fall from on high to the ground, and not only you, but also your city, which I gave to your fathers. And I will make you," he says, "a reproach and an everlasting disgrace that will never be blotted out by forgetfulness."

We know that this happened at the time of the Babylonian captivity; but it is fulfilled more fully and perfectly after the passion and resurrection of the Savior, when the Lord said: Your house will be left to you desolate. And this sentence will remain until the end.

Let us also put it another way, at least according to the Septuagint: λῆμμα means not only "taking up" but also "gift" and "present." Since the people were always promising themselves prosperity, he says that they must by no means say this any longer. For they are unworthy of God's gifts and presents; rather, they are to be cast off and utterly abandoned by God's help.

Things are also often indicated by words and by the interpretation of names. Thus the changed names of Abraham, Sarah, Peter and the sons of Zebedee signify a change in their state, and in this same prophet "Pashhur" is called "terror," or "removal" and "settler" or "stranger." Note that the Latin and Greek manuscripts do not have the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God, while the Hebrews read them in their own scrolls to their own refutation, since they properly signify the mystery of the Trinity.
BOOK FIVE

The fifth book of the commentaries on Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, will begin with the two baskets. One of them will show the sweetness of the right faith, the other the bitterness of the heretics' faithlessness. Hananiah son of Azzur opposes Jeremiah, Shemaiah the Nehelamite wants the prophet thrown into prison, and Zephaniah the priest conspires in the words of the false prophets. Even so, truth can be shut up and bound, but it cannot be conquered: it is content with the fewness of its own and is not frightened by the multitude of its enemies.

So lift up your hands to heaven with Moses and hang up the ancient serpent in the wilderness. At once Amalek will be destroyed and the venomous bites will not prevail, and the people of the Lord will cross the streams of the Jordan in safety with Joshua, and after the vast wilderness they will eat the bread that was born in our little village of Bethlehem.

The Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets (or, according to Symmachus, hampers) full of figs set before the temple of the Lord, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and his princes, and the craftsman and the setter, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon. One basket had very good figs, like the figs that come first in the season; and one basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten because they were so bad.

And the Lord said to me: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And I said: “Figs: the good figs very good, and the bad very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are so bad.” And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so will I regard the exiles of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans,

for good. And I will set my eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them back to this land; I will build them up and not tear them down, I will plant them and not uproot them. And I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.

And like the very bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are so bad, thus says the Lord, so will I give up (or, hand over) Zedekiah king of Judah, and his princes, and the rest of Jerusalem who remain in this city, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.

And I will give them up to vexation and affliction (or, dispersion) among all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach and a byword and a proverb and a curse in all the places to which I have driven them. And I will send among them the sword, famine and pestilence, until they are consumed from the land which I gave to them and to their fathers.”

Some interpret the two hampers or baskets of good and bad figs as the Law and the Gospel, the synagogue and the Church, the Jewish people and the Christian people, Gehenna and the kingdom of heaven: one of which belongs to the punishment of sinners, the other to the dwelling-place of the saints.

But we, knowing with the apostle Paul that the Law is good and holy, and the commandment good and holy, and that there is one God of both Testaments, should rather refer them to those who believed and those who did not believe at the coming of the Lord and Savior: so that those who, stirred up by the scribes and priests, cried out, “Crucify, crucify such a man,” are the basket of bad figs; while those of the people who believed after his ascension are to be referred to the good figs and to the excellent basket and hamper.

Let us, however, follow the plain and true historical sense: that he called the basket of good figs Jeconiah, who on Jeremiah's advice and at God's command had surrendered himself to the king of Babylon, and to whom the Lord also promises prosperity; and the basket of bad figs Zedekiah, who, resisting God's sentence, was captured, blinded, led to Babylon, and died there.

And so far did God set his eyes upon them for good, those who submitted to his command, and bring them back to their land, and build them up and not tear them down, and plant them and not uproot them, and give them a heart to know him, that he was the Lord, so that they became his people and he became their God, that even in captivity he set his eyes upon them and permitted them to till the land, build houses and plant orchards in the region of Babylon; Daniel, through miraculous signs, was suddenly made a ruler instead of a captive; the three young men were gloriously delivered from the fire of the furnace; and when the seventy years were completed, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the high priest, and Ezra and Nehemiah, the greater part returned to Jerusalem. Their number is recorded in the book of that same Ezra.

It should also be noted that this vision came to the prophet in the time of Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been led away into “deportation”; for he did not say “captivity,” because Jeconiah had surrendered of his own accord. By the craftsmen and setters we should understand either interpreters and teachers of the Law, or artisans and setters of gold and gems, a craft that is most highly prized among barbarian nations. For “setters” the Septuagint translated “prisoners,” to signify the evil of captivity, and they added “the rich” on their own, which is not in the Hebrew.

He compares the basket that had good figs, very good ones, to the figs of the first season (which in Greek are called πρόιμα), that is, to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and Aaron, Job and the other holy men, of whom one of the twelve prophets says: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, and like figs on the fig tree I found their fathers.” Hence we too are called children of Abraham, and on the other hand it is said to the Jews: “If Abraham were your father, you would do his works.” These baskets, which held the good and the bad figs, were not outside, beyond the Church, but before the temple of the Lord, because all things lie open to his knowledge.

Nor do the figs that are outside have as much bitterness as those which after confessing the faith have been changed by transgression; nor do the good figs that are not in the sight of God's temple (such as the philosophers of the world were, who by natural goodness and an understanding of the Creator strove not so much to follow the virtues as to praise them) have as much sweetness as the figs that are in God's temple. Among these were the prophets and apostles, of whom one fig said: “I gave you milk, not solid food,” and: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Hence it is said that in the sight of God's temple the good figs were very good and the bad figs were very bad.

And lest we be thought to be imposing our own meaning, Scripture itself makes it plain. “Like these good figs,” it says, “so will I regard the exiles of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good,” meaning Jeconiah and the princes who were captured with him.

And on the other hand, concerning the basket that had bad figs: “And like the very bad figs,” he says, “which cannot be eaten because they are so bad, so will I give up Zedekiah king of Judah, and his princes, and those who fled to Egypt, and those who remained in this city, to vexation and affliction among all the kingdoms of the earth,” when they were captured in Egypt too, and Nebuchadnezzar set up his throne in Tahpanhes, and the Lord sent upon them sword, famine and pestilence until they were consumed from the land which he had given to their fathers.

What he said of the good figs, “I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord,” is like the apostle's words: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish,” for not only our works but also our will rely on God's help.

At this point the ever-allegorizing interpreter raves and, eager to do violence to the historical truth, refers this to those who were taken captive from the heavenly Jerusalem and carried off to the land of the Chaldeans and who will return again to their former place, such as Jeremiah and the other holy prophets; while the others, who were sinners, are to die in this land and in the valley of tears. I have set out the whole pericope (περικοπή) of this vision at once, so as not to divide its meaning in the exposition.

The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judea (or, upon all the people of Judah) in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. These events come before the preceding vision; for that took place under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been carried off to Babylon, but this under Jehoiakim,

the son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah. For, as I have said before, prophecy was not concerned to preserve the chronological order that the laws of history require, but to write in whatever way it knew would be useful to hearers and readers. Hence some in the Psalter wrongly look for an order of the psalms following the sequence of history, which is not observed in lyric poetry.

That was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. This is not in the Septuagint. And there follows: which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim son of Josiah, the father of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar took power in Babylon, and so it came about that the year which was Nebuchadnezzar's first in Babylon was the fourth of King Jehoiakim in Jerusalem.

Then in the eighth year of his reign he led into captivity, with his mother and princes, Jeconiah, who had reigned only three months after the killing of his father Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim was killed in the eleventh year of his reign in Jerusalem.

From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, which is the twenty-third year, the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising early by night and speaking; and you have not listened.

In the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, who reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years, Jeremiah began to prophesy, and he prophesied under him for nineteen years. His son Jehoahaz succeeded him on the throne; when he was at once led into captivity by Necho king of Egypt, his brother Jehoiakim obtained the kingdom, and in the fourth year of his reign this word of the Lord came to Jeremiah. So it was the twenty-third year of Jeremiah the prophet since he began to speak to the people, and he never ceased to preach, but every day, rising at dawn and by night, he spoke to the people; “and you,” he says, “have not listened.”

But if, as the new heretics sprung from the old ones claim, the Law was given once and for all as a help, and commandments were established which we either do or do not do by the choice of our own free will, how is it that the prophet constantly presses himself upon them and daily repeats God's commandments, which, once received, would surely have sufficed for those to whom they were given? Is it not to show that we always need God's help, and that what has been given once can never suffice unless it is renewed daily by the Lord's admonition?

And the Lord has sent to you all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending them; and you have not listened. Not through one prophet but through all of them God continually admonished his people, and, as though himself stationed on watch and on guard, he rose at dawn to warn his people. “And you have not listened,” he says, so that the more frequent the warning, the greater were the sins of those who scorned it.

Nor have you inclined your ears to hear, when I said: Turn back, each of you, from his evil way and from your most wicked thoughts, and you shall dwell in the land which the Lord gave to you and to your fathers from age to age.

So great was the people's hardness that it would not even adopt the posture of a listener and incline its ear, though it was the Lord himself above all who was warning it, so that each might turn back from his evil way and from his most wicked thoughts. O boundless mercy, not to inflict punishment for crime, but to call to repentance both for evil works, signified by the evil way, and for most wicked thoughts, which are themselves counted as sin even without the deed!

And he promises a reward if they do what is commanded: that they shall dwell in the land which was given to their fathers and taken away because of the sons' vices. And when he says “from age to age,” or “from eternity to eternity,” he shows that God's gifts are everlasting, if those to whom they are given prove worthy.

And do not go after foreign gods to serve them and worship them, nor provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you; and you have not listened to me. “I warned your forebears of these things too,” he says, “that you should not serve foreign gods and worship them, and that by doing so you should not provoke me to anger through the works of your hands, so that I would do what I did not wish and afflict you; and you did not listen to me.”
What follows, says the Lord, so that you provoked me to anger with the works of your hands to your own harm, is not in the Septuagint.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you have not listened to my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant. “Because you provoked me to anger and did evil to your own destruction, and trampled with a proud foot the one who was calling you to repentance, I will send,” he says, “to all the families (or nations) of the north, and I will bring their ruler, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant.”

The Lord sends either angels to stir up the nations, or at any rate moves thoughts of such a kind that they do the Lord's will. And when he calls Nebuchadnezzar “his servant,” he is not called “servant” in the way the prophets and all the saints are, who truly serve the Lord, but because in the overthrow of Jerusalem he served the Lord's will; as the apostle also says: “whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.” That the Chaldeans lie to the north, in relation to the position of Jerusalem, no one doubts.

And I will bring them against this land and against its inhabitants and against all the nations that are round about it, and I will slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations.

These are the wages of those who scorn God's words and will not hear them; whatever evil, then, is brought upon us, our sins have caused it. And all the nations, as they were then brought against Jerusalem, so today are brought against a negligent Church, to slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations, so that they may be an example and a marvel to all. Hissing is a sign of wonder and astonishment, and everlasting desolation is found in those who do not have God as their protector.

And I will take away from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bride and the voice of the bridegroom, the sound of the millstone and the light of the lamp. And all its land shall become a desolation and an astonishment.

This is proved even today in the gathering of the wicked, where their teachers do not teach the word of God but hiss like snakes. And in them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness perish, so that they never hear the apostle's word: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice!” So too the voice of the bride, that is, of the Church's faith, and the voice of the bridegroom, the Lord and Savior, for he who has the bride is the bridegroom; the sound of the millstone, so that no grain is ground in it and given to the peoples to eat; and the light of the lamp, namely the teaching and knowledge of the prophets. Indeed, it is said of John the Baptist: “He was a burning lamp,” and another prophet says: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.”
“All the land of the heretics,” he says, “shall become a desolation and an astonishment, when its latter end has been shown to be folly.”

And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, says the Lord, for their iniquities, and the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it everlasting desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have spoken against it, everything that is written in this book, all that Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.

Just as Jerusalem after seventy years received back its former inhabitants and, its punishments completed, because it obeyed God's sentence, enjoyed its former happiness, so the king of Babylon, because he was lifted up in pride and thought that his rule over the nations was the work of his own strength and not of the Lord's will, will be destroyed when the Medes and Persians come.

Indeed, to this day only the remains of the city of Babylon survive, and the Lord has made it an everlasting desolation and fulfilled all the words contained in the book of this very prophet. For in what follows, Jeremiah's discourse describes the evils Babylon would suffer.

For they have served them, though they were many nations and great kings; and I will repay them according to their works and according to the deeds of their hands. This is not in the Septuagint. It means that Jeremiah prophesied not only against Babylon but also against the other nations that were in the Babylonian army and fought against the Lord's people.

Indeed, in what follows prophecies are spoken against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon and Idumea, against Damascus and Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor and Elam, and finally against Babylon and the land of Chaldea.

For thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, to me: Take this cup of the wine of wrath (or, of unmixed wine) from my hand, and make all the nations to which I send you drink of it; and they shall drink and be drunk (or, vomit) and go mad before the sword which I will send among them. And I took the cup from the Lord's hand and made all the nations drink to whom the Lord sent me.

The drinking of the cup, and of the cup of “neat” or “unmixed” wine, which in Greek is called ἄκρατος, is a sign of the Lord's wrath, so that all the nations that made war against God's people drink of the cup of the Lord's wrath; of which Isaiah also writes against Jerusalem: “You have drunk the bowl of wrath, the cup of ruin, and drained it; therefore arise!” This cup is drunk by all the nations so that they may vomit and go mad.

A perverse interpreter takes this in a good sense: that, like a purgative draught, it forces out whatever bile and phlegm and harmful humor is in the chest and restores former health. He also takes Jeremiah to stand for the Savior, because he gave the drink to all the nations to whom he was sent, so that they might cast off idolatry and devote themselves to the worship of God. What follows will show that this is contrary to Holy Scripture; for the cup of unmixed wine is given them to drink not as a remedy, as he would have it, but as a punishment.
to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and its kings and its princes, to make them a desolation and an astonishment and a hissing and a curse, as it is this day.

“I thought,” he says, “that I would give the drink to the nations alone, and so I had gladly offered myself for this ministry; but among the other nations, or rather before the other nations, I gave it to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah and its kings and princes, to make them an astonishment and a desolation and a hissing and a curse, as the present example also proves.” Hence he also says above: “You deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you were stronger, and you prevailed!”

To Pharaoh king of Egypt and his servants and his princes [?] and all his people, and to all without distinction. After Jerusalem, Pharaoh king of Egypt drank, and his allies; his princes drank, and the whole people, and everyone who is not indeed an Egyptian but dwells in his territories, whom the Septuagint rendered συμμίκτους, that is, “mixed,” a crowd not native to the land of Egypt but foreign and immigrant.

To all the kings of the land of Ausitis. In Hebrew it is called “Uz,” and the history tells that Job came from it: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis named Job.” Yet it should be known that this verse is not in the Septuagint, and that Theodotion rendered “Uz” as “island.”

And to all the kings of the land of the Philistines, and of Ashkelon and Gaza and Ekron and the remnant of Ashdod. He named the Philistines generally, that is, the land of the Palestinians, and specifically their cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod; he passed over only Gath, which is included in “the remnant.” This is what is written: “and the remnant of Ashdod”; for the district of the city of Gath is near and adjoining Azotus, which in Hebrew is called Ashdod. Isaiah too writes that the Palestinians were captured and laid waste by the Babylonians.

To Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon, and all the kings of Tyre and all the kings of Sidon. Idumea is where the mountains of Seir are, and in Hebrew it is called Edom; Moab and Ammon are the sons of Lot, near the Dead Sea. Tyre and Sidon are the leading cities on the coast of Phoenicia, and they too were overcome when the Babylonian came. Carthage is their colony; hence the Carthaginians are called Poeni, a corruption as it were of “Phoeni,” and their language is in large part closely related to Hebrew.
And to the kings of the islands beyond the sea. He passes on to Cyprus and Rhodes and the islands called the Cyclades (Κυκλάδες); for these too were occupied by the Babylonians.

And Dedan and Tema and Buz, and all who are shorn round the hair. These nations live in the desert, neighboring and intermingled with the territories of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, and of whom it is said: “who are shorn round the hair.”
And to all the kings of Arabia. This is not in the Septuagint. So after Dedan and Tema and Buz and the Ishmaelites, the sequence of regions follows.
And to all the kings of the west who dwell in the desert, and to all the kings of Zimri. This too is not in the Septuagint.

And to all the kings of Elam and all the kings of the Medes. Since Elam and the kings of the Medes follow Zimri, we think that Zimri too is a region of Persia, unless perhaps, because Arabia came before, these too are to be understood as kings of the desert. Elam is a region of Persia beyond Babylon; hence the Elamites, and also the Medes and Persians, by whom Babylon was captured and destroyed; for they too drank the cup of unmixed wine when Alexander, king of the Macedonians, gave it to them.

And to all the kings of the north, near and far. Since he had listed the regions of Persia and Babylon, of Elam and of the Medes, he now names generally all the kings of the north, those near and those far. For “north,” which in Hebrew is called “safun,” the Septuagint rendered ἀπηλιώτην, which we may call “the east wind.”

"Each one against his brother, and all the kingdoms of the earth that are on its face." To avoid the tedium of listing every region of the eastern province one by one, he spoke in general of "all the kingdoms of the earth," which dwell upon the earth. When he says "against his brother," the words "I gave the undiluted drink" are understood, so that all should rage, vomit, go mad and fight battles against one another. And what he added:

"And the king of Sheshach shall drink after them," which is not found in the Septuagint, has this sense: "All the nations round about," he says, "will be subject to Babylonian rule, and he will bring everything under his power, so that all the peoples whom the preceding passage listed will serve him and drink from his cup." Hence it is also written in the vision against Babylon: "Babylon is a golden cup that makes all the earth drunk." But the last king of Babylon will drink this drink himself, when Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians, the rider of the chariot, of the camel and of the donkey, hands him the cup.

How Babylon, which in Hebrew is called Babel, is to be understood as "Sheshach" will cost no great effort to anyone who has even a slight knowledge of the Hebrew language. Among us the Greek alphabet is read in order down to the last letter, that is, "alpha, beta" and so on to "omega"; and again, to help children's memory, we usually reverse the order of reading and pair the last letters with the first, so as to say "alpha omega, beta psi." So too among the Hebrews the first letter is aleph, the second beth, the third gimel, and so on to the twenty-second and last letter, tau, before which the second-to-last is shin.

So we read "aleph tau, beth shin," and when we come to the middle, kaph corresponds to lamed. And just as, read in the normal way, we read "Babel," so with the order reversed we read "Sheshach." The vowels between beth and beth and lamed (and between shin and shin and kaph) are not written in this name, in keeping with the idiom of the Hebrew language. I think the holy prophet prudently concealed it so as not to stir up openly against himself the fury of those who were besieging Jerusalem and were on the very point of taking it.

We read that the apostle did the same with regard to the Roman Empire, when he wrote of the Antichrist: "Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time" ("the Antichrist" is understood). "For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only he who now holds back will do so until he is taken out of the way. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming." By "he who holds back" he indicates the Roman Empire; for unless it is destroyed and taken out of the way, the Antichrist will not come before that, according to the prophecy of Daniel. Had he chosen to say this openly, he would foolishly have stirred up a frenzy of persecution against the Christians and the church that was then being born.

We have spoken about this passage at greater length than the brevity of a commentary allows, and perhaps the Greeks and Latins will find it tiresome, because it is not in their manuscripts. But what good will that do them, when later on this same prophet says: "How Sheshach has been taken, and the glory of all the earth seized! How Babylon has become an object of astonishment among the nations!"

Allegorical interpreters refer this whole passage to all the nations that the devil has made drunk with the most undiluted cup of sins; last of all, they say, he himself will drink punishments and torments, and of him the apostle writes: "whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth"; hence he also says in another place: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." It takes great powers to be able to reinterpret the names of the various nations according to their etymologies and to fit a particular vice to each particular name.

"And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk, and vomit and fall, and do not rise up before the sword that I will send among you!" "After you have handed the cup to all the nations," he says, "and fulfilled the Lord's command, you will again give this command in the Lord's words and say: Drink and be drunk, and vomit and fall, and do not rise up!" If "drinking,

being drunk, vomiting and falling" is a sign of salvation, so that, as with a purgative drink, everything harmful is expelled, how can there follow: "and do not rise up"? But what the drink is that makes them fall forever he states more plainly, namely: "before the sword that I will send among you."

"And if they refuse to take the cup from your hand to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: You shall surely drink, for behold, in the city on which my name is called I am beginning to bring affliction; and will you go unpunished, as if innocent (or: and will you be cleansed with cleansing)? You will not go unpunished (or: you will not be clean)."

He shows indirectly that those who refuse to carry out God's command willingly will accept it by necessity and will hear: "You shall surely drink." "Whether you will or not," he says, "God's sentence must be fulfilled. For if the city of Jerusalem, in which God's name was known — as the prophet says, 'In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel' — drank the undiluted cup of fury, how much less will you be clean, who worship idols in place of God's name!"

"For I am calling a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord of hosts." This is the most undiluted drink; this is the cup of the Lord's fury, which is called down not on Jerusalem alone but on the whole earth and on all the nations round about. Of it he had said above: "And I will send for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and against its inhabitants and against all the nations that are around it."

"And you shall prophesy to them all these words and say to them: The Lord will roar from on high (or: will give an answer), and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; he will roar mightily over his beauty (or: he will answer over his place); a shout like that of those treading grapes will be raised against all the inhabitants of the earth. The sound (or: the destruction) has reached to the ends (or: over a part) of the earth, for the Lord has a case against the nations; he enters into judgment with all flesh; the wicked he has handed over to the sword, says the Lord."

First let us explain the passage as the true translation has it. "To all the nations," he says, "you shall prophesy and say that the Lord roars from on high, that is, gives a sign of his fury, as it is written: 'The lion will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?'" "And from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice," so as to terrify all who hear it.

"He will roar over his beauty," that is, over the temple. And when he has roared, a shout will be raised like that of those treading in the winepresses, and amid the shedding of one another's blood a mournful song will be chanted, which Symmachus calls katalegma and Aquila iasmos [?]. The sound of this shout and song will reach to the ends of the earth, "for the Lord has a case against the nations."

But if the Lord has a case against the nations, the nations also differ in what they deserve. This serves to explain the passage, as some would have it: "He who does not believe is already judged." He is indeed judged in that he did not believe; but those who do not believe will themselves be visited with different punishments, one from another. "He enters into judgment with all flesh," so that no one goes away unjudged. But the wicked — that is, those who do not believe in the Lord — he hands over to the everlasting sword.

Allegorical interpreters, following the Septuagint, discuss this passage in such a way as to give the Lord's open threat a favorable sense. "The Lord," they say, "will give an answer from on high, namely to those whom he is going to save, and from his holy place he will utter his voice and give answer in his place. And they, like grape-gatherers full of its fruits, will answer that sentence. Destruction will come upon all the inhabitants of the earth — not upon the whole earth, but upon a part of the earth, namely of those who do not believe. For (the Lord) will have judgment among the nations, and he himself will enter into judgment with all flesh, but the wicked will be handed over to the sword."

"Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, affliction (or: evil) will go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind (or: storm) will go forth from the heights (or: the farthest parts) of the earth. And those slain by the Lord (or: wounded by the Lord) on that day will lie from one end of the earth to the other; they will not be mourned, or gathered, or buried; they will lie like dung on the face of the ground."

Let those blush for shame who try to do violence to holy Scripture by expounding in a favorable sense things that are full of threat. I think it was concerning this passage that the Lord too said: "Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom," and the rest of what that Gospel saying contains. Let us understand these things as having taken place historically,

when all the surrounding nations were subjugated by the Babylonian king and felt his cruel rule; or else, according to prophecy, as things that will happen long afterward at the consummation of the world. And they are called "slain by the Lord," not because the Lord himself strikes them, but because in the destruction of the worst people the will and command of the Lord are fulfilled.

"Wail (or: shout for joy), you shepherds, and cry out, and sprinkle yourselves with ashes, you leaders of the flock (or: lament, you rams of the sheep), for your days have been fulfilled for you to be slaughtered, and your scatterings, and you will fall like precious vessels (or: like choice rams). And flight will perish from the shepherds, and salvation from the leaders (or: the rams) of the flock."

Note that only in this passage had the Septuagint used "shouting for joy" in a bad sense; the other translators rendered it "wailing," as it is written in the Hebrew. The difference between shepherds and rams, or leaders of the flock, is this: shepherds are shepherds of rational beings, whereas rams and leaders refer to the rich, who are themselves also called part of the flock.

As for what he adds, "Your days have been fulfilled for you to be slaughtered": their days will be fulfilled when their sins have been filled up. "And they will be scattered and fall like precious vessels," so that once broken they cannot be restored, and the more precious they were before, the greater the loss in their breaking. Or "like choice rams," so that they become a fat victim for those eager to devour them.

"Flight will perish from the shepherds," he says, when they have not repented. So it is said to the Pharisees: "Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?" And in the Psalms we read: "Flight has perished from me." "And salvation," he says, "from the leaders of the flock" (or rams); "will perish" is understood from the shared construction.

"The sound of the cry of the shepherds and the wailing of the leaders of the flock (or: the shouting for joy of the rams), for the Lord has laid waste their pastures. And the fields (or: the beautiful places) of peace have fallen silent before the wrath of the Lord's fury." Here too note that in the Septuagint "shouting for joy" is put for "wailing."

The difference between shepherds and rams is this: the shepherds are understood to be those in the church who govern the flock with wisdom, learning and doctrine; the rams, those who indeed appear to be leaders among the people but have no doctrine or wisdom in them, and through excessive simplicity come close to foolishness.

But when we have peace and do not appreciate the goods or the beauties of peace, but give ourselves over to luxury, idleness and pleasures, then the goods of peace will come to rest, or fall silent, and be taken from us because of the wrath of the Lord's fury; and what is written will be fulfilled: "When they say, 'Peace and security,' then sudden destruction will come upon them"; and when it comes, all things will fall silent.

"Like a lion he has forsaken his shelter (or: his lair)" — or, more accurately, his tabernacle, for that is what the Hebrew soccho means — "for their land has become a desolation (or: impassable) before the wrath of the dove (or: before the great sword) and before the wrath of the Lord's fury."

The Lord, of whom he had said above, "He will roar from on high, and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; he will roar mightily over his beauty," will himself forsake his tabernacle. Of him it is written: "His place has been made in peace (or: in Salem), and his dwelling in Zion"; he himself will desert his seat and fulfill what he spoke through this same prophet: "I have left my house, I have forsaken my inheritance."

Like a lion he has left his lair, so that all the beasts may have power to lay waste his land; for while the lion guards and protects it, no one dares to approach it. "Their land has become," he says — no doubt the land either of the Jewish people or indeed of all the nations — "a desolation and impassable before the wrath of the dove."

No one will be surprised that the Lord's "dove" is understood as Nebuchadnezzar who has read above that he is called the Lord's "servant" — in place of which the Septuagint translated "great sword." We may, however, also take the "dove" as standing for Jerusalem, because she is angry and grieved that she has lost the protection of her lion and that her land has come to desolation.

"At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord: Stand in the court of the Lord's house and speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the Lord all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them; do not hold back a word! Perhaps they will listen and turn, each one from his evil way, and I may repent of (or: cease from) the evil that I intend to do to them because of the wickedness of their pursuits."

This prophecy is earlier than the preceding one, although it was given under the same king. For that one was given in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, but this one at the beginning of the same king's reign, as Scripture says: "At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying." So, as we have often said already, one should not try to weave a historical sequence out of the prophets, since in the present case, under the same king, earlier things are told later and later things earlier.

Whoever is going to speak the word of the Lord must stand with Moses and hear with the psalmist: "You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God."
