And he is commanded to speak to all the cities of Judah, although the Septuagint did not translate "cities," perhaps so that it would not seem unfitting to speak in the court of the Lord's house to cities that were not present. But when he speaks to the peoples and the citizens, he is speaking to the cities themselves. And he fittingly stands in the court and entrance of the Lord's temple, so that those who come to pray to the Lord and worship him are compelled to hear the prophet's words.

"Do not hold back a word," he says. "Though it is grievous, though the fury of your hearers is roused against you, still say what you have been commanded, fearing not the persecutions of those who will be roused against you, but the command of the Lord who gives the order!"

"Perhaps," he says, "they will listen and turn." The uncertain word "perhaps" cannot befit the majesty of the Lord, but he speaks in keeping with our human way of feeling, so that man's free will may be preserved, and he may not be compelled by God's foreknowledge, as if by necessity, either to do something or not to do it. For it is not because God knows that something will happen that it therefore will happen; rather, because it will happen, God knows it, as one who foreknows the future.

And yet we must recognize, according to this same Jeremiah, that if the Lord has foretold evils and the people repent, he too will repent of what he threatened to do; and if he has promised prosperity and the people behave carelessly, God changes his sentence and brings evils instead of good things. Something similar is found in the Gospel: "I will send my son; perhaps they will respect him," which is certainly said in the person of God almighty.

So in the present passage too he says: "If perhaps they listen and turn, each one from his evil way, then, when they have turned, I too may repent of my sentence and not do what I intend to do to them. And I intend to do it because of the wickedness of their pursuits; if these are changed, my sentence too will be changed." Let us read the story of Jonah and Nineveh.

"And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law, which I gave you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent to you, rising in the night and sending them, and you did not listen, I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth."

It is therefore within our power either to do something or not to do it, with this one proviso: that whatever good work we will, strive for and accomplish, we attribute to the grace of God, who, according to the apostle, has given us both to will and to accomplish. But if it is enough to walk once in the law that was given to us through Moses, as a foolish heresy supposes, how is it that he added, "to listen to the words of my servants the prophets"? They were certainly sent after the law, and not once but often, and not idly or carelessly, but continually and with anxious care.

"I sent you my servants," he says, "every day, rising even in the night; if you will not listen to them, I will make this house" — that is, the temple of God — "like Shiloh," where the tabernacle had been. And when the temple has been destroyed, the city in consequence will also become a curse to all the nations of the earth.

Just as, when the temple was built on the threshing floor of Ornan and on Mount Moriah, that is, "of vision," where Abraham is said to have offered his son Isaac, the worship at Shiloh ceased and no sacrifices were celebrated there afterward, so, when the church was built and spiritual victims were offered in it, the ceremonies of the law ceased and the city of the Jews was made a curse to all the nations of the earth. From this curse the Lord has freed us, as the apostle says: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us."

"And the priests and the prophets (or: the false prophets) and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking everything that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets (or: the false prophets) and all the people seized him, saying: Let him die the death, because he has prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying, 'This house will be like Shiloh, and this city will be made desolate, without an inhabitant.'"

The priests and prophets, whom the Septuagint more plainly translated "false prophets," are angry with Jeremiah because he proclaims the truth, and because, with the temple overthrown and the city deserted, their religion would perish, and with it the profits that came from religion. That is why they seize him and, with the people agreeing, mark him out for death, because he said in the name of the Lord: "This house will be like Shiloh, and the city will be made desolate, without an inhabitant."

If ever, then, priests or false prophets or a deceived people are angry with us because of the Lord's commands and the truth of the faith, let us not be much concerned, but carry out God's sentence, keeping our minds not on present evils but on future goods.

"And all the people gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. And the princes of Judah heard these words, and they went up from the king's house to the house of the Lord and sat at the entrance of the New Gate of the Lord."

Jeremiah was prophesying the words of the Lord in the temple and had said: "I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city a curse to all the nations of the earth." At once the priests, prophets and people stirred up an uproar, and the whole crowd gathered against the prophet in the temple, where the prophet was, held in the hands of the priests, the prophets and the mob.

When the princes of the city, who were in the royal house, heard of this, they crossed over, or went up, from the king's house to the house of the Lord. And note that going to the house of the Lord is always an ascent. "And they sat at the entrance of the New Gate of the Lord." For it was the princes' duty to sit in the gate of the Lord's house and there to find out the truth of a matter or a disturbance. The gate is called "new" because those who sat in it and presided over the trial withstood the false accusation of the priests and false prophets.

"And the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes and to all the people, saying: This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."

The princes of the city, who had hurried from the king's palace to the temple to quell the uproar of the people, were sitting in the gate of the temple, the New Gate, and the people had gathered in assembly; then the priests and false prophets brought their accusation. And the prophet would have perished, as far as it lay with the priests and prophets, if the accusers themselves had held the power of judgment. From this we understand that those who seemed devoted to religion were crueler toward the prophet, out of envy of his holiness, than those who were in charge of public affairs.

And Jeremiah spoke to all the princes and to the whole people, saying: The Lord sent me to prophesy to this house (or: against this house) and to this city (or: against this city) all the words that you have heard. Now therefore make your ways and your pursuits good, and listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you (or: and the Lord will cease from the evils that he has spoken against you).

But as for me, see, I am in your hands. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes (or: what is to your advantage)! But know and understand this: if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants. For in truth the Lord sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.

The princes of the city were sitting in the gate in the presence of the people. The priests and the prophets were accusing the prophet Jeremiah and pressing a capital charge against him. Jeremiah then speaks to the princes and to the whole people, whom the faction of the priests and false prophets had stirred up, and he speaks with prudence, with humility and with firmness all at once.

He speaks with prudence in saying that he had been sent by the Lord to speak against the temple and the city, and in giving them counsel: if they were willing to heed his counsel and repent, the Lord too would change his sentence. He speaks with humility in saying: See, I am in your hands; do with me what is good and right in your eyes! And he speaks with firmness in saying: In truth the Lord sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.

In other words he is saying: 'If you are angry that I have spoken against the temple and the city of the Lord, and if the safety of the city and the temple is your concern, why do you add sin to sin and make both the city and its inhabitants guilty of my blood?

' So if we too ever need humility in the straits of necessity, let us take it up in such a way that we do not abandon truth and firmness. For it is one thing to insult a judge arrogantly, which is a mark of folly, and another to avoid an impending danger in such a way that you take nothing away from the truth.
And the princes and all the people said to the priests and the prophets: This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God.

The people, who had earlier been led astray by the priests and false prophets, join the princes of the city and speak up for Jeremiah, saying that he is by no means guilty of death, but has prophesied in the name of the Lord and from his mouth. An uneducated crowd quickly changes its opinion once it hears a reason. But the resentment of the accusers, especially of the priests and false prophets, cannot be changed. So while they go on accusing and persist in their accusation, the people change their minds, because Jeremiah had given them hope of the Lord's pardon if they made their ways good and listened to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord too would turn aside his sentence.

And some of the elders of the land rose up and spoke to the whole assembly of the people, saying: Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord, and did not the Lord repent of the evil that he had spoken against them? So we are doing great evil against our own souls.

The princes of the city and the people understand where the truth of the case lies. The elders, whose particular business it was to know the past, recount the history and the prophecy of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied under King Hezekiah. They compare it with the prophecy of Jeremiah for which he is being charged with a capital crime, and they show that Micah had said harsher things and yet suffered nothing at the hands of the righteous King Hezekiah. Rather, because the people turned to repentance, the Lord changed his sentence for the better.

For Micah said: Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house a wooded height. Jeremiah, for his part, says: I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.

And they give their counsel. They think that what Micah foretold will by no means come about, since for a long time it has not happened, because the people repented. In the same way, they think, what Jeremiah has spoken will by no means come to pass if, following his counsel, they make their ways and their pursuits good and listen to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord does not bring upon them the evil with which he had threatened them.

At the same time they break the fury of the accusers and count themselves in with them, saying: So we are doing great evil against our own souls. They do not mean that they ought to do it, but that if they do, they will harm not the accused but their own souls, which they could set free by changing their verdict.

There was also a man who prophesied in the name of the Lord, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim, and he prophesied against this city and against this land in words just like those of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and princes heard his words, and the king sought to kill him. And Uriah heard of it and was afraid, and he fled and went into Egypt.

What follows, And King Jehoiakim sent men into Egypt, Elnathan son of Achbor and men with him into Egypt, is not found in the Septuagint. Then the text continues: And they brought Uriah out of Egypt and led him to King Jehoiakim, and he struck him down with the sword and threw his corpse into the graves of the common people. But the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, so that he was not handed over to the people to be put to death.

The question is asked why Uriah son of Shemaiah, from the town of Kiriath-jearim, who prophesied the same things as Jeremiah, fled to Egypt in terror and was dragged back from there and killed, while Jeremiah was able to escape. Jeremiah certainly did not flee. He boldly persisted in his earlier message, and he was set free against his accusers, the priests and false prophets, both by the verdict of the people and the princes and by the counsel of the elders.

To this we must answer briefly that God's judgment cannot possibly be known when, for the same cause and the same message, one man is punished and another set free. Unless perhaps we can answer that Uriah was slaughtered to the condemnation of both the accusers and the people, while Jeremiah was kept back by the judgment of God to preach to the remnant of the unhappy people and to draw them back to repentance. We read the same thing in the Acts of the Apostles: the apostle James at once suffered the sentence of Herod and was crowned with martyrdom, while Peter and the other apostles were kept back for teaching the Lord's doctrine.

We should also note the steadfastness of the prophet: not even when he was dragged back from Egypt did Uriah change his message. Though he saw death threatening him, he nonetheless spoke what the Lord had commanded. And the fact that he was afraid and fled and went into Egypt is a sign not of unbelief but of prudence, so that we do not expose ourselves to danger for nothing. Indeed, we read that the Lord our Savior himself slipped out of the hands of his persecutors, and that he instructed the apostles: When they persecute you in this city, flee to another!

It is also asked how Jehoiakim king of Judah, ruler of a small and weakened kingdom that was already on the verge of ruin, had the power to send men into Egypt and bring Uriah out from there. This is easily resolved if we consider that he had been made ruler by Neco king of Egypt, and that this prophecy too [?] was delivered at the beginning of his reign.

But although Jeremiah was set free by the Lord's help, credit is nevertheless also counted to the man through whom the Lord set his prophet free, namely Ahikam son of Shaphan. We shall read something similar later on, when Jeremiah is rescued from the danger of death out of the muddy cistern by the counsel and protection of Ebed-melech the eunuch.

In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying. This is not found in the Septuagint edition, and many think it is the beginning of the following chapter. That is by no means so. It should be joined to the preceding passage, so that we understand that everything reported there as said and done took place at the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign. That is why he had the power to send into Egypt, as though to a friendly king.

It seems to me that the Septuagint translators passed over this heading for the following reason: so as not to appear to say it a second time. For they had already put at the beginning: In the beginning of the reign of King Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying.

Thus says the Lord to me: Make yourself bonds and chains (or: collars, which in Hebrew are called mototh and in common speech are called boiae), and put them on your neck, and send them to the king of Edom, and to the king of Moab, and to the king of the Ammonites, and to the king of Tyre, and to the king of Sidon, by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah. And you shall command them to say to their masters: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters.

The previous vision came to the prophet at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. This one came under Zedekiah, who was the last to reign in Jerusalem and under whom the city was captured and overthrown.

Jeremiah is commanded to put chains, or wooden yokes, which, as we have said, are called mototh in Hebrew, on his neck, and to send them to the kings of Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, Tyre and Sidon by the envoys who had come to Zedekiah. He is to instruct them to tell their masters that they must serve King Nebuchadnezzar and obey him. The prophet's discourse goes on to develop this in what follows. And in case the envoys and the kings of these nations might reply, 'Why do you not command this to your own people?', he says similar things to King Zedekiah too, and to the priests and prophets.

The interpreter who is always allegorizing and runs away from the truth of history interprets this passage of the heavenly Jerusalem. He says that its inhabitants ought to take on bodies of their own free will and go down into 'Babylon', that is, into the 'confusion' of this world, which lies in the evil one, and serve the king of Babylon, by whom he doubtless means the devil. If they refuse to do this, he says, they will by no means bear heavy bodies, but will perish by sword and famine and pestilence, and will become not human beings but demons.

Let this be what he said, so that his defenders may not bring a false charge against us. For our part, let us follow the plain and true history, so as not to be wrapped up in clouds and conjuring tricks.

I made the earth, and man, and the beasts that are on the face of the earth, by my great strength and by my outstretched arm, and I have given it to whomever pleased me. Although Scripture speaks these things in human terms,

in the way that we humans can speak and understand, still the 'strength' of God and his 'arm' is the one of whom the apostle also says, 'Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God,' and Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? John the evangelist also writes: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. David too says in his song: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. And the words, I have given it to whomever pleased me, mean that all things have been bestowed on the human race by the grace of God. I made, he says, the earth, and man, and the beasts. The order is reversed: in Genesis the living creatures are made first and man last, but here he names man first and afterward the things that are subject to man.

And now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant; moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field as well, to serve him. And all nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son.

How unhappy Israel is, when in comparison with it Nebuchadnezzar is called 'servant of God'! It is written in the Gospel: The world was made through him, and the world did not know him; he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. So the Creator rightly hands over his creation to whomever he wishes. Indeed, the devil, of whom Nebuchadnezzar was a forerunning type, confesses: All these things have been handed over to me.

As for his adding, moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field as well, to serve him, we should either understand quite simply every kind of living creature, since along with man the things subject to him are also handed over, or else take the 'beasts' to be wild nations, which also serve, though previously they had not known how to serve. By 'his son' and 'his son's son', according to the Hebrew, he means Belshazzar and Evil-merodach, about whom Daniel writes.

Until the time of his land and of himself comes. Well put. So that Nebuchadnezzar's rule would not be thought everlasting, he says that he too will be captured by the Medes and Persians. That is what is meant by until the time of his land and of himself comes. But this too is not found in the Septuagint.

And many nations and great kings shall serve him. He did not say 'all', for that belongs properly to the kingdom of Christ. And yet in Symmachus we do not read, many nations and great kings shall serve him, but, many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude, meaning that he too, whom all nations had previously served, will serve the Medes and Persians.

What we have set down from the Hebrew, I have given him the beasts, to serve him, and all nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time of his land and of himself comes, and many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude, is not read in the Septuagint edition, as we have already said.

But the nation and the kingdom that will not serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and whoever will not bend his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will visit that nation with sword and famine and pestilence, says the Lord, until I have consumed them by his hand.

It is not only the Lord who subjects sinful nations to Nebuchadnezzar. The apostle too says of sinners: whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and in another place: I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. He also urges obedience to the authorities, not only because of wrath but also for the sake of conscience, so that we may not be condemned by them.

So do not listen to your prophets and diviners and dreamers and augurs and sorcerers, who say to you: You shall not serve the king of Babylon. For they prophesy a lie to you, so as to remove you far from your land, and drive you out, and you will perish. But the nation that bows its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, I will leave in its own land, says the Lord, and it shall till it and dwell in it.

Here too the allegorical interpreter raves. He urges those who dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem not to listen to their prophets and diviners, dreamers, augurs and sorcerers, but rather to serve Nebuchadnezzar and take on the body of humiliation: infancy, the wailing and the cradles of little children. For if they do this, he says, then when their service and the condition of human mortality are completed they will return to their own land and dwell in it and do the work they did before. And he says he suspects that those who have despised God's commands will be weighed down with human bodies, will become demons and unclean spirits, and will by no means regain their former seat.

But let us explain it plainly. Among the nations there are prophets, who pretend to foretell the future by a divine spirit; and diviners, about whom there is the common proverb, 'The wise, they say, are diviners'; and dreamers, who imitate Joseph and Daniel; and augurs, who announce what should or should not be done from the flight of birds and the cries of songbirds; and sorcerers, whom we may call poisoners or servants of the phantoms of demons, and who in Hebrew are called chassane.

'All these,' he says, 'deceive you and trip you up, so that you will not serve the king of Babylon.' For it is far better to accept servitude willingly, to have as a friend the one you serve, and to till your native land, than to serve as captives by force and compulsion.

And I spoke to Zedekiah king of Judah in accordance with all these words, saying: Bow your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why will you and your people die by sword, famine and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?

Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you: Do not serve the king of Babylon. For they are speaking a lie to you. For I did not send them, says the Lord, and they are prophesying falsely in my name, so that I will drive you out and you will perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you.

After all the nations he turns to Zedekiah king of Judah and speaks to him in the same words with which he had threatened the nations. For a man who has sinned as much as the other nations, or more, does not deserve the privilege of the Israelite nation. In the end, because the rebellious people refused to listen, they were consumed by sword, famine and pestilence.

It should be observed in holy Scripture that it uses the word 'prophets' in place of 'false prophets' for those who prophesy falsely in the name of the Lord. 'They do this,' he says, 'so that I will drive you out and you will perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you.' So the destruction of those who are deceived and of those who deceive is the same.

What we have set down from the Hebrew, under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why will you and your people die by sword, famine and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you, is not found in the Septuagint. I point this out so that the careful reader may understand how much is missing, passage by passage, from the Greek and Latin manuscripts.

And I spoke to the priests and to this people, saying: Thus says the Lord: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying: See, the vessels of the Lord will now soon be brought back from Babylon; for they are prophesying a lie to you. (What we have set down as 'now soon' is not found in the Septuagint, nor is what follows:) Do not listen to them, but serve the king of Babylon, so that you may live! Why should this city be given over to desolation?

After the nations and the king, he speaks to the priests and the people, since he had already announced destruction to the prophets above, saying: so that I will drive you out and you will perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. He tells them the same things he had told the king and the nations: they are not to listen to the words of their prophets, who say that the vessels of the Lord's temple, which had been carried off with Jeconiah, his princes and his mother, are about to be brought back right now. And he urges them to serve the king of Babylon and live, so that the city, by submitting of its own accord, would by no means be handed over to the flames. In this lies the Lord's mercy: he hands them over to a lighter punishment so that they will not suffer a heavier one.

And if they are prophets, and the word of the Lord is in them, let them go to meet (what follows, which we shall add down to the end of this chapter, is not found in the Septuagint) the Lord of hosts, so that the vessels that were left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem may not go

to Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts concerning the pillars and the sea and the stands (for which the Hebrew has mechonoth), and concerning the rest of the vessels that remained in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take when he carried Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, away from Jerusalem to Babylon, together with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem.

For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that were left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon, and there they shall remain until the day of their visitation, says the Lord; and I will have them brought back and restored to this place.

As we have said, these words are not found in the Septuagint but have been translated from the Hebrew original. In their place the Septuagint put something else that was not written there, saying: 'me, for thus said the Lord: And the rest of the vessels, which the king of Babylon did not take when he carried Jeconiah away from Jerusalem, shall go into Babylon, says the Lord.' They gave the sense rather than the words, perhaps because they thought it unreasonable for God to speak to pillars and the sea and stands and the rest of the vessels that had remained in Jerusalem. As though we did not read that the Lord rebuked the worm at dawn, and spoke to the sea: Be silent, be still!

And the words, let them go to meet me, or, the Lord of hosts, show that a true prophet can resist the Lord by his prayers. In this way Moses stood in the breach against the Lord, to turn away the wrath of his fury, and Samuel did the same. And the Lord said to Moses: Let me alone, that I may strike this people! When he says, Let me alone, he shows that he can be held back by the prayers of the saints. 'Let the prophets come forward,' he says, 'and

show that whatever they foretell has been fulfilled in fact, and then their prophecy will be proved true.' As for the pillars and the sea and the stands and the rest of the vessels, we read about them in Kings and at the end of this prophet's book, where the vessels carried off to Babylon are listed, when Zedekiah was captured, the city burned and the temple overthrown.

And it came to pass in that year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, that Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the Lord in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two more full years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the Lord.

Those whom the Hebrew calls 'prophets', that is, 'nebiim', the Septuagint rendered 'false prophets', to make the meaning plainer. So in the present passage too he is called a 'prophet', that is, 'nabi', and not a 'false prophet'. This word of the Lord comes under King Zedekiah, in the fourth year of his reign and in the fifth month, when the prophet Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been carried away with Jeconiah. And Hananiah has the confidence to speak against the prophet in the temple of the Lord, because he promises the people prosperity, and lies are gladly heard, especially lies that promise happy things.

Jeremiah had said that the rest of the vessels, too, whether of the temple or of the king's house and of the whole people, which Nebuchadnezzar had left behind, would be carried off to Babylon; this man, on the contrary, promises that even those which had already been carried off will be brought back.

which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took from this place and carried to Babylon. And Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles of Judah who went to Babylon, I will bring back to this place, says the Lord; for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.

In place of this the Septuagint translated: 'Jeconiah and the exiles of Judah, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon', briefly setting down the sense of the Hebrew truth rather than its words. Hananiah the 'prophet' — as he seemed to the people at that time — promises that not only the vessels but also King Jeconiah will be brought back to Jerusalem, and that the yoke of the Babylonian king will be broken, that is, his empire destroyed; and that this will happen before two years are complete, so that the nearness of the promised time might heighten the greatness of their joy.

And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet in the sight of the priests and in the sight of all the people who were standing in the house of the Lord — Jeremiah the prophet said: Amen! May the Lord do so! May the Lord fulfil the words which you have prophesied, so that the vessels of the house of the Lord and all the exiles may be brought back from Babylon to this place!

He wishes that what the false prophet falsely says might come true — for this is what 'amen' means, a word the Lord often uses in the Gospel: 'Amen, amen, I say to you' — and for the sake of the people's prosperity he would rather that the other man were telling the truth than himself. Hence another prophet also testifies, saying: 'Would that I were not a man who has the spirit, and spoke a lie instead!' Jonah, on the contrary, is grieved that he has turned out to be a liar, and is shown by the Lord that it is better for a prophet to be proved false than for so great a multitude to be ruined. And so as not to seem to approve the false prophet's prophecy, Jeremiah adds the truth, by way of the example of others and without insulting the liar:

Nevertheless, hear this word which I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people: the prophets who were before me and before you from of old prophesied against many lands and against great kingdoms of war and of affliction and of famine. As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when his word comes to pass, then it will be known that he is the prophet whom the Lord has truly sent.

Jeremiah could have said to Hananiah: 'You are speaking falsely, you are deceiving the people, you are not a prophet but a false prophet.' But if he had said this, the false prophet could have thrown the same words back at Jeremiah. So he does him no insult and speaks to him as to a 'prophet'.

'Not only am I a prophet, and you,' he says, 'but before me and you there were many others, among them Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, Amos and the rest. They prophesied', he says, 'against many lands and kingdoms — not small ones but great — announcing to them war and adversity and want of all things; and on the other hand there were others who promised peace and prosperity. The word of each was proved not by flattering lies but by the

outcome of events.' So under the example of others he speaks of himself and of Hananiah: that when the end of things arrives, then the truthfulness of the prophets is shown. The Lord said this same thing through Moses: that a prophet is revealed by the fulfilment of his prophecy. And we should notice that he rebukes the liar not with threats, not harshly, but with the confidence of truth, and defers the matter to the future, so that those who hear may wait for the outcome of events.

And Hananiah the prophet took the chain — or yoke, which in Hebrew is called 'mototh' — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it. And Hananiah spoke in the sight of all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord: So will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two full years. And Jeremiah the prophet went his way.

The Septuagint did not translate 'two years', nor did they call Hananiah a 'prophet', so as not to seem to call a man a prophet who was not a prophet — as if many things in holy Scripture were not said according to the opinion of the time in which the events are recounted, rather than according to what the truth of the matter was. Thus Joseph too is called the Lord's father in the Gospel, and Mary herself, who knew that she had conceived by the Holy Spirit and had answered the angel, 'How shall this be, since I do not know a man?', says to her son: 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow.'

At the same time we should consider Jeremiah's prudence, humility and patience. The false prophet insults him by deed, snatching the yoke from his neck and breaking it — which he certainly could not have done to an iron one — while Jeremiah stays silent and hides his pain; for it had not yet been revealed to him by the Lord what he should say. In this way holy Scripture shows implicitly that the prophets never speak merely by their own choice, but by the will of the Lord, especially about things to come, the knowledge of which belongs to God alone.
He went away, it says, and withdrew on his way as though defeated, fulfilling that prophetic word: 'I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no rebukes in his mouth.'

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after Hananiah the prophet had broken the chain — or yoke — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Go and say to Hananiah: Thus says the Lord: You have broken a wooden chain — or yoke — and you will make — or, I will make — in its place yokes — or chains — of iron.

For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. What follows — 'and they shall serve him; and I have also given him the beasts of the earth' — is not found in the Septuagint. In the present passage too, and in what follows, the Septuagint does not write that Hananiah is a 'prophet', so as not, as I said before, to seem to call a 'false prophet' a 'prophet'. But what has that to do with the Hebrew truth?

After Jeremiah the prophet had gone his way and swallowed the insult in silence, the word of the Lord came to him, so that the prophet would not speak to the false prophet, who was glorying in his lie, in his own words, but would say: 'Thus says the Lord' — although Hananiah too, when he broke the wooden yoke, had spoken with the same claim of authority in the presence of the Lord: 'Thus says the Lord'. For falsehood always imitates truth.

And what he added — 'You have broken wooden yokes, and you will make — or, you have made — chains of iron in their place' — shows that by rejecting a lesser punishment he became the cause of a greater torment for the people. Here too the allegorical interpreter talks nonsense, calling the wooden yokes

and chains the ethereal and airy bodies, namely those of demons and hostile powers, and the iron yokes or chains our grosser bodies, woven together of sinews and bones, flesh and veins. Thus, according to him, those who were unwilling to undergo lesser torments in the heavenly Jerusalem in proportion to their sin are condemned to the chains of our bodies, and must endure the wailing of infancy, the bonds and the filth of swaddling clothes, and serve the devil, the king of Babylon, that is, of this world — as Scripture says, 'The whole world lies in the evil one' — together with the beasts of the earth, which are souls bound into the bodies of brute animals.
An unlearned commentator, a follower of Grunnius's slanders, has forced me to set out openly another man's errors, which before I used to mention discreetly, leaving them to the reader's good sense.

And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: Listen, Hananiah: the Lord has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will send you away — or, cast you out — from the face of the earth; this year you shall die. What follows — 'because you have spoken against the Lord. And Hananiah the prophet died in that same year, in the seventh month' — is not found in the Septuagint, which has in its place only: 'And he died in the seventh month.'

Here too in the Septuagint Hananiah is not called a 'prophet', whereas according to the Hebrew holy Scripture does call him a 'prophet' — although where Jeremiah rebukes him, saying, 'Listen, Hananiah: the Lord has not sent you', it is silent about 'prophet'; for how could he call him a 'prophet' when he was denying that the Lord had sent him? But the truth and order of the narrative are preserved, as we said above, not according to what he was, but according to what he was thought to be at that time. 'You have deceived the people', he says, 'with a lie, so that they would not submit to God's sentence. Therefore know

that you will die this year!' If, when we die, we are freed from the prison of our bodies — according to that text which the heretics misinterpret, 'Bring my soul out of prison' — how is death now inflicted on the false prophet as a punishment? We should also note that Jeremiah, having been insulted by the false prophet, keeps silent while the word of the Lord has not yet come to him; but afterwards, when sent by the Lord, he boldly rebukes the liar and announces his approaching death.

As for his dying in the 'seventh' month: those who always interpret this number as signifying 'rest' will perhaps falsely claim that he died in the 'seventh' month in order to be freed from the evils of the body, according to the text they cite [?]: 'Death is rest to a man.' We, however, know that the bodies of believers are temples of God, provided that the Holy Spirit dwells in them.

And these are the words of the book which Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the remnant of the elders of the exile, and to the priests and to the prophets and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, after King Jeconiah had gone out, and the lady — or the queen — and the eunuchs and the princes of Judah and Jerusalem — or, from Jerusalem; or, the nobles — and the craftsmen from Jerusalem. It was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in Babylon. It said:

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens — or orchards — and eat their fruit. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply, and do not be few in number. And seek the peace of the city — or of the land — to which I have carried you, and pray to the Lord for it, for in its peace you will have peace.

This letter, or rather this little book, of the prophet Jeremiah is sent to Babylon by Zedekiah's envoys Elasah and Gemariah, to those who had been carried away by Nebuchadnezzar with Jeconiah and his mother, so that, taking the opportunity of the royal embassy, the prophet might also accomplish his own work and admonish the exiled people with what the Lord had commanded him.

And he put it well: 'King Jeconiah had gone out, and the lady, the eunuchs and the princes of Judah' and the rest; and: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon' — so that they may be seen to have been carried away not by the power of the king of Babylon but by the will of the Lord. And the word of God is addressed first to the elders, then to the priests, third to the prophets, fourth to all the people, so that the prophet's letter too might reach those being admonished in order of age.

He admonishes them not in his own words but in the Lord's, to build houses and live in them, to plant gardens or orchards and eat their fruit, to take wives and have sons and daughters, to multiply in the place of their exile and not be few in number, and to seek the peace of the city or land to which the Lord has carried them, and to pray to the Lord for it. And giving the reason, he says: 'for in the peace of that land you will have peace.'

Jeremiah, because captivity was soon to overtake Jerusalem, is commanded not to take a wife and not to have children. Hence it is said to us as well through the Apostle: 'The time has been shortened; it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none.' Now if, because of the shortness of the time, the use of wives is taken from those who have them, how much more are those who have none commanded not to take them!

The whole purpose of this prophetic message is that they should not give in to the false prophets, who were promising them a return to Jerusalem after a short time, but should know that they would stay a long time in Babylon — so long that they ought to take wives, plant orchards and sow gardens, build houses and have children. And what he added —

'Seek the peace of the city or of the land', and again, 'for in its peace you will have peace' — confirms that saying of the Apostle in which he commands: 'I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and chastity.'

Further, according to the mystical sense: when we have been cast out of Jerusalem, that is, the Church, because of our sins, and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar — of whom the same Apostle says, 'I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord', and again, 'whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme' — we must not be complacent, nor, sluggish with idleness, utterly despair of salvation. Rather, we must first build houses — not on sand but on rock — and such houses as the midwives in Exodus built, because they feared the Lord;

then plant gardens or orchards, such as the Lord planted in the paradise in Eden, placing in it the tree of life, of which it is written: 'She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and whoever holds her fast is blessed.' Third, we must take wives, one of whom is wisdom, of whom Solomon writes: 'Love her, and she will keep you; embrace her, and she will exalt you'; and in another place: 'I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty.' Nor is one wife, wisdom, enough for us unless we also have the others — courage, temperance and justice — so that we may beget many sons by them.

Let us also give our daughters to husbands, so that the truth of faith, which is signified by the sons, may be joined to good works, which refer to the daughters, and good works may be united to soundness of faith. And begetting such sons and daughters, let us multiply in number, so that, putting away childish things and growing up to the perfect man, we may be worthy to hear: 'I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning'; and may say with the Apostle to our children: 'For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the gospel.'

Let us also seek the peace of the Church, our city and our land, that we may be worthy to return to it, from which we were carried away by the Lord's judgement to dwell in the error of 'confusion'. For if she receives us back, we shall have peace. At the same time we should consider the Lord's mercy: he commands us to pray for our enemies and to do good to those who persecute us, so that we may not be content with our own salvation alone, but may seek the salvation of our enemies too.

For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets who are among you, and your diviners, deceive you, and do not heed your dreams which you dream, for they prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord. That there were prophets — or rather false prophets —

and diviners and dreamers in Babylon among those whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away with Jeconiah and his mother is attested by the prophet Ezekiel, who writes against the same people whom Jeremiah too commands them not to believe. But at the time this letter was sent, Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon; for this message is sent at the beginning of King Zedekiah's reign, whereas Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of Jeconiah's exile, which was also the fifth year of Zedekiah's reign.

Further, according to the tropological sense, we should understand as false prophets those who take the words of Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit means them; as diviners, those who pronounce the conjectures of their own minds and uncertain things about the future as though they were true, without the authority of the divine words; and as dreamers, those who do not heed what is written: 'Give no sleep to your eyes nor slumber to your eyelids' — of whom the apostle Jude also speaks: 'Likewise these dreamers defile the flesh and despise authority.' Their mind is never awake, but, weighed down by the sleep of arrogance and error, it is wrapped in the horror of night. To them the apostle Paul also says: 'Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light.'

For thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be completed in Babylon, I will visit you and fulfil my good word to you, to bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says the Lord, thoughts of peace and not of affliction, to give you an end and patience — or hope. And you will call upon me and go — or, according to Symmachus, you will find — and you will pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart; and I will be found by you — or, I will appear to you.

'Do not believe', he says, 'your false prophets, diviners and dreamers, who promise you a speedy return to Jerusalem! For unless seventy years are completed — when Cyrus king of the Persians sets the captives free — you will by no means return to your homeland. And then I will fulfil my promises, to bring you back to this place; for I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says the Lord.' He says that he knows what he is thinking, but that they, with their prophets, diviners and dreamers, do not know it; knowledge of the future, then, belongs to God alone. 'That I may give you', he says, 'an end

and patience' — an end to the captivity, and patience in present labours, or hope of things to come. 'Then you will call upon me and go to Jerusalem, and you will pray, and I will hear you.' Certainly the Lord could have fulfilled what he had promised without the captives calling on him and praying; but he urges them to prayer so that they may deserve to receive what was promised. 'You will seek and find me when you seek me with all your heart' — in keeping with the Gospel saying: 'Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.'

According to the anagogical sense, we live in the 'confusion' of this world until we are worthy to receive the 'rest' of the number seven, and, once we have repented, God fulfils what he promised, and we are brought back to our own place, the Church. For the Lord was seen to strike in order to heal, and he will give us an end of our labour and our patience. And we will call upon him and return to the Church and pray, and we will be heard. We will seek him and find him when we have sought him with all our heart, and then he will appear to us.

Someone interprets the 'seventy years' in light of what is written: 'The days of our years are seventy years'; when these are completed, then we return to the Lord with all our heart and are heard, and our labour and our patience come to an end — for now, he says, we possess all things in shadow and image.

[?] “And I will be found by you, says the Lord, and I will bring back your captivity and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I have driven you, says the Lord, and I will make you return from the place to which I made you go into exile. For you have said: The Lord has raised up prophets for us in Babylon.”

“For thus says the Lord to the king who sits on the throne of David, and to all the people who live in this city, and to your brothers who did not go out with you into exile; thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will send upon them the sword, famine and pestilence, and I will make them like bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are so very bad.”

“And I will pursue them with the sword, with famine and with pestilence, and I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, a curse and an astonishment and a hissing and a reproach among all the nations to which I am driving them, because they did not listen to my words, says the Lord, which I sent to them by my servants the prophets, rising up by night and sending them; and you did not listen, says the Lord. You, then, hear the word of the Lord, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon!” * Up to this point the passage is not found in the Septuagint.

I have marked these words with asterisks; as for the rest, where either single verses or a few words have been omitted by them, I was overcome by weariness and did not wish to note them, so as not to bore the reader. Now the Lord promises those who were in exile that after seventy years of captivity he will make them return from all the nations and from all the places to which he had driven them, and that, once the captivity is ended, they will recover their former state and their homeland.

“And since I,” he says, “will do these things of my own accord and will bring you back at a fixed time, you are deceived to no purpose in thinking that you have prophets in Babylon who promise you falsehoods. Know, then, that you ought by no means to hope for a return now, but to build houses, plant orchards, take wives and beget sons, increase in number, and wait for the promised time.”

Hear what the Lord says to Zedekiah, who now reigns in Jerusalem, and to all the inhabitants of his city, that is, to your brothers, who refused to obey my sentence and go to Babylon with you: that they will by no means be able to escape captivity, but will die by sword, famine and pestilence, and that he will make them like bad figs. Theodotion (and the first edition of Aquila) rendered this word as “sudrinas,” the second edition as “very bad,” and Symmachus as “last.” In Hebrew they are called “suarim,” but through the fault of copyists the Greek “delta” has crept in instead of “alpha” in the middle syllable or letter, so that “sudrim” is read instead of “suarim.”
And just as the basket or hamper that held good figs is said to have held “first-ripe” figs, so the other basket, which held bad figs, is described as having held “last” figs.

“And I will pursue,” he says, “those who now live in the city of Jerusalem with sword, famine and pestilence, so that first by the siege at once [?]; and those who manage to survive and escape will be scattered into all lands and will be an example of a curse, of astonishment, of hissing and of reproach to all those among whom I shall cast them out. For they did not listen to my words, says the Lord, which I spoke to them through my servants, rising up by night and sending them; and I never ceased to warn them to imitate you, who now in exile enjoy a secure leisure until the promise of the Lord is fulfilled. But you who obeyed my sentence and surrendered yourselves to the Babylonian king, hear what I am about to say.”

And in this place the raving interpreter dreams of the fall of the heavenly Jerusalem and supposes that the prophecy is addressed to those who live in the Babylonian region of this world: that they did well to descend willingly into these bodies and, in the land of the Chaldeans, to build houses, plant orchards, take wives and beget sons, and by good works to be restored after seventy years to their former place, the heavenly Jerusalem;

but that those who refused of their own will to descend to earthly things will suffer what the Lord threatens against Zedekiah and his people, who refused to imitate their brothers and come into Babylon: that he will send upon them sword and famine and pestilence, that is, a want of all things, and make them like very bad figs that cannot be eaten at all, and pursue them with an everlasting sword, and make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth — by which, you see, they become not men at all but demons, powers of the air, and among all the angels who preside over the individual provinces they become a curse and an astonishment and a hissing and a reproach to all the nations;

and that they will suffer this because they refused to hear, in the heavenly Jerusalem, the words of the prophets, who urged them to descend to earthly things and take on the body of humiliation, and, having done penance, to possess their former place after the true sabbath rest.

So he may say. When his disciples and the dung of Grunnius's household hear these things, they think they are hearing [?] mysteries, and us, who despise such things, they regard as brute animals and call us “Pelusiotes,” mud-dwellers, because, being set in the mud of this body, we cannot perceive heavenly things.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to Ahab son of Kolaiah and to Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy lies to you in my name: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them down before your eyes.”

“And because of them a curse will be taken up by all the exiles of Judah who are in Babylon, saying: May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire, because they committed folly — or iniquity — in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their friends — or fellow citizens — and spoke lying words in my name, which I did not command them. I am the judge and the witness, says the Lord.”

The Hebrews say that these are the elders who committed folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens, to one of whom Daniel says: “You who have grown old in wicked days,” and to the other: “Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you and lust has perverted your heart! This is how you treated the daughters of Israel, and they, out of fear, consorted with you; but a daughter of Judah would not endure your wickedness.”

And what the prophet now says, “and they spoke lying words in my name, which I did not command them,” they take to mean that these men deceived wretched little women, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, by telling them that, since they themselves were of the tribe of Judah, Christ was to be born of their seed; and the women, lured by desire, offered their bodies as though they would be the mothers of Christ.

But what is said here, “whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire,” seems to contradict the story in Daniel. For that story asserts that they were stoned by the people at Daniel's sentence, while here it is written that the king of Babylon roasted them in the fire. For this reason many, indeed nearly all, of the Hebrews do not accept that story, regarding it as a sort of fable, nor is it read in their synagogues.

“For how,” they say, “could captives have had the power to stone their own leaders and prophets?” They affirm instead that what Jeremiah writes is the truer account: that the elders were indeed convicted by Daniel, but that sentence was passed on them by the king of Babylon, who as victor and lord had authority over the captives.

How many there are from our own flock who, like Ahab and Zedekiah, prophesy lies in the name of the Lord and commit folly in Israel and commit adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens, who were born in the same city of the Church! These the true Nebuchadnezzar roasts in the fire of sin, as the prophet Hosea says: “All adulterers are like an oven heated by the baker.”

Happy is he who bears the yoke from his youth and sits alone, because he is filled with bitterness, and who can say with David: “I have not sat in the council of the wicked, and I will not go in with evildoers!”

And what the prophet has now added, “I am the judge and the witness, says the Lord,” has this sense: “What I say about the two false prophets, who speak lying words in my name which I did not command them, I have by no means learned from hearsay; I myself know it to be true, I from whom no one can hide and whose true judgment no one can escape.”

“And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say [?],” and what follows — “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have sent letters in your own name to all the people who are in Jerusalem” — is not found in the Septuagint; and again they have added on their own: “I did not send you in my name”; and then, in order: “and to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest,” and again from the Hebrew: “and to all the priests”; and then the narrative is woven together:

“The Lord has made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, so that you may be leader — or overseer and bishop — in the house of the Lord over every man who is possessed and prophesies, to put him in the stocks and in prison — or in custody and in the cataract, for which Symmachus put μοχλόν, “bar,” while Aquila put the Hebrew word itself, “sinac.”

“And now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who prophesies to you? For on this account he has sent to us in Babylon, saying: It will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their fruit!” So Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of the prophet Jeremiah.

Shemaiah, from the place “Nehelami,” which means “torrent,” had been taken to Babylon with King Jeconiah and was prophesying lies to the people, saying that they would soon return to Jerusalem. That he was a false prophet is shown by the words of Jeremiah that follow: “Thus says the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, and I did not send him.”

Jeremiah, then, had sent a letter to those who were in Babylon, saying: “Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their fruit; take wives and beget sons!” and after other things he had added: “Do not let your prophets who are among you and your diviners lead you astray!” and then: “For they prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord.” Shemaiah, understanding that this had been written against him under the general name of false prophets, sends a letter to Jerusalem, to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, and to the rest of the priests, against Jeremiah, asking why he is not rebuked by Zephaniah the priest, whose office it is to distinguish between prophets who speak by the Holy Spirit and those who speak by the opposing spirit, and why he is not ordered to be shut up in prison, so that he may pay the penalty for his lie and cease leading the people astray.

Jehoiada was the priest who handed the kingdom to Joash after Athaliah had been killed, and who killed the priest of Baal. This, then, is what he writes: “Why do you not imitate Jehoiada the priest and kill Jeremiah, the false prophet? For the Lord appointed you in place of Jehoiada, so that you might have charge of the temple and, above all, discern who speak by the Holy Spirit and who by a demonic one” — and the apostle too reminds us that the discernment of spirits is a gift of the Lord's grace —; “why,” he says, “have you not

rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth?” What he himself deserved as a false prophet he turns back upon the prophet, and gets in ahead of the truth with a lie. Hence the children of darkness are thought wiser in this generation than the children of light; and while we act patiently and wait for the salvation of the wretched, the heretics get in ahead of us and call us by their own name, the blind leading the blind into the pit.

“He has sent,” he says, “to us in Babylon, saying: It is far off.” This is the whole of his grievance: that against his lie Jeremiah wrote the truth, that the return was far off and that they would return to Jerusalem after seventy years, and that they should therefore build houses, plant orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and have sons, as the preceding passage related. When Zephaniah the priest received this letter, which had been addressed to him by name in particular, he read it to Jeremiah, as if taunting him and rebuking him by the very reading for daring to write such things to Babylon.

“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Send to all the exiles, saying: Thus says the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, and I did not send him, and he has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants; he shall have no man sitting in the midst of this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do for my people, says the Lord, because he has spoken rebellion against the Lord.”

Shemaiah the false prophet, truly a “Nehelamite,” who had drawn foreign and muddied waters from the “torrent,” is angry that Jeremiah had written the truth against his lie, and sends a letter to Zephaniah the priest asking why the prophet has dared to write the truth, and he wants him shut up in prison so that he may not speak. Zephaniah, too, covertly accuses the prophet when he reads the liar's letter and flaunts the fact that he has his accusation in hand.

How much more guilty of crime are those who defend false prophets, cherish liars, and make other men's wicked inventions their own sins! Let the false prophet, then, hear, and let the priest understand what he too deserves to hear through him: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit Shemaiah.” It is the Lord who says this, not the prophet: that he will visit Shemaiah the Nehelamite, not to heal the liar but to punish him, according to what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with scourges.”

And he visits not only the false prophet but also his seed, all the disciples whom he deceived by his error. “He shall have no man,” he says, “sitting in the midst of this people.” Let that most wicked stock be blotted out from the assembly of the saints, and let him not sit among those who are at rest, he who could not stand with those who stand and did not hear the words: “If he had stood in my substance.” And whereas the Lord promises the perfection of all virtues once the sevenfold period is completed, he will not see the good which he was claiming for himself in the present time.

And all this will happen because he spoke rebellion against the Lord, saying that, the captivity of sins being already loosed, they would return to Jerusalem — people such as the apostle threatens: “Already you are full! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you!”
BOOK SIX

The length of the book of the prophet Jeremiah defeats our intention of saying a great deal, however briefly. Hence this present sixth book of the commentaries on Jeremiah will contain the mystical promises which the Jews, and our own Judaizers, think are to be fulfilled at the consummation of the world; for they cannot prove that they were fulfilled under Zerubbabel.

We, however, following the authority of the apostles and evangelists, and especially of the apostle Paul, show that whatever is promised in a carnal sense to the people of Israel has been fulfilled spiritually in us and is being fulfilled today, and that there is no other dispute between Jews and Christians than this: that, while both they and we believe in Christ, the promised Son of God, the things that are to take place under Christ are said by us to have been fulfilled and by them to be still awaiting fulfillment.

Since, then, we believe that Christ has already come, we must teach that the things said to be future under Christ have been fulfilled, and that we are the children of Abraham, of whom it is written: “God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham,” to whom the promise was made: “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed.” The vessel of election, teaching that this blessing was fulfilled in Christ, says: “He did not say, ‘and to seeds,’ but ‘to seed,’ who is Christ.”

Pray, therefore, brother Eusebius, to the Lord [?] Christ, that with the same labor and grace of the Spirit with which we interpreted the promises of the other prophets, and especially of Isaiah, we may also be able to explain those of this prophet, who, however simple and easy he may seem in his words, is just as profound in the majesty of his meaning.

“This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, saying: Write in a book for yourself all the words that I have spoken to you! For behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel and Judah, says the Lord, and I will bring them back — or make them settle — in the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.”

When the false prophets in Babylon were promising that the people who had been taken captive with Jeconiah would soon return, and Hananiah son of Azzur was preaching the same thing in Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah had already declared that this would indeed come to pass, not within two years, as they falsely claimed, but when seventy years were completed; and now he is commanded to write in a book and commit to memory the things that the Lord foretells are to come.

From this it is clear that the time of the prophecy is by no means near, but that these things are to be fulfilled long afterward, when Israel and Judah are to return to their land, and that what Ezekiel prophesied is to be fulfilled: that two sticks are to be joined together and that King David will rule, of whom he writes: “And my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them.” So whatever we have said on that prophecy
is to be understood in the present passage as well, especially since Ezekiel in Babylon and Jeremiah in Jerusalem prophesied the same things at the same time.

“And these are the words that the Lord spoke concerning Israel and Judah: For thus says the Lord: We have heard a cry of terror — or fear —; there is dread, and there is no peace. Ask and see whether a male gives birth! Why then do I see every man with his hands on his loins like a woman in labor, and why have all faces turned sallow?”

First sad things are announced, so that joyful things may follow after great evils; for health is all the more welcome when sickness has been driven off, and great pain turns into great joy. What he says amounts to this: so great will be the fear and so great the dread that peace will be put to flight and everything will be filled with war and bloodshed, and even men, whose proper part is to fight against enemies, will be seized by a womanly terror and will put their hands not to their weapons but to holding their loins, as a woman in labor clutches her flanks and loins. Hence the faces of all will turn sallow, their pale countenances bearing witness to the terror in their hearts.

Some interpret this passage tropologically, citing that text: “From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and been in labor and given birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth,” and they compare to this example the apostle's words: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” But that plainly concerns not terror but joy, whereas the present scripture signifies the time of Israel's devastation and ruin.

“Alas, for that day is great, and there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob, and out of it he shall be saved.” He foretells the time of misery in order to bring in the time of joy. “Though,” he says, “such great evils have gone before that the pain of all men is compared to the pain of a woman in labor, yet the time of Jacob's distress, that is, of the people of God, will be changed into prosperity, and out of it” — supply “time” — “of which the discourse had spoken, he too shall be saved.” By “Jacob” understand the twelve tribes, which were saved not under Zerubbabel, as some wrongly think, but by the call of the gospel.

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will break his yoke from off your neck and burst his bonds, and foreigners shall no longer rule over him; but they shall serve — or work for — the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.”

This is the David whom the Gospel also mentions: that he would grant us that, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. For just as Scripture speaks of a first Adam and a second Adam according to the reality of the body, so too the Lord and Savior is David, since according to the flesh he is from David: holy Mary contributed to him everything he had from the stock of David, while he had his origin and conception from the Holy Spirit.
And as for his saying, “I will break his yoke from off your neck and burst his bonds,” there is no doubt that under the figure of Nebuchadnezzar the devil is to be understood.

"So do not fear, my servant Jacob, says the Lord, and do not be dismayed, Israel; for see, I will save you from a far-off land, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob will return and be at rest and abound in all things, and there will be no one for him to fear, for I am with you, says the Lord, to save you. For I will make a full end of all the nations among which I scattered you; but of you I will not make a full end. I will chasten you (or, instruct you) in judgment, so that you will not think yourself innocent" (or, "and in cleansing I will not cleanse you").

This passage is not found in the Septuagint, and in most manuscripts of the common edition it has been added from Theodotion under asterisks. The divine word makes a promise, and in a more intimate way calls Jacob and Israel "his servant," just as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are called "servants of God" (Moses and other prophets glory in this title too, and so does the apostle Paul at the opening of his letters). It does so in order that both the two tribes and the ten, that is, all twelve, may know that they are to be saved from a far-off land, that their captivity is to be ended, that peace is to be restored, and that they are to be filled with every abundance, as it says in the psalm: "May there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your towers!"

This will come about because they will enjoy the presence of the Lord, when the hostile nations that had taken them captive perish and they themselves are set free from among the nations. And he teaches them that they were handed over not to punishment but to instruction, so that they might be shown to be his own and not be destroyed as strangers. For "whoever does not believe is already judged," that is, judged beforehand for destruction.

As for what he adds, "so that you will not think yourself innocent," or, according to Symmachus, "and in cleansing I will not cleanse you," or, according to Aquila, "when I have instructed you through judgment, I will by no means make you innocent," it means that the whole world needs God's mercy, and that no one, however holy, can go to the Judge free of care. This stands against the heresy, new and old at once, which holds that in this age and in this mortal flesh, before this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality, there is perfection in anyone, and that a person can fulfill all the virtues at once.

"For thus says the Lord: Your fracture is incurable, your wound most grievous. There is no one to judge your cause so as to bind it up; healing remedies are of no use to you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they will not seek you. For I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, with cruel (or, harsh) chastisement.

Because of the greatness of your iniquity your sins have become hard (or, have been multiplied). Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your pain is incurable. Because of the greatness of your iniquity and because of your hard sins I have done these things to you."

He speaks as if to a beautiful woman, to whom he had said above, "I will chasten you in judgment, so that you will not think yourself innocent" (the word may be taken as feminine). By a metaphor he is speaking to Jerusalem: she has been grievously wounded by the judgment of God, and she can be healed by no one else but by the very one who struck her ("There is no one," he says, "to judge your cause"), nor can anyone else draw the skin of a scar over so deep a wound. Wherever you turn, there is nothing of use to you, because you have offended the one who is the true and only physician.

"All your lovers have forgotten you": whether the priests or the princes, or certainly the guardian angels by whom you were walled about before you offended the Lord. "They will not seek you": in this they act contrary to the apostle, who sought the believers themselves and not what belonged to the believers. "For I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, with cruel chastisement." A friend strikes in one way, an enemy in another;

a father in one way, a foe in another. The one beats in order to correct, the other strikes in order to kill. Hence the prophet says tearfully: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath!" This has happened because "because of the greatness of your iniquity your sins have become hard."

What follows, "Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your pain is incurable because of the greatness of your iniquity," is not found in the Septuagint, evidently because "because of the greatness of your iniquity and your hard sins" is said a second time, and the copyists thought it had been added from the beginning of the passage.

The sense is this: "That I struck you with the blow of an enemy, that I beat you with cruel chastisement, was the doing of the greatness of your iniquity and your hard sins, which could not be healed except by the most stinging powder, by the burning cautery, and by the sharpest blade, with which I might cut away flesh that was rotten and past healing. And yet I did this to you because of the greatness of your iniquity and your hard sins, not by my own will but because the logic of medicine compelled it."

"Therefore all who devour you will be devoured, and all your enemies will be led into captivity; those who lay you waste will be laid waste, and all who plunder you I will give up as plunder. For I will draw a scar over you and heal you of your wounds, says the Lord. Because they have called you an outcast (or, scattered), Zion: 'This is the one who had no one to seek her.'" We know that these things took place under Zerubbabel as well.

When the Babylonians and Chaldeans laid waste the Assyrians, that is, Nineveh, and the Medes and Persians in turn captured the Babylonians and Chaldeans and Babylon was destroyed, then Zion began to have the Lord seeking her, and a scar was drawn over her wound, and she was healed of her blows. This is fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ.

"Thus says the Lord: See, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have mercy on their dwellings (or, their captivity); the city will be built on its height, and the temple will be founded according to its proper order. And from them will come forth praise and the voice of those who make merry; and I will multiply them, and they will not be diminished." What follows, "and I will glorify them, and they will not be made small," is not found in the Septuagint.
