"And their children," he says, "will be as they were at the beginning, and their congregation will endure before me, and I will punish all who oppress them. Their leader will come from among them, and their ruler will be brought forth from their midst; I will bring him near, and he will approach me. For who is this who will set his heart to draw near to me? says the Lord." And again, what follows in the Hebrew is not found in the Greek: "And you will be my people," he says, "and I will be your God."

A type of these things went before in Zerubbabel and Ezra, when the people returned and the city began to be built on its height, and the worship of the temple began to be observed, along with the other things contained in the book of Ezra itself. But it was fulfilled more fully and perfectly in the Lord and Savior and his apostles, when the city was built on its height, the city of which it is written, "A city set on a hill cannot be hidden," and the temple was founded according to its proper order and rites, so that whatever was done in a carnal way among the former people might be fulfilled in a spiritual way in the Church.

Then came forth praise, or thanksgiving (for this is what "thoda" means), so that all the apostles would say: "Grace to you and peace"; and the voice of those who make merry, not with that merrymaking in which "the people ate and drank and rose up to play," but with that in which David danced before the ark of the Lord. They were multiplied and not diminished, so that the whole world believed in God the Savior; and they were glorified, so that what is written was fulfilled: "Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God!" And their children, that is, the apostles, were as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founders of the Israelite race, had been at the beginning.

Then the Lord punished all who had oppressed the people of God, namely the hostile powers. And their leader came from among them, for without doubt the Lord and Savior is of the race of Israel according to the flesh, and their ruler was brought forth from their midst. The Father brought him near to himself, and he approached him, so that the Son could say, "I am in the Father and the Father in me"; for no one can set his heart on the Lord in such a way, or be so joined to him, as the Son is to the Father.

And what he says according to the Hebrew alone, but not according to the Septuagint, "And you will be my people, and I will be your God," we see fulfilled in fact: in part in Israel, and wholly in the multitude of the nations.

"See, the whirlwind of the Lord, fury going forth, a rushing storm will settle on the head of the wicked. The Lord will not turn back the wrath of his indignation until he has carried out and fulfilled the purpose of his heart; in the last days you will understand it."

The whirlwind of the Lord's fury, the rushing storm and tempest, will settle on the head of the wicked, whether the demons or those who blasphemed the Son of God. And he will not turn back the wrath of his indignation until he has carried out and fulfilled the purpose of his heart, and Jerusalem is surrounded by an army and utterly destroyed. Just as a craftsman cannot be understood until his work is finished, nor the skill of medicine until health has been restored, so, when Jerusalem has been overthrown and the former people cast off, believers will then understand that the rejection of the Jews was the occasion of our salvation.

"At that time, says the Lord, I will be the God of all the families of Israel (or, of the race of Israel), and they will be my people." Unless the Lord's purpose has been fulfilled and his fury has come to rest on the head of the wicked, the Lord of all cannot be God to the families of Israel. He says this to the remnant who have been saved.

If the words "I will be God to the race of Israel," or "to all the families of Israel," are raised against us, let us take an example: "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of your father." And the apostle writes: "Look at Israel according to the flesh," by which he teaches that there is another Israel according to the spirit. That one, then, is Israel who sees God with the mind, or who is most upright before the Lord; and an Israel of this kind will be the people of God.

"Thus says the Lord: The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; Israel will go to his rest." The Septuagint: "Thus said the Lord: I found warmth in the wilderness with those who had perished by the sword; go, and do not kill Israel!"

In this place the Latin manuscripts, through the ambiguity of the Greek word, have absurdly translated "lupines" instead of "warmth"; for the Greek THERMON means both, and even that is not in the Hebrew. What is written there is "hen," which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated charin, that is, "grace." The Septuagint alone put "warmth," thinking the last letter was m. For if we read "hen" with the letter n, it means "grace"; if with m, it is rendered "heat."

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: the people of the Jews who survived the Roman sword, or at any rate were able to escape the wrath of the Lord's fury, found grace in the wilderness of the nations, so as to be saved in the Church amid the throng of the nations. And so Israel will go and find his rest, which he had always hoped for and which the prophecies of the prophets had promised him.

According to the Septuagint, on the other hand, the meaning is this: the Lord found the apostles and their companions warm and alive in the wilderness of the nations, among those who had been slain by their own unbelief and had no warmth of life. Therefore the angels, and those who are in God's service, are commanded not to kill everyone, so that Israel may not be utterly destroyed. And it is said to them: "Go, and do not kill Israel! Let there be some who live, some who are warm with the ardor of faith, some who escape the cold of unbelief and death, whom the Lord may find in the wilderness!"

"From afar the Lord appeared to me (or, to him): I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you to me in mercy. Again I will build you, and you will be built, virgin Israel. Once more you will be adorned with your tambourines (or, take up your tambourines) and go out in the dance of those who make merry. Once more you will plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; plant your plantings and gather the vintage! For there will be a day when the watchmen on Mount Ephraim will cry out: Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the Lord our God!"

Because Israel had offended the Lord and had said, "We have no king but Caesar," and, "Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours," and had withdrawn far from God, therefore the Lord appeared to him after a long time (not in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, since they were later taken captive again); but he loved him with an everlasting love, which no end will blot out, and drew him in mercy. For he was saved not by any merit of his own but by clemency.

"Again," he says, "I will build you, and you will be built, virgin Israel." Let us understand this properly of the Church; for those who long for a Jerusalem of gold and gems are raving, consecrating their own greed under the mystery of the city of the Lord. "Once more you will be adorned with your tambourines, so that you may sing to the Lord in the churches, once all the flesh of evil works in you has been consumed. And you will go out in the dance of those who make merry, together with the throngs of the nations; you will plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria": not in the valleys and low places, but on the mountains of Samaria, which after the captivity of the people of Israel were possessed by foreigners. To them it is said: "Plant your plantings and gather the vintage!"

Then came the day of the Lord on which the watchmen, namely the apostles and apostolic men, cried out on the mountain of Samaria and on Mount Ephraim, names of which the one means "watch" and the other "fruitfulness." What, then, do the watchmen of Samaria say, or rather, what do they cry out on Mount Ephraim? "Arise, you who lie prostrate; leave behind what is lowly; scorn the offerings of victims" ("the sacrifice to the Lord is a broken spirit"); "let us go up to Zion, that is, to the Church, where there is the watchtower and the beholding of God; and when we are in Zion, or rather have gone up to it, we will go up together to the Lord our God."

"For thus says the Lord: Exult with gladness, Jacob, and neigh against the head of the nations; sound aloud, sing, and say: Save your people, Lord, the remnant of Israel!" Significantly, it is not the whole of Israel that is saved, but the remnant of Israel, as the Lord commands and says: "Exult with gladness, you who are of Jacob, and neigh at the head of the nations, giving it all back to him, because what was once the tail has been turned into the head; sound aloud, sing, and say!" What is it that they are commanded to say?

"Save your people, Lord." Which people? The remnant of Israel, of course, which has been saved according to election, about which Paul too speaks, taking up the testimony of Isaiah: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah."

"See, I will bring them from the land of the north and gather them from the ends of the earth." What follows, "at the feast of the Passover; and she will bear many children," is not in the Hebrew but is read only in the Septuagint. In its place the Hebrew has: "Among them will be the blind and the lame, the woman with child and the one giving birth together, a great assembly returning here."

The remnant of the people of Israel is gathered by the apostles and apostolic men, of whom we read above, "The watchmen will cry out on the mountain," and who are commanded, "Sound aloud, sing, and say," so that the remnant of Israel may be saved.

And the Lord himself promises that he will bring them back from the land of the north, the harshest of winds, which nevertheless is called by name "right-handed": from unbelief, from coldness toward the Lord's love. And he promises to gather them from the ends of the earth, not at some other time but at the feast of the Passover, that is, in the days of the Lord's passion, when the Lord was crucified and what he himself had promised in the Gospel was fulfilled: "When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself." Then he begot a great people, so that the word of Isaiah was fulfilled: "For a nation was born at once"; for in a single day three thousand, and then five thousand, people believed. And as for what is written in the Hebrew:

"Among them will be the blind and the lame, the woman with child and the one giving birth together, a great assembly returning here": although this was also fulfilled according to the letter, in that the blind saw and the lame walked, it can be better understood according to the anagogical sense. Those who had once been blind through faithlessness afterward believed in the Savior; and the lame, to whom Elijah once said, "How long will you limp on both feet?", afterward walked; and the people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light; the lame ran; and the woman with child gave birth to children, a great assembly returning to the faith.

The Jews think this was fulfilled when, under Ezra, they came out of Babylon after the day of the Passover to return to Jerusalem. But that was a type, not the reality; nor will they be able to prove that everything we have read, and are yet to read, was fulfilled at that time.

"They will come (or, go out) with weeping, and with mercy I will lead them back; I will lead them by streams of waters, on a straight road, and they will not stumble (or, will not go astray) on it; for I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn."

If we read according to the Hebrew, "They will come with weeping" (for this is what "iabu" indicates), we will say that weeping is sometimes a sign of overflowing joy as well, as in the saying, "I weep for joy." But if we follow the Septuagint, which said, "They will go out with weeping, and with mercy (or, with consolation) I will lead them back," we will take the sense that is also expressed in the Psalms: "Going, they went and wept, carrying their seed; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves."

For they wept when they were led away captive, and received the greatest consolation when they were led back by the Lord's mercy. And the Lord led them by the apostles and apostolic men, who were full of waters and of a most abundant river, on a straight road, namely the road of faith, not in the faithlessness of the Jews. "And they will not stumble on it," he says, because they have ceased to be blind, they to whom it was once said: "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, 'We see'; your sin remains."

We may also understand Christ as the "straight road": whoever walks on it will not stumble. "I have become a father to Israel," he says, to Israel who has been led back, "and Ephraim is my firstborn"; for where sin once abounded, grace has abounded all the more. Scripture testifies that Ephraim is a type of the people gathered from the nations.

For he was the younger son of Joseph, and he took the birthright from Manasseh, who was by nature the firstborn. In the mystery of the cross, with Jacob's hands crossed, the one who stood at Jacob's left received the blessing of his right hand, while the one who had stood at his right was blessed by the left hand and reduced to second rank. And as Jacob took the birthright from Esau, so Ephraim took it from Manasseh; and the whole people of the ten tribes was called Ephraim, because Jeroboam son of Nebat, of this tribe, was the first to hold the kingship in Samaria.

Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and proclaim it to the islands that are far off, and say: He who scattered Israel will gather him and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock, for the Lord has redeemed Jacob and freed him from the hand of one more powerful—or stronger—than he. And they will come and give praise on Mount Zion, and they will stream to the good things of the Lord, to the grain and the wine and the oil and the young of the flocks and herds. Their soul will be like a watered garden—or like a fruitful tree—and they will hunger no more.

Then the virgin will rejoice in the dance—or the virgins—and young men and old together; and I will turn their mourning into joy, and I will comfort them and gladden them after their sorrow, and I will make the soul of the priests drunk with fatness—or of the sons of Levi—and my people will be filled with my good things, says the Lord.

The calling of the Gentiles is plainly shown when Scripture says: Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and proclaim it to the islands that are far off, and say! What do they proclaim to the islands that lie far off? That the Lord who scattered Israel will himself gather him—so their being scattered was by no means the work of their adversaries' power, but of the Lord's will—and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock—for the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep—for the Lord has redeemed Jacob at the price of his own blood and freed him from the hand of one more powerful, or stronger.

These words show that the hostile powers are stronger than frail human nature, and that, as far as the strength of each side goes, they are stronger by nature but we are stronger by faith—provided, that is, we are found worthy to be freed by him who can bind the strong man and plunder his house.

And they will come, he says—no doubt those freed from the hand of the powerful—and they will praise their deliverer on Mount Zion, that is, in the Church, and they will stream to the good things of the Lord, an abundance of all things, which is experienced not in crops and food for this flesh but in the variety of the virtues.

To the grain, he says, and the wine and the oil—from which the Lord's bread is made, and the type of his blood is fulfilled, and the blessing of sanctification is shown, as Scripture says: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions—and the young of the flocks, who are the simple ones in the Church, and of the herds, which are horned and toss their adversaries.

But so that we may know that these blessings have nothing to do with the body but belong to the soul, there follows: And their soul will be like a watered garden, or like a fruitful tree planted beside the streams of water, and the paradise of the Lord in delights.

And they will hunger no more, he says—not with that hunger of which it is written: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, but with the hunger that is changed by fullness and shuts out want of anything. Then the virgin will rejoice in the dance—of whom the apostle writes: For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ—and the young men—to whom John speaks: I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one—and the old, to whom the same apostle bears witness in mystical language: I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.

And I will turn, he says, their mourning into joy—so that those whom the cross had terrified the resurrection may gladden—and I will comfort them and gladden them after their sorrow—in keeping with what the Lord says: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted—and I will make drunk the soul of the priests, who have the knowledge of God, from whose mouth people seek the law of the Lord, who believe in him to whom the prophet sings: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.

What follows in the Septuagint, "of the sons of Levi," is not found in the Hebrew, and it is plain that this does not speak at all of the priests who are sons of Levi, but of those whose type Melchizedek prefigured. The "drunkenness" of the priests is also confirmed in the apostles, when they were fervent in faith and were said to be full of new wine. Hence the place where the Lord was arrested is called Gethsemane, which in our language means "valley of fatness."

And when the priests have been made fat with the Lord's teaching and, drunk at Joseph's banquet, have said: How excellent is your cup that makes drunk!, then this too will come to pass which the Lord now promises: And my people will be filled with my good things. All these things are now granted in part, but then they will be given in full, when we see face to face and the body of our lowliness has been transformed by the glory of the resurrection.

Thus says the Lord: A voice was heard on high, of lamentation, weeping and mourning, of Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted over her children, because they are no more. The Septuagint has: Thus said the Lord: A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and mourning, of Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be at rest, because they are no more.

Matthew took this testimony neither from the Hebrew nor from the Septuagint. For after his account of the slaughter of the infants we read: Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud wailing, Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more. From this it is plain that the evangelists and apostles did not follow anyone's translation from the Hebrew, but, as Hebrews born of Hebrews, expressed in their own words what they read in Hebrew.

Rachel, the mother of Joseph, as she was coming to Bethlehem, was suddenly seized with the pains of childbirth and bore a son. Because she was dying as she gave birth, the midwife named him Benoni, that is, "son of my sorrow"; but his father Jacob changed the name and called him Benjamin, that is, "son of the right hand."

So the question is raised how Matthew the evangelist applied the prophet's testimony to the killing of the little ones, when it was plainly written about the ten tribes, whose chief was Ephraim [?], and Ephrathah lies not in the tribe of Ephraim at all but in the tribe of Judah. For it is the same place as Bethlehem, a place with two names, and so the names of the two agree: "Bethlehem" means "house of bread," and "Ephrathah" means karpophoria, which we can render "fruitfulness."

Since, then, Rachel was buried in Ephrathah, that is, in Bethlehem—as both holy Scripture and the inscription on her tomb testify to this day—she is said to weep for the children who were killed near her and in her own district.

Some of the Jews interpret this passage as follows: when Jerusalem was taken under Vespasian, countless thousands of captives were sent to Rome along this road, by way of Gaza and Alexandria. Others say that in the last captivity under Hadrian, when the city of Jerusalem was also destroyed, a numberless multitude of every age and of both sexes was sold at the market of the Terebinth, and that for this reason the Jews hold it accursed to visit that most famous market.

Let them say what they like; we will say that the evangelist Matthew rightly took this testimony on account of the place where Rachel was buried, and that she wept for the children of the neighboring villages round about as though they were her own.

Thus says the Lord: Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord, and they will return from the land of the enemy—or of the enemies—and there will be hope for your last days, says the Lord, and your children will return to their own borders.

According to the letter this has not yet happened—for we do not read that the ten tribes, who are in exile in the cities of the Medes and Persians, have returned to the land of Judea—but according to the spirit it was fulfilled in the Lord's passion and is being fulfilled to this day, when Israel is saved from the whole world and it is said to Rachel: Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears! And the sense is: "Stop weeping—for the Lord has regarded your former works—and your children will return from the land of the enemy; do not be held fast by your present sorrow! For there is hope in your last days, says the Lord, and your children will return to their own borders, which their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob possessed."

But we do better to understand it of the little ones: that they have the reward of the blood they shed for Christ, and in place of the land of Herod, their enemy, they possess the kingdom of heaven, and they will return to their former home when, in place of the body of lowliness, they receive a glorious body. This is the hope of the last days, when the righteous will shine like the sun, and those who were once little ones and nursing infants will rise, without any growing older and without the injuries and toil of the body, to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ.

I have surely heard Ephraim going into exile—or lamenting—: You chastised me, and I was taught like an untamed bullock—or like a calf, and I did not learn—; turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are the Lord my God. For after you turned me—or I was taken captive—I repented, and after I came to know—or you showed me—I struck my thigh—or I groaned—; I was confounded and I blushed—or from the day of confusion, and I showed you—because I bore the reproach of my youth.

God tells what he heard Ephraim saying as he lamented. No one doubts that this signifies the ten tribes, over whom Jeroboam son of Nebat first ruled, who also made the golden calves in Dan and Bethel, so that the people, led astray by this error, would cease to worship and adore the God of Israel. You chastised me, he says, and I was chastised. Every correction serves for salvation; for the present it seems a matter of sorrow, but afterward it yields peaceful fruit.

And what he says, like an untamed bullock or calf, and I did not learn, means that he was trained with much labor and many blows so that he might turn to repentance, and yet made no progress. "Turn me," he says, "and I shall be turned"—so even this, our repenting, we cannot accomplish unless we rely on God's help—"for after you have turned me and I have been turned to you, then I shall know that you are the Lord my God, and not my errors and sins at all. And after you turned me,

I repented." See how great God's help is and how frail the human condition, that we are not able to accomplish even this, our repenting, unless the Lord first turns us. "And after," he says, "you showed me either repentance itself or the knowledge of you—or, I came to know you—I struck my thigh." This is the mark of one who grieves and mourns and weeps over his former error: he strikes his thigh with his hand and confesses that he was foolish before.

I was confounded, he says, and I blushed, or from the day of confusion. For what time is not a time of confusion for us, if we recall our old sins and call to mind all the wrong we have done? And what the Septuagint said, and I showed you, means that after he groaned and recognized his offenses, he then advanced so far that he even showed God to others who did not know him, in keeping with what David too says in his repentance: I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn to you. Because I bore,

he says, the reproach of my youth. He says that he sinned through the ignorance of his age, so as to obtain pardon more easily, in keeping with what David also sings: Remember not [?] the sins of my youth and my ignorances! Hence also in what follows the Lord calls him a "little one" and "abounding in delights." He says this because of the great wealth and the fertility of the land in which the tribe of Ephraim luxuriates to this day.

Is Ephraim an honored son to me—or a beloved one—is he a pampered child? For ever since I spoke of him—or, my words were in him—I will still remember him; therefore my heart is troubled over him; I will surely have mercy on him, says the Lord. When Ephraim repents and says at the beginning:

You taught me and I was taught like an untamed bullock, and at the end: because I bore the reproach of my youth, the Lord answers and, now that he has turned to him with his whole mind, sustains him with this oracle: "Ephraim is my beloved son, whom I loved so much from the beginning that I preferred him to his brother Manasseh."

An honored son, because, contrary to the order of nature, he received the honor of the firstborn by the Lord's favor; a pampered child, of whom Scripture writes: The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle; against whom and to whom the whole book of the prophet Hosea is addressed; whom Jacob blessed. Let us take "delights" in this place in the sense of what is said in the psalm: Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart, where the Greek and the Hebrew have: Abound in delights. Hence too the paradise in Eden is called the paradise "of delights."

"For," he says, "my words were in him; I will still remember him." So that the blessing might not be thought unearned, bestowed more by the indulgence of the giver than by the merit of the one who received it, he says: I will remember him, because my words were in him—not in his mouth, not on his lips, but in the deepest affection of his heart; and for this reason my heart is troubled over him. To him he also speaks through Hosea: What shall I do with you, Ephraim?

What shall I do with you, Israel? Shall I make you like Admah, and like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within me, my compassion is stirred. I will not carry out the fury of my wrath, and I will not destroy Ephraim. I will surely have mercy on him, says the Lord: "My words were indeed in him, and he received all my commandments with an eager mind and kept them in his heart; yet still I will surely have mercy on him"—to show that all human righteousness stands in need of God's mercy.

Set up watchtowers for yourself, make yourself bitter laments, direct your heart to the straight road on which you walked; return, virgin Israel, return to these your cities! How long will you go slack in delights, wandering daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing on the earth: a woman shall encompass a man.

The Septuagint has: Set up watchmen for yourself, inflict punishment, put your heart on your shoulders: the road on which you walked. Return, virgin Israel, return to your cities mourning! How long will you turn away, despised daughter? For the Lord has created salvation for you in a new planting; in your salvation men will go about.

Where we said, How long will you go slack in delights?, Symmachus put: How long will you sink into the deep? I have set out both versions in full to show that this most obscure passage, which contains the mysteries of the Church, was either not understood or passed over by the Septuagint—or by whoever else translated this prophet.

The Hebrew word sionim is rendered either "watchmen" or "watchtowers," as Aquila and Symmachus translated it. So I wonder what the common edition meant by putting "Zion" for sionim, that is, "watchmen," and confusing the reader's understanding, so that he would think God's word had suddenly turned from Ephraim to Zion and the tribe of Judah, when the whole discourse is addressed without a break to Ephraim, to whom he also spoke above: I have surely heard Ephraim, and: Ephraim is an honored son to me, or a pampered child, and to whom he now speaks: "Set up for yourself watchtowers, or watchmen, to announce to you beforehand that so great a happiness in all things is coming."

As for what follows, "bitter laments," which in Hebrew are called themruum and which Symmachus translated "change," this indicates that she ought to weep, either for her old sins or out of the greatness of her joy, and turn to God with her whole mind, and set or direct her heart on the road by which she set out; for it is by that road that she would return.

And what the Septuagint said instead, put your heart on your shoulders, means that she ought to join her thoughts to her works, or else look to the shoulders of those who carry her and bring her back from captivity; Isaiah sets this out more fully, declaring that they are to be brought back on camels and in chariots and litters. "Return,

" he says, "virgin Israel, return to your cities, which you left as a captive! How long will you go slack in negligence and wander in deep error? Consider what I am about to say, and attend carefully to the source from which you may hope for such great blessedness; hear what you never knew before! The Lord has created a new thing on the earth: without a man's seed, without any intercourse or conception, a woman will encompass a man in the bosom of her womb. As his age increases he will seem to advance in wisdom and stature through the cries of infancy, yet he will be a perfect man held in a woman's womb for the usual months.

" Symmachus and Aquila too translated in agreement with our edition. What the common edition meant in this place I could say, and I could find some sense in it, were it not sacrilege to reason about the words of God by human understanding. Theodotion too, agreeing with the common edition, translated: The Lord has created a new salvation; in salvation a man will go about, putting the singular for the plural. At the same time this too should be noted: the birth and conception of the Savior are called a "creation" of God.

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Once again they will speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity: The Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain! And Judah and all its cities will dwell in it together, farmers and those who drive flocks.

The Septuagint has: Thus said the Lord of powers, the God of Israel: Once again they will speak this saying in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I bring back its exiles: Blessed be the Lord upon his righteous, holy mountain, and those who dwell in the land of Judea and in every city of it with the farmer; and he will be lifted up in the flock.

According to the Hebrew, it is clear that when Israel returns and their captivity is turned back to their own land, the cities of Judah will be inhabited, and it will be said to each of them: The Lord bless you—he who is truly the beauty of righteousness and the holy mountain, and whoever dwells on it will fear no snares; and Judah will dwell without iniquity in its cities, and there will be farmers and a multitude of livestock. This seems to have been fulfilled in part under Zerubbabel and Ezra, but the full measure of the prophecy should be referred to the times of Christ: either to the first coming, when these things were done spiritually, or to the second, when all things are fulfilled—spiritually according to us, carnally according to the Jews and our own Judaizers.

Further, according to the Septuagint the sense is this: "Once again this saying will be spoken in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back its captivity." What will be said? Blessed be the Lord upon his righteous, holy mountain. The mountain that deserves to receive the name of righteousness and holiness is none other than the Savior; otherwise it is foolish, by Jewish error, to believe that an irrational and insensible mountain is "righteous and holy."

He it is of whom it is written in what follows: and in every city of it—understand: of the Savior—with the farmer. No doubt this signifies God, of whom it is written in the Gospel: I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer; hence the apostle too says: You are God's field, God's building. And what follows, and he will be lifted up in the flock, shows that the Lord himself, righteous and holy and the farmer, is lifted up in each flock and ascends to the heights in his servants and believers.
Because I have made the weary soul drunk—or, because I have made every thirsty soul drunk—and have satisfied every hungry soul—or, filled—therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me.

The change of speakers makes the meaning of the prophets obscure. The Lord had said: Once again they will speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity. And what will they say? No doubt what follows: The Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain, and so on. And again, when they have said this, the Lord answers: Because I have made the weary—or thirsty—soul drunk and have satisfied every hungry soul.

And when he has said this, the people who had come back from captivity answer: Therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me. For the Lord makes drunk the weary or thirsty soul, and says in the Gospel: Whoever is thirsty, let him come to me and drink, and: Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly; and he satisfies every soul that hungers and thirsts—a thirst and hunger to which he likewise bears witness in the Gospel: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.

It should be noted that "drunkenness" in this place is used in a good sense, as also in the Song: Eat, friends, drink and be drunk, beloved! With this drunkenness Joseph too was made drunk with his brothers at noon. And those who had been weary and hungry, now made drunk and satisfied, give thanks and answer: "I awoke and saw the Lord"—that is, rousing me and saying: Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light.
"And my sleep," he says, "was sweet to me, so that I might imitate the words of my Lord, who says: I slept and was sound asleep; and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me."

"Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of men and the seed of beasts. And just as I watched over them to uproot and to tear down, to scatter and to destroy and to afflict, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, says the Lord. In those days they will no longer say: 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But each one will die for his own iniquity; every man who eats sour grapes, his own teeth will be set on edge."

The words "house" and "house", that is, "the house of Israel and the house of Judah", are not in the Septuagint, which has only "Israel and Judah", so that it reads: "and I will sow Israel and Judah." And what he adds, "with the seed of men and the seed of beasts", we should refer to the rational and the simple. And just as it was said to Jeremiah at the beginning of his book, "Behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to scatter, to build and to plant," and "I watched over them to do what I had threatened," so, he says, "I will now watch over them to build and to plant; for you are God's

field, God's building." According to the Jews, and to our own Judaizers, all promises of this kind are supposed to be fulfilled in a kingdom of a thousand years. We, however, since the Apostle says, "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth," and since the prophet Isaiah records that the Savior is a builder of hedges and of houses, maintain that they were fulfilled spiritually at the first coming of Christ — and fulfilled in part, not in full, because "now we see in a mirror and in a riddle," and we do not know as we ought to know; "but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away" — or at any rate we believe that they are to be fulfilled at the second coming, when the Lord will appear in his majesty and the fullness of the Gentiles will have come in, so that all Israel may be saved, no longer in part, one by one, but that God may be all in all. As for what follows, "In those days they will no longer say:

'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge,'" and the rest, we discussed this more fully in our commentary on Ezekiel, when we explained the passage: "Son of man, what do you mean by this proverb among the children of Israel, who say, 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge'? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be used in Israel! For all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son: the soul that sins, it shall die." From this we learn that it is not the Lord who causes death, but sin; for "the soul that sins, it shall die."

And in the present passage it is said that Israel will by no means stand condemned forever for the sins of its fathers, but will be saved, after a long time, by its own merits and by faith in Christ. And it should be noted that vices and sins are called "sour grapes," so that the teeth of those who eat them are set on edge and cannot taste the sweetness of him of whom it is said: "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet!"

Whoever does not understand the Scriptures as the truth of the matter requires eats sour grapes. Hence all heretics too, believing perverse things, cannot eat the bread that comes down from heaven; their teeth are set on edge, not because the food is harsh, but because their teeth are faulty.

"Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make — or, I will arrange — with the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant — or, testament — not according to the covenant — or, testament — that I made with your fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, the covenant — or, testament — which they made void; and I was lord over them — or, I disregarded them —

says the Lord. But this will be the covenant — or, testament — that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law within them — or, in their mind — and I will write it on their heart; and I will be their God, and they will be my people.

And no longer will each one teach his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord,' for they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord; for I will be merciful toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."

The apostle Paul — or whoever else wrote the epistle — used this testimony in writing to the Hebrews, and all churchmen since then say that everything was fulfilled at the first coming of the Savior, and that the New Testament, that is, the Gospel, succeeded the Old Testament, by which the law of the letter was exchanged for the law of the Spirit, so that all the sacrifices, too, and circumcision and the Sabbath were fulfilled spiritually. Our putting "covenant" in place of "testament" follows the Hebrew original, although a testament is also rightly called a covenant, since it contains the will and the attestation of those who enter into the covenant.

When Israel was brought out of the land of Egypt, God's intimacy with that people was so great that he says he took it by the hand and gave it a covenant. This covenant they made void, and for that reason the Lord disregarded them.

But now, in the Gospel, after the cross, the resurrection, and the ascension, he promises to give a covenant not on tablets of stone but on fleshly tablets of the heart; and when the Lord's testament has been written in the mind of believers, he will be their God and they will be his people, so that they will by no means seek Jewish teachers and the traditions and commandments of men, but will be taught by the Holy Spirit — if, that is, they are worthy to hear: "You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you." But the Spirit breathes where it wills and has various gifts, and the knowledge of the one God is the possession of all virtues. "And this," he says,

"will come about because I will be merciful toward their iniquity and will remember their sin no more." From this it is clear that, according to the understanding of this passage, what precedes is to be understood of the first coming of the Savior, when both peoples, Israel and Judah, were joined to one another.

But if anyone is troubled as to why he said, "I will arrange with the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant — or, testament — not according to the covenant — or, testament — that I made with your fathers," let him understand that the first church of Christ was from the Jews, and that the Lord and Savior came to them and said, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and that the apostles confirmed the same thing: "It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles."

For it was not right to give the children's bread to the dogs; but since the children refused to receive the Father when he came to his own, he gave power to all, so that those who received him might become children of God.

"Thus says the Lord, who gives the sun for light by day, and the order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar — the Lord of hosts is his name: If these laws — or, these ordinances — cease before me, says the Lord, then the seed of Israel too will fail, so as not to be before me all the days."

In the beginning of Genesis, too, we read that the sun was placed in the heaven for light by day, and the moon and stars for light by night; and in the psalm: "Day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night," because day and night succeed one another in turn.

"Just as," he says, "the order of things, and especially of the heavenly stars, cannot be changed, and the waves of the roaring sea roll toward the shores, and the crash of its swelling waters and billows is heard with terror, yet it cannot go further than God's command has prescribed — according to the verse, 'You set a boundary which they shall not pass, nor shall they turn back to cover the earth' — so," he says, "by the Lord's will the seed and race of Israel will be everlasting and will never fail." Here "laws" are to be understood not as the laws of Moses, but as the constitution and order of nature.

Let us question the Jews: "If the heavens will perish and all will grow old like a garment, and it is said to God, 'But you are the same, and your years will not fail,' how can the seed of Israel be everlasting?" For either the seed of Israel will perish when the heavens perish, or, if it is everlasting, then the heavens will not perish either. But if Scripture cannot lie and the heavens are going to perish, then the seed of Israel will perish too, especially since Jacob also says to his sons: "Come, and I will tell you what will happen in the last days." And when it says "in the last days," it follows that the world will cease to exist and there will be another ordering of things. So much against them.

For our own people, moreover, the Gospel too shows that this world is not everlasting, when it says, "Heaven and earth will pass away," and, "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." Let us also put it another way: as long as this world lasts, the seed of Israel and the Jewish nation will endure, not in those who are now unbelievers, but in those who believed with the apostles and through the apostles, so that a remnant might be saved.

"Thus says the Lord: If the heavens above can be measured and the foundations of the earth below searched out, then I too will cast off all the seed of Israel for all that they have done, says the Lord." The Septuagint: "Thus says the Lord: If the heaven is raised higher, and if the floor of the earth is lowered beneath, then I will not reject the race of Israel, says the Lord, for all that they have done."

In this passage the Hebrew differs greatly from the common edition. Let us first explain it according to the Hebrew: "If the heavens above can be measured and their height known, or the foundations of the earth searched out and their extremities grasped by reason, then I too," he says, "will cast off all the seed of Israel for all that they have done, says the Lord. But just as it is impossible for us to know the heights of the heavens and the foundations of the earth, so too it will be impossible for me to cast off all the seed of Israel. But if I do cast off all the seed of Israel, then the height of the heavens and the extremities of the earth will be measured."

This syllogism is also constructed in the Gospel, where one impossibility is compared with another: "It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." For just as the one cannot happen, so neither can the other; but if the latter should happen, then the former, which was thought impossible, will happen too. So those who explain this passage otherwise are mistaken, when they cite also the testimony that the Son could have asked the Father and brought twelve legions of angels to his aid.

The Septuagint translated a sense contrary to this, saying: "If the heaven is exalted higher and the floor of the earth lowered beneath, then I," he says, "will not reject the seed of Israel, says the Lord, for all that they have done." If this is so, the nation of Israel will be rejected: for just as the heaven cannot be higher than it is, nor the earth lower than it is, so too the race of Israel can by no means be approved. If we see the Jews boasting of this testimony according to the Hebrew,
let us agree with them that not all the seed of Israel has been cast off; for not all have been cast off, but only those who were unbelievers.

"Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when the city will be built for the Lord from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring rule — or, according to Symmachus, line — will go out further, straight ahead over the hill of Gareb, and it will go around Goath — or, according to the Septuagint, with choice stones — and the whole valley of ruins — for which Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, Phagarim — and of ashes, and all Asaremoth — which we read better as Asademoth, which Aquila translated 'suburbs' — as far as the brook Kidron and as far as the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, holy to the Lord; it will not be uprooted or destroyed forever."

Those who accept a thousand-year reign of Christ in the land of Judea — namely the Jews and our own Judaizers — try to point out the tower of Hananel, the Corner Gate, the hill of Gareb, Goath, the valley of Phagarim, all Asademoth, the brook Kidron, and the site of the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east; and there, they say, the sanctuary of the Lord, that is, the temple, is to be built and is to remain forever.

And since they cannot show that this was fulfilled after the captivity, in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, they pass on to the times of Christ, who they say will come at the consummation of the world, so that, according to the Apocalypse of John, a Jerusalem of gold and jewels will descend and be built round about over this stretch of land, that is, from this place to that.

And they catch this faint breath of support for their surmise: that the foundations of the city are to be laid from the tower of Anathoth, which today is called Jeremiah's tower and lies three miles from Jerusalem, as far as the brook Kidron — which is mentioned in the Gospel and lies in the valley of Jehoshaphat, where there was the garden in which Judas the traitor betrayed the Savior.

"We shall read," they say, "in what follows that Hanamel, son of Shallum, was Jeremiah's cousin, whose field he bought; and this is the tower of Hananel." They are ignorant of the Hebrew original: for here, according to the Hebrew, it is written "from the tower of Hananel," with nun, that is, as the middle letter, whereas there it is "Behold, Hanamel son of Shallum, your cousin, will come to you," with m as the middle letter.

Calling, then, upon the Lord and Savior, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens; who also opened the sealed book of Isaiah and of all the prophets, and whom the twenty-four elders holding harps worshiped because he alone was able to unlock the divine mysteries — let us approach the building of the city to which the prophetic word is addressed: "Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God," and, "The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God."

The church, then, is built from the tower of "obedience," or "grace" and "the gifts of God" — for this is what Hananel means — to the Corner Gate. Although it seems to have a lofty beginning, as long as we remain in this flesh we cannot possess the straight line of truth; rather, we stand in a corner, with broken lines. And the measuring line goes out further, straight ahead of it, that is, of the Corner Gate, over the hill of Gareb, which in our language is rendered either "sojourning" or "scab," to teach us that we are strangers and pilgrims, and that we have itching ears and easily give our assent to novel and most wicked doctrines.

"And it will go around," he says, "Goath," for which the Septuagint translated "round about with choice stones," which roll over the face of the earth and are bound together by the cornerstone, as the apostle Peter says: "And you yourselves, like living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ."

"And the whole valley," he says, "of Phagarim" — which means "of ruins" — "and ashes" — understand "it will go around" — so that, although we may seem to ourselves to be on the hills, we may always fear ruin, and consider the ashes, and say in repentance with David: "For I have eaten ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping." Hence it is also said to those who have fallen: "Shall he who falls not rise again? says the Lord."

"And all," he says, "Sademoth," which we have rendered "region of death," dividing one name into two words: sade, which means "region," and moth, which is interpreted "of death"; for which Aquila rendered "suburbs," or "fields" and "countryside." Now the "region of death" is the region of sinners, and the "suburbs" are the region of pleasures, which extends as far as the brook Kidron — where the Lord was betrayed — which is interpreted "darkness."

See how many places the church contains, and how that saying of the Apostle, "that it may be without spot or wrinkle," is reserved for the future and for heaven. You hear of corners, you hear of scabs, you hear of ruins and ashes and the region of death and darkness — and you boast of your own virtue and sinlessness!

Next follows: "and as far as the corner of the gate." Here too it is a corner, so that no true righteousness and no sure victory may be displayed in this world. And this corner of the gate, although it is "toward the east," whence light comes forth, is nevertheless called "of the horses," to teach us that we need running and contest, so that at last we may be worthy to hear with the Lord: "You mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation."

At the eastern gate, at the gate of the chariots, is the sanctification of the Lord, so that we may consider ourselves perfect only when we say to the Lord: "The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice; the Lord is among them." A building of this kind, which is laid upon the foundation of Christ — of which the Apostle too speaks: "Like a wise master builder I laid a foundation" — is never destroyed, but will remain forever. Obscure and difficult passages must be discussed at greater length, so that we may run through the plain ones more briefly.

"The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah, king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the prison, which was in the house of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, 'Why do you prophesy, saying, Thus says the Lord?'"

Not only the words but also the deeds of the prophets serve us as an example for virtue. Jeremiah could have announced good fortune and enjoyed the friendship of King Zedekiah, but he preferred to obey God rather than men, and him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna rather than one who could have power only over the body.

And this should be considered: it was the tenth year of Zedekiah's reign, Jerusalem was already besieged and consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence, and captivity was near; and yet Zedekiah persists in his opinion. Some measure of his clemency is shown, however, in that he ordered him to be confined not in the prison itself but in the court of the prison — under open custody, that is, so that he could not escape — as though all Jerusalem, shut in by its fortifications, were not a common prison for its inhabitants.

This is the eighteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who began to rule in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. And the whole cause of the king's anger is this: that Jeremiah spoke in the name of the Lord the things he had been commanded.

"Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will take it. And Zedekiah, king of Judah, will not escape from the hand of the Chaldeans, but will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and his mouth will speak with his mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes. And he will lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he will remain until I visit him, says the Lord. But if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will have no success."

This was the cause of the king's anger: that Jeremiah preferred truth to falsehood and declared that both the city of Jerusalem and King Zedekiah would be taken; and, what was harder still, that he would see the face of the Babylonian king and, humbled and captive, would speak with that most unbridled king in his madness. For it is a heavier terror to see the one you fear, and to endure the rebuke of his words before the torment of his punishments. "And to Babylon," he says,

"he will lead Zedekiah, and there he will remain"; for which the Septuagint translated "and [?] Babylon." Of these, the one signifies being dragged against one's will, the other going there willingly. "And there," he says, "he will remain": he uses an ambiguous word so as not to seem to be prophesying torments and miseries. And what follows — "until I visit him, says the Lord.

And if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will have no success" — is not found in the Septuagint. He has prudently tempered the sentence so that it can be taken in either a good or a bad sense; for "visitation," as I have often said, signifies both "consolation" and "punishment."

And Jeremiah said: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Behold, Hanamel, the son of Shallum (or Salom), your cousin (in Hebrew, "dodach"), is coming to you to say: "Buy my field for yourself, the one in Anathoth; for the right to purchase it falls to you as next of kin."

No one could have known that the word of God had come to Jeremiah in secret unless he himself, to whom it came, made it known. And it is foretold to him that his cousin Hanamel would come to him and offer him possession of the field that had been his. This place was in Anathoth, among the pasture lands which by the law were given to the priests in each of the tribes and cities. It was not lawful for a possession to pass from one tribe to another, or from one family to another family. That is why the daughters of Zelophehad receive a portion among their brothers. Above all, the priests' pasture lands could not be sold to anyone, up to the year of release, except to the one who had a claim by blood kinship.

So his cousin comes to him and offers the purchase that is due to him by kinship. Hilkiah and Shallum were full brothers; Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, Hanamel the son of Shallum. "Hilkiah" means "portion of the Lord", and "Jeremiah" "loftiness of the Lord"; and it is fitting that "the height of the Lord" is born of "the portion of the Lord". "Shallum" is rendered in our language "peace" or "peaceful", and "Hanamel" "gift" or "grace of God". Nor should we wonder that "peace" and "grace" are joined together, since the apostolic letters also begin this way: Grace to you and peace. First, then, we earn peace with God, and after peace grace is born for us, which lies not in the choice of the one who possesses it but in the will of the one who gives it.

Now "the grace of God" offers the purchase to the one who is set "on high", so that, however exalted he may seem, he still needs the grace of God. As for what the bride often sings in the Song, my cousin (fratruelis), that is, adelphidos mou, in Hebrew it is "dodi". So it should be rendered not "fratruelis" (a brother's son) but "patradelphus", that is, "patruelis" (a father's brother's son). That Jeremiah son of Hilkiah was one of the priests who were in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin, the opening of this book also bears witness.

And Hanamel, my uncle's son, came to me, as the Lord had said, at the entrance (or court) of the prison, and said to me: "Take possession of (or buy) my field, the one in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. The inheritance falls to you and you are next of kin, so take possession of it" (or "buy it").

What the word of the Lord had told the prophet would happen was at once fulfilled in deed. "Hanamel came to me," he says (that is, "the grace of God"), "my uncle's son" (that is, "the son of peace"); "he came to the entrance of the prison and said to me what the Lord had foretold he would say."

This priestly field, whose purchase and possession was offered to Jeremiah, is in "Anathoth", in the land of "Benjamin". The first name means "obedience", the second "son of the right hand". It follows that he seeks to buy the place where the "obedience" and the "power" of the Lord dwelt. In place of "next of kin" the Septuagint translated presbyteron, that is, "elder", which does not suit this passage.

And I knew that this was the word of the Lord, and I bought the field from Hanamel, my uncle's son, the one in Anathoth, and I weighed out the money to him, seven staters and ten pieces of silver. And I wrote it in a deed and sealed it and called witnesses, and I weighed the silver on the scales. And I took the deed of possession, sealed, with its terms and conditions, and the seals on the outside.

It was certainly hard to accept, almost inconsistent and laughable, that the man who was prophesying that Jerusalem would be taken at any moment, and that all would be led captive or perish by the sword, famine and plague, should buy a field in Anathoth which he was never going to possess. "But I understood," he says, "that it was the word of the Lord, and that my purchase was to be made to fit the Lord's argument and prophecy. And so I submitted to his command to buy, knowing that the word of God had not come to me about such a matter in vain, and I weighed out seventeen shekels of silver." We have rendered these as "staters". A shekel is worth twenty obols, as is written in the last part of Ezekiel.

The prophet bought it for "seventeen" shekels. This is the number in which David, the servant of the Lord, sang on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and said: I will love you, O Lord, my strength! The Lord is my firm foundation and my refuge and my deliverer; my God, my helper, and I will hope in him; my protector and the horn of my salvation. That the number ten is mystical is shown by the Decalogue,

which was written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, and by the day of fasting and atonement in the seventh month. And that "seven", in which the true sabbath-rest and repose are found, is holy, we can prove by many testimonies of Scripture. I would have set down at least a few of them if it were not idle to teach what is already well known.

For this number, then, a prophet and priest buys a possession. It is written in a deed and sealed, witnesses are called, and the silver is carefully weighed, so that all the legal requirements of sale and purchase are observed and the possession is secure, confirmed by formal question and answer. Let this at least be heard by those who try to lay claim to estates with forged wills, and sometimes with no will at all, through witnesses they have brought in!

And I gave the deed of possession to Baruch son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, in the sight of Hanamel my cousin, in the sight of the witnesses whose names were written in the deed of purchase, and in the sight of all the Jews who were sitting in the court of the prison.

The possession would have to be abandoned at once; or rather, it was being bought for those who would come later, and bought by a man who had no children, for he had not taken a wife. Even so, obedient to the Lord's command, he carries out everything with due formality and gives the sealed deed of possession to Baruch son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah. "Baruch" in our language means "blessed". He was the son of "Neriah", which is interpreted "my lamp", as the prophet says: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a burning light to my paths. Neriah too, Baruch's father, was the son of "Mahseiah", that is, "the making" and "work of the Lord".

Let us take note, then, of how great were the virtues with which Baruch the disciple served Jeremiah, as David says: The one who walked in a blameless way, he ministered to me. So also Elisha, Elijah's servant, so pleased God that after his master was taken up he was found worthy to receive even a double portion of the spirit. I say this as a warning to those who make use of the services of wicked men and do not dare to cast off those whom their own bad consciences know to be bound to them as if by glue.

The deed is handed to Baruch, a man of such quality and stature. Hanamel, who had sold the field, looked on, along with the witnesses who had signed and whose names were recorded in the deed of purchase, and also, he says, all the Jews sitting in the court of the prison. These, no doubt, had come either to comfort the prophet or, out of zeal for the fear of God, because they wanted to hear the words of the Lord.

And I charged Baruch in their presence, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, this sealed deed of purchase and this deed which is open, and put them in an earthenware jar, so that they may last for many days. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be possessed in this land.

With all those named in the previous passage present and watching, Baruch, the servant and disciple, receives an order. It comes not from his teacher's words but from the command of God, who orders him to take the deeds, one sealed and the other open, and to put both in an earthenware jar so that they might last for many days. (This custom in purchases is kept to this day: what the seals hold closed within is displayed in an open copy to those who wish to read it.) That possession, then, was secure and would endure long afterward, since it was kept under such careful guard: the deeds of purchase would not lie exposed to theft, as they would if left outside, nor be ruined by the damp of the soil, as they would if buried in the ground.

All this is done so that those who saw it might understand that Jerusalem would be inhabited again and its fields possessed. They ought to have understood this for themselves without Jeremiah's word, yet they are reminded by the words of the Lord, and it is said to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be possessed in this land. This is what Jeremiah had said a little earlier: I knew that this was the word of the Lord; and that is why he bought a field he would never possess.

And after I had given the deed of possession to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to the Lord, saying: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God (or, "you who are, Lord God")! Behold, you made heaven and earth by your great strength and by your outstretched (or "lofty") arm. No word will be difficult (or "impossible") for you (or, according to the Septuagint, "nothing is hidden from you"). You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them. O most mighty, great and powerful one (in Hebrew, "gibbor"), the Lord of hosts (or "of powers") is your name!

You are great in counsel and beyond the reach of thought; your eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of Adam (or "of men"), to repay each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his schemes.

The purchase of the field has been lawfully completed, and the Lord has declared that houses, fields and vineyards will be possessed again. After this the prophet prays to the Lord and pours out the grief of his heart in groans, saying: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God. For this the Septuagint translated ho ōn, that is, "you who are, Lord God", in keeping with what is said to Moses: Go, say to the people of Israel: He who is has sent me. This does not mean that other beings do not exist; but it is one thing to exist by the gift of the Creator, so as to have being, and another to exist by an eternal nature.

He praises God and proclaims the Creator from his creatures. First he extols his power, mercy and justice toward the whole human race; then he turns to Israel and describes in ringing words how much God had bestowed on it. And after such great benefits, he says, they forgot his good gifts and provoked his kindness to bitterness, so that the city is now under siege and, before the enemy can break into it, has been consumed by sword, famine and plague.

He set all this out first so that he could go on to say what seemed to amount to a criticism of the divine decree: And you say to me, Lord God: "Buy the field with silver and call witnesses," when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans? That is the whole pericope of this passage for now; let us return to the details.

You made heaven and earth by your great strength. John too says of the Son: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. For this is the "strength" of the Lord, as the apostle confirms: Christ [?] the power of God and the wisdom of God.

And by your outstretched (or "lofty") arm: both words point to one who strikes. This is the "arm" of which Isaiah also speaks: And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? No word will be difficult for you; for what is impossible with men is possible with God. Or: from whom nothing is hidden, as the psalmist says: For darkness will not be dark to you, and the night will be lit up like the day.

You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them. Great is the Creator's kindness: he extends his mercy to a thousand generations, yet shows his justice at once in the next generation. Even this justice is mixed with mercy, for he does not punish the offender at once but waits for repentance, so that only if the children imitate their parents' vices is the long-deferred punishment repaid. O most mighty, great and powerful one,

the Lord of hosts (or "of powers") is your name! These names point to the Creator's power; but God's proper name is "Father", which is revealed in the Gospel by the Lord, who says: Father, I have made your name known to men. Great in counsel: and does anyone dare to pry into the Lord's secret and pass judgment on his judgments? And beyond the reach of thought: if thought cannot grasp him, how can speech? Whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of Adam: in vain, then, does a man think he can hide from God's knowledge.

And what he adds, to repay each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his schemes, shows that at times, because of his surpassing wisdom, God's judgments seem unjust. The apostle explains this more fully to the Romans: Do you not know that God's kindness is urging you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God's righteous judgment. So the later sinners are punished, the more just the punishment is. So it was with Pharaoh: he was warned by ten plagues, not punished, and when he persisted in his hardness he was at last overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea.

You performed signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day both in Israel and among men (or "the earth-born"), and you made a name for yourself, as at this day. And you brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with great terror.

And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey. And they came in and took possession of it; but they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all that you commanded them to do; and so all these evils have come upon them.

He passes from the general to the particular and briefly runs over what God had bestowed on Israel in particular. You performed, he says, signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, by which Egypt was afflicted, and to this day both in Israel and among men, or "the earth-born".

The phrase "to this day" should be joined to what follows, so that we read: "and in Israel and among all mortals your signs are fulfilled every day". Or another reading: "You performed signs and wonders not only in Egypt; to this day the same strength of your mercy has saved your people, and you come to the aid of the whole human race with the power of the Creator." Note also that he sets "Israel" apart from "men" and "the earth-born", in keeping with the saying: Israel is my firstborn son.

And you made a name for yourself, as at this day: "Your praises," he says, "are celebrated in the speech of the whole world." And you brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt: he does well to say "your people", for at the time they were brought out they were obeying the Lord's commands. "You brought them out with signs and wonders, with which Egypt was struck, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm and with great terror," when the Red Sea opened a way for the people of Israel as they crossed and overwhelmed the Egyptian army.

And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, namely Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. So they received the promised land not through their own merit but through the virtues of their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey. For they could not yet take solid food, but were nourished on the honey and milk of infancy; or at any rate, honey and milk stand for the richness and abundance of all things. And they came in and took possession of it. And at once there was nothing between possession and disobedience; for plenty breeds a sense of security, security breeds carelessness, and carelessness breeds contempt.

But they did not obey, he says, your voice or walk in your law. In vain, then, did they promise in the desert, saying: All that the Lord commands, we will do. For the reward lies not in the pledge but in the deed. This serves to check the impudence of those who think that a man can fulfill everything he has promised to do.

They did nothing of all that you commanded them to do; and yet they had certainly promised to do it. And so all these evils have come upon them: "evils" to those who suffer them, but "goods" in the Lord's judgment, since he repays each one according to his ways.

Behold, siege-works have been built against the city to take it, and the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it, because of the sword and famine and pestilence. Whatever you spoke has come to pass, as you yourself see; and yet you say to me, Lord God: "Buy the field with silver and call witnesses," when the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans? It was the tenth year of King Zedekiah, for it is written:

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the prison. And so it is rightly said now: "Behold, siege-works have been built against the city to take it, and the city has been handed over into the hand of the Chaldeans. They have no one left to conquer, only people to capture, for these have already been consumed by sword, famine and plague, and we see that whatever you said has been fulfilled. How then can you say to me, Lord: Buy the field with silver and call witnesses, when the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans?"

So he is not finding fault but asking. He wants to learn, not so much for his own sake as for the others who sat in the court of the prison and perhaps silently found fault with him: how could the same prophet, whom they believed to speak the truth, say that the city would be taken and yet buy a field as though he would possess it?

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh; will any word be difficult (or "impossible") for me (or "be hidden from me")? Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall take it.

And the Chaldeans will come (or "enter"), fighting against this city, and will set it on fire and burn it, together with the houses on whose roofs they sacrificed to Baal and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods to provoke [me].

He follows sad tidings with glad ones, and after the overthrow of Jerusalem he promises the captive people a return. But first he sets out the causes of the offence and of God's just fury, so that the greater the guilt of the sinners, the greater the Creator's kindness toward sinners may appear.

I am, he says, the Lord God of all flesh. He does not say "of all nations" or "of the people of Israel", nor indeed what he often says when speaking of the saints, "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob". He says the God of all flesh, so that we may believe he made both rational and irrational living creatures. For there are those who confess the Creator's providence as far as rational beings, but claim that irrational animals live or perish by chance. The prophetic word declares that nothing escapes God's providence and knowledge, since some things were created for their own sake and others for human use.

Will any word be difficult for me (or "impossible", or at any rate "hidden from me")? We said above as well: what is impossible with men is possible with God. Here and in many other places we should take "word" to mean "things". But what does it mean that the word came, Therefore thus says the Lord? What had come before, that he should use a causal conjunction and say: Therefore thus says the Lord?

"Because," he says, "it is my concern to govern all things, to order everything and to repay each one according to his ways, therefore I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and they shall take it." For first it is surrounded by an army and taken while Nebuchadnezzar is absent; then Zedekiah is led to Riblah and handed over to the king there.

And the Chaldeans, he says, will come, fighting against this city. Aquila does better here: where it is written "will come", he translated eiseleusontai, that is, they "will enter" the city. They were not absent, so they could not "come"; they had already surrounded Jerusalem, as Scripture testifies: At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and then: Behold, siege-works have been built against the city to take it, and the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans. How then could people who were already present "come"?

"But those who were besieging the city will enter it," he says, "and take it and set it on fire and burn it to the ground." (The Hebrew word "bau" is ambiguous and means both "they will come" and "they will enter".) "And the houses on whose roofs they sacrificed to Baal," the idol of the Sidonians, "and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods to provoke me." So they appeared to act not out of religious error but out of a kind of defiance, as if to insult the Creator.

Scripture says that the world will perish, according to what is written: Heaven and earth will pass away, because it lies in the power of the evil one. In the same way the very houses and places where crimes were committed lie under God's wrath. There are some who stubbornly apply to the places themselves the words: "the place where the Lord and Savior was crucified is spiritually called Gomorrah and Egypt." Others think that the whole world is meant by the names Egypt and Gomorrah: just as Gomorrah was destroyed by divine fire, so the world too will be burned up by the judgment of God.

For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have continually (or: alone) been doing evil in my sight from their youth. Aquila translated the Hebrew word 'ach' as πλήν, which means the conjunction 'nevertheless'. The first edition of Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as 'alone'.
