The second edition of Symmachus, however, rendered it διόλου, and we have followed him here in saying 'continually'.

So let us first explain it according to the Hebrew: the children of Israel and the children of Judah continually doing evil. 'Both the ten tribes and the two,' he says, 'did evil without ceasing, and they persevered constantly in the worst deeds.' But if this was constant and always so in the whole people, where is the righteousness that lasts for ever?

According to the Septuagint, on the other hand, which said: alone doing evil, a question arises. Did the other nations not do evil at the time when Israel and Judah were sinning? It is resolved like this. Whoever has knowledge of God and turns away from him alone sins in God's sight. Those who have remained unbelievers sin as though he did not see and did not care. So David too, a holy man, after he had fallen into the sin of Uriah's death and of Bathsheba, said later in his repentance: Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, that is, 'in your sight'.

Then it goes on: alone doing evil in my eyes and in my sight from their youth. What follows, the children of Israel, who to this day provoke me with the work of their hands, says the Lord, is not found in the Septuagint and has been added from the Hebrew. Because they sinned continually from their youth to the present day, God's sentence is just, and Scripture rightly continues:

This city has been to me a cause of fury and indignation from the day they built it to this day, when it is removed from my sight. From the time the city's foundations were laid until this day, when it has been captured, burned and taken away from the Lord's sight, it has always been steeped in vice and has provoked the Lord's indignation against itself. Where, then, as we have often said already, is any rest from sins?

Because of the wickedness, he says, of the children of Israel and the children of Judah, which they did to provoke me to anger, they and their kings, their princes, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Above he had said: This city has been to me a cause of fury and indignation from the day they built it to this day, when it is removed from my sight, and so he had shown in general that no one was without sin. Now he lists them part by part, kings, princes, priests and their prophets, and then takes them all in with a single phrase: the men, he says, of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
And he put it well. He did not say 'my kings, my princes, my priests and my prophets'. Because they had sinned, he said: their kings, their princes, their priests and their prophets.

And they turned their backs to me and not their faces. This matches what is written elsewhere: and they turned a stubborn shoulder against me. Someone who prays bends his neck and throws himself face down on the ground. But someone who turns his back shows by the very posture of his body that he ignores the one who threatens him. 'And they did this,' he says,

Though I taught them early and instructed them, and they would not listen to receive discipline. 'Once the darkness of error and all worship of idols had been driven away, I wanted every day to enlighten their hearts, [?] by my sentence, and to teach them what is right.' And to preserve their free will he adds: and they would not listen to receive discipline. There follows:

And they set up their idols in the house where my name is called upon, to defile it. It was not only at that time that Judah set up the statue of an idol in the temple of God, which we read of at the beginning of Ezekiel. To this day an idol is set up in the house of God, which means the church, or in the heart and soul of believers, whenever a new doctrine is constructed and, as Deuteronomy says, worshipped in secret. Do you not know, he says, that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?

And they built the high places (or: altars) of Baal which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to initiate their sons and their daughters to Moloch. For 'initiate' the Hebrew has 'ebir', which Aquila and Symmachus translated 'make pass over', and the Septuagint and Theodotion 'offer'. We have spoken more fully above about the 'valley of the sons of Hinnom', which in Hebrew is called 'Gehenna'. It lies below the springs of Siloam, and because it is a well-watered place, its pleasantness enticed the people to luxury, and the worship of idols follows luxury.

It should be noted that 'altars' and 'high places' are called 'bamoth' in Hebrew. I say this for the sake of those who are unsure what this word means in the books of Samuel and Kings. Moloch is an idol of the Ammonites, and the name translates as 'king'. Divine Scripture shows that in that place the people served not only the idol Baal but also Moab [?] and all the demons.

Which I did not command them, nor did it enter my heart, that they should do this abomination and lead Judah into sin. Strictly speaking, it was the tribes of Judah and Benjamin that venerated the images of the demons Baal and Moloch in their shrine. It is clear that the ten tribes, which were called Samaria, Joseph and Ephraim, worshipped the golden calves in Bethel and Dan. What the people did was so evil that God testifies he never thought of it and it never entered his heart that they would do such things. All of this, however, is said anthropopathōs, in human terms.

And now, because of these things, thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, concerning this city, of which you say that it is being given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine and by pestilence. To those who hoped for help and trusted in the strength of their walls it is prophesied that Jerusalem will be overthrown, that the people will be captured any moment now and will perish by sword, famine and pestilence before the captivity. In the same way, to those who despair and expect no salvation after the city's overthrow, he promises his help. So confidence and pride earn a just sentence, while despair and humility earn God's help.

Behold, I will gather them from all the lands to which I drove them in my fury, in my anger and in great indignation, and I will bring them back to this place and make them dwell securely. They shall be my people, and I will be their God. And I will give them one heart and one way, so that they may fear me all their days, and that it may go well with them and with their children after them.

And I will make with them an everlasting covenant (or: I will establish an eternal testament), and I will not cease to do them good. I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they do not turn away from me. And I will rejoice over them when I have done them good (or: and I will visit them to do them good), and I will plant them in this land in truth (or: in faith), with all my heart and with all my soul.

Many think this was fulfilled in the time of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied under Ezra the priest. Then the temple was built, and under Nehemiah the walls were raised all around. On this view, those whom he had earlier driven out of Jerusalem in fury, anger and great indignation and scattered through the whole world, he afterwards brought back and made to dwell securely, and they were the people of God and the Lord was their God, along with the rest of what Scripture goes on to say.

But how these words could fit that time cannot be proved at all: I will make them dwell securely and I will make with them an everlasting covenant (or: I will establish with them an eternal testament). For we read, and sacred history tells, that they were often captured, not only by neighbouring nations but also by the Persians, the Macedonians, the Egyptians and the Romans, and that they are in servitude to this day.

All these things, then, must be referred to the coming of the Saviour, and we see them fulfilled in our own time, the time of faith. The chosen remnant, as the apostle says, has been saved, and they dwell securely in Christ, and they have been given one heart, as it is written: Now the multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul.

And one way, he says: that is, him who says, I am the way, the life and the truth. So that they may fear me all their days, for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. All their days, he says. If this does not apply to the Jews, it must be understood of our people. It has gone well with us, it goes well, and it will go well, not only for them but also for their children after them. For he has made an everlasting covenant with us and will never cease to do us good.

Then follows: and I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they do not turn away from me. In saying this he grants free will in such a way that the fear which is given still remains the grace of the giver. 'And when,' he says, 'I have done them good, I will rejoice and be glad', glad, that is, that his creation has been saved. That is why there is joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents.

And I will plant them, he says, in this land in truth, or, as the Septuagint translated, in faith. This refers properly to the Christian people, whose religion is faith. With all my heart and with all my soul. If these are the words of the Lord the Saviour, then the heart and soul are rightly taken to be his, for he says in the Gospel: I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again. But if we take the words as spoken in the person of God the Father, they must be understood like this: My soul hates your new moons, your sabbaths and your feast days.

For thus says the Lord: Just as I have brought all this great evil upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I am promising them. And fields shall be possessed in this land, of which you say that it is desolate, because neither man nor beast remains, and that it has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans.

Fields shall be bought for money and recorded in a book, the seal shall be affixed, and witnesses shall be called, in the land of Benjamin and around Jerusalem, in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the plain (or: the Shephelah), and in the cities of the Negeb, that is, those that lie to the south. For I will turn back their captivity, says the Lord.

In the literal sense these things may have come first as a type after the return from the Chaldeans, when at the command of King Cyrus the people went back to Judea. Yet spiritually they are fulfilled more truly and more fully in Christ and in the apostles. Then both men and beasts were brought back into the church, as it is written: Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, that is, both the rational and the simple. Then fields were bought with money, so that we might make friends for ourselves by means of unrighteous mammon, who would receive us into the eternal dwellings. And they were recorded in a book, no doubt the book of the living. The seal was stamped, the standard of the Lord's cross and of his victory. And witnesses were called: the martyrs and the whole choir of the saints.

In the land of Benjamin, where the 'strength' of the Lord is; and around Jerusalem, where there is the 'vision of peace' and eternal security; in the cities of Judah, where there is true 'confession' of Christ; and in the cities of the hill country, one of which is the one of which he says: A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; and in the cities of the plain, which in Hebrew are called 'Shephelah', so that from the deep and low places we may advance over the level plains to the heights; and in the cities that lie to the south, which the Septuagint rendered 'nageb', where there is 'midday' and the full light of truth.

And when all these things have been done, what is written will be fulfilled: I will turn back their captivity, says the Lord. Of him it is written: Ascending on high he led captivity captive; he received (or, as the apostle says, gave) gifts to men.
